CSS Mastery

Everything between "I can centre a div" and "I can be trusted with the presentation layer of a production application." The cascade as an algorithm rather than a folk belief, the layout engines and the boxes they actually generate, colour in the spaces browsers now compute in, and the discipline that keeps a stylesheet legible after three years and four contributors.

How to use this course

  • This course assumes you have written some CSS. You should recognise a selector, a declaration and a media query. It does not assume you know why a declaration you wrote is being thrown away, what a formatting context is, or why z-index: 999 did nothing — those are what it is for.
  • CSS is not a small language. The reference lists 576 properties, 114 functions, 110 pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements, and 21 at-rules across 68 modules. This course does not enumerate them; it teaches the dozen systems they belong to, because once you know how the cascade, the box model and the layout algorithms work, an unfamiliar property is a lookup rather than a lesson.
  • CSS is designed not to fail. The specification requires a browser to discard a declaration it cannot understand and carry on. display: flexbox, overflow: none and color: #GGG are not errors — they are silence. The rule still applies, the page still renders, and the one line you wrote it for does nothing. That single property shapes how this course teaches: every example here was run through a real CSS grammar checker before it was written down, and the ones that are deliberately wrong are labelled.
  • The mechanism matters more than the syntax. Anyone can memorise justify-content. The expensive defects come from not knowing which box the value applies to, which containing block an absolutely positioned element resolved against, or that opacity: 0.99 created a stacking context.
  • Each section is Concept → Mechanism → Practice → Exercises with solutions.
  • The only setup you need is a browser and its developer tools:
mkdir ~/css-mastery && cd ~/css-mastery
printf '<!doctype html>\n<html lang="en">\n<head><meta charset="utf-8">\n<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">\n<title>Scratch</title>\n<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"></head>\n<body>\n<h1>Scratch</h1>\n</body>\n</html>\n' > index.html
touch style.css
python3 -m http.server 8000

A local server rather than file://, because @font-face, @import and anything involving CORS behave differently on the file protocol and you will lose an hour to it.

Every CSS example in this course was checked against the property grammars in mdn-data 2.33.0, through css-tree 3.2.1 — the same grammars a browser uses to decide whether to keep a declaration. Measurements were taken in a real browser, and the engine is named wherever the result depends on it.

What you are actually learning

Not a property reference. Five systems, and once you know how each one decides, an unfamiliar property is a lookup rather than a lesson:

  1. Error handling that never reports an error. An invalid declaration costs one line, an invalid selector the whole rule, an invalid at-rule its block, and an unclosed brace the rest of the file — silently in every case (§1).
  2. The cascade as a sort. Six criteria in order — origin and importance, cascade layer, scope proximity, specificity, source order, inheritance — with specificity fourth rather than first. That is why a weak selector in a later layer beats a strong one in an earlier layer, and why most specificity fights should be stopped rather than won (§3).
  3. Boxes and the formatting contexts that place them. Which box a value applies to, when margins collapse and how display: flow-root stops it, and what an absolutely positioned element resolves against (§6–§7, §10).
  4. Layout modes chosen on purpose. Flexbox when content decides the sizes along one axis, grid when the layout decides them or you need both, subgrid to align the insides of sibling components, and container queries when a component needs to know the space it was actually given (§8–§9, §13).
  5. Stacking and painting. z-index compares only within a stacking context, opacity: 0.99 creates one, and transform and opacity animate on the compositor while left and width re-run layout every frame (§10, §14).

By the end you should be able to explain why any declaration in front of you is or is not applying, choose a layout mode for a reason, and keep a stylesheet workable under many contributors with @layer and @scope (§16).

What this course is not

It is not a component library and it is not a list of recipes. It also does not teach HTML: the companion HTML course owns semantics, document structure, forms and the accessibility tree, and this course refers to it rather than repeating it. The division is the useful one — HTML decides what a thing is, CSS decides what it looks like and where it goes — and the places where that boundary leaks (a list-style that changes a screen reader's announcement, an order that desynchronises reading order from focus order) get a section of their own, because they are where the two languages actually collide.

SECTION 1

How CSS Reaches the Page

There is a version of CSS you can hold in your head as "a list of things I want to be true about the page". It works for a while. It stops working the first time a declaration you wrote does nothing, and the reason it stops working is that the browser is not reading a wish list. It is running a specified algorithm over a specified data structure, and that algorithm has an opinion about your stylesheet that you can read directly.

This section is about the front of that pipeline: what a stylesheet is made of, the four routes it can take into a document, what the browser does with the parts of it that do not parse, and the structure it produces before a single pixel is painted. Everything in the rest of the course sits on top of it. In particular, the one behaviour that surprises people most about CSS — that a mistake is silent — is not a browser bug or a leniency. It is required, it is precisely scoped, and once you know how far the damage spreads you can diagnose in seconds what otherwise takes twenty minutes of commenting-out.

1.1 What a Style Sheet Is Made Of

CSS is cascading style sheets, and the plural is not decoration — the whole language is built around several sheets from several parties arriving at once and being reconciled (§1.7). A style sheet is a sequence of two kinds of thing: rule sets and at-rules. Nothing else. The rest of the syntax is punctuation.

A rule set — the thing everyone calls "a rule" — is a selector list followed by a declaration block:

h1, .lede, [data-role="intro"] {
  font-size: 2rem;
  line-height: 1.2;
}

Four named parts, and it is worth having the names because every error message and every specification sentence uses them:

selector list
h1, .lede, [data-role="intro"] — one or more selectors separated by commas. Each one is tried independently against every element in the document.
declaration block
Everything between { and }. Semicolon-separated; the last semicolon is optional and you should write it anyway, for the reason §1.5 gives.
css declaration
font-size: 2rem — a property name, a colon, and a value. This is the atom the cascade operates on, and the atom the browser throws away when it cannot understand it.
value
Everything after the colon. Every property defines its own grammar for what is acceptable there, and §1.5 is about what happens when you miss it.

A css comment is /* ... */ and there is only one kind. CSS has no line comment: // like this is not a comment, it is garbage, and §1.5 explains exactly how much of your stylesheet it takes with it. This is the single most common way a developer who moves between JavaScript and CSS loses a rule.

/* This is the only comment syntax CSS has.
   It spans lines, and it does not nest — the first */ /* ends it. */

That second line is worth reading twice. Comments do not nest, so commenting out a block that already contains a comment terminates early and leaves the tail of the block live. It is a real way to break a stylesheet while trying to disable part of it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: cascading style sheets, css declaration and css comment.

1.2 At-Rules and Their Descriptors

An at-rule is a statement that begins with @. It is the mechanism CSS uses for everything that is not "apply these declarations to these elements": conditionals, resources, named things, and metadata.

At-rules come in two shapes, and the shape decides what may appear inside:

@charset "utf-8";
@import url("typography.css") layer(base);
@layer reset, base, components;

@media (min-width: 40rem) {
  .layout { display: grid; }
}

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
}

The first group are statement at-rules: a prelude and a semicolon, no block. The second are block at-rules. Within the block group there is a further split that matters more than it looks:

  • @media, @supports, @container, @layer, @scope contain rule sets. They are conditional wrappers; what is inside them is ordinary CSS.
  • @font-face, @property, @counter-style, @page, @position-try, @view-transition contain declarations that are not properties. They look identical — name: value; — but they live in a namespace of their own. These are at-rule descriptors.

That distinction is not pedantry. src and font-display are descriptors of @font-face; they are not CSS properties, and writing src: url(...) inside a normal rule set does nothing at all. Symmetrically, color: red inside @font-face does nothing, because color is not one of that at-rule's descriptors. The parser accepts the syntax in both directions and discards the declaration in both directions, silently, which is why a mistyped descriptor is one of the harder CSS bugs to see:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-dispay: swap;      /* discarded — the descriptor is font-display */
}

The font still loads. The swap behaviour you wrote the line for does not happen. Nothing is reported.

Every at-rule descriptor in this course is named as a descriptor when it is introduced, for exactly this reason.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: @view-transition.

1.3 The Four Routes Into a Document

CSS reaches a document by one of four routes, and they differ in more than convenience.

An external stylesheet, linked. This is the default and should stay the default:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">

It is cacheable across pages, it can be sent early by the server, and it keeps presentation out of the markup. The rel="stylesheet" value is what makes it a stylesheet — the HTML course owns the full rel vocabulary; here it is enough to know that the browser only treats the resource as CSS because of that keyword, and a <link> with a missing or misspelled rel fetches nothing.

A <style> element. Inline CSS in the document itself:

<style>
  .above-the-fold { contain: layout; }
</style>

It is not cacheable — it is re-sent with every copy of the page — but it costs no extra request, which is the whole argument for critical CSS in §1.9. A <style> element is legal in the body as well as the head, and applies to the whole document either way.

The style attribute. A declaration block with no selector, attached to one element:

<p style="color: rebeccapurple">Once.</p>

Its value is a bare declaration block — no braces, no selector. It sits at a special place in the cascade (§3.2) that makes it hard to override, which is exactly why it should be reserved for values a script computes at runtime rather than used as a styling technique.

@import. A stylesheet pulling in another:

@import url("reset.css");
@import url("typography.css") layer(base);
@import url("wide.css") screen and (min-width: 60rem);

@import must appear before any rule set in the file — after @charset and @layer statements, and before everything else — or it is dropped. Its two optional parts are why it survives at all in modern CSS: layer() assigns the imported sheet to a cascade layer (§3.6), which is the cleanest way to subordinate a third-party stylesheet, and a trailing media query makes the import conditional.

Its cost is real and worth stating plainly: an @import inside a linked stylesheet cannot be discovered until that stylesheet has been fetched and parsed, so it serialises two round trips that two <link> elements would have made in parallel. Use it for the layer assignment, not as a build system.

To have in hand before moving on: critical css.

1.4 @charset and How the Bytes Are Decoded

A stylesheet arrives as bytes and has to be decoded into characters before any of the above can happen. The browser decides the encoding in this order, and stops at the first answer it gets:

1
A Unicode byte order mark at the start of the file.
2
The charset parameter of the HTTP Content-Type header.
3
An @charset rule, which must be the very first thing in the file — byte zero, no comment or whitespace before it.
4
The encoding of the document that linked it.
5
UTF-8.
@charset "utf-8";

In practice you serve UTF-8, your server sends the header, and @charset never fires. It is in the course for two reasons: it is the one at-rule with a byte-offset requirement, and it is the explanation for a specific bug — a stylesheet full of content: "→" rendering mojibake because it was saved as UTF-8 and served with a Content-Type that claims otherwise. The header wins over the file. Fix the header.

1.5 CSS Error Handling: What Is Discarded, and How Much

This is the most important subsection in the section, and possibly in the first half of the course.

CSS has no error reporting. The specification requires a browser to recover from anything it does not understand and carry on, and it defines exactly how much it throws away in each case. There are three blast radii, and knowing which one you are in tells you immediately how far to look.

Here is a stylesheet with four deliberate defects. Six rules were written:

.a { color: red; colr: blue; background: GGG; font-size: 20px }
.b { color: green }
@medai (width > 0) { .c { color: red } }
.d { color: red }
.e:hovr { color: red }
.f { color: red }

Rendered in Chromium and read back out of document.styleSheets[0], this is what actually exists:

RULES PARSED: 4
.a { color: red; font-size: 20px; }
.b { color: green; }
.d { color: red; }
.f { color: red; }
--- .a computed: color=rgb(255, 0, 0) font-size=20px background-color=rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)

Read that against what was written. Six top-level rules went in and four came out: @medai and .e:hovr are gone, and so is the .c rule that was inside the at-rule, which makes three rule sets lost in total. The rule that did survive lost two of its four declarations. Nothing was reported anywhere.

Blast radius one: the invalid declaration. colr: blue is not a property, and background: GGG is a property with a value that does not match its grammar. Both are dropped individually. The rest of .a is untouched — color and font-size both applied, and the computed background is the initial transparent. This is the rule that makes CSS forward-compatible: you can write a declaration a browser has never heard of and the surrounding rule keeps working. It is also the rule that makes overflow: none invisible. none is not a value overflow accepts, so the declaration is dropped and the element keeps whatever overflow it had.

Blast radius two: the invalid selector. .e:hovr is not a valid selector, and an invalid selector invalidates the whole rule — the declaration block goes with it. Worse, it takes its siblings in the same selector list with it under the old rules: in .a, .e:hovr { ... } the entire rule set is discarded, including the part that would have matched .a. (This is precisely the problem :is() and :where() solve, and §2.9 covers their forgiving selector lists.) This is a bigger radius than most people expect and it is why a typo in one pseudo-class can make a rule vanish with no trace.

Blast radius three: the invalid at-rule. @medai is not an at-rule, so the browser discards the at-rule and everything in its block. .c never existed. An @ typo therefore costs you a whole section of the file.

And a fourth case that is not in the listing above but is the one people hit most: an unclosed construct swallows everything after it. A missing }, or a /* with no */, means the parser is still looking for the end of your rule when it reaches the end of the file. Everything after the mistake is consumed as part of it. This is why a // comment written out of JavaScript habit is so destructive — // is not a comment, so the parser reads it as the start of a selector and eats the following declaration block as that selector's rule.

The practical translation:

One declaration is dead
Suspect the value's grammar, or a property name typo. Look at that line only.
A whole rule is dead
Suspect the selector. Something in it does not exist.
Everything after a point is dead
Suspect an unclosed brace or comment at that point. Bisect the file.

The styles pane (§1.10) makes the first two visible directly: a dropped declaration is shown struck through, and a rule that never parsed is not shown at all.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: invalid declaration.

1.6 Vendor Prefixes, and Why They Nearly Stopped

A vendor prefix is a property or selector name carrying an engine marker: -webkit-, -moz-, -ms-, -o-. They exist because of §1.5's first rule — an unknown property is discarded harmlessly — so an engine could ship an experimental feature under a name no other engine would touch.

The experiment failed for a well-documented reason. Sites shipped -webkit- prefixed properties and never added the unprefixed version, so non-WebKit engines had to implement -webkit- prefixes to render the web, which defeated the entire mechanism. The industry response was to stop: new CSS features now ship unprefixed behind a browser flag, and are unflagged when they are ready.

What this means for what you write in 2026:

  • Do not write prefixes by hand. The set that is still needed is small, shrinking, and not memorable. If you have a build step, postcss with autoprefixer (§16.5) inserts them from real support data. If you do not, the honest answer for almost every property is that you do not need them.
  • A handful of genuinely non-standard prefixed things remain, because they never had an unprefixed equivalent: -webkit-line-clamp (now standardising as line-clamp), ::-webkit-scrollbar and its family, -webkit-text-fill-color. These are authoring choices, not mistakes.
  • A prefixed property is not a fallback for a modern one. -webkit-box-orient is not "old flexbox"; it is a different specification with different semantics. Feature-detect with @supports (§13.10) instead.

1.7 Origins, and the Place Where !important Turns Round

Three parties supply CSS to a document, and the specification calls each a cascade origin:

user-agent stylesheet
The browser's own defaults. Every element you have ever styled started here.
user stylesheet
CSS the reader has installed — an extension, an accessibility setting, a custom sheet. You will rarely see one and must never assume there is not one.
author stylesheet
Yours. Linked sheets, <style> elements and style attributes are all author origin.

The user-agent stylesheet is not a vague notion — it is a real stylesheet with real values, and it is the source of most "why does this element already have a margin?" questions. Measured in Chromium:

h1:         display=block         margin=21.44px 0px    padding=0px            font-size=32px      font-weight=700
p:          display=block         margin=16px 0px       padding=0px            font-size=16px      font-weight=400
ul:         display=block         margin=16px 0px       padding=0px 0px 0px 40px  font-size=16px   font-weight=400
li:         display=list-item     margin=0px            padding=0px            font-size=16px      font-weight=400
blockquote: display=block         margin=16px 40px      padding=0px            font-size=16px      font-weight=400
button:     display=inline-block  margin=0px            padding=1px 6px        font-size=13.3333px font-weight=400

Several things in that table are worth keeping. h1's margin is 21.44px because the UA sheet specifies 0.67em and the font size is 32px — a relative default, so it changes when you change the heading's size. ul's padding is a 40px left padding, not a margin, which is why margin: 0 alone never removes list indentation. li is display: list-item, a real display value you can set on anything (§7.3). And button has a font-size of 13.3333px that does not inherit from the page — form controls are the one family that ignores inherited typography, which is the reason essentially every reset in existence contains font: inherit for them.

The ordering of the origins is the surprising part, and it is the whole reason !important exists in the form it does. Normal declarations run weakest-to-strongest user agent → user → author; important declarations run in the opposite order, so that user important beats author important:

1
User agent !important — wins over everything. Vanishingly rare.
2
User !important — the reader's accessibility overrides.
3
Author !important — yours, and the one you actually reach for.
4
Author normal
5
User normal
6
User agent normal

That inversion is a deliberate accessibility guarantee: a reader who has set a minimum font size with !important cannot be overridden by a site. It is the only reason the keyword is defensible at all, and it is why an author's !important is a hierarchy escape hatch rather than a tool.

One measured consequence, because people get it backwards: an author !important beats an inline style attribute. Inline styles are author origin and normal weight; they sit at level 4 above, while !important sits at level 3.

<style>p { color: red !important }</style>
<p style="color: blue">Which colour?</p>

rgb(255, 0, 0)

Red. The style attribute lost. §3.2 gives the complete sort order that this is one row of, and §3.7 argues for !important being almost always the wrong fix.

In summary, the vocabulary here is user stylesheet, author stylesheet and cascade origin.

1.8 What the Browser Builds: CSSOM, Render Tree, Layout, Paint

Before anything appears, four structures are produced in order. Knowing their names is what turns a vague sense that "CSS is slow" into a specific question.

CSSOM
The CSS Object Model: every stylesheet parsed into rules and declarations, the structure §1.5's listing was read out of. Built from all origins, in parallel with the DOM.
render tree
DOM + CSSOM combined: every element that will generate a box, with its computed values attached. display: none elements are absent; visibility: hidden elements are present.
layout
Geometry: every box's size and position. Also called reflow. This is where flex, grid and flow (§7–§9) actually run.
paint & compositing
Pixels for each box, then layers assembled in painting order (§10.7). A repaint redraws without re-measuring; compositing reassembles layers without redrawing either.

The three verbs are a cost ladder, and it is the single most useful performance model in CSS:

  • Changing width, font-size, padding or anything geometric triggers style recalculation → layout → paint → composite. The whole ladder.
  • Changing background-color or box-shadow triggers paint → composite. No re-measurement.
  • Changing transform or opacity on an already-composited element triggers composite only. This is why §14 insists that animations be written in terms of those two properties and not in terms of left and top: the same visual motion costs a different number of stages per frame.

Style recalculation is the step between CSSOM and render tree where the cascade actually runs and each element gets its final value for each property. §3 is entirely about that step.

What to carry forward from this subsection: reflow, repaint and painting order.

1.9 Render-Blocking CSS and the Critical Path

CSS is render-blocking by default, and this is deliberate rather than a limitation. A browser that painted before the CSSOM was complete would show unstyled content and then rearrange it — the flash of unstyled content, and a large layout shift. So the browser holds the first paint until every stylesheet that applies to the current conditions has arrived and parsed.

Three consequences follow, and all three are actionable:

A stylesheet in the head delays first paint by its own round trip. That is the price of not flashing. It is worth paying, and worth minimising.

A media-qualified <link> is not render-blocking when its query does not match. The browser still downloads it, at low priority, but does not wait for it:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/wide.css" media="(min-width: 60rem)">

This is the cheapest real win available: split the sheets that only apply in conditions the current visit is not in.

Critical CSS is the technique of inlining, in a <style> element in the head, exactly the rules needed to paint what is above the fold, and loading the rest without blocking:

<style>/* the ~5 kB that styles the header and hero */</style>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css" media="print" onload="this.media='all'">
<noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css"></noscript>

The media="print" trick makes the link non-blocking on the way in, and the onload handler promotes it once it has arrived. It is a genuine improvement to first paint and it has a genuine cost: the inlined bytes are re-sent on every page, they can go stale against the real stylesheet, and generating them reliably needs tooling. Reach for it when a measurement says first paint is stylesheet-bound, not by default.

An @import inside a linked stylesheet is the pathological case of all three points at once: it is discovered late, it blocks rendering, and nothing can prefetch it. §1.3's advice stands.

1.10 Reading the Styles Pane

The developer tools' styles pane is not a convenience; it is the readout of §1.5 and §1.7, and using it well removes most CSS guesswork. Four things it tells you that nothing else will:

  • Struck-through declarations. A line with a strike through it lost. If it lost to another rule, that rule is above it in the list. If it is struck through with a warning marker and no competing rule, it was dropped as invalid — the §1.5 case, and the fastest way to spot overflow: none.
  • Rules in cascade order, most specific first. The pane lists every rule that matched, in the order the cascade resolved them, with the file and line each came from. A rule you expected that is not in the list at all did not match — that is a selector problem, not a specificity problem, and it is a completely different search.
  • The computed tab. One resolved value per property, with an expander showing which rule won and what it beat. When you cannot find why something is 16px, this is the answer, and it includes inherited values with the ancestor they came from.
  • The user-agent styles toggle. Off by default. Turn it on and §1.7's table stops being a mystery.

Those four are the whole of css debugging for the cascade; §16.15 adds the layout, accessibility and performance panels to them.

Two habits worth building. First, when a declaration does nothing, check whether it is struck through before you touch specificity — those are different diseases and the treatment for one does nothing for the other. Second, edit in the pane rather than the file while you are exploring: the changes are live, they are discarded on reload, and you will try five times as many things.

The terms above, gathered: css debugging.

1.11 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each, because the rest of the course assumes them:

  • A style sheet is rule sets and at-rules; a rule set is a selector list plus a declaration block of css declarations; the only comment syntax is /* */ and it does not nest.
  • At-rules either wrap rule sets (@media, @supports, @container, @layer, @scope) or contain at-rule descriptors, which are not properties (@font-face's src, @property's syntax).
  • CSS enters a document by rel="stylesheet", a <style> element, the style attribute, or @import — and @import costs a serialised round trip, so use it for layer(), not for structure.
  • @charset is the last-resort encoding declaration and loses to the HTTP header; serve UTF-8 and it never fires.
  • CSS error handling is specified and silent, with three blast radii: an invalid declaration costs one line, an invalid selector costs the whole rule, an invalid at-rule costs its whole block, and an unclosed brace or comment costs the rest of the file.
  • A vendor prefix is a historical artefact; do not hand-write them, and never treat one as a fallback for a standard property.
  • The three cascade origins are the user-agent stylesheet, the user stylesheet and the author stylesheet; !important inverts their order, which is why an author !important beats an inline style attribute and a user !important beats both.
  • The pipeline is CSSOM → render tree → layout (reflow) → paint (repaint) → compositing, and style recalculation is the step where the cascade runs.
  • CSS is render-blocking; a non-matching media attribute removes that, and critical css trades cacheability for first paint.
  • The devtools styles pane distinguishes "lost the cascade" from "was never valid" from "never matched", and those are three different bugs.

One line each, for reference: devtools styles pane.

Exercises

1. A colleague reports that half their stylesheet "stopped working" after they added one line. The file is 800 lines long. Describe the diagnosis, in the order you would actually do it, and say what single defect explains "everything after a point" better than any other.

Solution

The shape of the symptom names the defect. §1.5's three blast radii are diagnostic. "One declaration is dead" is a value or property problem. "One rule is dead" is a selector problem. "Everything after a point is dead" has essentially one cause: an unclosed construct — a missing } or a /* with no */. The parser is still consuming your file looking for the end of that construct, so every subsequent rule is being read as part of it.

The diagnosis, in order:

  1. Open the styles pane on an element that lost its styling. If its rule is not listed at all, the rule does not exist in the CSSOM — which is consistent with the parser having swallowed it. If the rule is listed but struck through, this is not the bug and the whole theory is wrong; that is a specificity question instead.
  2. Read document.styleSheets[0].cssRules.length in the console and compare it against roughly how many rules you believe the file has. This is the same measurement §1.5 used, and it turns "half the file stopped working" into a number.
  3. Bisect. Comment out the second half of the file — with a /* */ pair you are certain about — and see whether the survivors change. Four or five bisections locate an 800-line file's defect precisely.
  4. Look at the line they added. The bug is almost always adjacent to the last change, and the two shapes to look for are a // comment written out of JavaScript habit and a declaration block that was never closed.

Why // is the classic. CSS has no line comment. // TODO: fix later is parsed as the beginning of a selector, so the parser reads on looking for {, finds the next rule's brace, and consumes that rule's declaration block as the body of this imaginary selector. One line silently deletes the following rule — and if the writer then adds a second // the damage compounds.

The prevention, not the cure: run stylelint (§16.15) in the editor. Every one of these is a syntax error to a linter and none of them is a syntax error to a browser, which is the entire argument for having one.

2. Explain, with the mechanism rather than the rule of thumb, why each of these three does nothing. Then give the corrected line.

.panel { overflow: none; }
.title { colour: crimson; }
@media screen and (min-width: 40rem) { .grid { display: gird; } }
Solution

All three are §1.5 blast radius one: a single invalid declaration, dropped individually, with the surrounding rule intact and nothing reported.

overflow: none. overflow is a real property, so the property name is not the problem. Its grammar accepts visible | hidden | clip | scroll | auto (one or two of them, for the two axes). none is not in that list — it is a value that belongs to display, float, list-style and about forty other properties, which is exactly why the hand reaches for it. The declaration fails to match the grammar, so it is discarded and the element keeps overflow: visible. The corrected line is .panel { overflow: hidden; } — or, more often what was meant, overflow: clip, which does the same clipping without creating a scroll container (§6.14).

colour: crimson. The value is fine; the property does not exist. CSS property names are American-spelled without exception — color, text-decoration-color, border-color, color-scheme. There is no aliasing and no warning. .title { color: crimson; }.

display: gird. A real property with a value that matches no keyword in its grammar. The whole @media block is fine — the at-rule is spelled correctly and its condition parses — so the rule set inside it exists and the one declaration in it is dropped. That is the tell: if the media query itself had been misspelled (@medai) you would have lost the entire block, and .grid would not appear in the styles pane at all. Here it appears, with the declaration struck through. display: grid;.

The general lesson. All three of these look like typos to a human and like deliberate forward-compatibility to a browser, because there is no way for the parser to tell "author made a mistake" apart from "author is using a feature I have not implemented yet". That ambiguity is designed in and it is not going away, so the answer is tooling: a linter, or a checker that matches declarations against the real property grammars.

3. You have a 90 kB stylesheet and a first-paint problem. Your colleague suggests splitting it into six @import statements "so the browser can fetch them in parallel". Evaluate the suggestion, and give the change you would actually make.

Solution

The suggestion is backwards, and specifically so. @import is the one mechanism that prevents parallel fetching. An @import inside style.css cannot be discovered until style.css has itself been downloaded and parsed, because the browser has to read the bytes to know the import is there. Six imports at the top of one file therefore cost two serialised round trips, not one, and the preload scanner — which normally races ahead of the parser looking for resources to fetch — cannot see past the linked stylesheet into its contents.

Six <link> elements in the head would fetch in parallel, because they are all visible in the initial HTML. So the colleague's instinct about parallelism is right and their mechanism is precisely the one that defeats it.

What I would actually do, in order of value:

  1. Measure first. "First-paint problem" needs to become "first paint is blocked on style.css for N ms". If the block is on a font, a script or the HTML itself, everything below is wasted work.
  2. Split by condition, not by module. The genuine win from splitting is §1.9's: a stylesheet whose media does not match the current visit is downloaded at low priority and is not render-blocking. Print styles and styles for a breakpoint the visitor is not at can leave the critical path entirely.
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/base.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/wide.css"  media="(min-width: 60rem)">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print">
  1. Check compression before architecture. 90 kB of CSS is perhaps 12 kB over the wire with Brotli. If it is being served uncompressed, that is one server setting and it beats every other item on this list.
  2. Then consider critical CSS, with clear eyes about the cost: the inlined block is re-sent on every page rather than cached, and it goes stale against the real stylesheet unless it is generated by the build. Worth it when the measurement in step 1 says so, not by default.
  3. Keep the modular source, bundle the output. The reason people want six files is authoring, and that is a good reason. Six source files concatenated by the build into one response gives you both. If you want the source split to survive into the browser for cascade reasons rather than authoring reasons, that is what @layer is for (§3.6) — and @import ... layer(base) is the one use of @import this course endorses.

4. Take this fragment and say precisely what the browser ends up with, rule by rule. Then explain why the @font-face block is the one most likely to ship broken.

@import url("base.css");
.card { padding: 1rem }
@import url("theme.css");

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/f/inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-dispay: swap;
  color: black;
}
Solution

Rule by rule:

  • @import url("base.css") — applied. It is the first thing in the file, which is where @import is required to be.
  • .card { padding: 1rem } — applied. An ordinary rule set, nothing wrong with it.
  • @import url("theme.css") — dropped entirely. @import must precede every rule set in the stylesheet; once .card has appeared, any later @import is invalid and discarded. theme.css is never even requested. This is a §1.5 blast-radius-three case with an unusually quiet failure mode, because there is no typo to see — the rule is positional, and the file reads perfectly.
  • @font-face — the at-rule applies, and two of its four declarations are dropped. font-family and src are real descriptors and take effect, so the font loads and works. font-dispay is not a descriptor of @font-face (§1.2) and is discarded. color is a perfectly good CSS property and is still discarded, because @font-face has a descriptor namespace of its own and color is not in it.

Why @font-face is the one that ships broken. Every other defect here has a visible symptom: a missing theme.css makes the page look wrong immediately. The @font-face block, by contrast, works. The font downloads, the text renders in Inter, and the page looks exactly as intended in development on a fast connection.

What was lost is font-display: swap — the descriptor that governs what the reader sees during the download. Without it the browser uses its default block period, so a visitor on a slow connection gets invisible text for up to three seconds where they should have got fallback text immediately. That defect is invisible on the developer's machine, invisible in review, invisible in a screenshot test, and shows up only as an unexplained metric in the field.

The fix, and the general habit:

@import url("base.css");
@import url("theme.css");

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/f/inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
}

.card { padding: 1rem }

Both imports first, font-display spelled correctly, and color removed rather than left in as decoration. The habit worth taking from this: when a declaration inside an at-rule does nothing, check the descriptor list rather than the property list. They are different vocabularies that share a syntax, and that is the whole trap.

SECTION 2

Selectors and Combinators

A selector answers one question: which elements? Everything else in CSS is about what to do with the answer.

That makes selectors the half of the language with the highest leverage. A stylesheet whose selectors describe the document accurately needs very little machinery to keep working; a stylesheet whose selectors describe the markup as it happened to be written last Tuesday needs a class on every element and breaks whenever someone moves a <div>. And since 2023 the vocabulary has changed enough that advice from before then is actively wrong in places: :has() made CSS able to select an element by its contents, :is() and :where() decoupled grouping from specificity, and nesting removed the main reason people reached for a preprocessor.

Every claim in this section about which element wins was measured in Chromium rather than recalled, because this is an area where the widely published answer and the specified answer have diverged more than once.

2.1 The Anatomy of a Selector

Three words, used precisely throughout the specifications and throughout this course:

simple selector
One condition: a, .card, #main, [href], :hover, ::before.
compound selector
Simple selectors written together with no space: a.card:hover. All of them must match the same element.
complex selector
Compound selectors joined by combinators: nav > ul a.card:hover. Describes a relationship between several elements.

In a complex selector, exactly one element is styled: the subject, which is the last compound selector in the chain. nav > ul a styles the a, and the nav and ul are conditions on it. This left-to-right-reads, right-to-left-applies asymmetry is the single most common source of confusion for beginners, and it has a mechanical explanation: browsers match selectors right to left, starting from the candidate element and walking up, because that fails fast. Given nav > ul a, the engine finds every a, then checks each one's ancestors — it does not find every nav and walk down.

A selector list is several complete selectors separated by commas, each tried independently:

h1, h2, h3 { text-wrap: balance; }

§1.5 established what happens when one item in that list is invalid: the whole rule is discarded, including the valid items. That behaviour is what :is() and :where() were introduced to change, and §2.9 measures the difference.

2.2 The Basic Selectors

Five, and their differences are about coupling, not capability.

p            { margin-block: 1em; }      /* type: every <p> */
.card        { padding: 1rem; }          /* class: every element with class="card" */
#checkout    { position: sticky; }       /* id: the one element with id="checkout" */
*            { box-sizing: border-box; } /* universal: every element */
[data-open]  { display: block; }         /* attribute: §2.3 */

A type selector names an element and is case-insensitive in HTML (P and p are the same selector). A class selector matches an element whose class attribute contains that word — an element can have many classes, and their order in the attribute means nothing. An id selector matches the one element with that id; ids are required to be unique, and if you duplicate one, the selector matches all of them and everything else about your document breaks quietly.

The universal selector * matches every element. It is the one whose reputation is worst and mostly undeserved: * { box-sizing: border-box } is fine, because the engine does not evaluate it per element in the naive way people imagine (§16.10 covers selector performance honestly). Where * does deserve care is in a descendant position — .card * { margin: 0 } is a large, indiscriminate hammer whose effects show up three refactors later.

The practical guidance, and the reason for it:

  • Class selectors are the default. They decouple styling from element choice, so changing a <div> to a <section> for semantic reasons does not disturb the CSS.
  • Type selectors belong in exactly two places: a reset or base layer that establishes document-wide defaults, and inside a scoped context where the element choice is genuinely part of the contract (.prose h2, .table td).
  • Id selectors should not appear in stylesheets. Not because they are slow — they are the fastest thing available — but because they carry a specificity (§3.3) that nothing but another id or an !important can beat, and they cannot be reused. Keep id for fragment links, for/id label pairing, and aria-labelledby, which are its real jobs.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: universal selector and box-sizing:.

2.3 Attribute Selectors, All Six Operators

An attribute selector matches on the presence or value of an attribute, which makes it the bridge between CSS and the state HTML is already carrying. Presence alone is often the most useful form:

[href]          { text-decoration: underline; }
[disabled]      { opacity: 0.5; }
[data-loading]  { cursor: progress; }

Presence means the attribute exists, and an empty value still counts. Measured: an element written <p title=""> matches [title], and also matches [title=''].

The six value operators, each with the job it is actually for:

[attr=value]
Exact match on the whole value. [type="checkbox"].
[attr~=value]
The value is a whitespace-separated list and value is one of its words. This is what a class selector is underneath: .card is [class~="card"].
[attr^=value]
Begins with. [href^="https://"], [href^="#"].
[attr$=value]
Ends with. [href$=".pdf"] — the classic document-type icon.
[attr*=value]
Contains, as a raw substring anywhere. The bluntest one, and the one that surprises: [class*="btn"] also matches class="subtle-button".
dash-match selector
[lang|="en"] — exactly en, or en followed by a hyphen. Built for language subtags and used for essentially nothing else.

The dash-match selector is worth a measurement because its purpose is not obvious from its syntax. [lang|="en"] matches lang="en", lang="en-GB" and lang="en-US", but not lang="english". Measured against <p lang="en-GB" title="">:

[lang|=en]   -> matched   (color applied)
[title]      -> matched   (presence, despite the empty value)
[title='']   -> matched

Case sensitivity is the trap in this family, and it is asymmetric. Attribute names are case-insensitive in HTML. Attribute values are case-sensitive by default — except for a specific list of HTML attributes (type, dir, and others) that the HTML specification declares case-insensitive. Custom data-* attributes are not on that list. Measured:

[data-x="Foo"]   { color: red; }        /* does NOT match data-x="foo" */
[data-x="Foo" i] { font-weight: 700; }  /* DOES match data-x="foo" */

color=rgb(0, 0, 0)   weight=700

The i flag before the closing bracket makes it a case-insensitive attribute selector, forcing an ASCII case-insensitive match; there is a matching s flag that forces case-sensitivity where the default would have been insensitive. Reach for i whenever you are matching a value that a human types or a CMS generates.

Two patterns worth stealing outright. Style by state, not by class, when HTML already carries the state — [aria-expanded="true"], [aria-current="page"], [open], [disabled] — because then the CSS cannot drift out of sync with the accessibility semantics; there is only one source of truth and assistive technology reads the same attribute your stylesheet does. And flag the links that behave unexpectedly:

a[href^="http"]:not([href*="example.com"])::after { content: " ↗"; }
a[href$=".pdf"]::after { content: " (PDF)"; }
a[href^="mailto:"]::before { content: "✉ "; }

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: [attr=value], [attr~=value], [attr^=value], [attr$=value], [attr*=value] and case-insensitive attribute selector.

2.4 Combinators

Four, and the two sibling combinators are the ones people underuse.

.prose p        { max-inline-size: 65ch; }  /* descendant: any depth below */
.menu > li      { display: contents; }      /* child: exactly one level down */
h2 + p          { margin-block-start: 0; }  /* next-sibling: immediately after */
h2 ~ p          { color: #444; }            /* subsequent-sibling: any later sibling */

The descendant combinator is a space, which makes it the only operator in CSS you can type by accident. .a.b and .a .b are entirely different selectors, and a stray space is a bug that reads as correct.

The child combinator is the one to prefer whenever the structure is known, because it says what you mean and it stops matching things you did not intend three levels down. .menu > li styles the menu's own items and not the items of a submenu inside them.

The next-sibling combinator + matches an element that immediately follows another with the same parent. Its canonical use is the one above: collapse the margin between a heading and the paragraph that follows it. Its other classic use is the "lobotomised owl", which sets spacing between siblings without setting it around the group:

.stack > * + * { margin-block-start: 1.5rem; }

Read it as "every child that follows another child" — which excludes the first, so the group gains no leading margin. Modern layout has a better tool for this (gap, §8.10), but the owl still earns its place in flow layout where gap does not apply.

The subsequent-sibling combinator ~ matches any later sibling, not just the adjacent one. It is what makes the input-driven patterns work: #toggle:checked ~ .panel { display: block } styles a panel that appears anywhere after the checkbox.

There is one hard limitation and it is worth stating plainly, because it explains the shape of a decade of CSS: there is no parent or previous-sibling combinator. You cannot walk up or backwards with a combinator. :has() (§2.10) is the feature that finally provides that capability, and it does so as a pseudo-class rather than a combinator precisely so that the right-to-left matching model still works.

To have in hand before moving on: descendant combinator, child combinator, next-sibling combinator, subsequent-sibling combinator and :checked.

2.5 Pseudo-Classes and the Structural Family

A pseudo-class selects on a state or position that is not expressible as an attribute. It is written with one colon, and there are around 80 of them. They fall into five groups, and this course treats them group by group: structural (here), link and interaction (§2.7), form state (§2.8), logical (§2.9 and §2.10), and element state (§2.11).

The structural family selects by position in the tree:

:root                { color-scheme: light dark; }
article :empty       { display: none; }
li:first-child       { border-block-start: 0; }
li:last-child        { border-block-end: 0; }
p:only-child         { margin: 0; }
tr:first-of-type     { font-weight: 600; }
img:only-of-type     { margin-inline: auto; }

:root matches the root element, which in an HTML document is always <html>. It is worth using in preference to html for one reason: it has class-level specificity (0,1,0) rather than type-level (0,0,1), which makes custom properties declared there marginally harder to clobber by accident — and it is the conventional home for them (§5.3).

:empty matches an element with no children at all, and "no children" includes text nodes. An element containing a single space is not empty. This makes :empty far less useful than it looks for hiding blank containers, because server-rendered markup is full of whitespace; a container that renders as <div class="alerts">\n</div> will not match. Comments are ignored, so <div><!-- nothing --></div> does match.

The -of-type variants restrict counting to siblings of the same element type. p:first-of-type is the first <p> among its siblings even if a <h2> came first; p:first-child requires the <p> to be the very first child of its parent. The distinction matters most in prose content where the element sequence is not under your control.

:scope names the element the selector is being evaluated against. In a stylesheet it is equivalent to :root unless you are inside @scope (§2.15), where it means the scoping root — and that is where it earns its keep.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: :scope and :first-of-type.

2.6 :nth-child() and the An+B Microlanguage

:nth-child() and its three relatives take a small language of their own, and learning it properly replaces about a dozen classes.

The argument is an+b, where n counts from 0 upwards and the result is a 1-based position:

:nth-child(3)
The third child. a is 0.
:nth-child(2n)
2, 4, 6, … Spelled even as a keyword.
:nth-child(2n+1)
1, 3, 5, … Spelled odd.
:nth-child(n+4)
The fourth onwards — "all but the first three".
:nth-child(-n+3)
The first three. Negative a counts downwards from b.
:nth-last-child(2)
Second from the end. The same language, counted from the other side.

Combining two of them gives ranges without any arithmetic in your head: li:nth-child(n+3):nth-child(-n+6) is items three to six inclusive — "from the third" intersected with "up to the sixth".

The genuinely new capability is the of S clause, and it is not what most people assume. :nth-child(2 of .x) means the second element among the siblings that match .x — the filter is applied first, then the counting. It is not "the second child, if it also matches .x". Measured on a list of four items where the first, third and fourth carry the class:

<ul>
  <li class="x">1</li>
  <li>2</li>
  <li class="x">3</li>
  <li class="x">4</li>
</ul>

li:nth-child(2 of .x) { outline: 1px solid red; }

0:1:none | 1:2:none | 2:3:solid | 3:4:none

The outline landed on the third <li> — the second one carrying .x. Without of S there is no way to express this: .x:nth-child(2) would ask for an element that is both .x and the second child, which here is nothing at all. The of S clause is what makes "stripe the visible rows" work in a filterable table, where hidden rows must not consume a position in the count.

:nth-of-type() and :nth-last-of-type() take the same an+b language and count only siblings of the same element type. Note that of S is available on :nth-child() and :nth-last-child() only — the -of-type variants are effectively a special case of it, and there is little reason to reach for them once you have of S.

In summary, the vocabulary here is :nth-last-child(), :nth-of-type() and :nth-last-of-type().

2.7 Links, Interaction and Focus

Five pseudo-classes for links, and they must be written in a specific order.

a:link    { color: #0645ad; }
a:visited { color: #663; }
a:hover   { text-decoration-thickness: 0.15em; }
a:active  { color: #b00; }

:link matches an unvisited link, :visited a visited one, and :any-link matches either — which is what you almost always want when setting properties that are not about visitedness. Note all three require an href: an <a> without one is not a link and matches none of them.

The order matters because these have equal specificity, so the later rule wins where they overlap. LVHA — link, visited, hover, active — is the order that makes all four observable. Put :hover before :visited and a visited link never shows a hover state.

:visited is subject to a privacy restriction that is unlike anything else in CSS, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising. History sniffing — reading a user's browsing history by styling visited links and measuring the result — was a real, exploited attack. Browsers responded by restricting :visited to a tiny set of colour properties (color, background-color, border-color, column-rule-color, outline-color, and the SVG fill and stroke colours), and, critically, by lying to getComputedStyle: script reading the computed style of a visited link is given the unvisited value. So you cannot change a visited link's size, weight, background image or content, and you cannot detect the difference from JavaScript. Design accordingly: a colour change is the only tool you have.

:target matches the element whose id equals the document's URL fragment. It is the mechanism behind a scroll-to-section highlight with no script at all:

:target { scroll-margin-block-start: 6rem; background: #fffbdd; }

That scroll-margin line is the more valuable half — it stops a sticky header from covering the element you just jumped to (§10.14).

The three focus pseudo-classes are distinct and all three are needed:

  • :focus — the element has focus, however it was obtained. Styling this alone is what produces the "why does the button get a ring when I click it" complaint.
  • :focus-visible — the element has focus and the browser judges that a visible indicator is appropriate. In practice: keyboard navigation yes, mouse click on a button no, click into a text field yes. This is what you should style, and §15.9 covers the indicator design rules.
  • :focus-within — the element or any of its descendants has focus. This is the one people forget exists, and it is how you highlight a whole form field group, or keep a dropdown open while something inside it is focused.
.field:focus-within { outline: 2px solid CanvasText; }
button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid; outline-offset: 2px; }

:hover deserves one warning that becomes a section later: on a touch device there is no hover, and a :hover-only affordance is invisible until tapped. §13.9's hover media feature is how you ask whether hovering is even possible.

What to carry forward from this subsection: :link, :any-link and hover media feature.

2.8 Form State

HTML's form controls carry a large amount of state, and CSS can read essentially all of it. This is the family that removes the most JavaScript.

input:enabled            { background: Field; }
input:disabled           { opacity: 0.6; cursor: not-allowed; }
input:checked            { accent-color: rebeccapurple; }
input:indeterminate      { outline: 1px dashed; }
option:default           { font-weight: 600; }
input:required           { border-inline-start: 3px solid; }
input:optional           { border-inline-start: 3px solid transparent; }
input:read-only          { background: Canvas; }
input:read-write         { background: Field; }
input:placeholder-shown  { text-overflow: ellipsis; }
input:autofill           { background: #fdf6d8; }

:indeterminate matches a checkbox whose indeterminate property has been set from script — the visual third state — and also a radio group with nothing chosen, and a <progress> with no value. :default matches the control that is the form's default: the default submit button, or a pre-checked checkbox.

:read-only is broader than it sounds: it matches every element that is not user-editable, which includes ordinary paragraphs. Scope it to controls.

Validation state is where the modern advice differs from the old advice, and it matters:

input:valid          { border-color: green; }
input:invalid        { border-color: red; }
input:user-valid     { border-color: green; }
input:user-invalid   { border-color: red; }
input:in-range       { }
input:out-of-range   { }

:invalid matches from the moment the page loads. A required field that the user has not reached yet is invalid, so styling :invalid red paints an empty form in errors before anyone has typed a character — hostile, and a genuine accessibility problem because it makes the real errors indistinguishable.

:user-invalid and :user-valid are the fix. They match only after the user has interacted with the control and the browser has decided it is worth reporting — after a blur, or after a submit attempt. They are what you should style in essentially every case. :in-range and :out-of-range are the numeric-specific pair for min/max on <input type="number"> and friends, and they do not fire for an empty field, so they compose well with :user-invalid.

The HTML course owns constraint validation itself — what makes a field invalid, the ValidityState object, and how to write the error message. This section owns only the selectors that read the result.

The terms above, gathered: :indeterminate, :default, :in-range, :out-of-range, :user-valid and :read-only.

2.9 :is(), :where() and :not() — Grouping Without Specificity

These three take a selector list as an argument, and they solve two different problems: repetition, and specificity.

:is() factors out a common part. These are the same rule:

:is(h1, h2, h3, h4) > :is(code, kbd, samp) { font-size: 0.9em; }

h1 > code, h1 > kbd, h1 > samp,
h2 > code, h2 > kbd, h2 > samp,
h3 > code, h3 > kbd, h3 > samp,
h4 > code, h4 > kbd, h4 > samp { font-size: 0.9em; }

Twelve selectors written as one. The saving is not just typing: the twelve-selector version has to be edited in twelve places when the rule changes.

Their specificity behaviour is the important part, and the three differ. Measured in Chromium:

  • :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument. :is(#id, p) has specificity (1,0,0) — the id's — even when it matched the p.
  • :not() does the same. p:not(#zz) has specificity (1,0,1), and it beat p.c at (0,1,1). The #zz does not even need to exist in the document: it contributes specificity by being written.
  • :where() always has specificity zero, no matter what is inside it. Measured against a plain type selector:
:where(#a) { color: red; }
p          { color: green; }

rgb(0, 128, 0)

Green. A bare type selector at (0,0,1) beat an id inside :where(), because :where() contributed nothing at all.

That makes :where() the correct tool for anything a consumer is expected to override — a reset, a base layer, a component library's defaults. :where(.btn) { padding: 0.5em 1em } can be overridden by a single class, which is exactly what you want from a default. Reach for :is() when you want the grouping and the specificity, and for :where() when you want the grouping and not the specificity, which is more often than you would think.

All three take a forgiving selector list, and this is a real behavioural difference from a plain selector list. §1.5 showed that one invalid selector kills a whole rule. Inside :is() and :where(), an invalid branch is pruned and the rest survives. Measured — the stylesheet as written, and what Chromium actually kept:

.a, .e:hovr        { color: red }     <- written
:is(.b, .e:hovr)   { color: green }   <- written
:where(.c, :nosuch){ color: blue }    <- written

RULES KEPT: 3
:is(.b) { color: green; }
:where(.c) { color: blue; }
:nth-child(1 of .g) { color: teal; }

The first rule is gone entirely — .a was never styled. The second and third survived, and the browser has rewritten them, pruning the invalid branch out of the list. That is the forgiving behaviour, and it is a genuine compatibility tool: :is(::-moz-thing, ::-webkit-thing) degrades to whichever one the current engine understands instead of dropping the rule.

One limitation to know: pseudo-elements may not appear inside :is() or :where(). :is(::before) is invalid and, being a whole-argument problem rather than one branch, invalidates the selector.

2.10 :has(), the Relational Pseudo-Class

:has() is the largest addition to CSS selectors in a decade, because it removes the constraint §2.4 ended on: it lets a selector's subject be chosen by what is inside or after it.

.card:has(img)              { grid-template-rows: auto 1fr; }
label:has(input:checked)    { font-weight: 600; }
article:has(> h2)           { padding-block-start: 0; }
h2:has(+ p)                 { margin-block-end: 0.25em; }
figure:has(figcaption)      { padding-block-end: 0.5rem; }
form:has(:user-invalid)     { border-inline-start: 3px solid red; }
body:has(dialog[open])      { overflow: hidden; }

The argument is a relative selector list: each item is evaluated with the subject as its anchor, and a leading combinator is allowed. :has(> h2) means "has a direct child h2"; :has(+ p) means "is immediately followed by a p", which is a previous-sibling combinator by another name.

Two of those examples are worth dwelling on. h2:has(+ p) styles the heading based on what follows it — a relationship CSS could not express at all before. And body:has(dialog[open]) is the scriptless version of the "lock scrolling while the modal is open" pattern, driven entirely by an attribute the browser sets for you.

Its specificity takes its most specific argument, like :is(). Measured:

div:has(#x) { color: red; }    /* (1,0,1) */
div.c       { color: green; }  /* (0,1,1) */

rgb(255, 0, 0)

Red — the id inside :has() counted.

And here is the fact that is most often stated wrongly: :has() is not forgiving. It takes a relative selector list, not a forgiving relative selector list — the specification was changed to make it so, and browsers followed. Measured in the same run as §2.9's:

.d:has(:nothere) { color: purple }   <- written, and NOT in the parsed rules

.d came back with the default colour, and the rule was absent from cssRules entirely. One unknown pseudo-class inside :has() therefore destroys the whole rule, exactly like a plain selector list. If you need the forgiving behaviour, nest one inside: :has(:is(:nothere, .real)).

Two more constraints. :has() cannot be nested inside another :has(), and pseudo-elements are not valid inside it. Both restrictions exist to keep the matching tractable.

On performance: the old advice that :has() is expensive is largely obsolete. Engines optimise it heavily, and the cases that are genuinely costly are the unbounded ones — :has(.thing) with no combinator, on a very large subtree, invalidated on every DOM change. Prefer a combinator (:has(> .thing)) when you can, and measure rather than avoid.

2.11 Element State: Components Without Script

A newer group of pseudo-classes reads state the browser maintains for built-in components. Each of these replaces a class that used to be toggled from JavaScript.

details:open              { border-inline-start: 3px solid; }
dialog:modal              { max-inline-size: 40rem; }
[popover]:popover-open    { animation: pop 150ms; }
video:fullscreen          { object-fit: contain; }
my-widget:defined         { display: block; }
  • :open matches an element in its open state — <details> that is expanded, a <dialog> that is showing, a <select> whose picker is dropped down. It generalises the older [open] attribute selector to elements that have open state without an attribute.
  • :modal matches an element that is excluding interaction with the rest of the page: a <dialog> opened with showModal(), and a fullscreen element. It does not match a non-modal <dialog> opened with show(), which is exactly the distinction you want when styling a backdrop.
  • :popover-open matches a popover that is showing. Because a popover is in the top layer (§10.14), this is how you attach an entry animation to it.
  • :fullscreen matches the element the Fullscreen API has promoted.
  • :defined matches every built-in element, and a custom element only once customElements.define() has run. This is the correct way to avoid a flash of unstyled custom element: style my-widget:not(:defined) to reserve space, and my-widget:defined for the real thing.
  • :host and :state() belong to shadow DOM and web components; §16.8 develops them, with ::part() and ::slotted().
  • :dir() and :lang() match on the element's resolved text direction and language rather than on a state it entered — :dir(rtl) and :lang(ja). §15.3 develops both, because they exist to serve writing modes and internationalisation rather than component state.

One line each, for reference: :open, :modal, :popover-open, :fullscreen, :state(), :dir() and :lang().

2.12 Pseudo-Elements: ::before, ::after and Generated Content

A pseudo-element selects something that is not an element in the document at all — a box the browser generates, or a region of one. It is written with two colons. (One colon is also accepted for the four that existed in CSS2 — :before, :after, :first-line, :first-letter — for compatibility; write two.)

::before and ::after create a box as the first or last child of the element, inside it:

.tag::before  { content: "#"; opacity: 0.6; }
.external::after { content: " ↗"; }

The two rules of these that catch everyone:

The content property is mandatory. With no content declaration, the pseudo-element is not generated at all — not an empty box, nothing. content: "" is the idiom for a purely decorative box you will size and colour yourself.

They cannot be applied to replaced elements. <img>, <input>, <br>, <video> have no place to put a child box, so img::after does nothing. This is a frequent and frustrating discovery; the workaround is to style a wrapper.

Generated content is available to assistive technology in most browsers, which cuts both ways. Decorative content should be marked as such, and the cleanest way is an empty alt in the content value's alternative-text syntax:

.external::after { content: " ↗" / ""; }
.required::after { content: "*" / " (required)"; }

The part after the slash is the alternative text: an empty string removes the symbol from the accessibility tree, and a real string replaces it with something readable. Use it. A decorative arrow announced as "north east arrow" in every link is a real annoyance, and a * announced as "asterisk" tells nobody that the field is required.

content accepts more than strings: a url() for an image, attr(data-label) to pull an attribute value, counter() for generated numbering (§12.13), and open-quote/close-quote driven by the quotes property.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: the content property.

2.13 The Rest of the Pseudo-Elements

Fifteen more, grouped by what they select.

Regions of text. ::first-letter selects the first letter of a block (plus any leading punctuation), and accepts only a limited set of properties — font, colour, background, margin, padding, border, and a few text properties. ::first-line selects the first formatted line, which is a genuinely dynamic selection: resize the window and a different set of words is selected. ::selection styles the user's highlight and accepts only color, background-color, text-decoration, text-shadow and a couple of others. ::target-text styles text a "scroll to text fragment" URL has highlighted.

::selection      { background: #ffe08a; color: #000; }
::target-text    { background: #d0f0c0; }
.lede::first-line { font-variant-caps: small-caps; }
.drop::first-letter { initial-letter: 3; margin-inline-end: 0.1em; }

Parts of form controls and built-in widgets. ::placeholder styles the placeholder text — and note that low-contrast placeholder text is a common accessibility failure, so this is a place to be deliberate. ::file-selector-button styles the button inside <input type="file">, which was un-styleable for years. ::marker styles a list item's bullet or number, and accepts font, colour and content. ::details-content styles the revealed body of a <details>, which is what makes animating it possible (§14.7). ::picker() styles the dropdown of a customisable <select>.

::placeholder            { color: #666; opacity: 1; }
::file-selector-button   { border-radius: 0.25rem; padding-inline: 0.75rem; }
li::marker               { color: rebeccapurple; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
details::details-content { block-size: auto; }

The opacity: 1 on ::placeholder is not decoration: Firefox applies a default opacity to placeholder text, and resetting it is required for the colour you set to be the colour you get.

Overlays and scrolling. ::backdrop styles the layer behind a top-layer element — a modal <dialog>, a popover, a fullscreen element — and is the correct place for the dimming that people usually build with an extra div. ::scroll-marker and ::scroll-marker-group generate the dot indicators of a CSS-only carousel, and ::scroll-button() generates its previous and next controls.

dialog::backdrop { background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5); backdrop-filter: blur(2px); }

Shadow DOM. ::part() styles an element a component has deliberately exposed, and ::slotted() styles content passed into a slot. Both are §16.8.

Highlights. ::highlight() styles ranges registered through the CSS Custom Highlight API, which is how a search-within-page feature highlights matches without touching the DOM.

Two structural rules apply to all of them. A pseudo-element must be last in its compound selector — p::before:hover is invalid, p:hover::before is correct. And with the exception of ::part() and ::slotted(), you cannot select inside a pseudo-element, because there is nothing there to select.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: ::first-letter, ::first-line, ::selection, ::backdrop, ::file-selector-button, ::details-content, ::target-text, ::highlight(), ::picker() and ::scroll-button().

2.14 CSS Nesting and the & Nesting Selector

css nesting lets a rule contain other rules, with the outer selector implied:

.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border-radius: 0.5rem;

  & .title { font-size: 1.25rem; }
  & > img  { inline-size: 100%; }

  &:hover  { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15); }

  @media (min-width: 40rem) {
    padding: 2rem;
  }
}

The nesting selector & refers to the enclosing rule's selector. In most positions it is optional — .title { } nested inside .card behaves as .card .title — but it is required when the nested selector must attach directly to the parent (&:hover, &.active) rather than descend from it, and writing it always is a habit worth having because the two cases look identical otherwise.

Three things about native nesting that differ from the preprocessor version people are used to:

  • & cannot be concatenated with text. Sass's &__title producing .card__title has no equivalent in CSS. The nesting selector is a selector, not a string, so BEM-style name building does not work natively (§16.2).
  • The parent selector is wrapped in an implicit :is(). .a, .b { & .c {} } behaves as :is(.a, .b) .c, which means it inherits :is()'s specificity rule from §2.9: the specificity is that of the most specific branch, applied to all of them. A nested rule under .card, #special is therefore an id-specificity rule everywhere.
  • Nesting is not free of the cascade. A nested rule is an ordinary rule at its computed selector; it is not "scoped" and it does not win by virtue of being nested. @scope (§2.15) is the feature for actual scoping.

The depth guidance is the same as it has been since preprocessors: two levels, occasionally three. Every level of nesting adds specificity and couples the CSS to the markup's shape. The value of nesting is co-location — the states and media queries of a component next to the component — not the tree drawing.

2.15 @scope, and Styles With a Floor

Nesting keeps related rules together. @scope does something different: it limits which elements a rule may match, in both directions.

@scope (.card) {
  img { border-radius: 0.5rem; }
  :scope { padding: 1rem; }
}

The scoping root is .card, and inside the block, selectors only match elements within a .card subtree. :scope refers to the root itself. So far this is a descendant combinator with extra steps.

The part that has no other expression in CSS is the scoping limit:

@scope (.article) to (.comments) {
  p { line-height: 1.7; }
  a { text-decoration: underline; }
}

That styles paragraphs and links inside .article but stops at .comments — the limit element and everything below it is excluded. This is the "donut scope" problem, and before @scope it required either a class on everything or a :not() chain that broke whenever the markup changed. It is the natural tool for embedded third-party content, for a rich-text region that must not style the widgets inside it, and for design-system boundaries.

Two behaviours to know. @scope adds no specificity — the rules inside it have exactly the specificity their selectors have, which keeps it composable. And it introduces scope proximity into the cascade: when two scoped rules of equal specificity and layer both match, the one whose scoping root is nearer the element wins. That is a genuinely new tie-breaker, it sits above source order in the sort, and §3.2 places it in the full ordering. It is what makes nested themes work — a .dark inside a .light inside a .dark resolves to the nearest ancestor without any specificity escalation.

A scoping root can also be implicit. @scope { ... } inside a <style> element scopes to that element's parent, which is the closest CSS has to a component-scoped stylesheet without a build step.

To have in hand before moving on: scoping limit.

2.16 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • A simple selector is one condition, a compound selector several on one element, a complex selector several elements joined by combinators; the styled element is the subject, and matching runs right to left.
  • The basic selectors are the type selector, class selector, id selector and universal selector; prefer classes, confine type selectors to base layers, and keep ids out of stylesheets for specificity reasons rather than speed ones.
  • An attribute selector matches presence or value with six operators — [attr=value], [attr~=value], [attr^=value], [attr$=value], [attr*=value] and the dash-match selector — and attribute values are case-sensitive unless you add the i flag.
  • The four combinators are descendant combinator (a space), child combinator, next-sibling combinator and subsequent-sibling combinator; there is no parent combinator, which is what :has() exists for.
  • The structural family — :root, :scope, :empty, :first-child, :last-child, :only-child, :first-of-type, :last-of-type, :only-of-type — selects by position, and :empty counts whitespace as content.
  • :nth-child(), :nth-last-child(), :nth-of-type() and :nth-last-of-type() take the an+b microlanguage, and of S filters before counting.
  • Links use :link, :visited, :any-link, :target, :hover, :active in LVHA order; :visited is restricted to colour properties and lies to getComputedStyle for privacy.
  • Focus splits three ways: :focus, :focus-visible (style this one) and :focus-within.
  • Form state is readable directly: :enabled, :disabled, :checked, :indeterminate, :default, :required, :optional, :read-only, :read-write, :placeholder-shown, :autofill, :in-range, :out-of-range, and :user-valid/:user-invalid rather than :valid/:invalid.
  • :is() and :not() take their most specific argument's specificity; :where() always contributes zero; all three have forgiving selector lists that prune invalid branches.
  • :has() is the relational pseudo-class, takes a relative selector list, takes its argument's specificity — and is not forgiving, which was measured rather than assumed.
  • Element state has its own selectors: :open, :modal, :popover-open, :fullscreen, :defined, plus :host and :state() for shadow DOM.
  • ::before and ::after require the content property, do not work on replaced elements, and should carry / "" alternative text when decorative.
  • The other pseudo-elements select regions (::first-letter, ::first-line, ::selection, ::target-text), control internals (::placeholder, ::file-selector-button, ::marker, ::details-content, ::picker()), overlays (::backdrop), carousel controls (::scroll-marker, ::scroll-marker-group, ::scroll-button()), shadow boundaries (::part(), ::slotted()) and script-registered ranges (::highlight()).
  • css nesting with the nesting selector & co-locates rules; the parent is wrapped in an implicit :is(), & cannot be concatenated with text, and two levels is the limit.
  • @scope bounds matching between a scoping root and an optional scoping limit, adds no specificity, and introduces scope proximity as a cascade tie-breaker.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: :last-child, :only-child, :last-of-type, :only-of-type, :active, :enabled, :disabled, :required, :optional, :valid, :placeholder-shown, :autofill and :read-write.

Exercises

1. You are given a filterable table. Rows the user has filtered out carry hidden. Write the zebra striping so that the visible rows alternate, and explain why the obvious selector cannot work.

Solution 
tbody tr:not([hidden]):nth-child(odd of :not([hidden])) {
  background: Canvas;
}
tbody tr:nth-child(even of :not([hidden])) {
  background: color-mix(in oklab, Canvas 94%, CanvasText);
}

Or, more simply, just the one that needs a background:

tbody tr:nth-child(even of :not([hidden])) {
  background: color-mix(in oklab, Canvas 94%, CanvasText);
}
