Why the obvious selector cannot work. tr:nth-child(even) counts every row, hidden or not. Hide the third row of ten and the stripes below it all shift by one position — but the hidden row still consumes position three, so what the user sees is two adjacent rows with the same background, then the pattern resuming. It looks like a rendering bug and it is a counting bug.

tr:not([hidden]):nth-child(even) does not fix it either, and this is the instructive part. That selector reads to a human as "the even ones among the visible", but it is a compound selector: both conditions apply to the same element independently. It means "an element that is not hidden and is the second, fourth, sixth… child of its parent" — the counting still happens over all siblings. The two conditions do not compose the way the English does.

of S is the only construct that changes what is counted. :nth-child(even of :not([hidden])) applies the filter first, builds the list of matching siblings, then takes every second one from that list. This is the same semantics §2.6 measured: :nth-child(2 of .x) landed on the third <li>, because it was the second one carrying .x.

Two implementation notes. Use hidden (or display: none) rather than visibility: hidden — of S filters on the selector, not on rendering, so visibility: hidden rows would still be counted by :not([hidden]), and would still occupy space anyway. And prefer color-mix() against the system Canvas and CanvasText colours over a hardcoded grey, so the stripe survives forced-colours mode and dark mode (§11.5, §15.12).

2. A component library ships this rule. A consumer complains they cannot override the padding without !important. Diagnose it, then rewrite it so that a single class in the consumer's stylesheet wins.

:is(.btn, #cta-button) { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; }
Solution

The diagnosis: :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument, and it does so unconditionally. The #cta-button branch gives this selector a specificity of (1,0,0) — the same as a bare id — and it keeps that specificity even when it matched via the .btn branch. So a consumer writing .btn-compact { padding: 0.25rem } at (0,1,0) loses, and there is no amount of class stacking that reaches (1,0,0). Their only routes are another id, an inline style, or !important — all three bad.

This was measured in §2.9: :is(#id, p) behaves as (1,0,0), and p:not(#zz) beat p.c even though #zz matched nothing in the document. Specificity inside these functions is computed from what is written, not from what matched.

The rewrite. Split the branches so the id's specificity is confined to the rule that needs it:

:where(.btn) { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; }

:where() contributes zero specificity regardless of contents, so the whole selector is (0,0,0) and any consumer rule beats it — a single class, a type selector, even another zero-specificity rule later in the sheet. This is the right default for a library's base styles: they should be the floor, not the ceiling.

If #cta-button genuinely needs different padding, it gets its own rule, where its specificity is honest and local:

:where(.btn) { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; }
#cta-button  { padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem; }

The better answer for a library, though, is a cascade layer:

@layer components {
  .btn { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; }
}

Anything the consumer writes outside a layer beats everything inside one, whatever the specificity (§3.6). That gives the library normal, readable selectors and guarantees overridability, and it is the reason @import url("lib.css") layer(components) from §1.3 is the recommended way to bring in third-party CSS. :where() and layers solve the same problem at different scales: :where() per selector, layers per stylesheet.

3. Write CSS that highlights a form field group when any control inside it is focused by keyboard, and separately marks the group when any control inside it has failed validation after the user touched it. No JavaScript, no extra classes.

Solution 
.field-group:has(:focus-visible) {
  outline: 2px solid CanvasText;
  outline-offset: 4px;
}

.field-group:has(:user-invalid) {
  border-inline-start: 3px solid;
  padding-inline-start: 0.75rem;
  color: color-mix(in oklab, CanvasText 70%, red);
}

Why each piece is what it is.

:has(:focus-visible) rather than :focus-within. Both would work for "something inside is focused", but they answer different questions. :focus-within matches when a descendant has focus however it was obtained, so clicking a button inside the group would light the whole group up — the same complaint §2.7 raised about styling bare :focus. :focus-visible is the browser's own judgement about whether an indicator is warranted: keyboard yes, mouse-click-on-button no, click-into-a-text-field yes. Combining it with :has() gives "a descendant that the browser thinks deserves a focus ring", which is exactly the intent.

:user-invalid rather than :invalid. :invalid matches from page load, so a group containing a required field would be marked red before the user has seen it — §2.8's point, and a real accessibility problem, because it makes genuine errors indistinguishable from fields nobody has reached yet. :user-invalid matches only after interaction or a submit attempt.

:has() rather than a class toggled from script. The state already exists in the platform; mirroring it into a class introduces a second source of truth that can drift.

Two refinements worth making in real code. First, add the group's own state to the announcement, not just the colour — colour alone is not an accessible indicator, so the border and the padding shift are doing real work here, and the field's own error message (which the HTML course owns) is doing the rest. Second, note the specificity: :has(:user-invalid) is (0,2,0), because :has() takes its argument's specificity from §2.10 and both parts are pseudo-classes. If a later rule needs to beat this one, it needs two classes' worth, which is worth knowing before you are surprised by it.

4. Explain why each of these four rules does nothing, and give a working version of each.

.card:has(:nosuchthing, img)::after { content: "★"; }
img::after                          { content: " (image)"; }
.list :empty                        { display: none; }
p::before:hover                     { color: red; }
Solution

1. :has() is not forgiving. §2.10 measured this: a rule whose :has() contains one unknown selector is discarded in its entirety, exactly like an ordinary selector list. It does not behave like :is(), which prunes the bad branch and keeps the rest — and this is the single most common wrong belief about :has(), because the two functions were specified together and the forgiving behaviour was removed from :has() later. The fix is to nest a forgiving list inside it, so that a branch this engine does not understand is pruned rather than taking the rule with it:

.card:has(:is(:popover-open, img))::after { content: "★"; }

2. ::before and ::after do not work on replaced elements. An <img> is replaced content — its box is filled by an external resource — so there is no place inside it for a generated child box. img::after parses fine, matches fine, and generates nothing. The fix is to style something that has a content box:

figure:has(img)::after { content: " (image)" / ""; }

Note the / "" alternative text from §2.12: without it, screen readers announce the parenthetical on every image.

3. :empty counts whitespace. An element written across two lines in the source contains a text node — the newline and the indentation — so <div class="alert">\n</div> is not empty and never matches. This is why the selector appears to do nothing on server-rendered markup while working perfectly in a hand-minified test. There is no selector-level fix; either produce genuinely empty elements, or select on something real:

.list [hidden], .list:not(:has(> *)) { display: none; }

4. A pseudo-element must be last in its compound selector. p::before:hover is asking for the hover state of the pseudo-element, and the grammar does not permit anything after a pseudo-element (with the narrow exception of certain pseudo-classes on ::part()). The whole selector is invalid, so the rule is dropped — §1.5's blast radius two. What was almost certainly meant is "the ::before of a hovered p", which reverses the order:

p:hover::before { color: red; }

The pattern across all four: two of them fail loudly enough to see in the styles pane (1 and 4 produce no rule at all), and two of them fail invisibly (2 and 3 produce a rule that matches nothing or generates nothing). The invisible ones cost the most time, which is the argument §1.10 made for checking whether a rule is present, struck through, or absent before touching anything else.

SECTION 3

The Cascade, Layers, Specificity and Inheritance

Most CSS that is hard to work with is not hard because of layout. It is hard because nobody on the team can predict which declaration will win, so every change is made by adding a more specific selector than the last person used, and the file ratchets upwards until !important is the only tool left.

The cascade is not a heuristic and it is not "the most specific one wins". It is a sort with six criteria applied in a fixed order, and specificity is the fourth of them. Two of the three criteria above it — cascade layers and scope proximity — are recent enough that a lot of published advice predates them, and both of them beat specificity outright. That is the single most useful thing in this section: you can stop fighting specificity by moving the fight to a criterion that outranks it.

Everything below was measured in Chromium. Several of the results are the opposite of what the folk model predicts.

3.1 What the Cascade Is For

More than one declaration can apply to the same element for the same property. That is not a failure mode — it is the design. A browser default, a reset, a design system, a component, a utility class and a page-specific override may all have an opinion about a heading's margin-block-start, and all six are legitimate. The cascade is the algorithm that picks one.

It runs per element, per property. There is no such thing as "this rule won"; a rule can win for color and lose for background-color on the same element in the same pass. This is why the developer tools' computed tab (§1.10) is organised by property rather than by rule, and why "why is this rule not applying?" is usually the wrong question — the right one is "which declaration won for this property, and what did it beat?".

The output of the cascade is the cascaded value: at most one declared value per element per property. Everything after that — inheritance, defaulting, computation — happens downstream, and §3.13 walks that pipeline.

In summary, the vocabulary here is declared value.

3.2 The Sort Order, in Full

Six criteria — the cascade sort order — applied in order. The first one that distinguishes two declarations decides it; ties fall through to the next.

1
Origin and importance
The six-row table from §1.7. Transition declarations sit above everything; animation declarations sit just below important author styles.
2
Cascade layer
Within one origin, later layers beat earlier ones, and unlayered styles beat every layer. Reversed for !important. §3.6.
3
Scope proximity
The declaration whose @scope root is nearer the element wins. Unscoped counts as infinitely far. §3.8.
4
Specificity
The three-number selector weight. §3.3. This is the fourth criterion, not the first.
5
Order of appearance
Last declaration in document order wins. §3.5.
6
Inheritance
Only if nothing declared a value at all. §3.9 — this is defaulting, not a competition.

Criterion 2 beating criterion 4 is the one worth proving, because it inverts a decade of habit. An id plus two classes, in an earlier layer, against a bare type selector in a later one:

@layer base, theme;
@layer base  { #x.y.z { color: red; } }
@layer theme { p       { color: blue; } }

rgb(0, 0, 255)

Blue. A specificity of (1,2,1) lost to (0,0,1), because layer order is decided before specificity is ever consulted. Nothing you can write in the base layer's selector will change that — which is precisely the property that makes layers useful.

What to carry forward from this subsection: cascade sort order.

3.3 Specificity, Computed Properly

Specificity is a triple, conventionally written (A, B, C), compared left to right like a version number. It is not a base-10 number: a hundred classes do not add up to an id.

A
Id selectors.
B
Class selectors, attribute selectors, and pseudo-classes.
C
Type selectors and pseudo-elements.

Worked examples, and the ones that catch people are at the bottom:

*                                   0,0,0
li                                  0,0,1
li::before                          0,0,2      <- pseudo-elements count in C
ul > li                             0,0,2
.card                               0,1,0
[type="text"]                       0,1,0      <- attribute selectors are class-weight
input:disabled                      0,1,1
a:hover                             0,1,1      <- pseudo-classes are class-weight
#nav                                1,0,0
#nav .item a                        1,1,1
:where(#nav) .item                  0,1,0      <- :where() contributes nothing
:is(#nav, .item)                    1,0,0      <- :is() takes its most specific branch
p:not(#zz)                          1,0,1      <- ...even for an id that matches nothing
div:has(#x)                         1,0,1
.a.a.a                              0,3,0      <- repetition is legal and counts

Four rules that are not obvious and that §2.9 measured directly:

  • Combinators contribute nothing. >, +, ~ and the descendant space are free. body > div > p and p differ only by the two extra type selectors.
  • :where() is always zero, whatever it contains. :is(), :not() and :has() take the specificity of their most specific argument, computed from what is written rather than from what matched.
  • The style attribute is not part of specificity at all. It is handled at criterion 1 as its own row in the origin table (§1.7), which is why an author !important beats it.
  • Repetition is a real technique. .btn.btn.btn is (0,3,0) and is a legitimate, if ugly, way to raise specificity without introducing an id. It is the escape hatch of last resort before !important — and if you find yourself needing it, layers (§3.6) are the actual answer.

The practical discipline is not "use low specificity"; it is keep specificity flat. A stylesheet where nearly everything is (0,1,0) is trivially predictable. A stylesheet ranging from (0,0,1) to (1,3,2) requires everyone to hold the whole file in their head.

3.4 Where Specificity Does Not Apply

Three places, and knowing them prevents a category of wasted debugging:

  • Between origins. A user's !important beats your !important no matter what the selectors are. Specificity only breaks ties within one origin-and-importance bucket.
  • Between layers. As measured in §3.2.
  • Between an element and its ancestor. Inheritance is not a competition. A directly-targeted declaration with specificity (0,0,0) beats an inherited value from a parent styled with an id, because the parent's declaration is not competing for the child's property at all — it only reaches the child if nothing declared a value there. This is why .card * { color: black } overrides #special-card { color: red } for the descendants: the universal selector declares a value on the descendant, and the id only ever offered one for inheritance.

3.5 Order of Appearance

When origin, layer, proximity and specificity all tie, the last declaration wins. "Last" means last in the concatenation of all stylesheets in the order the document links them, with <style> elements and <link> elements interleaved in document order, and an @imported sheet appearing where its @import is.

Two practical consequences:

  • Ordering your link elements is a cascade decision, not a housekeeping one. A reset linked after a component sheet undoes the components.
  • Within one file, later overrides earlier at equal specificity, which is the mechanism behind every "utilities last" convention. It is also fragile: it depends on a file ordering that a bundler, a code splitter or a lazily loaded chunk can change without anyone noticing. Layers make the same intent explicit and order-independent, which is the argument for them.

3.6 Cascade Layers

@layer creates an explicitly ordered bucket inside the author origin. It is the most significant change to the cascade since the beginning, because it gives you a criterion above specificity that you control.

Declare the order once, at the top, before any of the layers have content:

@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

That single line fixes the order. Layers can then be filled in any sequence, in any file, and the order stays what the declaration said:

@layer components {
  .card { padding: 1rem; border-radius: 0.5rem; }
}

@layer reset {
  *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
}

Three rules govern them, and all three were measured:

Later layers win. With @layer a, b; a declaration in b beats one in a, regardless of specificity.

Unlayered styles beat every layer. Anything written outside a layer is, in effect, in a final implicit layer at the end:

@layer a, b;
@layer b { p { color: blue; } }
@layer a { p { color: red; } }
p { color: green; }

rgb(0, 128, 0)

Green. This is worth internalising because it makes migration cheap: you can put a legacy stylesheet into a layer and every unlayered rule you write afterwards beats it, whatever selectors the legacy sheet used.

!important reverses the layer order. An important declaration in an earlier layer beats an important declaration in a later one:

@layer base, theme;
@layer base  { p { color: red !important; } }
@layer theme { p { color: blue !important; } }

rgb(255, 0, 0)

Red. The reversal is the same principle as §1.7's origin inversion: importance is an escape hatch for the party that would otherwise be weakest, so it flips whatever ordering it applies within. The practical reading is that an important declaration in your reset layer is nearly unbeatable, which is almost never what anyone wants — so keep !important out of low layers.

Layers can nest (@layer components.card), and an anonymous layer is created by @layer { ... } with no name — it takes a position in the order but cannot be referred to again, which makes it useful only for third-party code you never need to append to.

The two highest-value uses:

@import url("normalize.css") layer(reset);
@import url("vendor-widget.css") layer(vendor);

Subordinating a stylesheet you do not control, so that its selectors — however aggressive — cannot beat yours. And giving a design system a documented override story: anything in the utilities layer beats anything in components, which is a sentence a team can actually follow, unlike "keep your specificity below 0,2,0".

The terms above, gathered: normalize.css.

3.7 !important, and Why It Is Usually the Wrong Fix

!important moves a declaration into a different bucket at criterion 1. Within the author origin it beats every normal declaration regardless of specificity, layer or proximity.

It has exactly three defensible uses:

  • User stylesheets, where the inversion in §1.7 is the entire point and the reader's needs must beat the site's.
  • Utility classes, where the class's whole contract is "this wins" — .hidden { display: none !important } is honest, because a utility that can be silently overridden is not a utility. Better still, put utilities in the last layer and drop the keyword.
  • Overriding a third-party stylesheet you cannot edit — and even here, @import ... layer() is now the better tool, because it fixes the problem for the whole sheet at once rather than one declaration at a time.

Everywhere else it is a symptom. The reason is mechanical rather than moral: !important does not resolve a conflict, it escalates one. The next person who needs to override your declaration has no criterion left except another !important later in the file, so the escalation is one-way and the endgame is a stylesheet where importance is meaningless because everything has it.

The replacement, in order of preference:

  1. Move the losing declaration to a later layer. This is what layers are for and it is order-independent.
  2. Lower the winner's specificity by wrapping part of its selector in :where() (§2.9).
  3. Fix the selector so that only one rule matches, which is often the real bug.

3.8 Scope Proximity

@scope (§2.15) introduced a genuinely new criterion, and it sits above specificity and source order.

When two declarations match, tie on origin, importance and layer, and both come from scoped rules, the one whose scoping root is nearer the element wins. Measured both ways round, to show that it is proximity and not source order doing the work:

@scope (.outer) { p { color: red; } }
@scope (.inner) { p { color: blue; } }

@scope (.inner) { p { color: blue; } }
@scope (.outer) { p { color: red; } }

first stylesheet:  rgb(0, 0, 255)
second stylesheet: rgb(0, 0, 255)

Blue in both cases — .inner is nearer the paragraph, so it wins whether it is written first or last. Identical selectors, identical specificity, and source order never got a look in.

This is the mechanism that makes nested theming work without any specificity escalation. A .theme-dark inside a .theme-light inside a .theme-dark resolves to the nearest ancestor, automatically, and adding a fourth level of nesting requires no change to any selector. Before @scope, the same effect required either increasingly specific selectors or a JavaScript pass, and both broke as soon as the nesting got deeper than the author had anticipated.

An unscoped declaration is treated as infinitely distant, so any scoped rule that matches beats it on proximity — but only after origin, importance and layer have tied, which is why an unlayered unscoped rule still beats a scoped rule inside a layer.

3.9 Inheritance

Inheritance is what happens when the cascade produces nothing for an element and property. It is not part of the competition; it is the default that applies in the competition's absence.

Each property is either inherited or non-inherited by specification. The split is not arbitrary — it follows what would be useful to propagate:

inherited property
Typography and text: color, font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, letter-spacing, text-align, text-indent, text-transform, white-space, word-break, visibility, cursor, list-style, quotes, direction, and custom properties.
non-inherited property
Everything about the box: display, position, margin, padding, border, background, width, height, overflow, opacity, transform, z-index, and the layout properties.

A useful test for which bucket a property is in: would applying it to every descendant be sensible? Inheriting color is; inheriting border would draw a border around every element inside a bordered box.

What is inherited is the computed value, not the specified one, and this is the mechanism behind the single most useful piece of typography advice in CSS. Measured on two identically structured pieces of markup where the only difference is how line-height was written on the parent:

#a   { font-size: 20px; line-height: 1.5;  }   /* unitless number */
#a p { font-size: 40px; }

#b   { font-size: 20px; line-height: 30px; }   /* a length */
#b p { font-size: 40px; }

a p lineHeight=60px    b p lineHeight=30px

The unitless 1.5 inherits as the number, and each descendant multiplies it by its own font size — so the 40px paragraph gets 60px of leading, proportionally correct. The 30px version computes to a length on the parent and inherits that length, so the 40px paragraph gets 30px of leading and its lines overlap. This is why line-height should be written unitless essentially always, and it generalises: a value that computes to an absolute length before inheriting is frozen at the ancestor's context.

Two things inheritance does not do. It does not cross the shadow DOM boundary for non-inherited properties (§16.8), and it does not reach form controls for typography by default — §1.7's measurement showed a <button> at 13.3333px regardless of the page's font size, which is why font: inherit on form controls is in every reset.

One line each, for reference: non-inherited property.

3.10 inherit, initial, unset, revert, revert-layer

Five keywords, valid on every property, that let you declare a defaulting behaviour rather than fall into one. The inherit keyword, the initial keyword, the unset keyword, the revert keyword and revert-layer are the complete set, and each means something different. They are frequently confused, so here they are measured side by side on the same setup: an inherited color of teal from the parent, a .t { color: red } in layer a, and a .t.u { color: blue } in layer b.

inherit
Take the parent's computed value. Works on non-inherited properties too, which is its main use — border: inherit is meaningful.
initial
The property's specification-defined initial value. Not the browser's default for that element — display: initial is inline, even on a <div>.
unset
inherit for inherited properties, initial for the rest. The "act as if I said nothing" keyword.
revert
Roll back to the value the previous origin would have produced — for author CSS, the user or user-agent stylesheet. This is the one that restores browser defaults.
revert-layer
Roll back to the value the previous cascade layer would have produced. Same origin, one layer down.

Applied to four paragraphs that are otherwise identical:

@layer a { .t   { color: red; } }
@layer b { .t.u { color: blue; } }
/* the parent's colour is teal */

@layer b {
  #p1 { color: revert; }
  #p2 { color: revert-layer; }
  #p3 { color: unset; }
  #p4 { color: initial; }
}

p1=rgb(0, 128, 128)   p2=rgb(255, 0, 0)   p3=rgb(0, 128, 128)   p4=rgb(0, 0, 0)

Four different answers from four keywords on one property:

  • revert gave teal. It discarded the whole author origin, and the user-agent stylesheet has no color rule for <p>, so the value fell through to inheritance from the teal parent.
  • revert-layer gave red. It discarded only layer b, so layer a's .t { color: red } won — the declaration that would have applied if layer b had never existed. This is the keyword that makes layers composable: a later layer can selectively step aside.
  • unset gave teal, because color is inherited, so unset behaved as inherit.
  • initial gave black, the specified initial value of color, ignoring both the cascade and the parent entirely.

The one that surprises people is initial, and the general warning is worth stating: initial means the property's initial value, never the element's usual appearance. display: initial on a <div> gives inline, font-size: initial gives the root default rather than the heading size. When you mean "put it back how the browser had it", the keyword is revert.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: inherit keyword, initial keyword, unset keyword and revert keyword.

3.11 all

The all property sets every property at once — every one except direction, unicode-bidi and custom properties — and it accepts only the five keywords above. It is a nuclear option with two real uses.

button.reset { all: unset; }

Measured on an <a href="#"> given all: unset: colour became the inherited black, text-decoration-line became none, cursor became auto, and display stayed inline. Every trace of the link's appearance is gone — including the affordances that told a sighted user it was a link, so this is a starting point for restyling and never an end state.

b { all: revert; }

Measured: font-weight came back as 700. all: revert restores the entire user-agent presentation, which makes it the correct way to undo an over-aggressive reset for one element rather than editing the reset.

all is also the honest way to build an isolation boundary — a widget that must not inherit the host page's typography can open with all: initial and then declare everything it wants. It is expensive to reason about and should be rare, but it is the only thing that reliably severs inheritance for every property at once.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the all property.

3.12 Shorthands, Longhands, and the Reset Trap

A shorthand property sets several longhands in one declaration, and each longhand property can also be written on its own. background, font, border, margin, grid, flex, animation, transition, inset, place-items and text-decoration are all shorthands.

The rule that causes the most lost time: a shorthand sets every one of its longhands, including the ones you did not mention, resetting them to their initial values. Measured with the same two declarations in the two possible orders:

.a { background-color: red; background: linear-gradient(red, blue); }
.b { background: linear-gradient(red, blue); background-color: red; }

a bg-color=rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)     b bg-color=rgb(255, 0, 0)

In .a the shorthand came second and wiped background-color back to transparent. In .b the longhand came second and survived. This is not a special case for background; it is how every shorthand works, and it is why a shorthand written after a longhand in a different rule — or in a different file, or in a different layer — silently undoes it.

Three specific shorthand hazards worth carrying:

  • font is the most destructive shorthand in CSS. It resets font-style, font-variant, font-weight, font-stretch, line-height and font-size-adjust, so font: 16px/1.5 system-ui also sets font-weight: normal — which is why applying it to a <strong> un-bolds it.
  • background resets background-color, as measured, and also background-position, background-size, background-repeat, background-attachment, background-clip and background-origin.
  • grid resets the implicit-grid longhands (grid-auto-rows, grid-auto-columns, grid-auto-flow) to their initial values, which is a common source of "my implicit rows stopped being 200px" (§9.9).

The other side of the coin is that shorthands are the correct tool for a deliberate shorthand reset. border: 0 is one declaration that clears twelve longhands; writing the twelve is worse in every way. The guidance is simply to know which of the two you are doing — an intentional shorthand reset is the cleanest way to clear a property family, and an accidental one is the bug measured above.

One more asymmetry: a shorthand cannot express every combination of its longhands. background cannot set background-position-x alone; flex: 1 sets flex-basis: 0% and there is no way to say "grow and shrink but keep an auto basis" in the shorthand. When a shorthand cannot say what you mean, the longhands are not a fallback, they are the answer.

To have in hand before moving on: shorthand property and longhand property.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: shorthand reset.

3.13 From Declaration to Pixel: The Six Values

The specification gives a property's value six names as it moves through the engine. Knowing them makes several otherwise-mysterious behaviours obvious.

declared value
Every value any matching declaration proposed. Possibly many per property.
cascaded value
The winner of §3.2's sort. At most one. May be absent.
specified value
The cascaded value, or — if there was none — the inherited or initial value. Always present.
computed value
Resolved as far as it can be without layout: em becomes px, var() is substituted, relative URLs are made absolute. This is what inherits.
used value
Resolved with layout: percentages against a real containing block, auto against real available space, fr against a real track size.
actual value
The used value after device constraints — rounded to whole pixels, clamped to available colours.

The computed-value time boundary is the one that carries weight. It is where em is resolved, which is why §3.9's unitless line-height behaves differently from a length: the number survives computation and the length does not. It is also where var() is substituted, which is why a custom property that is invalid at computed-value time cannot be recovered from (§5.5).

Measured, with an element whose parent is 400px wide and 20px in font size:

.outer { width: 400px; font-size: 20px; }
.inner { width: 50%; margin: 0 auto; padding: 1em; line-height: 1.5; }

width=200px   padding=20px   lineHeight=30px   marginLeft=80px

Every number there is a resolution of something relative. 50% became 200px against the parent's width — a used value, because it needed layout. 1em became 20px at computed-value time. 1.5 became 30px against the element's own font size. And margin: 0 auto became 80px, which is the interesting one: the content box is 200px, the two 20px paddings make the border box 240px, and the leftover 160px was split. None of those numbers exists in the stylesheet.

In summary, the vocabulary here is specified value and actual value.

3.14 What getComputedStyle Actually Returns

Despite the name, getComputedStyle does not return the computed value for every property. For the layout-dependent ones — width, height, margin, padding, top, left, and others — it returns the used value, which is why the measurement above reported 200px for a declared 50%.

This is genuinely useful, because "what is this element's actual width" is usually the question. But it has three consequences that bite:

  • You cannot read back what you wrote. A script that reads getComputedStyle(el).width to check whether an author specified a percentage gets a pixel count and no way to tell the difference. el.style.width reads the inline declaration only; the specified value from a stylesheet is not exposed at all.
  • Reading it forces layout. Asking for a used value requires the engine to have laid out the page, so a read immediately after a style write flushes pending layout work. Alternating writes and reads in a loop is the classic layout-thrashing pattern (§16.12).
  • :visited lies to it, as §2.7 established — a privacy measure, and the one case where the returned value is deliberately not the truth.

For a property that does not depend on layout, getComputedStyle really does return the computed value: line-height: 1.5 came back as 30px, resolved but not laid out, and color comes back as an rgb() triple regardless of how it was written.

3.15 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • The cascade picks one cascaded value per element per property, by a six-criterion sort: origin and importance, cascade layer, scope proximity, specificity, order of appearance, then inheritance as the fallback.
  • Specificity is the fourth criterion, written (A, B, C) for ids / classes-attributes-pseudo-classes / types-pseudo-elements, compared left to right and never carrying.
  • Specificity calculation ignores combinators, gives :where() zero, and gives :is(), :not() and :has() their most specific argument's weight from what is written.
  • @layer declares an order once; later layers win, unlayered beats every layer, and !important reverses the layer order — all three measured.
  • !important is defensible in user stylesheets, in utilities, and against unfixable third-party CSS; everywhere else it escalates rather than resolves, and layers or :where() are the fix.
  • Scope proximity puts the nearer @scope root first, above specificity and source order, measured in both writing orders.
  • An inherited property propagates its computed value to descendants; a non-inherited property does not; unitless line-height inherits as a number and a length inherits as a length.
  • inherit, initial, unset, revert and revert-layer gave four distinct measured results on one property; initial is the specification's initial value and revert is the browser default.
  • The all property sets everything at once and takes only those keywords; all: unset strips a link bare and all: revert restores user-agent presentation.
  • A shorthand property resets every longhand it covers, including the unmentioned ones — measured on background — and font, background and grid are the three that cost the most.
  • The value pipeline is declared → cascaded → specified → computed → used → actual; em and var() resolve at computed-value time, percentages and auto resolve at used-value time.
  • getComputedStyle returns used values for layout-dependent properties, forces layout when read, and cannot tell you what was specified.

What to carry forward from this subsection: specificity calculation.

Exercises

1. A design system ships .button { padding: 0.5rem 1rem }. A page needs one button with padding: 0. List every mechanism that would make the page's rule win, in the order you would consider them, and say what each one costs.

Solution

In order of preference, with the criterion each one exploits:

1. Put the design system in a layer and write the page rule unlayered — criterion 2, and the cleanest of all.

@import url("design-system.css") layer(components);
.button-flush { padding: 0; }        /* unlayered — beats every layer */

Cost: a one-line change at the import, and it fixes the problem for the whole system rather than for this button. Requires that you control the import. This is the right answer if you can reach it.

2. Put the page's overrides in a later layer — same criterion, when everything is already layered.

@layer components, overrides;
@layer overrides { .button-flush { padding: 0; } }

Cost: nothing, if the layer order is already established. Needs team agreement on what the layers mean.

3. Match the specificity and rely on source order — criteria 4 and 5.

.button.button-flush { padding: 0; }

Cost: fragile. It works only while the page's stylesheet is loaded after the system's, which a bundler, a code-split chunk or a lazily loaded route can change without touching either file. It also starts a specificity ratchet: the next person needing to override this has to reach (0,3,0).

4. Repeat the class — criterion 4, brute force.

.button-flush.button-flush { padding: 0; }

Cost: it works and it is honest about being a hack, but it is a signal that the architecture has no override story. §3.3's point: reach for this only as a stopgap with a comment.

5. !important — criterion 1.

.button-flush { padding: 0 !important; }

Cost: the highest. It does not resolve the conflict, it escalates it: the next override has no move left except another !important later in the file. §3.7.

6. An inline style. Beats every normal declaration but loses to any author !important (§1.7's measurement), cannot be reused, cannot be media-queried, and puts presentation in the markup. Only correct when a script computes the value at runtime.

What I would actually do: option 1 or 2. The point of the exercise is that options 3–6 are all attempts to win specificity, and specificity is only the fourth criterion — there are two criteria above it that are explicit, order-independent and designed for exactly this.

2. Explain, with reference to the value pipeline, why the first of these produces readable text at every size and the second produces overlapping lines. Then say what line-height: 150% does, and why it is a third distinct behaviour.

article { font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.5; }
article { font-size: 16px; line-height: 24px; }
Solution

The mechanism is §3.13's computed-value boundary, and §3.9 measured it. What inherits is the computed value, so the question is what each form computes to on the ancestor.

line-height: 1.5 — the number survives computation. line-height is the one property whose specification says a unitless number computes to itself, not to a length. So the ancestor's computed value is the number 1.5, that number is what inherits, and every descendant multiplies it by its own font size. Measured on a 20px parent with a 40px child: the child's line height came out at 60px. Proportional at every size, forever.

line-height: 24px — the length computes on the ancestor and freezes. The computed value is 24px, and 24px is what inherits. A descendant with font-size: 40px gets 24px of leading regardless — measured at 30px for a 30px declaration, unchanged by the child's 40px font. The lines overlap because the leading is smaller than the text.

line-height: 150% is the third behaviour, and it sides with the length. A percentage on line-height resolves against the element's own font size at computed-value time, so on a 16px ancestor it computes to 24px — and that absolute 24px is what inherits. It looks like the proportional form and behaves like the frozen one, which makes it the most misleading of the three. This is a case where percentages and unitless numbers are genuinely different, unlike most of CSS where they are interchangeable.

The general rule this is an instance of: a value that fully resolves before computed-value time inherits as a resolved value; a value that survives computation inherits as a formula. em resolves at computed-value time, so padding: 1em on an ancestor does not stay proportional for descendants either — it just does not matter as often, because padding is not inherited.

Practical consequence: write line-height unitless on anything that has descendants — :root, body, article. Absolute line heights are correct only on a single-line element where nothing will inherit from it, such as a button label or a table cell.

3. This stylesheet produces a card with no background colour and a bold heading that is not bold. Explain both, and fix the file without deleting any rule.

.card       { background-color: #fff; }
.card       { background: url("/paper.png") no-repeat; }
.card h2    { font: 1.25rem/1.2 Georgia, serif; }
.card h2 b  { font-weight: 700; }
Solution

Both symptoms are the same defect: §3.12's shorthand reset.

No background colour. The second rule's background is a shorthand, and a shorthand sets every longhand it covers, including the ones not written. background covers background-color, and since the declaration does not mention a colour, background-color is reset to its initial value — transparent. The first rule's #fff is not overridden by a competing colour; it is wiped by a shorthand that has an opinion about a property it never names. Measured in §3.12: writing background-color: red and then background: linear-gradient(...) produced rgba(0, 0, 0, 0), and reversing the order preserved the red.

The heading is not bold. font is the most destructive shorthand in CSS. font: 1.25rem/1.2 Georgia, serif sets font-size, line-height and font-family explicitly, and silently resets font-style, font-variant, font-weight and font-stretch to normal. <h2> gets its boldness from the user-agent stylesheet's font-weight: bold (§1.7 measured it at 700), and the shorthand overwrote it with normal. The fourth rule then restores 700 — but only for a <b> inside the heading, so the heading itself stays light and any <b> in it looks correct, which is exactly the sort of half-working symptom that makes this hard to spot.

The fix, without deleting a rule — put the colour into the shorthand, and stop using font:

.card       { background-color: #fff; }
.card       { background: #fff url("/paper.png") no-repeat; }
.card h2    { font-size: 1.25rem; line-height: 1.2; font-family: Georgia, serif; }
.card h2 b  { font-weight: 700; }

The first rule is now redundant rather than broken, which is what "without deleting any rule" costs.

The habits worth taking away. Never write a shorthand after a longhand it covers, in any file, in any layer — the ordering that makes it safe is not local and cannot be seen from the rule you are editing. And treat font as a reset rather than as a convenience: it is the right tool for font: inherit on form controls (§1.7) and for all: revert-style deliberate wiping, and the wrong tool for setting a couple of typographic properties.

4. A team has a reset layer, a components layer, and utilities written outside any layer. Someone adds .visually-hidden { position: absolute !important; ... } to the reset layer to "make sure it always wins". Explain what actually happens, and what they should have done.

Solution

What actually happens is the opposite of what they intended — and then, awkwardly, it works anyway, for the wrong reason.

§3.6 measured the rule: !important reverses the layer order. For normal declarations, later layers beat earlier ones and unlayered beats everything. For important declarations the whole ordering inverts, so an important declaration in the earliest layer is the strongest important declaration in the author origin. reset is the earliest layer, so their !important there beats an !important in components, beats an !important in any later layer, and beats every !important written in unlayered code.

So the utility does win. It wins more than they meant, and that is the problem:

  • Nothing in the author origin can now override it. Not a later layer, not an unlayered rule, not another !important. The only remaining tools are a user stylesheet or an inline style — and an inline style loses to it too (§1.7). If a component ever needs to make a visually-hidden element visible on focus, which is the standard skip-link pattern, that rule cannot be written.
  • They have made reset the most powerful layer in the file for any important declaration. The next person who adds an !important to the reset layer for an unrelated reason acquires the same unbeatable status without knowing it, and the layer order now means the opposite of what its name suggests to everyone reading it.
  • The intent is unexpressed. A reader seeing !important in a reset layer has no way to know whether it is load-bearing or cargo-culted.

What they should have done: put it in a last layer and drop the keyword.

@layer reset, components, utilities;

@layer utilities {
  .visually-hidden:not(:focus):not(:active) {
    position: absolute;
    inline-size: 1px; block-size: 1px;
    margin: -1px; padding: 0; border: 0;
    overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%);
    white-space: nowrap;
  }
}

The utilities layer is last, so it beats reset and components for normal declarations regardless of their specificity — §3.2's measurement showed (0,0,1) in a later layer beating (1,2,1) in an earlier one. That is exactly the "always wins" guarantee they wanted, expressed by the mechanism designed for it, and it leaves !important available as a genuine escape hatch instead of spending it.

The :not(:focus):not(:active) is the reason overridability matters here rather than being an abstract concern: a visually-hidden skip link must become visible when focused, and that requires the utility to be beatable. §15.14 covers the pattern in full.

SECTION 4

Values, Units and Math Functions

Every property in CSS defines a grammar for what may follow its colon, and §1.5 established the consequence: a value outside that grammar is discarded silently. So knowing the value types is not vocabulary study — it is the difference between a declaration that works and a declaration that is not there.

This section covers the types themselves, the units that instantiate them, and the twenty-odd functions that let CSS compute rather than merely state. That last part is the most under-used capability in the language. A stylesheet that can say clamp(1rem, 0.5rem + 2vw, 2rem) needs far fewer breakpoints than one that can only say 1rem, and a stylesheet that can say round(var(--h), var(--grid)) can enforce a baseline grid that no amount of hand-entered numbers will hold.

Every number in this section was measured in a real browser at a 900×700 viewport with a 16px root font size.

4.1 Value Types, and How to Read a Grammar

The specification writes each property's grammar in a small notation you will meet constantly in documentation and in error messages. overflow's is [ visible | hidden | clip | scroll | auto ]{1,2}, and background-color's is <color>.

The angle-bracket names are value types, and the ones that appear everywhere are:

<length>
A distance: 16px, 2rem, 50vh. Always carries a unit — except 0, which is the one length that may be written bare.
<percentage>
A proportion of something the property defines. §4.6 — the "of what" is never obvious.
<number>
A bare number: 1.5, 0.6, -2. Distinct from a length; line-height, opacity, flex-grow and z-index take these.
<angle>
45deg, 0.25turn, 1.57rad, 50grad. Rotations, gradient directions, hues.
<time>
200ms, 0.3s. Transitions and animations. A bare 0 is not valid here — 0s is required.
<color>
§11 in full.
<string>
Quoted text: "Inter", '→'. Either quote character; escape the same one inside with a backslash.
<custom-ident>
An author-chosen name: a grid line, an animation, a layer, a container. §4.14.

The notation itself is worth ten minutes because documentation assumes it: | is a choice, || is "one or more of these in any order", && is "all of these in any order", [ ] groups, ? is optional, * is zero or more, + is one or more, {1,2} is a count range, and # means a comma-separated list. So <line-width> || <line-style> || <color> — the grammar of border — tells you immediately that all three parts are optional and their order does not matter.

The terms above, gathered: <string>.

4.2 Absolute Lengths

Six absolute units, and exactly one of them is real.

1in  = 96px       1cm  = 37.7812px
1pc  = 16px       1mm  = 3.76562px
1pt  = 1.32812px  1Q   = 0.9375px

Those are measured values, not conversions from a table, and they carry a detail worth having: 1cm should be 96 / 2.54 = 37.7953px, but the browser reported 37.7812. Chromium stores lengths in a fixed-point unit of 1/64 px, so every computed length is quantised to the nearest sixty-fourth. 37.7812 is 2418/64. You will see this again in §4.8, where 400px / 3 came back as 133.328px rather than 133.3333px.

The important fact about the whole family is that px is not a physical pixel and the physical units are not physical. CSS defines them all in terms of each other with 1in = 96px fixed by specification, so on a phone with a 3× display, 1in of CSS is not an inch of glass. The reference pixel is an angular measure — roughly the size a pixel appears at arm's length on a typical screen — and the whole system is anchored to it.

The practical guidance follows directly: use px for hairlines and small fixed offsets — a 1px border, a 2px outline offset — where a physical-ish minimum is what you actually want, and use the relative units for everything sized in relation to text or the viewport. cm, mm, in, pt and Q have one real use, which is print stylesheets (§13.16), where the output medium genuinely has physical dimensions.

4.3 Font-Relative Lengths

These resolve against a font, and which font is where the interest is. Measured on an element with font-size: 20px inside a document with a 16px root:

1em   = 20px        the element's own font-size
1rem  = 16px        the root element's font-size
1ex   = 9.17188px   the font's x-height
1ch   = 10px        the advance width of "0" in the font
1cap  = 13.0938px   the font's cap height
1lh   = 40px        the element's own line-height (2 × 20px here)

The em unit is the element's own computed font-size — with one exception that trips everyone: on the font-size property itself, em refers to the parent's font size, because the element's own is what is being defined. That is what makes em compound. Measured on a two-level nesting where both levels declare font-size: 2em against a 16px root:

:root  { font-size: 16px; }
.p     { font-size: 2em; }         /* 32px  — 2 × the root's 16px */
.p .c  { font-size: 2em;           /* 64px  — 2 × the parent's 32px */
         padding: 1em;             /* 64px  — 1 × its OWN font size */
         margin: 1rem; }           /* 16px  — 1 × the root's */

fontSize=64px   padding=64px   margin=16px

Three different resolutions in one rule. font-size: 2em looked at the parent, padding: 1em looked at the element's own newly computed 64px, and rem ignored both.

rem is the unit for anything that should scale with the user's browser font-size setting but not compound. That covers most spacing and most type. Do not set :root { font-size: 62.5% } to make 1rem = 10px: it looks convenient and it silently overrides a reader who has set a larger default size, which is one of the few genuinely important accessibility settings a browser offers. If you want round numbers, use calc() or a custom property.

ch is the most useful of the obscure ones. It is the advance width of the 0 glyph, which makes max-inline-size: 65ch a direct expression of the classic 45–75 character measure for readable prose. It is an approximation — proportional fonts vary — but a far better one than guessing a pixel width.

lh and its root-relative sibling are newer and solve a real problem: expressing a margin as a whole number of lines, so that a baseline grid survives a change of line height.

One line each, for reference: the em unit and max-inline-size:.

4.4 Viewport Units

Six axes of viewport measurement, each in four variants. Measured at a 900×700 viewport:

100vh   = 700px      100vw   = 900px
100svh  = 700px      100vmin = 700px   (the smaller axis)
100lvh  = 700px      100vmax = 900px   (the larger axis)
100dvh  = 700px      100vi   = 900px   (the inline axis)
                     100vb   = 700px   (the block axis)

On a desktop browser all four height variants agree, and that is exactly why they exist: they only diverge on mobile, where the browser chrome grows and shrinks as you scroll.

svh
Small: the viewport when the browser UI is at its largest. The safe one — content sized in svh is never cut off.
lvh
Large: the viewport when the browser UI is retracted. Content sized in lvh may be hidden behind the toolbar on arrival.
dvh
Dynamic: whatever it is right now. Correct at every instant, and it changes during scrolling, which can cause layout on every frame.
vh
The original. Equals lvh on mobile, which is why "100vh is too tall on my phone" was a universal complaint for a decade.

The practical answer for a full-height hero is min-block-size: 100svh — never cropped, never jumping. Use dvh only when a genuinely dynamic fit is required and you have measured that the reflow cost is acceptable.

vi and vb are the writing-mode-relative pair (§15.4): vi follows the inline axis and vb the block axis, so they swap with writing-mode: vertical-rl. In a horizontal English page, vi is vw and vb is vh, as the measurement shows.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: vmin, vmax and writing-mode:.

4.5 Container Query Units

A container query unit measures against the nearest ancestor that has declared itself a query container (§13.11), rather than against the viewport. This is what lets a component size itself relative to the space it was given rather than relative to the window.

cqw   1% of the container's width      cqi   1% of its inline size
cqh   1% of the container's height     cqb   1% of its block size
cqmin  the smaller of cqi and cqb      cqmax  the larger

Measured on a 400×200 container declared with container-type: inline-size, inside a 900×700 viewport:

.c { container-type: inline-size; width: 400px; height: 200px; }
.i { width: 50cqw; height: 10cqh; font-size: 5cqi; }

width=200px   height=70px   fontSize=20px

50cqw gave 200px and 5cqi gave 20px — both 50% and 5% of the container's 400px width, as expected.

10cqh gave 70px, and that is not 10% of 200px. It is 10% of the viewport's 700px height. This is the container-unit trap and it follows directly from the containment type: container-type: inline-size establishes a query container on the inline axis only, so the block axis has no container to measure against and the units fall back to the small viewport. Nothing warns you; the declaration is valid and the number is wrong.

The fix is to use container-type: size, which establishes both axes — but that requires the container's block size to be independent of its contents, which for most containers it is not. In practice: use cqi/cqw freely, and treat cqh/cqb as needing container-type: size and a deliberately sized container.

4.6 Percentages, and What They Resolve Against

A percentage is meaningless without a basis, and CSS's choice of basis is per-property and occasionally surprising:

width, max-width, left, right
The containing block's width. Unsurprising.
padding and margin, all four sides
The containing block's width — including padding-top and margin-bottom. This is the surprising one, and it is what makes the classic padding-top: 56.25% aspect-ratio hack work.
height
The containing block's height — and it is ignored if that height is itself auto, which is why height: 100% so often does nothing.
font-size
The parent's font size. Equivalent to em.
line-height
The element's own font size, resolved at computed-value time — which is why §3.9's warning about it applies.
transform: translate()
The element's own border box, not its container. This is what makes translate(-50%, -50%) a centring idiom.
background-position
The difference between the box and the image, which is why 50% centres rather than offsetting by half.

Percentages resolve at used-value time (§3.13), not computed-value time, which is why getComputedStyle reports them as pixels and why a percentage can depend on a layout that has not happened yet.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: translate().

4.7 Angles, Times, and the Other Dimensions

Angles. Four units, all interchangeable: deg (360 per turn), grad (400), rad (2π), and turn (1). The deg unit is the default choice; turn is more readable for whole rotations (0.5turn beats 180deg in a keyframe); rad is what the trigonometric functions in §4.11 return.

Times. s and ms. There is no bare 0 here — transition-duration: 0 is invalid and discarded, while 0s works. This is a real and frequent one-character bug.

Resolutions. dpi, dpcm, dppx, and x as an alias for dppx. They appear in image-set() and in the resolution media feature: 1dppx is a standard-density screen, 2dppx a typical "retina" one.

Ratios. <ratio> is 16 / 9, or a bare number where the second term is 1. It is what aspect-ratio (§6.13) and the aspect-ratio media feature take.

The fr unit is unique in that it is not a length at all — it is a flexible length, valid only in grid track sizing (§9.6), where it means "a share of the leftover space". Measured: width: 1fr on an ordinary block is invalid and discarded, while grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr on a 300px grid resolved to 100px 200px.

To have in hand before moving on: deg unit, fr unit, grid-template-columns:, image-set() and transition-duration:.

4.8 calc()

calc() performs arithmetic on values, and it is valid anywhere a <length>, <number>, <angle>, <time>, <percentage> or <frequency> is. Its real power is that it can mix units that are not resolvable against each other until layout runs:

.o { width: 400px; font-size: 20px; }
.a { width: calc(100% - 2em); }
.b { width: calc(100% / 3); }
.c { width: calc(50px + 10%); }

a=360px   b=133.328px   c=90px

100% - 2em mixes a percentage that needs layout with a font-relative length that resolves at computed-value time, and that is exactly what nothing else in CSS can do. Note b: 400 / 3 is 133.3333, and the browser reported 133.328 — the 1/64 px quantisation from §4.2, showing up in a place where it is easy to mistake for a bug.

Three syntax rules, and the first is the one everyone hits:

  • + and - require whitespace on both sides. calc(100%-2em) is invalid, because -2em parses as a negative length rather than a subtraction. * and / do not need the spaces, but write them anyway for consistency.
  • calc() nests, and can be omitted when nesting: calc(100% - calc(2em + 4px)) is legal, and so is calc(100% - (2em + 4px)).
  • It is type-checked, and this is more interesting than it sounds. Measured, with the ones that were discarded shown as gone:
calc(2px * 3px)             -> discarded    a length times a length is an area
calc(100px + 10)            -> discarded    a length plus a number has no type
calc(1s * 100px)            -> discarded    time times length has no type
calc(10 % 3 * 10px)         -> discarded    % is a percentage sign, not modulo
calc(100px * 2)             -> 200px        length times number is a length
calc((100px / 10px) * 5px)  -> 50px         a ratio of lengths IS a number

That last pair is typed arithmetic in action: dividing a length by a length yields a <number>, which can then multiply a length. Chromium serialises it as calc((100px * (1 / 10px)) * 5px), showing the type it tracked. But width: calc(100px / 2px) is discarded — not because the arithmetic is illegal, but because the result is a number and width does not accept a number. The error is at the property, not in the expression.

And note the fourth line: % in CSS is a unit, not an operator. Use mod() (§4.10).

Named once more, since each is referred to later: typed arithmetic.

4.9 min(), max() and clamp()

Three functions that replace a great many media queries, and their names read backwards until you internalise what they are doing.

.a { width: min(300px, 50%); }         /* on a 400px parent -> 200px */
.b { width: max(300px, 50%); }         /* on a 400px parent -> 300px */
.c { width: clamp(100px, 50%, 150px); } /* on a 400px parent -> 150px */

a=200px   b=300px   c=150px

The max() function sets a minimum, and min() sets a maximum. min(300px, 50%) never exceeds 300px, so min() is a ceiling. max(300px, 50%) is never below 300px, so max() is a floor. The confusion is universal and the way out is to read the function as "pick the smaller/larger of these", not as "the minimum/maximum size".

clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX) is exactly max(MIN, min(PREFERRED, MAX)), and the measurement confirms it: the preferred 50% was 200px, the maximum was 150px, so 150px won.

Both take any number of arguments and any mix of units, and both may contain full expressions without a nested calc():

h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.25rem + 2.5vw, 3rem); }
.page { padding-inline: max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-left)); }
.card { inline-size: min(100% - 2rem, 60ch); }

That first line is fluid typography and it is the single highest-value idiom in this section: a heading that grows smoothly with the viewport, with a hard floor and ceiling, and no breakpoints at all. §12.15 covers how to choose the numbers.

The third line is worth stealing verbatim: "as wide as the container allows minus a gutter, but never wider than 60 characters" is a complete responsive width rule in one declaration.

One accessibility rule about these: never write a viewport unit as the sole term of a font-size. font-size: 4vw cannot be enlarged by page zoom in the way users expect, because zooming changes the viewport in the same proportion. Always combine it with a rem term, as 1.25rem + 2.5vw does — the rem part responds to the user's font-size setting, and that is what makes the result zoomable.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the max() function and page zoom.

4.10 Stepped-Value and Exponential Functions

Eight functions that were unavailable in CSS until recently and remove a category of preprocessor work. All measured:

.d { width: round(105px, 25px); }        /* 100px — nearest */
.e { width: round(up, 101px, 25px); }    /* 125px — ceiling to the step */
.f { width: mod(105px, 25px); }          /*   5px */
.g { width: rem(105px, 25px); }          /*   5px */
.h { width: calc(abs(-30px)); }          /*  30px */
.j { width: calc(pow(3, 2) * 1px); }     /*   9px */
.k { width: calc(sqrt(16) * 1px); }      /*   4px */
.l { width: calc(hypot(3px, 4px)); }     /*   5px */

d=100px  e=125px  f=5px  g=5px  h=30px  j=9px  k=4px  l=5px

round() takes an optional strategy — nearest (the default), up, down, to-zero — then a value and a step. round(var(--h), 1lh) snaps a height to a whole number of lines, which is a baseline grid enforced by the browser rather than by discipline.

mod() and rem() differ only for negative operands: mod() takes the sign of the divisor, rem() the sign of the dividend. For positive inputs they agree, as the measurement shows. Note the unfortunate name collision — rem() the function has nothing to do with rem the unit.

abs() and sign() do what they say. One measured caution: calc(100px * sign(-5)) computed to -100px, and the element rendered at 0px, because width clamps negatives to zero. The function worked; the property refused the result. That distinction — an expression being valid but its result being out of range for the property — is worth remembering, because the symptom looks identical to a dropped declaration.

pow(), sqrt(), hypot(), log() and exp() operate on plain numbers, with hypot() as the exception that accepts dimensions. They are how you compute a modular type scale directly in CSS: font-size: calc(1rem * pow(1.25, var(--step))) gives you a scale where changing the ratio changes every size.

What to carry forward from this subsection: round(), abs() and pow().

4.11 Trigonometry and progress()

.a { width: calc(sin(90deg) * 100px); }   /* 100px */
.b { width: calc(cos(0) * 100px); }       /* 100px */
.c { width: calc(tan(45deg) * 100px); }   /* 100px */

a=100px   b=100px   c=100px

sin(), cos() and tan() take an <angle> or a bare <number> interpreted as radians, and return a number. asin(), acos(), atan() and atan2() are the inverses and return angles. Their canonical use is placing things on a circle without JavaScript:

.dial-mark {
  --angle: calc(var(--i) * 30deg);
  translate: calc(cos(var(--angle)) * 8rem) calc(sin(var(--angle)) * 8rem);
}

progress() returns how far a value sits between two others, as a number from 0 to 1 — measured with progress(75px, 50px, 100px) giving 0.5, so calc(100px * progress(...)) came out at 50px. It is the building block for interpolating anything against anything: an opacity that tracks a width, a colour that tracks a scroll position.

4.12 Counting the Tree: sibling-index()

sibling-index() returns an element's 1-based position among its siblings, as a number usable in any expression. Measured on three list items each declaring width: calc(sibling-index() * 10px):

li: 10px, 20px, 30px

sibling-count() gives the total. Together they replace the --i: 1; --i: 2; --i: 3 custom-property ladders that staggered-animation demos have been written with for years:

li { transition-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 60ms); }

They are new enough that a fallback matters in production, and @supports (§13.10) is how to write one. But the direction of travel is clear: CSS is gaining the ability to compute from the document's own shape.

4.13 attr(), url() and env()

attr() reads an attribute from the element. Its classic form pulls a string into generated content, and its newer form can produce a typed value for any property:

.a::before { content: attr(data-label); }

The newer form takes a type and a fallback, and produces a value for any property:

.b { width: attr(data-w type(<length>), 10px); }

  markup:   <div class="b" data-w="120px"></div>
  measured: width=120px

The second line is the significant one: with a type() argument and a fallback, attr() becomes a general bridge from markup to any property, so a server can emit data-w="120px" and the stylesheet consumes it without a custom property or a script. Treat the data as untrusted — it comes from your markup, which may come from your database.

url() references an external resource. Its argument may be quoted or not; quote it, because unquoted URLs have escaping rules that bite on parentheses and whitespace. Relative URLs in a stylesheet resolve against the stylesheet's own location, not the document's — which is why moving a CSS file breaks its background images and moving the HTML does not.

env() reads a user-agent-defined environment variable, with an optional fallback. The safe-area-inset-* family is the important one: it reports the notch and rounded-corner insets on modern phones.

.page { padding-inline: max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-left)); }

Measured, with a caution attached. env(safe-area-inset-left, 12px) returned 0px, not the 12px fallback — because on a desktop browser the variable is defined, with a value of zero. env(titlebar-area-x, 5px) returned 5px, because that one is genuinely undefined there. The fallback fires only when the variable does not exist, never when it exists and is zero, so wrapping the env() in max() as above is the pattern that actually works.

4.14 Identifiers, Strings and Escaping

A <custom-ident> is a name you invent: a grid line, a @keyframes name, a layer name, a container name, a counter, a view-transition name. The rules are the same as for a CSS identifier anywhere: letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, not starting with a digit, and not starting with a hyphen followed by a digit.

Anything outside that needs escaping with a backslash, and the escapes are worth being able to read even if you never write them. Measured in standards mode:

.a\.b     { color: red; }    /* matches class="a.b"  — a literal dot in a class name */
#\31 23   { color: green; }  /* matches id="123"     — \31 is "1", the space ends the escape */
.\--x     { color: teal; }   /* matches class="--x" */

All three matched. That middle one is the form to recognise: a numeric escape is a backslash, up to six hex digits, and a space that terminates the escape rather than being part of the selector. This is exactly what utility-first frameworks generate for class names like w-1/2 and p-[3px].

Class and id matching is case-sensitive in standards mode. Measured: .Foo matched class="Foo" and did not match class="foo". (In quirks mode it matches both, which is one of many reasons a document without a doctype is not worth debugging.) By contrast, type selectors and property names are case-insensitive, as are keyword values — RED, Red and red are one colour.

A <string> is quoted, and inside content a newline must be written \A rather than as a literal line break.

4.15 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • A property's grammar is written with |, ||, &&, [ ], ?, *, +, {1,2} and #, and a value outside it is discarded silently.
  • The core types are <length>, <percentage>, <number>, <angle>, <time>, <color>, <string> and <custom-ident>; 0 is the only bare length, and <time> does not accept a bare 0.
  • The absolute length units are fixed to each other with 1in = 96px; only the px unit is worth using outside print, and Chromium quantises every computed length to 1/64 px.
  • Font-relative length: the em unit is the element's own font size except on font-size itself where it is the parent's; the rem unit is the root's; the ex unit, ch unit and cap measure glyph geometry; the lh unit is one line.
  • Viewport unit variants svh, lvh and dvh differ only where browser chrome moves; svh is the safe default, dvh costs layout while scrolling, and vw unit/vh unit/vmin/vmax/vi/vb complete the family.
  • A container query unit (cqw, cqi, cqh, cqb, cqmin, cqmax) measures the nearest query container — and cqh silently falls back to the viewport under container-type: inline-size, which was measured.
  • A percentage resolves against a per-property basis; vertical padding and margin resolve against width, translate() against the element's own box, and all of them at used-value time.
  • deg unit, grad, rad and turn are interchangeable angles; dppx measures resolution; <ratio> is 16 / 9; the fr unit is valid only in grid track sizing.
  • calc() mixes units across resolution times, requires spaces around + and -, and is type-checked — a length over a length is a number, and % is not modulo.
  • min(), max() and clamp() are ceiling, floor and both; never use a viewport unit as the sole term of a font-size.
  • round(), mod(), rem(), abs(), sign(), pow(), sqrt() and hypot() were each measured; a valid expression can still produce a value the property refuses.
  • sin(), cos(), tan() and their inverses place things on circles; progress() normalises a value between two others.
  • sibling-index() and sibling-count() read the element's position in the tree.
  • attr() with a type() argument produces typed values for any property; url() resolves relative to the stylesheet; env() falls back only when the variable is undefined, not when it is zero — which is why safe-area-inset is usually wrapped in max().
  • A <custom-ident> is an author-chosen name; backslash escapes let any character appear in one, and class and id matching is case-sensitive in standards mode.

The terms above, gathered: px unit, rem unit, ex unit, ch unit, lh unit, vw unit and vh unit.

Exercises

1. Write a single font-size declaration for a page heading that is 1.75rem on a 360px-wide phone, 3rem on a 1400px-wide desktop, and scales linearly between. Show the arithmetic, and say why a bare vw value would be wrong.

Solution 
h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.1477rem + 2.6786vw, 3rem); }

The arithmetic. We want a line through two points: 28px at 360px viewport, 48px at 1400px. (1.75rem and 3rem at the 16px default.)

The slope is (48 − 28) / (1400 − 360) = 20 / 1040 = 0.0192307 px of font per px of viewport. As a viewport unit, 1vw is 1% of the viewport, so the slope is 0.0192307 × 100 = 1.92307vw.

The intercept is 28 − (0.0192307 × 360) = 28 − 6.923 = 21.077px, which is 21.077 / 16 = 1.3173rem.

So the preferred term is 1.3173rem + 1.9231vw. Checking it: at 360px that is 21.077 + 6.923 = 28px ✓, and at 1400px 21.077 + 26.92 = 48px ✓.

h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.3173rem + 1.9231vw, 3rem); }

clamp() then does the rest: below 360px the floor holds at 1.75rem, above 1400px the ceiling holds at 3rem, and in between the preferred term runs the line — §4.9 measured that clamp(MIN, PREF, MAX) is exactly max(MIN, min(PREF, MAX)).

Why a bare vw value would be wrong, for two independent reasons:

Accessibility. font-size: 3.4vw cannot be enlarged by the reader. Page zoom scales the viewport and the font size together, so the text occupies the same proportion of the screen at every zoom level — the zoom does nothing. A reader who has set a larger default font size is likewise ignored, because vw has no relationship to the font setting. The rem term is what fixes both: it responds to the user's preference, and it is the reason the combined form is the accessible one. This is a WCAG 1.4.4 failure in its pure form.

It has no floor or ceiling. At a 320px viewport 3.4vw is under 11px; at a 2560px monitor it is 87px. The clamp is not decoration.

A refinement worth knowing: if the page might be viewed in a narrow container rather than a narrow window, swap vw for cqi (§4.5) and declare the container — then the heading responds to the space it was actually given, which is what §13.11 argues is almost always the better question.

2. A component uses container-type: inline-size and sets padding-block: 2cqh on a child. In testing the padding is enormous and unrelated to the component's height. Explain, and give two fixes with their trade-offs.

Solution

The explanation is §4.5's measurement. container-type: inline-size establishes a query container on the inline axis only — that is the whole point of the value, and it exists because containing the block axis requires the container's height to be independent of its contents, which for a text-bearing component it is not.

With no block-axis container, cqh and cqb have nothing to resolve against, and the specification says they fall back to the small viewport units. So 2cqh is not 2% of the component's height; it is 2svh — 2% of the viewport height. On a 700px-tall viewport that is 14px, and on a 1440px monitor it is 29px, neither of which has anything to do with the component. Measured directly: 10cqh inside a 200px-tall inline-size container came back as 70px, which is 10% of the 700px viewport.

Nothing reports this. The declaration is valid, the value is a real number, and the only symptom is that the number is wrong.

Fix 1 — use the inline axis.

.child { padding-block: 2cqi; }

Trade-off: none technically, but it changes the design intent — the padding now tracks the component's width rather than its height. In practice this is almost always what you wanted anyway, because a component's block size is a result of its content and padding, so sizing padding from it is close to circular. This is the right answer in the large majority of cases.

Fix 2 — establish a size container.

.component { container-type: size; block-size: 20rem; }
.child     { padding-block: 2cqh; }

Trade-off: real and significant. container-type: size applies containment on both axes, which means the container's block size can no longer be determined by its contents — you must give it one. If you do not, it collapses. So this fix converts a content-sized component into a fixed-height one, and any overflow becomes your problem. Use it when the component genuinely has a designed height (a chart, a media tile, a fixed-ratio card), and not otherwise.

A third option worth mentioning: if what you actually want is "padding proportional to this component's own font size", the answer is not a container unit at all — it is em, which needs no container declaration, no containment, and no fallback story.

The general lesson: container-type is not a switch you turn on; it is a statement about which axes are sized independently of content, and the units follow from that. inline-size is the safe default precisely because a block's width usually is independent of its contents and its height usually is not.

3. Explain why each of these is discarded, and rewrite each to do what was intended.

.a { width: calc(100%-2rem); }
.b { transition-duration: 0; }
.c { width: calc(100px / 2px); }
.d { margin-top: calc(10 % 3 * 1rem); }
Solution

.a — + and - require whitespace on both sides. Without them, -2rem is not a subtraction; it is a single token, a negative length. calc(100% -2rem) is therefore two lengths side by side with no operator between them, which is a syntax error, and calc(100%-2rem) is worse still. The rule exists because CSS identifiers may contain hyphens, so the parser cannot tell a-b apart from a - b without the spaces. * and / have no such ambiguity and do not need spaces, but write them consistently.

.a { width: calc(100% - 2rem); }

.b — <time> has no unitless zero. <length> allows a bare 0 because every length unit is a scaling of the same quantity and zero of any of them is the same zero. <time> does not get that dispensation, so 0 is a <number> and transition-duration does not accept numbers. The declaration is dropped and the element keeps its previous duration — which is usually 0s anyway, making this bug invisible until the day someone adds a duration higher up the cascade.

.b { transition-duration: 0s; }

.c — the arithmetic is legal and the result has the wrong type. §4.8 measured this pair: calc((100px / 10px) * 5px) was kept and produced 50px, so dividing a length by a length is perfectly valid — it yields a <number>. The problem is that .c stops there, and width does not accept a <number>. The failure is at the property, not inside the expression, and the fix depends on the intent. If a half-size was wanted:

.c { width: calc(100px / 2); }     /* 50px — divide by a number */

If a ratio was wanted for use elsewhere, keep it as a number and multiply it back into a length:

.c { width: calc((100px / 2px) * 1px); }   /* 50px, via a number */

.d — % is a unit, not an operator. CSS has no infix modulo; the % character is exclusively the percentage sign. 10 % 3 is therefore 10 followed by % 3, which is not a valid expression, and the whole calc() fails.

.d { margin-top: calc(mod(10, 3) * 1rem); }   /* 1rem */
