mod() and rem() (§4.10) are the two remainder functions, and they differ only in sign handling for negative operands — mod() follows the divisor's sign, rem() the dividend's.

What links all four: each is a type or tokenisation error rather than a spelling one, so none of them can be caught by knowing property names, and all four are invisible in the browser — §1.5's blast radius one, a single dropped declaration and no message. This is the class of defect that a grammar-aware checker exists to catch.

4. You need a card whose padding snaps to a 4px grid, whose corner radius is half its padding, and whose maximum width is the smaller of "the container minus a 2rem gutter" and "60 characters". Write it, and say which parts would have required a preprocessor five years ago.

Solution 
.card {
  --pad-raw: 2.5vw;
  --pad: round(up, var(--pad-raw), 4px);

  padding: var(--pad);
  border-radius: calc(var(--pad) / 2);
  max-inline-size: min(100% - 2rem, 60ch);
}

How each part works.

round(up, var(--pad-raw), 4px) is §4.10's stepped-value function. The strategy keyword up ceilings to the step rather than taking the nearest, so a fluid 2.5vw — which is 22.5px at a 900px viewport — becomes 24px, and the card's padding lands on the grid at every viewport width without a single breakpoint. Using nearest (the default, written by omitting the keyword) would be equally valid and would round 22.5px down to 20px.

calc(var(--pad) / 2) divides a length by a number, which §4.8 confirmed yields a length. The radius therefore tracks the padding automatically — change the grid step or the fluid rate and the corners follow, which is exactly the kind of relationship that goes stale when it is written as two independent numbers.

min(100% - 2rem, 60ch) is §4.9's ceiling function doing two jobs at once. 100% - 2rem is the container minus a gutter; 60ch is the readable measure from §4.3, expressed in the width of the font's 0 glyph rather than a guessed pixel count. min() takes whichever is smaller, so the card is gutter-limited on a narrow screen and measure-limited on a wide one, with no media query and no breakpoint to maintain.

What would have needed a preprocessor five years ago:

  • The rounding. There was no round() in CSS at all. A 4px grid was enforced by hand, or by a Sass function that could only round static values — and 2.5vw is not static, so even the preprocessor could not have done this one. This is the part that was not merely inconvenient but impossible.
  • The derived radius. padding / 2 needed a Sass variable and a math.div(), and the relationship existed only at build time: the browser received two unrelated numbers, so nothing survived into the cascade. Here --pad is a real custom property (§5), so a media query or a container query can change it and the radius follows at runtime.
  • The measure-or-gutter width. This needed a media query with a hand-computed breakpoint at the viewport width where 60ch happened to equal 100% - 2rem — a number that changes whenever the font does. min() expresses the intent instead of the consequence.

What did not need a preprocessor, and never did: the nesting-free structure, the custom property, and the ch unit. The genuine remaining reasons to run a preprocessor are covered in §16.5, and they are fewer than most teams assume.

SECTION 5

Custom Properties, `@property` and CSS-Native Functions

A preprocessor variable is a build-time find-and-replace. It has no existence in the browser, it cannot change at runtime, it does not respond to a media query, and JavaScript cannot read or write it.

A custom property is none of those things. It is a real CSS property that participates in the cascade, inherits down the tree, can be redefined per element, per media query, per container, per state, and can be read and written from script. That difference is not a convenience — it changes what is expressible. A theme that is a set of custom properties on :root can be switched by adding one class; a theme that is a set of Sass variables requires a second stylesheet.

This section covers the mechanism, the registration system that makes custom properties typed and animatable, and the two functions — if() and @function — that are turning CSS into something with actual computation in it. Nine behaviours below were measured, and one of them is the most commonly misunderstood thing in modern CSS.

5.1 What a Custom Property Actually Is

A custom property is any property whose name begins with two hyphens. That is the entire definition.

:root {
  --brand: #5b21b6;
  --space: 1rem;
  --shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.2);
}

The value is stored as an almost-uninterpreted token stream. The browser checks that it is syntactically well-formed CSS tokens and nothing else — it does not know whether --brand is a colour, and it will happily store --brand: hello world; or --brand: 4px solid; or --brand: }{; (well-formed tokens, meaningless value).

Two consequences follow immediately, and both are load-bearing:

  • A custom property can hold a fragment, not just a complete value. --shadow-offset: 0 1px composes into box-shadow: var(--shadow-offset) 3px black. This is impossible with a typed system and it is what makes custom properties good at composition.
  • Nothing is validated until the value is used. A typo in a custom property is not an error where it is written; it becomes an error where it is substituted, which is §5.5's subject and the source of the section's most surprising measurement.

Custom property names are case-sensitive, unlike every other property name in CSS. Measured:

:root { --A: red; --a: blue; }
.p    { color: var(--A); background-color: var(--a); }

root --A=[red]  --a=[blue]  |  p color=rgb(255, 0, 0)  bg=rgb(0, 0, 255)

Two distinct properties. This is a real source of bugs in a large token set and an argument for a mechanical naming convention.

One line each, for reference: box-shadow:.

5.2 var() and Its Fallback

var() substitutes a custom property's value. It takes an optional second argument, after a comma, used when the property is not defined:

.button {
  background: var(--button-bg, var(--brand, #5b21b6));
  padding: var(--button-pad, 0.5rem 1rem);
}

The var() fallback may itself contain var(), so chains like the above work. It may also contain commas — everything after the first comma is the fallback, which is why var(--pad, 0.5rem 1rem) works and why you cannot have a fallback that is "a list, or else another list" without care.

A custom property that is defined but empty does not trigger the fallback. This is the distinction between "undefined" and "defined as nothing", and it is measured:

.a { --x: ;  color: var(--x, red); }   /* --x is DEFINED, as the empty token stream */
.b { --y: ;  width: calc(10px var(--y)); }

a color=rgb(0, 0, 0)     b width=10px

.a did not become red. The fallback never fired, because --x exists; its value substituted into color: as nothing, producing color: with an empty value, which is invalid — and §5.5 explains why that gives black rather than red. .b shows the same substitution being useful: the empty value vanished and left calc(10px).

That second behaviour is the basis of the space toggle trick (§5.14), which is how people built conditionals in CSS before if() existed.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: var() fallback.

5.3 Where to Declare Them, and How They Inherit

Custom properties are inherited properties (§3.9). That is the single most important thing about how to organise them.

:root  { --c: red; }
.a     { color: var(--c); }          /* red — inherited from :root */
.b     { --c: blue; color: var(--c); } /* blue — redefined locally */

a color=rgb(255, 0, 0)     b color=rgb(0, 0, 255)

.b did not need to know where --c came from; it shadowed it for itself and its subtree. This is what makes theming work: define the token set on :root, and any subtree can override any token without touching anything else.

Three placements, each with a purpose:

:root
Global tokens — the palette, the spacing scale, the type scale. Everything inherits from here.
A component
The component's own knobs, given defaults that reference the globals: --card-pad: var(--space-4). This is the component's public API (§5.14).
A state or a query
Redefine inside @media, @container, :hover or a theme class. Because custom properties cascade, one redefinition retunes everything downstream.

That last one is the pattern with the highest leverage in the whole language:

:root          { --gap: 1rem; }
@media (min-width: 60rem) { :root { --gap: 2rem; } }

.grid  { gap: var(--gap); }
.stack > * + * { margin-block-start: var(--gap); }
.card  { padding: var(--gap); }

One media query, three components retuned. The alternative — a media query per component — is the thing that makes stylesheets grow without bound.

5.4 Whitespace, Types and What Is Preserved

The value of a custom property is everything between the colon and the semicolon, with leading and trailing whitespace trimmed but internal whitespace preserved exactly. --x: 1px solid red ; stores 1px solid red.

Because the value is a token stream, none of the type machinery from §4 applies to it at the point of declaration:

  • --n: 5 is not a number, it is the token 5. width: var(--n) is invalid, because width needs a length.
  • calc() is how you attach a unit. width: calc(var(--n) * 1px) works, and this is the standard idiom for a unitless custom property.
  • You cannot build a unit by concatenation. width: var(--n)px does not work: substitution happens at the token level, and 5 followed by px is two tokens, not the dimension 5px.

The fix for all three is either calc(), or registration (§5.6), which gives the property a real type.

5.5 Invalid at Computed-Value Time

This is the most surprising behaviour in this section and the most valuable to know.

When a var() substitutes a value that the receiving property cannot accept, the declaration is not discarded in the way §1.5 described. It is invalid at computed-value time, and the specification says such a property becomes unset — that is, inherit for an inherited property and initial for the rest.

The consequence is that it does not fall back to a previous declaration in the cascade. Measured:

.x { color: green; color: var(--bad); }

rgb(0, 0, 0)

Not green. Black. The color: green declaration was overridden by the second declaration in the ordinary way — the cascade ran and color: var(--bad) won on source order — and only afterwards, at computed-value time, did the substitution fail. By then the green is gone. color is an inherited property, so unset meant inherit, and the inherited value from <body> is black.

This is the opposite of how an ordinary invalid value behaves. color: green; color: gibberish gives green, because gibberish is rejected at parse time and never reaches the cascade. The two look identical in the source and behave completely differently:

Invalid at parse time
color: gibberish. Dropped before the cascade. The previous declaration survives. The styles pane shows it struck through.
Invalid at computed-value time
color: var(--bad). Wins the cascade, then fails. The property becomes unset, and the previous declaration is already lost.

The reason for the design is unavoidable rather than arbitrary: the parser cannot know what var(--bad) will contain, because the cascade has not run yet. It has to accept the declaration provisionally, and by the time the truth is known the competition is over.

The other measured cases in the same family:

.c { color: var(--nope, green); }   /* green  — fallback fired: the property is undefined */
.d { color: var(--nope); }          /* black  — no fallback: unset, so inherit */
.e { --w: banana; width: var(--w); color: teal; }

c color=rgb(0, 128, 0)   d color=rgb(0, 0, 0)   e color=rgb(0, 128, 128), width unaffected

.e confirms the blast radius is still one declaration: the invalid width did not take color with it.

The practical rules that follow:

  • Always give var() a fallback for anything that matters. It converts a silent unset into a defined value.
  • Do not rely on a preceding declaration as a fallback. It is not one.
  • Register the property (§5.6) if you can. A registered property with an initial-value cannot produce this failure at all, which is measured next.

5.6 @property: Giving a Custom Property a Type

@property registers a custom property with the browser, giving it three at-rule descriptors:

@property --len {
  syntax: "<length>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 10px;
}
syntax descriptor
A string naming a value type: "<length>", "<color>", "<number>", "<percentage>", "<angle>", "<image>", a list with + or #, alternatives with |, or literal keywords. "*" means "anything", which is the unregistered behaviour.
inherits descriptor
true or false. Required. This is the only way to make a custom property non-inherited, which is often what a component-local knob should be.
initial-value descriptor
The value used when nothing declares one. Required unless syntax is "*", and it must itself match the syntax.

All three are descriptors, not properties (§1.2), and a misspelled one is discarded silently.

What registration buys, measured against the same @property --len declaration above:

.a {                  width: var(--len); }   /* never set     */
.b { --len: banana;   width: var(--len); }   /* invalid value */
.c { --len: 3rem;     width: var(--len); }   /* valid         */

a=10px   b=10px   c=48px

.a got the initial-value rather than nothing. And .b — the important one — got 10px, not unset. An invalid value assigned to a registered property is rejected at the custom property itself and replaced with the registered initial value, so §5.5's failure mode cannot occur. That alone is a strong argument for registering any custom property that a theme, a script or a user can set.

Registration is also available from JavaScript with CSS.registerProperty(), taking the same three fields. The CSS form is preferable: it lives with the stylesheet, and it applies before the first paint rather than after a script has run.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: syntax descriptor, inherits descriptor and initial-value descriptor.

5.7 Registered Properties Animate

The second thing registration buys is interpolation, and the contrast is stark. The same animation, run to exactly 50% progress, with and without registration:

@keyframes k { from { --n: 0; } to { --n: 100; } }
.a { --n: 0; width: calc(var(--n) * 1px); animation: k 10s linear -5s paused; }

unregistered:   width=100px   --n=100

@property --n { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0; }
@keyframes k  { from { --n: 0; } to { --n: 100; } }
.a { width: calc(var(--n) * 1px); animation: k 10s linear -5s paused; }

registered:     width=50px    --n=50

Halfway through the animation the unregistered property reads 100 and the registered one reads 50.

The mechanism is §14.3's: animation between two values requires the browser to know how to interpolate them, and an unregistered custom property is an untyped token stream with no interpolation defined. Such values animate discretely — they flip from the start value to the end value at the halfway point, which is exactly what the measurement shows. Registering the property as <number> tells the browser it is a number, and numbers interpolate.

This is what makes animated gradients, animated conic-gradient angles and animated shadows possible at all:

@property --angle { syntax: "<angle>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0deg; }

.spinner {
  background: conic-gradient(from var(--angle), #0000, var(--brand));
  animation: spin 2s linear infinite;
}
@keyframes spin { to { --angle: 360deg; } }

Without the @property block that animation is a jump, not a spin.

5.8 The Guaranteed-Invalid Value

An unregistered custom property that has never been declared has the guaranteed-invalid value. It is a real concept with a real behaviour: substituting it makes the whole declaration invalid at computed-value time unless a fallback is present. That is exactly what §5.5's .d measured.

You can also assign it deliberately, and this is occasionally useful:

.card        { --accent: var(--brand); }
.card.plain  { --accent: initial; }        /* back to guaranteed-invalid */
.card        { border-color: var(--accent, transparent); }

Setting a custom property to initial resets it to guaranteed-invalid, which re-arms every var() fallback downstream. It is the closest CSS has to "unset this token", and it is more precise than assigning an empty value — which, as §5.2 measured, does not re-arm the fallback.

5.9 Design Tokens and Theming

A design token is a named design decision. Custom properties are the natural home for them, and the structure that scales is two layers:

:root {
  /* 1. Primitives — the raw palette and scale. No meaning attached. */
  --violet-600: oklch(48% 0.24 295);
  --gray-050:   oklch(98% 0.002 285);
  --gray-900:   oklch(20% 0.01 285);
  --size-1: 0.25rem;  --size-2: 0.5rem;  --size-4: 1rem;  --size-8: 2rem;

  /* 2. Semantic tokens — what a thing means. These are what components use. */
  --surface:       var(--gray-050);
  --text:          var(--gray-900);
  --accent:        var(--violet-600);
  --space-inline:  var(--size-4);
  --radius:        var(--size-1);
}

Components reference the semantic layer and never the primitive one. That is what makes a theme a small diff:

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --surface: var(--gray-900);
  --text:    var(--gray-050);
}

Five lines change the whole application, because §5.3's inheritance carries the new values to every descendant, and because no component ever named a grey directly. A theme that has to restate every component's colours is a theme built on the primitive layer, and it will drift.

Three conventions worth adopting:

  • Name semantically, not visually. --surface-raised, not --white. The day dark mode arrives, --white: black is a sentence nobody wants to write.
  • Put the theme on an attribute, not a class, so [data-theme="dark"] and [data-theme="light"] are mutually exclusive by construction and a script sets one attribute rather than juggling two classes.
  • Register the tokens that animate or that scripts write (§5.6). Colours in particular: a <color>-registered token transitions smoothly and an unregistered one snaps.

5.10 light-dark()

light-dark() picks between two values according to the element's used colour scheme. It removes the media query from the common case entirely:

:root { color-scheme: light dark; }
.a    { color: light-dark(red, blue); }
.b    { color-scheme: dark;  color: light-dark(red, blue); }
.c    { color-scheme: light; color: light-dark(red, blue); }

a=rgb(255, 0, 0)   b=rgb(0, 0, 255)   c=rgb(255, 0, 0)

.a followed the browser's preference (light, in this measurement). .b and .c overrode it locally, so one element can be dark inside a light page with no query at all.

light-dark() requires color-scheme to be set — it reads the used colour scheme, and an element with no declared scheme resolves to light. Declaring color-scheme: light dark on :root is the one line that makes the whole mechanism work, and it does a second job at the same time: it tells the browser to render form controls, scrollbars and the canvas background in the matching scheme, which is covered in §11.9.

The trade-off against @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) is worth stating. light-dark() is per-value, so it composes beautifully with tokens and cannot get out of sync. A media query is per-rule, so it can change anything — including layout — and it can respond to a user's manual override only if you drive it from a class. Most codebases want both: light-dark() for token values, and a [data-theme] attribute for the manual override.

To have in hand before moving on: prefers-color-scheme.

5.11 Style Queries: Reading a Custom Property Back

A style query asks whether an ancestor has a particular custom property value. It is the mechanism that lets a token drive behaviour, not just a value:

.wrap { container-name: card; }

@container style(--variant: danger) {
  .title { color: red; }
}

rgb(255, 0, 0)

Measured, with --variant: danger set on the wrapper. Note two things: a style query does not require container-type to be declared — every element is a style container by default — and it queries the computed value of the custom property on the nearest matching container.

This turns a custom property into a component variant switch that inherits. Set --variant: danger once on a subtree and every card, button and icon inside it can respond, without a class on each one and without a JavaScript pass. §13.13 develops container queries in full.

5.12 if()

if() brings conditionals into a value, rather than into a rule. It takes a sequence of condition-and-value pairs and an else:

.badge {
  background: if(style(--variant: danger): crimson;
                 style(--variant: warn):   goldenrod;
                 else:                     var(--surface));
}

The conditions it accepts are style(), media() and supports(), which makes it a single-value equivalent of @container style(), @media and @supports.

Its advantage over the at-rule forms is that it works inside a value, so a component can vary one declaration without duplicating the rule. Its status is worth stating plainly: at the time of writing if() is available in Chromium-based browsers only, with a Baseline status of limited. It belongs in a stylesheet behind @supports (§13.10) or with a preceding declaration as a fallback — and note that this is one of the cases where a preceding declaration does work as a fallback, because an unsupported function is invalid at parse time (§5.5's first row), not at computed-value time.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: baseline status.

5.13 @function

@function defines a reusable computation with parameters — the feature that closes the last real gap between CSS and a preprocessor:

@function --spacing(--multiplier <number>: 1) {
  result: calc(var(--size-4) * var(--multiplier));
}

.card { padding: --spacing(2); }

The result descriptor is the returned value. Parameters are custom-property names, may declare a type, and may declare a default after a colon. The body may contain conditional at-rules, so a function can return different values under different media conditions — which is something no preprocessor function can do, because a preprocessor has no runtime.

Like if(), @function is Chromium-only at the time of writing, with a Baseline status of limited. It is in this course because the direction matters: the arguments for running Sass are getting shorter every year, and §16.5 revisits them.

5.14 Two Patterns Worth Knowing

A component API. Expose a component's knobs as custom properties with defaults, and consumers can retune it without overriding a single rule:

.card {
  --card-pad:    var(--space-inline);
  --card-radius: var(--radius);
  --card-bg:     var(--surface);

  padding: var(--card-pad);
  border-radius: var(--card-radius);
  background: var(--card-bg);
}

.sidebar .card { --card-pad: var(--size-2); }

The consumer sets a token; they do not need to know which property it feeds, and the component can change its internals without breaking them. This is a genuine encapsulation boundary and it costs three lines.

The space toggle. Before if(), this was how CSS did conditionals, and it still works everywhere:

.thing        { --on: ; }                        /* "true":  empty value    */
.thing.off    { --on: initial; }                 /* "false": guaranteed-invalid */

.thing { border: var(--on, 1px solid transparent) var(--on-alt, 2px solid red); }

It relies on exactly the two measured behaviours from §5.2 and §5.8: an empty custom property substitutes as nothing and does not trigger the fallback, while a property set to initial is guaranteed-invalid and does. It is clever, it is unreadable, and it should be commented wherever it appears — but knowing how it works means you can recognise it in someone else's stylesheet instead of deleting it.

5.15 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • A custom property is any property named with a leading --; its value is a token stream that is not validated where it is written, and its name is case-sensitive.
  • var() substitutes it; the var() fallback fires only when the property is undefined, not when it is defined as empty — measured.
  • Custom properties inherit, which is what makes :root tokens, per-subtree overrides and one-media-query retuning work.
  • Whitespace inside a value is preserved, no type is attached, and var(--n)px cannot build a unit — calc(var(--n) * 1px) is the idiom.
  • Invalid at computed-value time makes a property unset rather than falling back to the previous declaration: color: green; color: var(--bad) measured black, not green.
  • @property registers a custom property with the syntax descriptor, inherits descriptor and initial-value descriptor; a registered custom property given an invalid value falls back to its initial value rather than to unset — measured at 10px.
  • Animating a custom property requires registration: at exactly 50% progress an unregistered property read 100 (discrete) and a registered <number> read 50 (interpolated).
  • The guaranteed-invalid value is what an undeclared custom property holds, and assigning initial restores it, re-arming every downstream fallback.
  • A design token set works in two layers — primitives and semantics — and theming changes only the semantic layer.
  • light-dark() picks per value from the used colour scheme and requires color-scheme to be declared.
  • A style query reads a custom property from an ancestor and needs no container-type.
  • if() puts a conditional inside a value and @function defines a parameterised computation with a result descriptor; both are Chromium-only today and belong behind @supports.

In summary, the vocabulary here is animating a custom property.

Exercises

1. This rule is meant to fall back to green when the token is missing. It renders black. Explain precisely what happened, and give two different correct fixes.

.notice { color: green; color: var(--notice-color); }
Solution

What happened, step by step.

  1. Both declarations are syntactically valid at parse time. var(--notice-color) is a well-formed function call, and the parser cannot know what it will contain, so it accepts the declaration.
  2. The cascade runs (§3.2). Two declarations for color on the same element, same origin, same layer, same specificity — so criterion 5, order of appearance, decides. The second one wins. color: green is now gone.
  3. Computed-value time arrives and --notice-color turns out to be undefined, so it substitutes the guaranteed-invalid value (§5.8). There is no fallback in the var(), so the declaration is invalid at computed-value time.
  4. The specification says such a property becomes unset. color is an inherited property, so unset means inherit, and the inherited colour from the ancestors is black.

Measured exactly this way: color: green; color: var(--bad) produced rgb(0, 0, 0).

Why the intuition fails. With an ordinary bad value — color: green; color: gibberish — you do get green, because gibberish is rejected at parse time and never enters the cascade at all. The two cases look identical in the source and are governed by completely different rules. This is the distinction the section's table draws, and it is the single most valuable thing to carry away from it.

Fix 1 — put the fallback where the substitution happens.

.notice { color: var(--notice-color, green); }

The var() fallback fires when the property is undefined, which is the actual condition you were trying to express. One declaration, no reliance on cascade order.

Fix 2 — register the property, so it can never be invalid.

@property --notice-color {
  syntax: "<color>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: green;
}

.notice { color: var(--notice-color); }

Measured behaviour (§5.6): a registered property that is never set yields its initial-value, and one set to something that does not match its syntax also yields its initial-value rather than going invalid. So this version is robust against both "nobody set it" and "someone set it to banana" — which Fix 1 is not, since a defined-but-nonsense value still reaches color: and still produces black.

Which to use. Fix 1 for a one-off. Fix 2 for anything in a design token set, anything a script writes, and anything that needs to animate — registration is the only route to all three.

2. A spinner is built with a conic-gradient whose start angle is animated from 0deg to 360deg through a custom property. It does not rotate; it flips once, halfway through. Explain, and fix it.

Solution

The mechanism. An unregistered custom property is an untyped token stream (§5.1). The browser does not know that 0deg and 360deg are angles — as far as it is concerned they are two token sequences with no defined way to get from one to the other. The specification's rule for a property with no interpolation is that it animates discretely: it holds the start value until 50% progress and then holds the end value.

Measured on exactly this shape — an animation paused at 50% progress:

unregistered:   --n=100   (already at the end value)
registered:     --n=50    (interpolated)

So the "flip halfway" symptom is not a bug in the keyframes or the timing function. It is the correct, specified behaviour for an untyped value, and it will look the same with any easing, any duration and any number of intermediate keyframes.

The fix is one at-rule:

@property --angle {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}

.spinner {
  background: conic-gradient(from var(--angle), transparent, var(--accent));
  animation: spin 2s linear infinite;
}
@keyframes spin { to { --angle: 360deg; } }

syntax: "<angle>" tells the browser the value is an angle, angles have a defined interpolation, and the gradient now sweeps.

Three details worth getting right in the real thing.

  • inherits: false is correct here. The angle is the spinner's own state; letting it inherit would mean a nested spinner silently inherits its parent's animated angle, which is never what you want for a component-local knob. Registration is the only way to make a custom property non-inherited (§5.6).
  • initial-value: 0deg is required, because the syntax is not "*". It is also what the element shows before the animation's first frame.
  • Prefer animating --angle over rotate only when the thing rotating is the gradient rather than the element. If the whole element is spinning, rotate: 360deg is cheaper — it is a compositor-only property (§1.8), whereas repainting a conic gradient every frame is paint work. §14.12 covers the distinction.

And the broader lesson: whenever something animated "jumps instead of moving", the first question is whether the animated value has a type the browser can interpolate. That covers unregistered custom properties, and also display, content-visibility and overlay, which are discretely animated by specification — §14.6's transition-behavior: allow-discrete exists for exactly those.

3. Design the token layer for an application that needs (a) a light and a dark theme, (b) a user override that beats the OS preference, and (c) a "high contrast" variant. Write the CSS, and justify each structural choice.

Solution 
:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;

  /* 1. Primitives — no meaning, just values. */
  --violet-500: oklch(58% 0.20 295);
  --violet-700: oklch(38% 0.20 295);
  --gray-000:   oklch(100% 0 0);
  --gray-100:   oklch(96% 0.002 285);
  --gray-800:   oklch(28% 0.01 285);
  --gray-950:   oklch(14% 0.01 285);

  /* 2. Semantics — what components actually use. */
  --surface:      light-dark(var(--gray-000), var(--gray-950));
  --surface-sunk: light-dark(var(--gray-100), var(--gray-800));
  --text:         light-dark(var(--gray-950), var(--gray-000));
  --accent:       light-dark(var(--violet-700), var(--violet-500));
  --border:       color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 20%, transparent);
}

/* (b) the user override — an attribute, so the two states are exclusive */
[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
[data-theme="dark"]  { color-scheme: dark; }

/* (c) high contrast, driven by preference or by the same attribute */
@media (prefers-contrast: more) {
  :root { --border: var(--text); --surface-sunk: var(--surface); }
}
[data-contrast="more"] { --border: var(--text); --surface-sunk: var(--surface); }

Justifying each choice.

Two layers, and components touch only the second. A component that writes background: var(--gray-000) has hard-coded a light theme, and no amount of theming can rescue it. Referencing --surface means the component never learns what colour it is. This is the difference between a theme that is a five-line diff and one that is a second stylesheet.

light-dark() for the light/dark axis, not a media query. §5.10 measured that it reads the used colour scheme, which means requirement (b) falls out for free: setting color-scheme: dark on an element flips every light-dark() beneath it, so the user override is one attribute and one declaration rather than a duplicate of the whole token block. With @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) you would need the media query and a class-based duplicate of it, and the two would drift.

color-scheme: light dark on :root is load-bearing twice. It is what makes light-dark() resolve at all — an element with no declared scheme is light — and it tells the browser to render form controls, scrollbars and the canvas in the matching scheme (§11.9). Without it, a dark theme has light scrollbars.

An attribute rather than a class for data-theme. [data-theme="dark"] and [data-theme="light"] cannot both be set, so a script writes one attribute instead of adding one class and remembering to remove the other. It also reads better in the DOM inspector.

High contrast redefines semantics, not primitives. --border: var(--text) at full strength rather than a 20% mix, and sunk surfaces collapsed into the base surface so that contrast comes from borders rather than from fills. Note it is expressed twice — once for prefers-contrast: more and once for the manual attribute — which is the same both-routes structure as the theme, for the same reason.

What I would add for production, and why they are omissions rather than oversights: register the animated tokens with @property ... syntax: "<color>" so theme transitions interpolate instead of snapping (§5.7); and add a @media (prefers-reduced-transparency) branch if any surface uses alpha, since the color-mix() border does. Both are in §11 and §15.

SECTION 6

The Box Model, Sizing and Overflow

Every element that renders generates at least one box, and the whole of layout is arithmetic on those boxes. This section is that arithmetic: the four rectangles a box is made of, the six properties that size it, the three ways it can be sized by its contents instead, and what happens when the contents do not fit.

None of it is difficult, and all of it is worth knowing precisely, because the box model is where the largest number of "it is two pixels off" hours are spent. The specific things that cost the most time are margin collapsing — which has three separate rules, all counter-intuitive — and the difference between overflow: hidden and overflow: clip, which sounds cosmetic and is not.

Everything below was measured.

6.1 The Four Boxes

The box model is the arithmetic that decides how much room an element occupies. A box is four nested rectangles, and the box model is the set of rules governing how the four relate:

margin box — transparent space outside the border. Backgrounds do not reach here. Can be negative. Collapses (§6.6).
border box — the border itself. This is what offsetWidth reports.
padding box — space inside the border. The background does reach here. Cannot be negative.
content box — the text or the replaced content. What width sizes by default.

Four facts about them that matter downstream:

  • The background paints under the padding box by default, not just the content box, and background-clip (§11.7) changes which of the four it stops at.
  • Margins can be negative; padding cannot. A negative padding is an invalid value and is discarded.
  • Only margins collapse. Padding and borders never do, and adding either is one way to stop a collapse (§6.7).
  • The margin box is what participates in layout. Flex and grid space items by their margin boxes, and gap is added between margin boxes.

What to carry forward from this subsection: box model.

6.2 box-sizing

The default is box-sizing: content-box, which means width sizes the content box and padding and border are added outside it. Measured on two boxes given identical declarations:

.a, .b { width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; }
.b     { box-sizing: border-box; }

.a  offsetWidth=250   computed width=200px
.b  offsetWidth=200   computed width=200px

.a occupies 250px — the 200px content plus 40px of padding plus 10px of border. .b occupies exactly the 200px it asked for, and its content box has been reduced to 150px to make room.

Note that getComputedStyle().width reported 200px for both: Chromium reports the value as measured by the element's own box-sizing, so the number you read back is not comparable between two elements unless they share the setting. clientWidth (content + padding) was 190 and offsetWidth (content + padding + border) was 200, and those two are unambiguous.

border-box is what almost everyone wants almost always, because "this element is 200px wide" is a statement about the space it occupies. The universal opener:

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

The ::before/::after part is not optional — pseudo-elements do not inherit box-sizing from anything, because box-sizing is a non-inherited property, and the universal selector does not match them. This is the single most-copied rule in CSS and it is worth knowing why all three selectors are there.

6.3 width, height, and the Minimum and Maximum Overrides

The width property and the height property set a preferred size; min-width:, max-width:, min-height: and max-height: constrain it. The resolution order is fixed and it is not the intuitive one. Measured:

.a { width: 500px; max-width: 300px; }                   /* -> 300px */
.b { width: 100px; min-width: 300px; }                   /* -> 300px */
.c { min-width: 400px; max-width: 200px; width: 300px; } /* -> 400px */

a=300px   b=300px   c=400px

.c is the one to remember: min-width beats max-width. The specification resolves the preferred width, clamps it to the maximum, and then clamps it to the minimum — so the minimum has the final say and a contradictory pair is not an error, it is a defined outcome. The same holds on the block axis.

A percentage height is ignored when the containing block's height is auto, which is the mechanical reason height: 100% so often does nothing: the parent has no height to take a percentage of, so the declaration resolves to auto. The fixes, in order of preference, are height: 100% on every ancestor up to :root (fragile), a flex or grid parent that stretches its items (usually right), or 100svh if what you meant was the viewport (§4.4).

The logical equivalents — the inline-size property, the block-size property, min-block-size: and max-inline-size: — do the same job on the writing-mode-relative axes and are covered in §15.6. Prefer them; they cost nothing and they survive a change of writing mode.

The terms above, gathered: the width property, the height property, min-height:, max-height:, the block-size property and the inline-size property.

6.4 Padding

The padding property is the space between content and border. It cannot be negative, it is always painted with the element's background, and it is the shorthand for four longhands in the usual clockwise order — top, right, bottom, left.

The one thing worth knowing beyond that is from §4.6 and it is genuinely surprising: a percentage padding resolves against the containing block's width, on all four sides. padding-top: 50% is half the container's width, not half its height. That is not a quirk; it is deliberate, because resolving vertical padding against height would make a box whose height depends on its padding which depends on its height.

It is also what made the pre-aspect-ratio ratio hack work:

/* the historical technique — aspect-ratio (§6.11) replaces it */
.ratio-16-9 { padding-block-start: 56.25%; block-size: 0; position: relative; }

9 / 16 = 0.5625. You will still meet this in older stylesheets, and now you know why it is a padding and why it is a percentage.

One line each, for reference: the padding property.

6.5 Margin, auto, and Negative Values

The margin property is space outside the border. Unlike padding, it accepts negative values and the keyword auto.

Measured inside a 400px container, on 100px-wide blocks:

.a { width: 100px; margin-left: -20px; }
.b { width: 100px; margin-inline: auto; }
.c { width: 100px; margin-left: auto; }

a  ml=-20px  mr=0px       b  ml=150px  mr=150px       c  ml=300px  mr=0px

An auto margin absorbs the free space. Two of them split it equally, which is the classic horizontal centring idiom. One of them takes all of it, which pushes the element to the opposite side — margin-inline-start: auto is how you push a single item to the end of a flex row without changing justify-content for its siblings, and it is a much better tool than people realise.

margin: 0 auto only centres an element that has a definite width narrower than its container. On a full-width block there is no free space to absorb, which is why it appears to do nothing.

A negative margin pulls the box in that direction, and — on the end sides — pulls subsequent content along with it. Two legitimate uses survive modern layout: cancelling a container's padding for a full-bleed child, and the negative-margin/positive-padding pair that keeps a grid's outer gutters even. Both are better expressed with grid or gap today; know them because you will read them.

auto margins do not work on the block axis in normal flow. margin-block: auto computes to 0 for an ordinary block, which is why vertical centring was hard for so long. It does work in flex and grid containers, where it is often the neatest tool available (§8.14).

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: the margin property, negative margin, grid container and margin-block:.

6.6 Margin Collapsing

Adjacent vertical margins in normal flow collapse into one, and its size is the larger of them — not their sum. There are three distinct cases and all three are measured below.

Case one: adjacent siblings. A 30px bottom margin meeting a 20px top margin:

.a { margin-bottom: 30px; }
.b { margin-top: 20px; }

gap between a and b = 30

30, not 50. Two adjoining margins produce one margin of the maximum size. (With a negative involved, the rule generalises: the result is the largest positive plus the most negative.)

Case two: parent and first/last child. This is the one that produces bug reports, because the margin escapes the parent entirely:

.q       { background: #ddd; }
.q > p   { margin-block: 40px; }

.q height=18

The parent is 18px tall — just the line box. The child's 40px top and bottom margins did not push the parent's content down; they collapsed through the parent and became the parent's own outer margins. The visible symptom is a background that does not cover the space you expected, and space appearing outside the element instead of inside it.

Case three: an empty block's own margins collapse together. A block with no content, padding, border or height collapses its own top and bottom margin into one.

Two things that never collapse, and it is worth being explicit: horizontal margins never collapse, and margins never collapse out of a box that establishes a new block formatting context — which is the whole of §6.7.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: adjoining margins.

6.7 Stopping a Collapse

Anything that puts something between the two margins stops them adjoining. Measured on the same 40px-margin child in three differently configured parents:

.q { }                          /* nothing between      */
.r { padding-block-start: 1px; }/* one pixel of padding */
.s { display: flow-root; }      /* a new BFC            */

.q height=18    .r height=59    .s height=98

Read those three numbers carefully, because they tell the whole story:

  • .q is 18px — both margins escaped.
  • .r is 59px — 1 + 18 + 40. The single pixel of padding blocked the top collapse, so the top margin is now inside. The bottom margin still escaped, because nothing was placed between the child's bottom margin and the parent's. A one-sided fix produces a one-sided result, which is exactly the confusing half-working state people report.
  • .s is 98px — 40 + 18 + 40. Both margins are contained.

display: flow-root (§7.7) is the right tool: it creates a new block formatting context whose entire purpose is to contain its contents' margins and floats, and it has no other visual effect. The alternatives all have side effects — overflow: hidden creates a scroll container (§6.13), display: flex or grid changes the children's layout, padding: 0.05px is a hack, and position: absolute removes the element from flow.

The cleanest modern answer is often to sidestep the whole thing: margins that only ever exist between siblings do not collapse if there are no margins. A parent with display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 1rem — or display: grid; gap — spaces its children without any margins at all, and margin collapsing does not apply in flex or grid layout in the first place.

To have in hand before moving on: grid layout.

6.8 margin-trim

margin-trim: tells a container to discard the margins of its edge children, which is the declarative version of the :first-child/:last-child margin resets that appear in every stylesheet:

.prose { margin-trim: block; }

That removes the first child's leading margin and the last child's trailing margin, so the container's own padding is the only spacing at its edges.

The rule it replaces is one that appears in essentially every stylesheet ever written:

.prose > :first-child { margin-block-start: 0; }
.prose > :last-child  { margin-block-end: 0; }

Those two rules exist because a container's padding and its first child's margin add up, so a card with padding: 1rem and a heading with margin-block-start: 1.5rem shows 2.5rem of space at the top and 1rem at the sides. The :first-child and :last-child pair cancels the outer margins so the padding is the only spacing — and it has to be repeated for every container that holds flowing content, and it breaks the moment someone wraps the first child in a <div>, because :first-child then matches the wrapper rather than the heading.

margin-trim: says the same thing structurally rather than by selector: the container declines its children's edge margins, so no descendant needs a rule and no wrapper breaks it. Its support is currently limited to Safari, which was confirmed by feature-testing rather than assumed, so treat it as a progressive enhancement — write margin-trim: for the browsers that have it and keep the :first-child reset alongside until it is widely available.

Note also that it trims only the edge margins on the axis named. margin-trim: block leaves the margins between children untouched, which is exactly right: those are the spacing you designed, and only the ones touching the container's edge are the accident.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: :first-child and margin-trim:.

6.9 Borders

The border property is the shorthand for border-width:, border-style: and border-color: — in any order, all optional, per §4.1's || notation.

The rule that catches people: border-style defaults to none, so a border with a width and a colour but no style draws nothing. border: 2px red is a valid declaration that produces no border. Conversely border: solid alone gives you a medium (3px) border in currentColor, which is often exactly what you want.

The four sides have their own longhands, and each side has its own width, style and colour — so border-block-end: 1px solid is a single-side declaration in logical terms (§15.7). border-radius:, border-image: and corner-shape: are appearance rather than box structure and live in §11.9.

One measurement-adjacent note: a border's width contributes to the border box, so under content-box sizing it adds to the element's footprint and under border-box it eats into the content. That is §6.2's whole subject, and borders are where it bites hardest because a 1px border on a border-box element with width: 100% fits, while the same border under content-box overflows by 2px.

In summary, the vocabulary here is border-width:, border-style:, border-color:, border-image: and corner-shape:.

6.10 Intrinsic Sizing

Three keywords let the content decide the size, and they are the tools that removed a lot of JavaScript measurement. Measured on the string "Hello wonderful world" inside a 600px container:

.a { width: min-content; }   /* 65.77px  */
.b { width: max-content; }   /* 146.64px */
.c { width: fit-content; }   /* 146.64px */
.e { width: stretch; }       /* 600px    */
min-content
The narrowest the content can be without overflowing — the width of the longest unbreakable run. Here, the word "wonderful" at 65.77px.
max-content
The content laid out with no wrapping at all. The whole string, 146.64px.
fit-content
Exactly min(max-content, max(min-content, available)) — shrink-to-fit. Here the string fits in 600px so it matches max-content.
stretch
Fill the containing block's available space — 600px. Unlike 100%, it accounts for the element's own margins.

fit-content is the practical star: a heading with inline-size: fit-content gets a background exactly as wide as its text, and max-inline-size: fit-content combined with a border-block-end gives an underline that stops at the end of the words.

One measured caution: fit-content() — the function, with a length argument — is not valid as a width value. Declaring width: fit-content(120px) produced an empty rule and the element fell back to its container's 600px. The function form exists only for grid track sizing (§9.7); the keyword form is what works on width.

The other place intrinsic sizes appear is as the automatic minimum size of flex and grid items, which is the cause of the "why won't my flex item shrink" problem in §8.13.

What to carry forward from this subsection: intrinsic size.

6.11 aspect-ratio

aspect-ratio: gives a box a preferred ratio, so that setting one dimension determines the other:

.a { width: 200px; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }              /* 200 x 112.5 */
.b { width: 200px; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; height: 50px; }/* 200 x 50    */
.c { width: 100px; aspect-ratio: 1; }                   /* 100 x 100   */

a=200x112.5   b=200x50   c=100x100

.b shows the precedence: an explicit height wins. aspect-ratio only fills in a dimension that is otherwise automatic.

And the trap, measured. A ratio-boxed element whose content is taller than the ratio allows:

.d      { width: 200px; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
.d > p  { height: 300px; margin: 0; }

d=200x300

The box is 300px tall, not 112.5px. aspect-ratio sets a preferred size, and the automatic minimum size of a block (min-height: auto) still lets content push it out. Nothing is reported; the ratio is simply not honoured. The fix is to say what should happen to the overflow:

.d { width: 200px; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; overflow: auto; }
/* or, when clipping is right: */
.d { width: 200px; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; min-height: 0; overflow: clip; }

For images and videos, aspect-ratio is usually unnecessary: a replaced element with width and height attributes has a natural aspect ratio the browser already knows, which is what makes those two attributes the cheapest fix for layout shift.

6.12 Replaced Elements, object-fit and object-position

A replaced element — <img>, <video>, <iframe>, <canvas>, most form controls — has content the CSS box model does not lay out. It has natural dimensions of its own, and the interesting question is what happens when the box and the content disagree.

object-fit: answers it:

fill
The default. Stretch to the box, distorting the ratio.
cover
Fill the box, preserve the ratio, crop the overflow. The one you want for a thumbnail grid.
contain
Fit inside the box, preserve the ratio, leave empty space. The one for a logo.
none / scale-down
Natural size, cropped; or the smaller of none and contain.

object-position: places the content within the box, taking the same values as background-position. With cover, this is what decides which part gets cropped — object-position: 50% 20% biases towards the top, which is the difference between a portrait thumbnail with a face in it and one with a forehead in it.

.thumb img { inline-size: 100%; aspect-ratio: 1; object-fit: cover; object-position: 50% 25%; }

The terms above, gathered: object-fit:.

6.13 overflow and What Makes a Scroll Container

The overflow property decides what happens when content exceeds its box. The four values differ in ways that are not obvious, so here they are measured. Each box is 100×50 with a 300×200 child; scrollTop was set to 50 and read back:

overflow: hidden    scrollTop after setting 50 = 50   -> IS a scroll container
overflow: clip      scrollTop after setting 50 = 0    -> is NOT
overflow: auto      scrollTop after setting 50 = 50   -> IS a scroll container
overflow: visible   scrollTop after setting 50 = 0    -> is NOT
visible
The default. Content spills out and is painted. Nothing is clipped.
hidden
Clipped — and it is a scroll container. There are no visible scrollbars, but the content can still be scrolled programmatically, and it will be scrolled by the browser when something inside it receives focus.
clip
Clipped and not a scroll container. Nothing can scroll it, by script or by the browser. This is what most people meant when they wrote hidden.
auto
A scroll container with scrollbars when needed. The right default for a scrollable region.
scroll
A scroll container with scrollbars always reserved, whether needed or not.

The hidden versus clip distinction is the practically important one, and it explains a real bug: a decorative element clipped with overflow: hidden on a container that also holds focusable content will jump when a keyboard user tabs into something off-screen, because the browser scrolls a scroll container to reveal the focused element. With clip it cannot, because there is nothing to scroll. Use clip when you mean "cut this off", and hidden only when you also want programmatic scrolling.

A scroll container matters for more than scrollbars: it is the element that position: sticky sticks within (§10.6), that scroll snapping applies to (§10.14), and that scroll-driven animations measure (§14.10).

One line each, for reference: the overflow property.

6.14 The Two Axes Are Not Independent

overflow is a shorthand for overflow-x: and overflow-y:, and one value sets both. But the two axes are coupled by a rule that surprises everyone. Measured:

.a { overflow-x: hidden; }
.b { overflow-x: hidden; overflow-y: visible; }

a  x=hidden  y=auto        b  x=hidden  y=auto

.b explicitly asked for overflow-y: visible and computed to auto. When one axis is anything other than visible, a visible on the other axis computes to auto. The specification requires it, because a box cannot simultaneously clip one axis and let content spill on the other — the clip has no boundary to stop at.

The consequence in practice: overflow-x: hidden on <body> to suppress a horizontal scrollbar quietly turns the body into a vertical scroll container too, which breaks position: sticky on anything inside it. That is one of the most common "why has sticky stopped working" causes, and §10.6 returns to it. overflow-x: clip does not have this effect, because clip pairs with visible, which is a strong reason to prefer it.

6.15 Scrollbars and the Rest of the Family

text-overflow: decides how clipped inline text ends. It needs three declarations together, and all three are load-bearing:

.truncate {
  white-space: nowrap;      /* or the text wraps instead of overflowing */
  overflow: hidden;         /* or there is nothing to truncate          */
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}

For more than one line, the standard line-clamp: property is specified but not yet shipping — §12.11 measures it — so the prefixed -webkit-box recipe is still what works.

scrollbar-gutter: reserves space for a scrollbar whether or not one appears, which removes the layout shift when content grows past one screen. Measured on a 100px-wide box with scrollbar-gutter: stable: clientWidth was 85 against an offsetWidth of 100, so 15px was reserved.

:root { scrollbar-gutter: stable; }

scrollbar-width: takes auto | thin | none, and scrollbar-color: takes a thumb colour and a track colour. Both are the standard replacements for the ::-webkit-scrollbar pseudo-elements. A warning attached to scrollbar-width: none: it hides the scrollbar without removing the ability to scroll, which leaves no visible affordance that a region is scrollable — an accessibility problem unless something else signals it.

overscroll-behavior: controls what happens when a scroll container reaches its end. contain stops the scroll from chaining to the page behind, which is the one-line fix for "scrolling a modal scrolls the page underneath". none additionally suppresses the platform's overscroll effect.

resize: makes an element user-resizable, and requires overflow to be something other than visible to have any effect. The scroll-behavior property with the value smooth makes programmatic and fragment-link scrolling animate — and should be wrapped in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference), for the reason §15.11 gives.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: scrollbar-color:, overscroll-behavior:, resize:, the scroll-behavior property and line-clamp:.

6.16 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • A box is four rectangles — content box, padding box, border box, margin box; the background reaches the padding box, margins may be negative and padding may not, and only margins collapse.
  • box-sizing: defaults to content-box, where padding and border are added outside width; border-box includes them, measured at 250px versus 200px for identical declarations.
  • min-width: beats max-width: — measured — and a percentage height is ignored when the containing block is auto.
  • A percentage padding resolves against the containing block's width on all four sides.
  • Auto margins absorb free space: two split it, one takes all of it; negative margins pull content along; block-axis auto margins do nothing in normal flow but work in flex and grid.
  • Margin collapsing takes the larger of two adjoining margins — measured at 30, not 50 — and a child's margins escape a parent that has no padding, border or new formatting context, measured as an 18px-tall parent.
  • One-sided padding produces a one-sided fix (measured at 59px); display: flow-root contains both margins (98px) and has no other visual effect.
  • margin-trim: removes edge children's margins declaratively.
  • The border property needs a border-style: — border: 2px red draws nothing.
  • Intrinsic size keywords min-content, max-content and fit-content were measured at 65.77px, 146.64px and 146.64px; stretch fills the container; fit-content() the function is not valid on width.
  • aspect-ratio: is a preferred size that an explicit height overrides and that content can override — measured at 200×300 for a 16/9 box.
  • A replaced element has natural dimensions; object-fit: and object-position: decide how the content meets the box.
  • The overflow property: hidden and auto are scroll containers and clip and visible are not — measured by setting scrollTop — which is why clip is usually what was meant.
  • overflow-x: and overflow-y: are coupled: visible computes to auto when the other axis is not visible, measured, and this is a common cause of broken position: sticky.
  • text-overflow: needs nowrap and overflow alongside it; scrollbar-gutter: reserved a measured 15px; scrollbar-width:, scrollbar-color:, overscroll-behavior:, resize: and scroll-behavior: complete the family.

Exercises

1. A card has padding: 1rem and a coloured background. Its first child is an <h3> with the browser's default margin. The heading's space appears above the card rather than inside it, and the card's background does not cover it. Explain, and give three fixes ranked by preference.

Solution

Wait — check the premise first. With padding: 1rem on the card, this should not happen: §6.7 measured that a single pixel of padding on the block-start side is enough to stop the top collapse. So either the padding is on the inline axis only (padding-inline: 1rem), or a padding: 0 is winning the cascade for the block axis. That is worth establishing before fixing anything, because it changes which fix is correct.

Assuming the block-start padding really is zero, here is the mechanism.

§6.6 case two: parent and first child. When nothing separates a parent's top border edge from its first child's top margin — no padding, no border, no new block formatting context — the two margins are adjoining and collapse into one, which becomes the parent's margin. The heading's margin is therefore outside the card, and the card's background starts below it, because backgrounds paint to the padding box and a margin is outside that.

Measured on exactly this shape: a parent whose only child had margin-block: 40px came out 18px tall — the line box alone, with both 40px margins escaped.

Fix 1 — display: flow-root on the card. Preferred.

.card { display: flow-root; }

It creates a new block formatting context, whose defining job is to contain its contents' margins and floats. Measured: the same parent became 98px — 40 + 18 + 40, both margins inside. It has no other visual effect at all, which is what distinguishes it from every alternative.

Fix 2 — give the card block padding. Usually what the design wanted anyway.

.card { padding: 1rem; }

Caveat, and it is the instructive part: padding on one side fixes one side. Measured, a parent with only padding-block-start: 1px came out at 59px — 1 + 18 + 40 — with the top margin contained and the bottom margin still escaping. A half-fix here produces a half-symptom, which is why this bug so often gets reported twice.

Fix 3 — remove the margins and space with gap.

.card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 1rem; }
.card > :is(h1,h2,h3,p) { margin-block: 0; }

Margin collapsing does not exist in flex or grid layout, so this removes the category of bug rather than this instance. It is the most invasive change and the best long-term one for a component library.

Fixes I would not use, and why: overflow: hidden works but silently creates a scroll container (§6.13), which changes focus-scrolling behaviour and breaks position: sticky for descendants. padding-top: 0.05px is the same as fix 2 with the intent obscured. position: absolute or float both work by removing the element from flow, which is a large side effect for a margin problem.

2. A hero section uses .hero { aspect-ratio: 21 / 9 } and looks right on a wide screen. On a phone the section is far taller than 21:9 and the background image is stretched. Diagnose both symptoms.

Solution

Symptom one: the box is taller than its ratio. §6.11 measured this directly — a width: 200px; aspect-ratio: 16/9 box containing a 300px-tall child rendered at 200×300, not 200×112.5.

aspect-ratio sets a preferred size, and a block-level element's automatic minimum block size (min-height: auto) still lets its content push it out. On a wide screen the hero's text fits inside 21:9 and the ratio holds; on a phone the same text wraps to five lines, exceeds the ratio's height, and the box grows. Nothing is reported, because nothing is wrong — the ratio was a preference and the content outvoted it.

The fix depends on what should happen to the extra content:

/* let the box grow, but stop pretending it is ratio-controlled below a width */
.hero { aspect-ratio: 21 / 9; min-block-size: 60svh; }
@media (max-width: 40rem) { .hero { aspect-ratio: auto; } }

/* or: hold the ratio and deal with the overflow explicitly */
.hero { aspect-ratio: 21 / 9; min-block-size: 0; overflow: clip; }

The second form needs min-block-size: 0 as well as overflow, because it is the automatic minimum that is doing the overriding — and clip rather than hidden, so the hero does not become a scroll container that the browser can scroll when something inside it takes focus (§6.13).

An extreme aspect ratio on a narrow viewport is usually a design error rather than a CSS one: 21:9 of a 390px-wide phone is 167px tall, which cannot hold a headline and a button. Changing the ratio at a breakpoint — or dropping it entirely and letting content size the section — is the honest fix.

Symptom two: the background image is stretched. This is a separate defect with a separate cause. If the image is an <img>, its default object-fit is fill, which stretches the content to the box and ignores the natural ratio (§6.12). If it is a background-image, the equivalent default is background-size: auto, which does not stretch but does tile and crop unhelpfully.

.hero img { inline-size: 100%; block-size: 100%; object-fit: cover; object-position: 50% 30%; }
/* or */
.hero { background-size: cover; background-position: 50% 30%; }

cover preserves the ratio and crops the overflow, and object-position decides which part survives the crop — which matters more on a phone than anywhere else, because that is where the crop is most severe. Biasing towards the upper third is the usual choice for photographs with people in them.

Why the two symptoms appeared together: both are properties whose default is "distort or overflow rather than refuse", which is the same design principle as §1.5's silent recovery. CSS very rarely fails; it produces a result, and the job is to notice when that result is not the one you asked for.

3. Explain the difference between these four, and say which you would use for: a decorative shape that must not cause scrolling; a message list that scrolls; a <body> that must not scroll sideways; and a truncated single-line label.

overflow: hidden      overflow: clip      overflow: auto      overflow-x: hidden
Solution

The measured distinction. Four 100×50 boxes with a 300×200 child, scrollTop set to 50 and read back:

hidden   -> 50    IS a scroll container
clip     -> 0     is NOT
auto     -> 50    IS a scroll container
visible  -> 0     is NOT

hidden and clip look identical on screen — both cut the content off with no scrollbars — and differ entirely in whether the box is a scroll container. That single bit governs: whether script can scroll it, whether the browser will scroll it to reveal a focused descendant, whether position: sticky inside it sticks to it, whether scroll snapping applies, and whether a scroll-driven animation can measure it.

A decorative shape that must not cause scrolling → overflow: clip.

.blob-container { overflow: clip; }

hidden would work visually and would introduce a real bug: a keyboard user tabbing to a control positioned off-screen inside that container makes the browser scroll the container to reveal it, and the decoration lurches. clip cannot be scrolled, so it cannot lurch. Add overflow-clip-margin if the shape should be allowed to bleed a few pixels past the box before being cut.

A message list that scrolls → overflow: auto.

.messages { overflow: auto; overscroll-behavior: contain; }

auto shows scrollbars only when needed; scroll reserves them always, which is uglier but avoids a layout shift — and scrollbar-gutter: stable gets that benefit without permanent scrollbars, measured at 15px of reserved space. overscroll-behavior: contain stops the page behind from scrolling when the list hits its end, which is the fix for the classic modal-scroll-through.

A <body> that must not scroll sideways → overflow-x: clip, not hidden.

body { overflow-x: clip; }

This is the case where the distinction is most consequential, because of §6.14's coupling rule. Measured: setting overflow-x: hidden made overflow-y compute to auto — even when overflow-y: visible was written explicitly. So overflow-x: hidden on the body silently makes the body a vertical scroll container, and every position: sticky inside it stops working, because sticky positions relative to the nearest scroll container and that is now the body rather than the viewport. clip pairs legally with visible, so it suppresses the horizontal overflow without the side effect.

Better still: find what is overflowing. A horizontal scrollbar on <body> is nearly always one element wider than the viewport, and hiding it hides a real layout bug.

A truncated single-line label → overflow: hidden, as part of the three-declaration set.

.label { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }

All three are required: without nowrap the text wraps instead of overflowing, without overflow there is nothing for text-overflow to act on. hidden is conventional here and clip also works — the element is a single line of text with nothing focusable in it, so the scroll-container distinction has nothing to bite on. For multiple lines, the prefixed -webkit-box recipe in §12.11 is still what works; the standard line-clamp: property is specified but was measured unsupported.

SECTION 7

Normal Flow: Display, Formatting Contexts, Floats and Columns

Flex and grid get the attention, and they deserve it. But every page still begins in normal flow, every piece of running text is laid out by it, and most of the confusing behaviour people attribute to CSS in general is actually a property of flow: margins that collapse, a container with zero height, a mysterious four-pixel gap under an image, a <div> that will not sit next to a float.

None of these are quirks. They fall out of two ideas — the formatting context and the line box — and once you have those two, the rest of this section is consequences.

Everything below was measured.

7.1 Normal Flow

Normal flow is the default layout mode. Boxes are laid out one after another: block-level boxes stack down the block axis, one per line, filling the inline axis; inline-level boxes flow along the inline axis, wrapping into new lines when they run out of room.

That is the whole model, and everything else — floats, positioning, flex, grid — is a departure from it.

Two consequences are worth stating before anything else, because the rest of the section assumes them.

A block-level box fills the inline axis by default and takes exactly the block-axis space its content needs. That asymmetry is why width: auto and height: auto behave so differently: auto on the inline axis means "fill the containing block", and auto on the block axis means "be as tall as the content". Everything in §6.3 about a percentage height doing nothing follows from it.

An element is out-of-flow if it is floated or absolutely positioned, and only then. Being out-of-flow means the box takes no space in its parent's layout: the parent's height is computed as though it were not there, and its siblings lay out into the space it occupies. That is why a container of nothing but floats has zero height (§7.9, measured), and it is the single fact behind most "why has my container collapsed" questions.

Everything else is in flow, including position: relative elements — a relatively positioned box keeps its original space in the flow and merely paints at an offset, so its siblings do not move (§10.2). A block-level box and an inline-level box are both in flow; the difference between them is which axis they stack on, not whether they participate.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: block-level box and out-of-flow.

7.2 display, and the Two-Value Syntax

The display property is two properties wearing one name. Every box has an outer display type, which says how it behaves in its parent's layout, and an inner display type, which says how it lays out its own children.

The two-value display syntax makes this explicit:

.a { display: block flow; }        /* an ordinary block               */
.b { display: inline flow-root; }  /* an inline-block                 */
.c { display: block flex; }        /* a flex container, block-level   */
.d { display: inline grid; }       /* a grid container, inline-level  */

Measured, with what each computes to:

display: block            -> block
display: inline flow-root -> inline-block
display: inline-block     -> inline-block
display: flex             -> flex
display: block flex       -> flex
display: list-item        -> list-item
display: contents         -> contents
display: flow-root        -> flow-root

inline flow-root and inline-block are the same thing, and the browser serialises both to the legacy spelling. That equivalence is the single most useful thing the two-value syntax teaches: an inline-block is not a special box type, it is an inline-level box whose inside is a block formatting context. Similarly display: flex is shorthand for block flex — a block-level box whose children are laid out by the flex algorithm — which is why a flex container still occupies a full line.

The legacy single values all map onto pairs:

block
block flow
inline
inline flow
inline-block
inline flow-root
flow-root
block flow-root — a block-level BFC (§7.7)
list-item
block flow list-item — generates a ::marker
table-cell
An internal display type — §7.13

Note that list-item is a value you can set on anything. A <div> with display: list-item gets a ::marker, which is occasionally the right way to build a stepped list out of non-list markup — though §15.14 has a warning about what that does and does not do for a screen reader.

To have in hand before moving on: the display property, outer display type, inner display type and two-value display syntax.

7.3 Block-Level and Inline-Level Boxes

The difference is not cosmetic; it changes which properties do anything. Measured on identical <span>s given width: 200px; height: 100px; margin: 20px; padding: 10px:

inline:        rect = 56 x 37    marginTop=20px   paddingTop=10px
inline-block:  rect = 220 x 120  marginTop=20px   paddingTop=10px

The inline box ignored width and height entirely and sized itself to its text. But notice that margin-top and padding-top computed to their declared values — they are not discarded, they are applied and painted, they simply do not affect the height of the line. That is why padding on an inline element overlaps the lines above and below it rather than pushing them apart, which is the correct behaviour for something like a highlighted phrase running across two lines.

The rules in one place:

  • On an inline-level box: width, height, and the vertical margins have no effect on layout. Horizontal margins, all padding and all borders do apply, and vertical padding and borders paint without affecting line height.
  • On a block-level box: everything applies.
  • inline-block is the hybrid: it participates in a line like an inline box, and is sized like a block box. The measurement shows it honouring all four dimensions.

7.4 The Inline-Block Whitespace Gap

Inline-level boxes are separated by the whitespace in the source, because that whitespace is real text content. Measured with two 100px inline-blocks, once with a newline between the tags and once without:

<div class="o"><span>a</span>
<span>b</span></div>
<div class="o"><span>a</span><span>b</span></div>

with a newline:    left = 8, 112   -> a 4px gap
without:           left = 8, 108   -> no gap

Four pixels of gap that exist in the markup, not the stylesheet. At a 16px font size a collapsed run of whitespace renders as one space, and that space is about 4px wide.

This is the defining annoyance of inline-block layout, and the historical workarounds — font-size: 0 on the parent, HTML comments between the tags, negative margins — are all bad. The modern answer is not to use inline-block for layout. display: flex or display: grid with gap (§8.10) ignores whitespace between children entirely, which is one of the quiet reasons flex replaced inline-block so completely.

7.5 The Gap Under an Image

The same mechanism produces a different famous symptom. An <img> is an inline-level replaced element, so it sits on the baseline of its line — and a line box reserves room below the baseline for descenders. Measured, with a 100px-tall image in a <div>:

img { display: block }    -> div height = 100
img { display: inline }   -> div height = 104

Four pixels of red background under the image, from nowhere. There is no margin and no padding; the extra height is the line box's descender space.

Three fixes, in order of preference: img { display: block } when the image is not part of a run of text; img { vertical-align: middle } (or bottom) to remove the descender allowance; or line-height: 0 on the container. The first is the one to put in a reset:

img, svg, video, canvas { display: block; max-inline-size: 100%; }

7.6 display: none, visibility and display: contents

Three ways to make something not appear, and they differ in every respect that matters.

display: none
No box at all. Not in the render tree, takes no space, not in the accessibility tree, not focusable, and its descendants cannot be shown by any rule. Cannot be transitioned without allow-discrete (§14.6).
visibility: hidden
A box exists and reserves its space; it is simply not painted. Removed from the accessibility tree, not focusable — but a descendant can set visibility: visible and reappear, because the visibility property is inherited.
display: contents
The element's own box is removed; its children are laid out as if they were children of its parent. The element is still in the accessibility tree.

display: contents measured, on a wrapper inside a four-column grid:

<div class="g"><i>1</i><div class="wrap"><i>2</i><i>3</i></div><i>4</i></div>

wrap box = 0 x 0
children left edges: 8, 109, 210, 311

All four <i> elements landed on the four grid tracks, including the two inside the wrapper. The wrapper has no box at all, so its background, padding and border — all declared in the measurement — produced nothing.

That is display: contents' entire purpose: promoting grandchildren into a flex or grid container without changing the markup. Two cautions. Any box-level property on the element is silently lost, which is the measured result above. And historically browsers also removed such elements from the accessibility tree — that bug is fixed in current browsers, but the general rule holds: do not put display: contents on an element whose semantics matter, such as a <ul> or a <table>, because removing the box can still disturb the roles of its children.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the visibility property.

7.7 Formatting Contexts

A formatting context is a region with its own layout rules, inside which a set of boxes are laid out together and — critically — isolated from the boxes outside it.

A block formatting context is created by the root element, and by any element that is floated, absolutely positioned, an inline-block, a table cell, a flex or grid item, an element with overflow other than visible, an element with contain: layout — and, most usefully, display: flow-root, which exists to create one and do nothing else.

A BFC does three things, and all three are the answer to a common problem:
