It contains its floats. Measured, with a floated 100×60 child:

parent with no BFC:            height = 0
parent with display:flow-root: height = 60
parent with a clear:both child: height = 78

A float does not contribute to its parent's height, so a container of nothing but floats collapses to zero. This is the "clearfix" problem, and display: flow-root is the whole solution — the ::after { content: ""; clear: both } hack exists only because flow-root did not.

Its margins do not collapse with its children's. §6.7 measured this: flow-root on the parent brought a child's escaping 40px margins back inside.

It does not overlap outside floats. Measured, with a 100px-wide left float and a following block:

ordinary block:      left = 8    width = 400
display: flow-root:  left = 108  width = 300

The ordinary block's box is the full 400px and sits under the float — only its line boxes are shortened, which is what produces text wrapping around an image. The flow-root block is pushed aside entirely and narrowed. That is the mechanism behind every "media object" layout built before flexbox, and it is still the correct way to make a sidebar sit beside a float rather than under it.

An inline formatting context is what a block with only inline content establishes. Inside it, boxes are laid into line boxes, and the properties that govern it are line-height, vertical-align, text-align and white-space.

7.8 Line Boxes, Baselines and vertical-align

A line box is as tall as it needs to be to contain the inline boxes on it, aligned by their baselines. That is why an inline element with a larger font on one line makes that line taller, and why line-height on a container affects the spacing of every line inside it.

vertical-align: aligns an inline-level or table-cell box within its line. It is one of the most misunderstood properties in CSS, for one reason: it does not vertically centre things in a block. It has two entirely separate jobs:

  • On an inline-level or inline-block box, it aligns that box relative to the line's baseline: baseline (the default), top, middle, bottom, text-top, text-bottom, sub, super, a length, or a percentage of the line height.
  • On a table-cell box, it aligns the cell's content within the cell — and here middle really does centre vertically. Measured: display: table-cell; vertical-align: middle computed to middle and centres.

That second behaviour is why display: table-cell was the vertical-centring technique for a decade. Today it is align-content: center on a block, or a flex or grid container, and vertical-align is for what it was designed for: superscripts, aligning an icon with its label, and fixing §7.5's image gap.

7.9 Floats and clear

The float property takes an element out of normal flow, shifts it to one side of its containing block, and lets line boxes flow around it. That last clause is the whole point: floats were designed for exactly one thing, which is text wrapping around an image, and they are still the only tool that does it.

figure.pull { float: inline-start; margin-inline-end: 1rem; inline-size: 12rem; }

The clear property moves an element below any floats on the specified side: left, right, both, and the logical inline-start/inline-end. Measured, a container holding a 60px float plus a clear: both sibling came out 78px tall — the float's 60px plus the cleared line.

Everything else floats used to do has a better tool now:

  • Multi-column layouts → grid or flex.
  • Containing floats (clearfix) → display: flow-root.
  • Sitting a block beside a float → grid, or a BFC as measured in §7.7.

What survives is text wrap, plus one genuinely modern use: a float inside a <p> with shape-outside.

7.10 shape-outside

shape-outside: changes the shape that line boxes wrap around, from the float's rectangle to any basic shape or an image's alpha channel:

.pull {
  float: inline-start;
  inline-size: 120px; block-size: 120px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  shape-outside: circle(50%);
  shape-margin: 10px;
}

shape-outside: circle(50%)   shape-margin: 10px

border-radius makes the element round; shape-outside makes the text believe it. Both are needed, and forgetting the second is why a rounded pull-quote still has square text wrap. shape-margin: adds a gap between the shape and the text — the shape equivalent of a margin, which the element's own margin cannot express because the margin box is rectangular.

shape-outside only affects floats. It does nothing on a grid item, a flex item or a positioned element.

In summary, the vocabulary here is basic shape.

7.11 The Containing Block

Every box's percentages, and every positioned box's offsets, resolve against a containing block. Which box that is depends on position, and getting it wrong is the cause of most position: absolute surprises:

static / relative
The content box of the nearest block-level ancestor.
absolute
The padding box of the nearest positioned ancestor — §10.4.
fixed
The viewport — unless an ancestor has a transform, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, contain or will-change, in which case that ancestor takes over. §10.5.
the root
The initial containing block: a viewport-sized rectangle anchored at the document origin.

Note the padding-box/content-box difference in the first two rows. An absolutely positioned child with inset: 0 fills its positioned ancestor's padding box, so it covers the padding — which is usually what you want for an overlay and occasionally a surprise.

7.12 Anonymous Boxes

The box tree is not the element tree. When a block container holds a mix of inline and block content, the browser wraps the inline runs in anonymous block boxes so that the "all block or all inline" invariant holds:

<div>
  text before
  <p>a paragraph</p>
  text after
</div>

That <div> generates three block boxes: an anonymous one holding "text before", the <p>, and another anonymous one. You cannot select an anonymous box, style it, or give it a class — it inherits from its parent and that is all the control you have. It is why "why is this stray text not aligned with my paragraphs" has no CSS answer: wrap it in a real element.

The same machinery produces anonymous table boxes (§7.13) and anonymous flex and grid items around stray text inside a flex or grid container.

7.13 Table Layout

display: table and its family are a complete internal layout mode, and they are still the right answer for one thing: tabular data. (For layout, they are not — grid does everything they did, better.)

The internal display types are table, table-row, table-cell, table-row-group, table-header-group, table-footer-group, table-column, table-column-group and table-caption. Missing levels are filled in with anonymous boxes, which is why a table-cell with no table-row ancestor still works.

Four properties govern the appearance:

border-collapse: chooses between the two border models. Measured:

border-collapse: collapse   border-spacing reported as 2px (unused)
border-collapse: separate   border-spacing: 8px, honoured

Under separate, each cell has its own border and border-spacing: puts a gap between them; border-spacing has no effect at all under collapse, though it still computes to whatever you set. Under collapse, adjacent borders merge into one and a conflict-resolution algorithm picks the winner — which is why a border-bottom on a row can be overridden by a border-top on the next.

table-layout: is the one with real consequences. The default auto measures every cell's content before deciding column widths, so the table cannot be laid out until all of it has arrived, and a single long word can widen a column arbitrarily. fixed takes the widths from the first row (or from <col> elements) and ignores the rest. Measured on a 300px table whose second cell holds a long string:

table-layout: auto    cells = 16 / 89     (content-driven)
table-layout: fixed   cells = 150 / 150   (first row decides)

fixed is dramatically faster for large tables and is the only way to make a table's columns predictable. Pair it with word-break or text-overflow (§6.15) for the content that no longer fits.

caption-side: puts the <caption> above or below, and empty-cells: decides whether an empty cell's border is drawn under separate.

7.14 Multi-Column Layout

Multi-column layout, driven by the columns property and its longhands, flows a single block of content into several columns — the newspaper model, which no other layout mode in CSS does. Grid makes columns and places different items in them; multi-column takes one item and fragments it.

.article { column-count: 3; column-gap: 2rem; column-rule: 1px solid; }
.article { column-width: 20rem; }        /* or: as many as fit */

column-count: 3   column-gap: 20px   column-rule width: 1px
column-width: 120px on a 400px container -> about 3 columns
column-count
Exactly this many columns, whatever the width.
column-width
An ideal width; the browser fits as many as it can. This is the responsive one — it needs no media query.
columns
The shorthand for both. columns: 20rem 3 means "at most 3, each about 20rem".
column-gap, column-rule
The gutter and a line drawn in it. column-rule takes the same width/style/colour grammar as border — and needs a style, for §6.9's reason.
column-span
all makes a child break out across every column — a heading spanning the page.
column-fill
balance (the default) evens the columns out; auto fills each in turn.

The honest limitation: multi-column has no way to control the height of the flow other than the container's height, and a reader scrolling a multi-column region vertically has to scroll up again to read the next column. It is excellent for short, print-like passages and poor for a long article on a screen.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the columns property, column-count:, column-width: and column-gap:.

7.15 Fragmentation

Fragmentation is what happens when a box is split across column, page or region boundaries — and its properties are shared between multi-column and print (§13.17).

h2         { break-after: avoid; }
figure     { break-inside: avoid; }
.chapter   { break-before: page; }

break-before:, break-after: and break-inside: take auto, avoid, page, column, avoid-page, avoid-column and a few more. They replace the older page-break-* properties entirely; those are now defined as aliases and should not be written in new code.

The three that earn their place every time: break-inside: avoid on figures and cards so they are not split down the middle, break-after: avoid on headings so a heading is never the last thing in a column, and break-before: page for a print stylesheet's section boundaries.

Support is genuinely uneven — engines honour avoid as a strong hint rather than a guarantee, and they will break anyway rather than leave a column badly underfull. Write the declarations; do not build a layout that fails without them.

7.16 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • Normal flow stacks block-level boxes down and flows inline-level boxes along the line; floated and absolutely positioned boxes are out-of-flow.
  • The display property carries an outer display type and an inner display type; the two-value display syntax makes it explicit, and inline flow-root and inline-block are measurably the same thing.
  • On an inline box width and height do nothing and vertical margins do not affect layout — measured at 56×37 versus 220×120 for the inline-block.
  • Whitespace between inline-level boxes is real content: a newline between two inline-blocks produced a measured 4px gap, and an inline <img> added a measured 4px of descender space below it.
  • display: none removes the box and the accessibility node; the visibility property keeps the space and is inherited; display: contents removes only the element's own box — measured at 0×0 with its children promoted into the grid.
  • A formatting context isolates layout; a block formatting context contains floats (measured 0 → 60px), contains margins, and does not overlap outside floats (measured left 8 → 108) — and display: flow-root creates one with no other effect.
  • An inline formatting context lays boxes into line boxes aligned on the baseline; vertical-align: aligns within a line, and centres vertically only in a table-cell.
  • The float property takes a box out of flow and wraps line boxes around it; the clear property moves past it; shape-outside: and shape-margin: change the wrap shape and only work on floats.
  • A containing block is the content box of the nearest block ancestor, the padding box of the nearest positioned ancestor for absolute, and the initial containing block at the root.
  • Anonymous boxes are generated to keep the box tree consistent and cannot be selected or styled.
  • display: table and its internal display types still suit tabular data; border-collapse: chooses the border model, border-spacing: only applies under separate, and table-layout: fixed made a measured 150/150 split where auto gave 16/89.
  • Multi-column layout fragments one element into columns via columns:, column-count:, column-width:, column-gap:, column-rule:, column-span: and column-fill:.
  • Fragmentation is controlled by break-before:, break-after: and break-inside:, which supersede page-break-* and are honoured as strong hints.

The terms above, gathered: column-rule:, column-span: and column-fill:.

Exercises

1. A gallery renders four thumbnails as inline-block items with width: 25%. They wrap onto two lines, and there is a small gap under each image inside its frame. Explain both symptoms with the mechanism, and rewrite the layout.

Solution

Both symptoms are the same underlying fact: inline-level boxes live in an inline formatting context, where whitespace in the source is content and boxes sit on a baseline.

Why four 25% items do not fit on one line. Each item is exactly 25% of the container, so four of them are exactly 100% — with nothing left for the whitespace between them. But the newlines in the markup are real text, and §7.4 measured what they cost: two 100px inline-blocks separated by a newline sat at left = 8, 112, a 4px gap, where the same pair written with no whitespace sat at 8, 108. Three gaps of about 4px is 12px more than the container has, so the fourth item wraps.

This is why the historical fixes were all so unpleasant — font-size: 0 on the parent (which breaks any em inside it), HTML comments between the tags, or removing the newlines and accepting unreadable markup. None of them is a styling solution, because the problem is in the content.

Why there is a gap under each image. §7.5 measured it: a <div> containing a 100px image rendered at height = 100 when the image was display: block and at height = 104 when it was display: inline. An <img> is an inline-level replaced element, so it sits on the line's baseline, and the line box reserves space below the baseline for descenders. Those four pixels are the descender allowance, and they show up as the frame's background peeking out under the image.

The rewrite:

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(12rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
.gallery img { display: block; inline-size: 100%; block-size: auto; }

Both symptoms disappear, for different reasons. Grid ignores whitespace between children entirely — the anonymous boxes that would have held it are not generated — so the 25%-plus-gaps arithmetic never arises. And img { display: block } takes the image out of the inline formatting context, so there is no baseline and no descender space.

The repeat(auto-fill, minmax(12rem, 1fr)) is a bonus: the number of columns now follows the available width with no media query at all (§9.8), which the 25% version could not do.

Worth putting in the reset, because this class of bug recurs:

img, svg, video, canvas, iframe { display: block; max-inline-size: 100%; }

2. A card component has a floated icon and a body of text. The card's background has zero height, and a "read more" link that should sit under everything is instead beside the icon. Explain both, and give the one-declaration fix.

Solution

Both symptoms come from the same property of floats: a float is out of flow, so it does not contribute to its parent's height and it is not something following blocks avoid.

Zero height. Measured (§7.9): a container whose only child was a floated 100×60 box came out at height = 0. A float is removed from normal flow, so the parent's height calculation — which sums the in-flow children — has nothing to sum. The background paints over a zero-height box, which is why it appears to be missing entirely rather than merely short.

The link beside the icon. Measured (§7.7): an ordinary block following a 100px left float had left = 8, width = 400 — its box is the full container width and sits underneath the float. Only its line boxes are shortened to avoid the float, which is exactly the text-wrap behaviour floats exist for. So the link's box starts at the container's left edge, and its text is pushed right by the float, giving the appearance of sitting beside the icon.

The one-declaration fix:

.card { display: flow-root; }

flow-root creates a block formatting context, and a BFC contains its floats. Measured: the same zero-height container became 60px tall. The card's background now covers its contents, and the float is enclosed rather than overflowing into whatever follows.

Why not the alternatives:

  • overflow: hidden also creates a BFC and is what most stylesheets historically used — but §6.13 measured that it makes the element a scroll container, which changes focus-scrolling behaviour, breaks position: sticky for descendants, and clips anything you later want to overflow (a dropdown, a focus ring, a tooltip).
  • A clearfix pseudo-element (.card::after { content: ""; display: block; clear: both }) works and was the standard answer for a decade. It exists only because flow-root did not, and it costs you the ::after pseudo-element on every card.
  • clear: both on the link fixes the second symptom and not the first, which is the classic half-fix.

And the fix I would actually ship, because the float is doing no wrapping work here:

.card { display: grid; grid-template-columns: auto 1fr; gap: 1rem; }
.card__icon { grid-row: span 2; }

Floats have exactly one job left in modern CSS — running text around a shape (§7.10) — and an icon beside a block of text is not that job. If the text is genuinely meant to wrap around the icon and continue underneath it, keep the float and add display: flow-root.

3. Explain why display: contents on a <div> wrapping two grid items works, why it silently discards that <div>'s background and padding, and give a case where you should not use it.

Solution

Why it works. Grid and flex only lay out their direct children. A wrapper <div> between the container and the items makes the wrapper the grid item and the real content its descendants, so the items no longer participate in the grid — a very common problem when markup structure is fixed by a template or a framework.

display: contents sets the element's outer display type to nothing: the element generates no box at all, and its children are laid out as though they were children of its parent. Measured on a four-column grid with two of the four items inside a display: contents wrapper:

wrap box = 0 x 0
children left edges: 8, 109, 210, 311

All four landed on the four tracks. The wrapper is still in the DOM, still in the accessibility tree, still selectable — it just has no box.

Why the background and padding vanish. They have nothing to paint on. background, padding, border, box-shadow, width, overflow, transform — every property that describes a box — requires a box, and there is not one. Measured: the wrapper's declared background: red; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid produced a 0 x 0 rect and no visible output. Nothing is reported; the declarations are valid, they simply have no subject. This is a §1.5-adjacent failure: not an invalid declaration, but a valid one with nowhere to apply.

The consequence for authoring: an element with display: contents cannot be a visual grouping. If you need a background behind those two items, you need a real box — which means either grid-column: span 2 on a real wrapper that is itself a grid, or subgrid (§9.13), which is the feature designed for exactly this and does not throw the box away.

Where not to use it. On any element whose box or semantics are load-bearing:

  • A <ul>, <ol> or <table>. Removing the box can disturb the roles of the children — a <li> whose <ul> has no box may lose its listitem role in some engines, and a table stripped of its box loses the grid semantics entirely. §15.14 covers the related list-style: none case, which has the same shape.
  • A focusable element, or one carrying a role that assistive technology navigates by. The element remains in the tree, but anything about it that was communicated by its geometry — a focus ring, a target size (§15.10) — is gone.
  • Anything you might later want to animate, transform or give a background to. The failure mode is silent, and it appears months later when someone adds a hover state.

The safe use is exactly the measured one: an inert structural wrapper — a <div> or a <span> with no role, no semantics and no visual treatment — that exists only because a template put it there.

SECTION 8

Flexbox

Flexbox lays out boxes in one dimension and distributes the space left over. That is its whole job, and it is worth being precise about it, because the most common source of flexbox frustration is asking it to do two-dimensional work that grid does better.

The mental model that makes it click is not "a row of things". It is: every flex item starts at a hypothetical size, then grows or shrinks to consume or relieve the free space, and the alignment properties decide what happens to whatever is still left over. Once you can say what the free space is at each step, the behaviour stops being surprising.

Everything below was measured in Chromium.

8.1 The Container, the Items and the Two Axes

display: flex makes an element a flex container; its direct children become flex items. Grandchildren are not items, and text directly inside the container is wrapped in an anonymous flex item (§7.12).

Two axes, and every flexbox property names one of them:

main axis
The direction items are laid along, set by flex-direction. Sizes along it are main size; justify-* properties act on it.
cross axis
Perpendicular to the main axis. Sizes along it are cross size; align-* properties act on it.

The mapping is worth memorising in this form, because it is the thing that stops you guessing: justify- is always the main axis, align- is always the cross axis. In a default row, justify-content is horizontal and align-items is vertical; set flex-direction: column and they swap. Nothing else about the properties changes.

One line each, for reference: main size and cross size.

8.2 flex-direction, flex-wrap and flex-flow

flex-direction: takes row (the default), row-reverse, column, column-reverse. Note that row follows the writing mode's inline direction, so it is right-to-left in an Arabic or Hebrew page automatically — which is one of the reasons flexbox is preferable to floats in an internationalised interface (§15.5).

flex-wrap: takes nowrap (the default), wrap, wrap-reverse. The default is the one that surprises: flex items do not wrap unless you ask, so a row that runs out of room shrinks its items rather than moving one to a second line.

flex-flow: is the shorthand for both: flex-flow: row wrap.

Once items wrap, each row is a flex line, and a container with more than one line behaves differently in one important respect — see §8.9.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: flex line.

8.3 flex-basis, and What It Beats

flex-basis: is an item's size along the main axis before growing or shrinking. Its default is auto, which means "look at width (or height in a column) and, if that is also auto, use the content size".

When both are specified, flex-basis wins. Measured:

.f { display: flex; width: 600px; }
.a { width: 100px; flex-basis: 300px; flex-grow: 0; flex-shrink: 0; }

width = 300

The width: 100px was ignored entirely. This is worth knowing because it explains the otherwise baffling case where changing width on a flex item does nothing: something set flex-basis, very often the flex: 1 shorthand (§8.5).

flex-basis: 0 deserves its own note. It means "this item's hypothetical size is zero", so all the container's space is free space and gets distributed by flex-grow — which is what makes equal columns equal regardless of content.

8.4 flex-grow and flex-shrink

flex-grow: distributes positive free space; flex-shrink: distributes negative free space. Only one of them is ever active at a time, and which one depends on whether the items' bases add up to less or more than the container.

flex-grow is a simple proportion: with items at 1, 2 and 1, the leftover space is split into four parts and handed out 1:2:1.

flex-shrink is weighted by each item's basis, which is not obvious and is measurable:

.f { display: flex; width: 300px; }
.a { flex: 0 1 200px; }
.b { flex: 0 1 400px; }

a = 100.00    b = 200.00

The bases total 600px in a 300px container, so 300px of overflow must be removed. Both items have flex-shrink: 1, but they did not lose 150px each: .a lost 100 and .b lost 200, in proportion to their bases. The reasoning is sound — shrinking a 400px item by 200px is proportionally the same injury as shrinking a 200px item by 100px — and the practical consequence is that two items with equal flex-shrink do not shrink equally unless their bases are equal.

8.5 The flex Shorthand, and flex: 1 versus flex: auto

flex: sets all three at once, and its expansions are not what the words suggest. Measured:

flex: 1     ->  flex-grow: 1   flex-shrink: 1   flex-basis: 0%
flex: auto  ->  flex-grow: 1   flex-shrink: 1   flex-basis: auto
flex: none  ->  flex-grow: 0   flex-shrink: 0   flex-basis: auto

The flex: 1 case is the one that matters: a bare number sets flex-basis to 0, not to auto. That single difference changes the layout completely, and here it is with the same two items of very different content lengths in a 600px container:

flex: 1     ->  300 / 300
flex: auto  ->  162 / 438

flex: 1 gives equal columns: every item's basis is zero, so the entire 600px is free space and is split evenly. flex: auto gives content-proportional columns: each item starts at its content width and the leftover is split evenly on top, so the item with more text stays wider.

Both are useful, and choosing between them is the most frequent real decision in flexbox:

  • flex: 1 for a set of things that should be the same size — equal-width cards, a toolbar of equal buttons.
  • flex: auto for things that should be sized by their content and then share the slack — navigation items, a label-and-value pair.
  • flex: none for something that must not resize at all — an icon, a fixed-width sidebar.
  • flex: 0 0 20rem for an explicit fixed track. This is the honest spelling of a sidebar.

Always write flex rather than the three longhands. The shorthand sets all three, so a stray flex-grow: 1 written later without a basis produces exactly the confusion above (§3.12 has the general rule).

8.6 The Automatic Minimum Size

This is the single most-reported flexbox problem and it has a one-declaration fix.

A flex item's min-width (or min-height in a column) defaults to auto, and auto there means "the item's min-content size" — not zero. So an item cannot shrink below the width of its longest unbreakable word, however aggressive its flex-shrink. Measured, with a long word in the first of two flex: 1 items in a 300px container:

.f { display: flex; width: 300px; }
.f > div { flex: 1; }

default:        items = 215 / 85
min-width: 0:   items = 150 / 150

With the default, "Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious" forced its item to 215px and squeezed its sibling into 85px. With min-width: 0 the two items are the 150/150 that flex: 1 promised.

The symptom takes several forms and they all have this cause: a flex item that overflows its container; two flex: 1 items that are not equal; text-overflow: ellipsis that never appears; a <pre> or a long URL that blows out a layout.

.f > * { min-inline-size: 0; }     /* the fix, in logical terms */

One measured refinement worth knowing: an item with overflow other than visible already has an automatic minimum of zero. In the truncation test above, adding min-width: 0 changed nothing, because overflow: hidden had already zeroed it. That is why text-overflow: ellipsis sometimes works without the fix and sometimes does not — it depends on where the overflow declaration sits relative to the flex item.

8.7 justify-content — the Main Axis

Distributes leftover main-axis space. The three "space" values differ in where the space goes, and the measured numbers make it obvious. Three 60px items in a 400px container — 220px of free space, item left offsets relative to the container:

space-between:   0,   170,  340
space-around:    37,  170,  303
space-evenly:    55,  170,  285
space-between
All the space between items, none at the ends. 220 ÷ 2 = 110 per gap.
space-around
Each item gets equal space on both sides, so the end gaps are half the inner ones. 220 ÷ 6 = 36.67 at the ends, 73.3 between.
space-evenly
Every gap equal, including the ends. 220 ÷ 4 = 55.

The other values are flex-start, flex-end, center, start, end, left and right. Prefer start/end (the box-alignment spellings) over flex-start/flex-end: they mean the same thing in flexbox and they also work in grid and block layout, so one habit covers all three.

8.8 align-items and align-self — the Cross Axis

align-items: sets the default cross-axis alignment for every item; align-self: overrides it on one.

The default is stretch, which is why flex items in a row are all as tall as the tallest — and why equal-height cards are free in flexbox and were a genuine problem before it. The others are flex-start, flex-end, center, start, end, and baseline.

Baseline alignment lines up the items' first text baselines rather than their box edges. Measured with a 16px item and a 32px item side by side:

"small" top = 23      "BIG" top = 8

The boxes start at different heights precisely so that the text sits on one line. This is what you want for a label beside a large number, or a row of headings with mixed sizes, and it is invisible until you compare it with center, which lines up the boxes and leaves the text looking wrong.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: align-items:, align-self: and baseline alignment.

8.9 align-content — and Why It Often Does Nothing

align-content: distributes space between flex lines on the cross axis. It takes the same values as justify-content, plus stretch.

The catch, measured on a 200px-tall container with a single 40px item and align-content: center:

flex-wrap: nowrap  ->  child top offset = 0     (no effect)
flex-wrap: wrap    ->  child top offset = 80    (centred)

align-content has no effect on a single-line flex container. With nowrap there is only one line, and there is nothing to distribute. This is a frequent "why is align-content: center not working" — and the answer is almost always align-items: center, which aligns items within a line rather than lines within a container.

The two are easy to keep straight once stated: align-items positions items in their line; align-content positions the lines in the container. In a single-line container only the first exists.

8.10 gap

The gap property — with row-gap: and column-gap: as its longhands — puts space between items and not around them. It is a much better tool than margins for the job:

.toolbar { display: flex; gap: 0.5rem; }

Three reasons it wins over margin-inline-end plus a :last-child reset. It adds no space at the container's edges, so no reset is needed. It survives flex-wrap, adding the row gap between wrapped lines too, which margins do not. And it composes with justify-content: gap is subtracted from the free space first, and whatever remains is distributed — so space-between with a gap gives you a guaranteed minimum separation.

gap also removes §7.4's whitespace problem entirely: the space between flex items comes from the property, not from the newlines in the markup.

To have in hand before moving on: the gap property and row-gap:.

8.11 order, and Why to Be Careful

The order property takes an integer (default 0) and re-sorts items visually. Measured on two items given order: 2 and order: 1:

"1"@76   "2"@8

The visual order is reversed while the DOM order is unchanged.

That last clause is the problem. order changes the paint order and not the reading order, the focus order, or the order a screen reader announces. A keyboard user tabbing through the reordered row above moves right to left, which is disorienting and is a WCAG 2.4.3 failure when the visual order implies a meaning.

The rules to work by:

  • Use order for purely visual rearrangement of equivalent items — a media object whose image moves from left to right at a breakpoint, where nothing depends on sequence.
  • Never use it to fix a markup ordering problem. Fix the markup, or use grid placement, which has the same hazard but at least makes the intent explicit.
  • reading-flow: is the fix that is arriving, and §15.8 covers it: it lets a container declare that the accessibility and focus order should follow the visual order rather than the DOM order. Its support is currently Chromium-only.
  • flex-direction: row-reverse and column-reverse carry exactly the same hazard and the same guidance.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the order property and reading-flow:.

8.12 Auto Margins in Flex

§6.5 measured that an auto margin absorbs free space. In a flex container this becomes one of the most useful tools available, because it works on both axes — unlike normal flow, where block-axis auto margins compute to zero.

Measured, with a third item given margin-inline-start: auto in a 400px row:

a@8   b@76   c@348

The third item was pushed to the far end while the first two stayed together. That is a common navigation layout — logo, links, then a right-aligned account menu — and doing it with justify-content would require splitting the children into two wrapper elements.

.nav        { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
.nav .push  { margin-inline-start: auto; }

Two more idioms from the same mechanism: margin-block: auto on a flex item centres it vertically in its line, and margin: auto on a single flex item centres it in both directions — which is the shortest true centring in CSS.

An auto margin consumes the free space before justify-content sees it, so the two do not compose: if any item has an auto margin on the main axis, justify-content has nothing left to distribute.

8.13 The Box Alignment Shorthands

justify-content, align-content, align-items and justify-items come from the box alignment specification, which is shared between flexbox, grid and block layout. That sharing is why the same keyword vocabulary appears everywhere and why learning it once pays three times.

Two shorthands: place-content: sets align-content then justify-content, and place-items: sets align-items then justify-items. place-self: does the same for align-self and justify-self. Measured:

.g { place-content: center start; place-items: end center; }

alignContent=center   justifyContent=start
alignItems=end        justifyItems=center

Note the order: block axis first, then inline axis — the same order as margin: <block> <inline> in the two-value form. A single value sets both.

One flexbox-specific gap: justify-items and justify-self do nothing in a flex container. There is no per-item main-axis alignment in flexbox, because the main axis is where sizing happens; the auto-margin technique in §8.12 is what fills that role. In grid they both work (§9.16).

Safe alignment is the last piece: align-items: safe center falls back to start when centring would push content out of the container where it cannot be scrolled to. Centred content that overflows is clipped at both ends and the beginning becomes unreachable, which is the one alignment bug that loses data rather than just looking wrong.

In summary, the vocabulary here is place-content:, place-items: and place-self:.

8.14 When to Use Flexbox and When to Use Grid

The honest rule is about which dimension you are controlling, and it decides correctly nearly every time:

Flexbox
The content should decide the sizes, and you are arranging along one axis. A toolbar, a navigation bar, a row of tags, a label beside a control, a card's footer. Items are sized by what is in them.
Grid
The layout should decide the sizes, or you need both axes at once. A page skeleton, a card gallery, a form with aligned labels, anything where things must line up across rows.

The give-away that you have chosen wrong is a flex container full of percentage widths and calc() subtracting gaps. That arithmetic is what grid-template-columns does for you, and §9 is next.

They compose freely: a grid page skeleton whose header is a flex row is the normal arrangement, not a compromise.

8.15 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • Flexbox lays out along one axis; display: flex makes a flex container and its direct children flex items.
  • Main axis and cross axis are set by flex-direction:; justify-* acts on the main axis and align-* on the cross axis, and main size and cross size name the two dimensions.
  • flex-wrap: defaults to nowrap, so items shrink rather than wrapping; each wrapped row is a flex line, and flex-flow: is the shorthand for direction plus wrap.
  • flex-basis: is the pre-growth size and beats width — measured at 300px over a declared 100px.
  • flex-grow: splits positive free space proportionally; flex-shrink: splits negative free space weighted by basis — measured at 100/200, not 150/150.
  • flex: expands 1 to 1 1 0% and auto to 1 1 auto, which measured as 300/300 versus 162/438 — equal columns versus content-proportional ones.
  • A flex item's automatic min-width: auto is its min-content size, measured at 215/85 until min-width: 0 restored 150/150; overflow other than visible already zeroes it.
  • justify-content: measured space-between at 0/170/340, space-around at 37/170/303 and space-evenly at 55/170/285.
  • align-items: defaults to stretch, which is why equal-height cards are free; baseline alignment lines up text rather than boxes, measured at tops of 23 and 8.
  • align-content: distributes lines and therefore does nothing with flex-wrap: nowrap — measured as an offset of 0 versus 80.
  • The gap property, with row-gap: and column-gap:, spaces items without edge space, survives wrapping, and is subtracted before justify-content distributes.
  • The order property changes visual order only — measured — and leaves focus and reading order untouched, which is a WCAG failure unless the items are genuinely equivalent.
  • Auto margins absorb main- and cross-axis free space in flex, measured pushing an item to 348, and pre-empt justify-content.
  • Box alignment is shared with grid: place-content:, place-items: and place-self: take block-then-inline, justify-items:/justify-self: do nothing in flex, and safe alignment prevents unreachable overflow.
  • Choose flexbox when content decides the sizes on one axis and grid when the layout decides them or you need both axes.

What to carry forward from this subsection: min-width: auto, justify-items: and justify-self:.

Exercises

1. A navigation bar has a logo, five links and a "Sign in" button. The button should sit hard against the right edge and the links should stay grouped next to the logo. Write it two ways — with and without extra wrapper elements — and say which you would ship.

Solution

Without wrappers, using an auto margin:

.nav       { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1rem; }
.nav .signin { margin-inline-start: auto; }

<nav class="nav">
  <a class="logo" href="/">Acme</a>
  <a href="/a">Products</a> <a href="/b">Pricing</a> <a href="/c">Docs</a>
  <a href="/d">Blog</a> <a href="/e">About</a>
  <a class="signin" href="/in">Sign in</a>
</nav>

§8.12 measured exactly this: a third item given margin-inline-start: auto in a 400px row landed at 348 while its siblings stayed at 8 and 76. The auto margin absorbs all the free space, so everything before it stays packed at the start and the button is pushed to the end.

With a wrapper, using justify-content:

.nav       { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; }
.nav__left { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1rem; }

<nav class="nav">
  <div class="nav__left"><a class="logo" href="/">Acme</a> … </div>
  <a class="signin" href="/in">Sign in</a>
</nav>

Which I would ship: the auto-margin version. Three reasons.

It needs no extra element, so the markup describes the navigation rather than the layout — and a <div> that exists only to be a flex parent is exactly the kind of thing that later needs display: contents to undo (§7.6).

It degrades better. If a sixth link is added, the auto-margin version simply has less free space to absorb and everything still works; the wrapper version is unaffected too, but the wrapper has to be maintained as the markup changes.

And it composes with gap correctly. gap: 1rem applies uniformly between every item including across the auto margin, so the button never ends up closer than 1rem to the last link on a narrow screen.

The one thing to watch, and it is worth stating because it surprises people: §8.12's measurement also implies that justify-content becomes inert once any item has a main-axis auto margin. There is no free space left for it to distribute. So you cannot combine margin-inline-start: auto with justify-content: center and expect both to act — the margin wins.

For the narrow-screen version, add flex-wrap: wrap and the auto margin still behaves, because it absorbs the free space on whichever line the button lands on.

2. Two sibling panels are given flex: 1 each. They render at unequal widths, and the left one overflows its container when it contains a long URL. Diagnose both, then explain when flex: 1 and flex: auto are each the right choice.

Solution

Both symptoms are §8.6's automatic minimum size.

A flex item's min-width defaults to auto, and in a flex item auto resolves to the item's min-content size — the width of its longest unbreakable run. A long URL has no break opportunity, so its min-content size is the whole URL, and flex-shrink cannot take the item below it however much overflow there is.

Measured with a 34-character unbreakable word in the first of two flex: 1 items in a 300px container:

default:        items = 215 / 85
min-width: 0:   items = 150 / 150

So the "unequal widths" and the "overflow" are one defect seen twice: the item is being held at 215px by its content, its sibling gets the 85px remainder instead of the promised 150, and when the content is longer than the container the item pushes past the edge.

The fix:

.panels > * { min-inline-size: 0; }

And for the URL itself, so it does not merely overflow silently once the item can shrink:

.panels .url { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }   /* or: text-overflow: ellipsis + overflow: hidden */

A measured refinement: an item that already has overflow other than visible has an automatic minimum of zero already, which is why the same layout sometimes appears to work. In a test where the item carried overflow: hidden for truncation, adding min-width: 0 changed nothing.

flex: 1 versus flex: auto. §8.5 measured them on two items with very different content in a 600px container:

flex: 1     ->  300 / 300      (equal)
flex: auto  ->  162 / 438      (content-proportional)

The difference is entirely in flex-basis: flex: 1 expands to 1 1 0% and flex: auto to 1 1 auto.

  • flex: 1 when the items should be the same size regardless of content: a two-panel split, a row of equal cards, columns in a dashboard. The basis of zero makes the whole container free space, so the split is even by construction.
  • flex: auto when content should set the proportions and the leftover should be shared: navigation items where a longer label deserves a wider hit area, a label-and-value pair, a row of tags.
  • flex: none for anything that must not resize — an avatar, an icon button.
  • flex: 0 0 20rem for a fixed sidebar, which is the honest spelling of that intent and much clearer than width: 20rem on an item whose flex-basis might be set elsewhere (§8.3 measured flex-basis beating width).

3. A designer asks for a card grid: three equal columns on desktop, two on tablet, one on mobile, with a 1.5rem gutter and all cards the same height per row. Write it in flexbox, then in grid, and say which is correct and why.

Solution

In flexbox:

.cards {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1.5rem;
}
.cards > * {
  flex: 1 1 calc((100% - 3rem) / 3);
  min-inline-size: 0;
}
@media (max-width: 60rem) { .cards > * { flex-basis: calc((100% - 1.5rem) / 2); } }
@media (max-width: 40rem) { .cards > * { flex-basis: 100%; } }

In grid:

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(18rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

Grid is correct, and the flex version demonstrates why.

The arithmetic is the tell. calc((100% - 3rem) / 3) is the developer computing what the gutters cost so the basis comes out right — and it has to be recomputed at every breakpoint, because the number of gaps changes with the number of columns. Two gaps at three columns, one at two, none at one. §8.14's rule names exactly this smell: a flex container full of percentages and calc() subtracting gaps is a grid that has not been written yet. grid-template-columns does that arithmetic itself, because 1fr means "a share of what is left after the gaps".

The equal-height-per-row requirement is a two-dimensional one. Flexbox stretches items within a flex line, so cards on the same wrapped row do come out equal — that part works. But nothing in flexbox relates one line to another, so a card's internal parts (a title, a body, a footer) will not line up across rows. Grid rows are shared structure, and with subgrid (§9.13) the internal parts line up too:

.cards > * { display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-row: span 3; }

That is not expressible in flexbox at all.

The breakpoints disappear. repeat(auto-fill, minmax(18rem, 1fr)) fits as many 18rem-minimum columns as the space allows and stretches them to fill — three on a wide screen, two on a tablet, one on a phone, with no media queries and no maintenance. It also responds to the container rather than the viewport if you pair it with a container query (§13.11), which the media-query version fundamentally cannot.

When the flex version would be right after all: if the last row should have its items stretch to fill the leftover space rather than leaving a gap — a tag cloud, a photo strip — flexbox's flex-grow does that naturally and grid's auto-fill deliberately does not. That is a real difference in intent, and it is the one case where the flex answer is the better answer. auto-fit (§9.8) is the middle ground.

SECTION 9

Grid

Grid layout is the first thing in CSS that lets you describe a layout as a layout. Before it, every two-dimensional arrangement was an emergent property of one-dimensional rules — floats that happened to line up, percentage widths that happened to add to 100, tables pressed into service. Grid replaces all of that with a declaration of the structure itself, into which items are placed.

The consequence is that grid stylesheets are shorter and, more importantly, that they say what they mean. grid-template-areas is the only construct in CSS you can hand to a designer and have them read.

This section covers the model, the seven ways to size a track, the four ways to place an item, and subgrid — which is the piece that makes nested components line up and which nothing before it could do. Everything below was measured.

9.1 The Model: Lines, Tracks, Cells and Areas

display: grid makes an element a grid container and its direct children grid items. The container defines a set of grid lines; the space between two adjacent lines is a grid track (a row or a column); the intersection of a row track and a column track is a grid cell; and a rectangle of one or more cells is a grid area.

grid line
Numbered from 1 at the start, and from −1 at the end. A three-column grid has four column lines: 1, 2, 3, 4 — which are also −4, −3, −2, −1.
grid track
A row or a column. Everything in §9.5–§9.9 is about sizing these.
grid cell
One row × one column. The smallest unit an item can occupy.
grid area
Any rectangle of cells, bounded by four lines. Items occupy areas.

Items are placed against lines, not into cells. That is the single idea that makes the placement properties in §9.10 make sense: grid-column: 2 / 4 means "from line 2 to line 4", which is two columns wide, not two-to-four.

Grid comes in two halves. The explicit grid is what you declare with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. The implicit grid is the tracks the browser creates automatically when items land outside the explicit one, and it is sized by grid-auto-columns and grid-auto-rows. Most real grids use both, and a great many "why is that row the wrong height" questions are about implicit tracks nobody declared.

9.2 Declaring Tracks

grid-template-columns: and grid-template-rows: take a list of track sizes:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 200px;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  gap: 1rem;
}

Any length, percentage, auto, min-content, max-content, fr, minmax() or fit-content() may appear, and they may be mixed freely. Measured on a 400px container, the resolved tracks:

minmax(100px, 1fr) 2fr        ->  133.328px  266.672px
auto 1fr                      ->   89.7656px 310.234px
min-content max-content 1fr   ->   64.8906px 100.891px 234.219px
fit-content(80px) 1fr         ->   80px      320px

Read the third line against §6.10: min-content gave the longest word, max-content gave the untruncated string, and 1fr took what was left. And note the fourth: fit-content() — the function — does work here, unlike on width, where §6.10 measured it being discarded. It means "max-content, but capped at this size", which is the natural way to say "as wide as the label needs, up to 80px".

9.3 repeat()

repeat() replaces a hand-written list:

grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 100px 1fr);   /* the pattern repeats  */
grid-template-columns: 200px repeat(2, 1fr) 200px;  /* and composes    */

Its first argument may also be auto-fill or auto-fit, which is where it becomes genuinely powerful — §9.8.

9.4 minmax() and fr

minmax(min, max) gives a track a floor and a ceiling. The min may not be an fr; the max may.

The fr unit is a fraction of the leftover space — the space remaining after every fixed-size track, every gap and every content-sized track has taken what it needs. That is why 1fr is not 33.33% in a three-column grid with gaps: the percentage would be of the whole container and would overflow by the width of the gaps, while 1fr accounts for them automatically. This is the arithmetic §8.14 said grid does for you.

An fr track has an implicit minimum of auto, and that is a trap. 1fr is exactly minmax(auto, 1fr), so the track will not shrink below its content's minimum size — the grid analogue of §8.6. Measured, with an unbreakable 20-character word in the first of two tracks in a 200px grid:

1fr 1fr                        ->  122.953px  77.0469px
minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(0, 1fr)  ->  100px      100px

minmax(0, 1fr) is the spelling that means "genuinely equal". Reach for it whenever a grid track must be a fixed share regardless of content — which, in a layout with text or images in it, is most of the time.

9.5 auto, min-content, max-content and fit-content()

The content-based track sizes, with what each is for:

auto
As large as its content needs, and it stretches to absorb leftover space when there is no fr track to take it. This last part distinguishes it from max-content.
min-content
The narrowest without overflow. Measured at 64.89px for "hello wonderful".
max-content
No wrapping at all. Measured at 100.89px for the same content.
fit-content(N)
max-content capped at N. Measured at exactly 80px for fit-content(80px).

Those four are intrinsic track sizing: the track is measured from what is in it rather than from a number you chose. auto is the right default for a track whose content sets its size — a label column, a sidebar of navigation links. Pair it with an fr track and you get "this one is as wide as it needs, the other takes the rest", which is one of the two or three most useful two-track layouts there is.

The terms above, gathered: intrinsic track sizing.

9.6 Gaps

The gap property works identically to flexbox's (§8.10), with row-gap: and column-gap: as longhands. In grid it is even more clearly correct than in flex, because fr accounts for gaps when distributing space — so adding a gap never causes an overflow.

The old grid-gap spelling is a deprecated alias. Write gap.

9.7 Named Lines

A track list may carry named grid lines in square brackets, and a name may sit on the same line as another:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns:
    [full-start] 1fr
    [main-start] 2fr
    [main-end] 1fr
    [full-end];
}
.hero { grid-column: full-start / full-end; }
.body { grid-column: main-start / main-end; }

Measured, the resolved tracks with their names, and where the items landed in a 400px container:

cols = [full-start] 97.5px [main-start] 195px [main-end] 97.5px [full-end]
items: hero x=0 w=400 | body x=103 w=195

Named lines are the difference between a layout you can read and one you have to count. grid-column: 2 / 3 requires the reader to reconstruct the track list in their head; grid-column: main-start / main-end does not, and it survives someone inserting a track.

A convention worth adopting: name lines in -start/-end pairs. It is not merely tidy — a pair named foo-start and foo-end creates an implicit grid area called foo, so grid-area: foo then works.

One line each, for reference: grid-area: and named grid line.

9.8 auto-fill and auto-fit

Passing auto-fill or auto-fit to repeat() lets the browser decide how many tracks fit. This is the single most valuable line in grid, because it is a responsive layout with no media query:

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(150px, 1fr));
  gap: 10px;
}

The two keywords differ only when there are fewer items than tracks, and the difference is stark. Measured, two items in a 600px container:

auto-fill:  tracks = 193.328px 193.328px 193.328px   items = 193 / 193
auto-fit:   tracks = 295px     295px     0px         items = 295 / 295

auto-fill keeps the empty track. Three tracks were created, two were filled, and the third sits there at full width — so the items stay at their "natural" grid size and the row is left-aligned with a hole at the end.

auto-fit collapses the empty track to zero, and the 1fr maximum then distributes its space to the surviving tracks — so two items stretch to fill the whole row.

Which you want is a design decision, not a technical one:

  • auto-fill when items should keep a consistent size across pages, so a page with two cards shows them at the same width as a page with eight.
  • auto-fit when items should always fill the row, so a two-item row shows two wide cards rather than two normal cards and a gap.

Both are usually paired with minmax(), because repeat(auto-fill, 150px) gives fixed tracks and leaves a ragged remainder, while repeat(auto-fill, minmax(150px, 1fr)) gives "at least 150, then share the rest".

9.9 The Implicit Grid

Items placed outside the explicit grid — or simply more items than declared cells — create implicit tracks. They are auto-sized unless you say otherwise:

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  grid-auto-rows: minmax(120px, auto);   /* every implicit row */
  gap: 1rem;
}

grid-auto-rows: and grid-auto-columns: size the implicit tracks. minmax(120px, auto) is the idiom worth remembering: a floor so short rows do not look collapsed, and auto so long ones still fit.

grid-auto-flow: decides how unplaced items are inserted: row (the default), column, and either plus dense.

Auto-placement normally works forwards only: once the algorithm has passed a position it never goes back, so a large item that does not fit leaves a hole. Dense packing changes that. Measured on a three-column grid holding a normal item, an item spanning all three columns, and two more normal items:

sparse:  1(c1,r1) 2(c1,r2) 3(c1,r3) 4(c2,r3)    container height = 124
dense:   1(c1,r1) 2(c1,r2) 3(c2,r1) 4(c3,r1)    container height = 82

Without dense the grid is three rows tall and row 1 has two empty cells. With it, items 3 and 4 went backwards into those cells and the grid is two rows tall.

The cost is stated in the specification and is worth taking seriously: dense packing disconnects visual order from DOM order, exactly as order does in flexbox (§8.11). Items 3 and 4 now appear before item 2 visually while following it in the document, so a keyboard user tabs in an order that does not match what they see. Use dense for content where sequence carries no meaning — a photo wall — and not for anything a reader is expected to work through.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: grid-auto-columns:, grid-auto-flow: and auto-placement.

9.10 Placing Items: Lines, Spans and Negative Numbers

grid-column: and grid-row: are shorthands for a start and an end line, separated by a slash. Four spellings, all measured on a four-column 400px grid:

.a { grid-column: 1 / -1; }      /* full width          */
.b { grid-column: 2 / span 2; }  /* from line 2, 2 wide */
.c { grid-column: -3 / -1; }     /* the last two        */

a  x=0    w=400
b  x=100  w=200
c  x=200  w=200
Line numbers
2 / 4 — from line 2 to line 4, so two tracks wide.
The span keyword
2 / span 2 or just span 2. Says how many tracks rather than which line, so it survives the grid changing size.
Negative line numbers
Counted from the end. 1 / -1 is "the whole explicit grid" and is the idiom for a full-bleed row. Note: negative numbers only address the explicit grid.
Named lines
main-start / main-end, from §9.7.

grid-area: sets all four at once, in the order row-start / column-start / row-end / column-end — an order nobody remembers, which is why it is mostly used in its other form: with a single name, referring to an area from grid-template-areas.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: span keyword.

9.11 grid-template-areas

The most readable construct in CSS. Each string is a row; each word in it is a named grid area; a repeated word spans; a . is an empty cell:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "sidebar header"
    "sidebar main"
    "sidebar footer";
  gap: 1rem;
}
.page > header { grid-area: header; }
.page > nav    { grid-area: sidebar; }
.page > main   { grid-area: main; }
.page > footer { grid-area: footer; }

Rewriting the layout at a breakpoint is then a rewrite of the picture, and nothing else changes:

@media (max-width: 40rem) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas: "header" "main" "sidebar" "footer";
  }
}

Three rules that the syntax enforces for you: every row must have the same number of columns; an area must be a rectangle (an L-shape is invalid and the whole declaration is discarded); and an area name is a <custom-ident>, so it must not be quoted individually and must not be span or auto.

Named areas create named lines automatically. An area called head implicitly defines lines head-start and head-end on both axes. Measured — an item placed with grid-column: head-start / head-end on a grid whose only definition of head came from grid-template-areas spanned the full 300px width. This is why the -start/-end naming convention from §9.7 is worth following: it makes the two systems interoperate in both directions.

grid-template: is the shorthand for rows, columns and areas together, and there is a form that puts the track sizes into the picture:

grid-template:
  "sidebar header" auto
  "sidebar main"   1fr
  "sidebar footer" auto
  / 200px 1fr;

Row sizes at the end of each line, column sizes after the slash. It is dense, and for a layout you will edit often the separate properties read better.

To have in hand before moving on: grid-template: and named grid area.

9.12 The grid Shorthand and Its Reset

grid: is the shorthand for grid-template-* plus the three implicit properties — and that last part is the hazard. §3.12's rule applies with unusual force here. Measured, with the two declarations in each possible order:

.a { grid-auto-rows: 200px; grid: auto-flow / 1fr 1fr; }
.b { grid: auto-flow / 1fr 1fr; grid-auto-rows: 200px; }

a  gridAutoRows = auto      b  gridAutoRows = 200px

In .a the shorthand came second and reset grid-auto-rows to auto, silently. The symptom — "my implicit rows stopped being 200px" — has nothing in it that points at the grid declaration, because that declaration never mentions rows.

The guidance is simple: use grid-template or the individual properties, and reserve grid: for the auto-flow form where you are deliberately setting the implicit behaviour too.

9.13 subgrid

Grid's original limitation was that the grid stopped at the container: a grid item that was itself a grid had its own, unrelated tracks. So a row of cards could be the same width, but the title, body and footer inside them could not line up, because each card sized its own rows independently.

subgrid removes that. A nested grid can adopt its parent's track sizing on either axis:

.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 10px; }
.card  {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: subgrid;
  grid-column: span 3;
  gap: inherit;
}

Measured on a 400px outer grid:

card cols = subgrid [] [] [] []      items = 127 / 127 / 127

The card's three children landed on the outer grid's three tracks exactly. (400 − 20) / 3 is 126.67, and the measurement is rounded to whole pixels, so all three read 127. Note that the computed value serialises as subgrid plus the inherited line-name slots, which is how you can confirm in developer tools that a subgrid is actually subscribing rather than falling back.

The canonical use is the one that motivated it — a row of cards whose internals align:

.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
  grid-row: span 3;         /* title, body, footer */
}

Every card's title occupies the same row track, so every title bottom aligns even when one wraps to two lines. There is no way to do this in flexbox at all, which is the point §8.14 made.

Two details. A subgridded axis inherits the parent's line names as well as its sizes, so grid-column: main-start / main-end works inside a subgrid. And gap: inherit is worth writing: a subgrid does not inherit the gap automatically, and a mismatched gap is the commonest way a subgrid looks almost right.

9.14 What About Masonry?

A masonry layout — items packed into columns of unequal heights, as in a photo wall — is the one common arrangement grid does not do. grid-auto-flow: dense (§9.9) fills holes but keeps the row structure, so it is not the same thing.

grid-template-rows: masonry has been specified and prototyped, and the design is still being argued over. Measured in current Chromium:

grid-template-rows: masonry   ->   computed as 18px

The declaration was not honoured — the value was not recognised and the track fell back. Treat masonry as a thing to watch rather than a thing to use: today it needs either JavaScript or a CSS-columns approximation (§7.14), and the columns approach has the ordering problem that multi-column reads top-to-bottom-then-across rather than across-then-down.

9.15 Alignment in Grid

Grid uses the same box alignment vocabulary as flexbox (§8.13), with one important addition: justify-items: and justify-self: do work here, because grid has a real inline axis per item.

The four container-level properties, and what each moves:

justify-items
Items within their track, on the inline axis. Default stretch.
align-items
Items within their track, on the block axis. Default stretch.
justify-content
The whole grid within the container, on the inline axis — only visible when the tracks do not fill it.
align-content
The whole grid within the container, on the block axis. Unlike flexbox (§8.9), this works with a single row.

Measured, on a two-track grid with 100px columns and an 80px row, holding 40×20 items:

.g { justify-items: center; align-items: end; }
.s { justify-self: end; align-self: start; }

item 0  x=30   y=60      item 1 (.s)  x=160  y=0

Item 0 took the container defaults: centred in its 100px track (x = 30), pushed to the bottom of the 80px row (y = 60). Item 1 overrode both with justify-self/align-self and went to the end of its track and the top of the row.

place-items: center is the shortest full centring in CSS — one declaration on the container centres every item on both axes — and place-content: center centres the grid itself.

Safe alignment applies here as in flexbox: align-items: safe center degrades to start rather than producing content that overflows in a direction that cannot be scrolled to.

9.16 Reading a Grid in Developer Tools

Grid is the layout mode with the best tooling, and not using it is a waste. In Chromium's Elements panel, a grid container carries a grid badge; clicking it overlays the container with its line numbers, its named lines and its area names drawn on the page, and the Layout pane lists every grid on the page with toggles for line numbers, area names and track sizes.

Three things to look for when a grid misbehaves:

  • Are the tracks the sizes you think? The overlay labels each one. An unexpectedly wide track is almost always §9.4's implicit auto minimum.
  • Are there implicit tracks you did not declare? The overlay draws them with a dashed line. An item placed on a line that does not exist creates them silently.
  • Is the item where you placed it, or where auto-placement put it? Removing a grid-area and watching nothing change means the rule is not matching at all — a §1.10 problem, not a grid one.

9.17 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • Grid layout gives a grid container a set of grid lines; between them are grid tracks, whose intersections are grid cells, and rectangles of cells are grid areas. Items are placed against lines.
  • The explicit grid is declared; the implicit grid is created for anything outside it.
  • grid-template-columns: and grid-template-rows: accept lengths, auto, min-content, max-content, minmax(), fit-content() and fr — measured at 133.328/266.672 for minmax(100px,1fr) 2fr and exactly 80px for fit-content(80px).
  • repeat() compresses a track list and takes auto-fill or auto-fit as a count.
  • The fr unit divides the leftover space and therefore accounts for gaps; 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr), so minmax(0, 1fr) is the spelling for genuinely equal tracks — measured at 122.953/77.047 versus 100/100.
  • auto-fill keeps empty tracks and auto-fit collapses them: measured 193/193 across three tracks versus 295/295 across two.
  • grid-auto-rows:, grid-auto-columns: and grid-auto-flow: govern the implicit grid; dense packing backfills holes — measured, a 124px-tall grid became 82px — at the cost of separating visual from DOM order.
  • grid-column:, grid-row: and grid-area: place items by line-based placement, the span keyword or a negative line number — measured at x=0/100/200 for 1 / -1, 2 / span 2 and -3 / -1.
  • Named grid lines make placement readable; grid-template-areas: draws the layout, requires rectangles, and creates implicit -start/-end lines that were measured working.
  • grid-template: combines rows, columns and areas; grid: additionally resets the three implicit properties, measured wiping a grid-auto-rows: 200px written before it.
  • subgrid adopts the parent's tracks and line names — measured at 127/127/127 across a parent's three tracks — and is the only way to align the insides of sibling components; write gap: inherit with it.
  • Masonry is not yet available: grid-template-rows: masonry was measured falling back.
  • Grid uses box alignment, and unlike flexbox justify-items: and justify-self: work — measured at x=30/y=60 for the container defaults and x=160/y=0 for the per-item overrides.
  • The grid inspector overlay draws line numbers, area names and implicit tracks, and is the fastest route to a grid diagnosis.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: grid-template-areas: and line-based placement.

Exercises

1. Write a page skeleton: a header and footer spanning the full width, a 220px sidebar on the left, and a main area taking the rest — collapsing to a single column below 45rem, with the sidebar after the main content in the mobile order. Explain why your solution does or does not create an accessibility problem.

Solution 
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "sidebar header"
    "sidebar main"
    "sidebar footer";
  gap: 1rem;
  min-block-size: 100svh;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
}
.page > header { grid-area: header; }
.page > nav    { grid-area: sidebar; }
.page > main   { grid-area: main; }
.page > footer { grid-area: footer; }

@media (max-width: 45rem) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas: "header" "main" "sidebar" "footer";
  }
}

The breakpoint rewrites the picture and nothing else. No item's placement rule changes, because each one refers to a name, and the name moves.

The accessibility question is the real content of this exercise, and the answer is: it depends entirely on the DOM order, which the CSS does not show.

Grid placement, exactly like order in flexbox (§8.11) and dense packing (§9.9), changes visual order and leaves DOM order untouched. DOM order is what determines the tab sequence, the reading order for a screen reader, and the order content is announced in. So:

  • If the markup is header, nav, main, footer, the desktop layout puts the sidebar visually to the left of the header — which a sighted keyboard user sees as "focus starts in the header, then jumps left and down into the nav". The visual order (nav appears first, top-left) disagrees with the focus order (header first). That is a WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) concern.
  • If the markup is nav, header, main, footer, the desktop order matches, and the mobile layout is the one that disagrees, because the sidebar has been moved after main visually but still precedes it in the DOM.

Either way, one of the two layouts has a mismatch — which is the honest answer, and it is why "just reorder with CSS" is not free.

What I would actually do:

  1. Choose the DOM order that matches the more-used layout, and accept the mismatch in the other. For most sites that is the mobile order, so: header, main, nav, footer, and let the desktop layout do the reordering. The mismatch on desktop is then between a header at top-right and a sidebar at left, which is a weak visual sequence anyway.
  2. Keep a skip link (<a href="#main">Skip to content</a> as the first focusable element), which makes the mismatch far less costly for keyboard users regardless of which order won.
  3. Watch reading-flow: (§15.8). It is designed for exactly this: a grid or flex container can declare that focus and reading order should follow the visual order rather than the DOM. It is Chromium-only today, so it is an enhancement rather than a solution.

A min-block-size: 100svh note, since the skeleton has one: svh rather than vh for §4.4's reason, and grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto so the footer is pushed to the bottom on short pages — which is the modern replacement for the sticky-footer hack.

2. A card gallery uses repeat(auto-fill, minmax(18rem, 1fr)). The designer complains that with two cards they sit at the left with a gap on the right, and asks for them to fill the row. Separately, one card contains a long unbroken product code and is wider than its siblings. Fix both, and explain the mechanism of each.

Solution

Symptom one: auto-fill keeps the empty track.

Measured (§9.8) with two items in a 600px container:

auto-fill:  tracks = 193.328  193.328  193.328   items = 193 / 193
auto-fit:   tracks = 295      295      0         items = 295 / 295

auto-fill creates as many tracks as fit and keeps them all, so the third track exists at full width with nothing in it, and the two cards stay at their natural grid width with a hole at the end. auto-fit creates the same tracks and then collapses the empty ones to zero width; the 1fr maximum redistributes that space, so the two survivors stretch.

.cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(18rem, 1fr)); }

One word. And note that this is a genuine design choice rather than a bug fix — auto-fill is right when card width must be consistent between a page with two items and a page with eight, which is often what a catalogue wants. The designer has asked for the other behaviour; both are defensible.

Symptom two: an fr track will not shrink below its content.

1fr is exactly minmax(auto, 1fr), and the auto minimum is the track's min-content size — the widest unbreakable run in it. A long product code has no break opportunity, so it sets a floor that the fr distribution cannot go below, and that track ends up wider than its siblings. Measured (§9.4) on a 200px grid with a 20-character word in the first track:

1fr 1fr                        ->  122.953  77.047
minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(0, 1fr)  ->  100      100

This is the grid twin of §8.6's flexbox min-width: auto, and it has the same shape: the automatic minimum is content-based, not zero.

Two fixes, and they address different things:

/* 1. make the tracks genuinely equal */
.cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(18rem, 100%), 1fr)); }
.cards > * { min-inline-size: 0; }

/* 2. deal with the content that caused it */
.card__code { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }

min-inline-size: 0 on the item removes the item's contribution to the track's minimum. The min(18rem, 100%) inside minmax() is a related and separately useful guard: without it, a viewport narrower than 18rem makes the track wider than the container and the whole grid overflows — a very common bug on small phones that only shows up below 288px.

And overflow-wrap: anywhere on the offending content is the fix that makes the layout right rather than merely contained. Forcing the track to 1fr while the code still cannot wrap just moves the overflow inside the card.

3. Three cards sit in a row. Each has a title of one or two lines, a body, and a footer button. The buttons do not line up because one title wraps. Show why flexbox cannot fix this, then fix it.

Solution

Why flexbox cannot fix it.

Flexbox aligns items within a flex line (§8.8). align-items: stretch — the default — makes the three cards equal in height, and that part works. But each card's internal layout is its own independent formatting context: card one lays out a two-line title, card two a one-line title, and nothing relates the two. The title in card one is taller, so everything below it starts lower, and the buttons are at different heights.

The usual flexbox workaround is margin-block-start: auto on the footer inside each card, which pushes the button to the bottom of its own card. That aligns the buttons — because the cards are equal height — but it does not align the bodies, so the second card gets a large gap between its one-line title and its body, and the visual rhythm is still broken. It is a fix for the symptom the designer noticed and not for the cause.

Fundamentally: flexbox has no concept that could relate card one's title row to card two's title row. There is no shared structure between siblings' interiors.

The fix is subgrid (§9.13), which creates exactly that shared structure:

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(18rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
  grid-row: span 3;          /* title, body, footer */
  gap: inherit;
}

The outer grid now has three implicit row tracks, sized by the tallest content in each across all cards. Each card subscribes to them with grid-template-rows: subgrid and grid-row: span 3, so every card's title occupies the same row track, every body the same track, and every footer the same track. A two-line title in one card makes the title track two lines tall for all of them, and the bodies and buttons all move down together.

Measured on the column axis, which behaves identically: a subgridded card's three children landed on the parent's three tracks at 127 / 127 / 127 in a 400px grid with 10px gaps — (400 − 20) / 3 exactly. The card adopted the parent's sizing rather than computing its own.

Two details that catch people:

  • gap: inherit is not optional cosmetics. A subgrid does not inherit the parent's gap, so without it the card's internal rows use the default 0 and the alignment is right while the spacing is not — the "almost right" failure that is hardest to diagnose.
  • The span 3 must match the number of rows the card actually has. If a card sometimes has no footer, it spans 2 and its rows no longer correspond to the others'. Give every card the same structure, using an empty element or grid-row: span 3 with a deliberately empty final cell.

The honest alternative if subgrid is unavailable in a target browser: give the title a fixed min-block-size of two lines (min-block-size: 2lh, using §4.3's unit). It is a worse solution — it wastes space when every title is one line and breaks when one is three — but it degrades predictably, and it is what @supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) should fall back to.

SECTION 10

Positioning, Stacking Contexts and Anchor Positioning

Positioning is the layout mode people reach for when the other three will not do, and it is the one that most often produces behaviour nobody can explain: a fixed element that is not fixed to the viewport, a z-index: 9999 that loses to a z-index: 1, a sticky header that quietly stops sticking after an unrelated change three files away.

None of those is mysterious. Each is a consequence of one of three mechanisms — the containing block, the stacking context, and the scroll container — and this section is those three, followed by the feature that finally replaced the JavaScript most positioning code was written to support: anchor positioning.

Everything below was measured, and two of the measurements are the ones that explain most positioning bug reports.

10.1 The Five Values

The position property takes five values, and they divide into two groups by whether the box stays in normal flow:

static
The default. In flow. Offsets and z-index do not apply.
relative
In flow — it keeps its original space — but painted at an offset.
sticky
In flow, until a scroll threshold is crossed; then offset within its scroll container.
absolute
Out of flow. Removed from layout; positioned against the nearest positioned ancestor.
fixed
Out of flow, positioned against the viewport — usually. §10.5.

An element with any value other than static is positioned, and that word matters: it is what absolute looks for when it hunts for a containing block, and it is what z-index requires.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the position property.

10.2 static and relative
