Static positioning is the default and needs no discussion except one point: inset and z-index are ignored on a static box. They are not invalid — measured, z-index: 5 on a position: static element computes to 5 and simply has no effect, which is why it is not struck through in the styles pane and gives you no clue.

Relative positioning offsets a box from where it would have been, without disturbing anything else. The original space is preserved, so siblings do not move, and the box may overlap them. This makes it a very cheap adjustment — but it has two other jobs that are used far more often than the offsetting:

.card { position: relative; }        /* 1. become a containing block */
.badge { position: absolute; inset-block-start: 0; inset-inline-end: 0; }

.icon { position: relative; z-index: 1; }   /* 2. become z-index-able */

position: relative with no offsets at all is the standard way to make an element a containing block for its absolutely positioned descendants, and the standard way to make it participate in z-index. Both are §10.4 and §10.8.

What to carry forward from this subsection: static positioning.

10.3 The Offset Properties

The top property, the right property, the bottom property and the left property are the physical offsets. inset: is the shorthand for all four (in the usual clockwise order), and inset-block: and inset-inline: are the logical pairs (§15.8).

Two behaviours worth knowing:

  • inset: 0 on an absolutely positioned element with width: auto stretches it to fill its containing block. This is how an overlay is written, and it is more robust than width: 100%; height: 100% because it accounts for the containing block's padding.
  • When both offsets on an axis are specified along with a definite size, the two conflict, and inset-inline-start wins in a left-to-right writing mode. Setting left, right and width is a declaration of something impossible, and the resolution is defined rather than an error. If you want centring instead, set both offsets to 0 and use an auto margin — which does work on an absolutely positioned box, on both axes.
.centred { position: absolute; inset: 0; inline-size: 20rem; block-size: 10rem; margin: auto; }

The terms above, gathered: the top property, the right property, the bottom property, the left property, inset-block: and inset-inline:.

10.4 absolute and the Containing Block

An absolutely positioned box is removed from flow — it occupies no space, and its siblings lay out as if it were not there — and its offsets resolve against the padding box of the nearest positioned ancestor. If there is no positioned ancestor, the containing block is the initial containing block (§7.11).

The padding-box part is measurable and occasionally surprising. An outer box with 200px of content and 30px of padding, holding a child with inset: 0:

.o { position: relative; width: 200px; height: 200px; padding: 30px; }
.a { position: absolute; inset: 0; }

outer 260 x 260    abs 260 x 260    offset 0

The absolutely positioned child is 260×260 — it covers the padding as well as the content. For an overlay that is exactly right; for a "border" drawn with an absolutely positioned pseudo-element it is a 30px surprise.

The failure mode to recognise: an absolutely positioned element that has jumped to the top-left of the page, or to somewhere far away, is almost always one whose intended parent is not position: relative. The offsets are resolving against a much more distant ancestor, or against the initial containing block.

10.5 fixed, and the Transform Trap

position: fixed positions against the viewport and does not move when the page scrolls — which is what everyone expects, and which is not always what happens.

A transform, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, contain: paint, contain: layout or will-change on any ancestor makes that ancestor the containing block for fixed descendants. Measured, with two identical position: fixed; inset: 0 children, one inside an ordinary 200×200 box and one inside the same box with transform: translateZ(0):

no transform ancestor:   900 x 700 at 0,0        <- the viewport
transform ancestor:      200 x 200 at 58,300     <- the ancestor's box

The second element is 200×200, positioned inside its ancestor, and it scrolls with the page. Nothing about the element's own declarations changed. This is the mechanism behind an enormous number of "my modal is trapped inside a card" and "my sticky header scrolls away" reports, and the ancestor causing it is often several levels up and was given transform: translateZ(0) or will-change: transform as a performance measure.

The diagnosis is mechanical: walk up the ancestors in the elements panel and look at each one's computed transform, filter, will-change and contain. The fix is either to remove the property from the ancestor, or — better — to move the fixed element out of that subtree entirely. Which is exactly what the top layer (§10.13) does for you.

One line each, for reference: will-change:.

10.6 sticky, and the Two Ways It Silently Fails

position: sticky is relative until the element reaches a threshold in its scroll container, and fixed-like afterwards, but confined to its parent's box.

thead th { position: sticky; inset-block-start: 0; background: Canvas; }

Three things are required and each is a distinct failure when missing:

1. At least one offset. position: sticky with no top, bottom, inset-block-start or equivalent never sticks, because there is no threshold to cross. This is the commonest cause and it produces no symptom at all — the element simply behaves as static.

2. A scroll container that actually scrolls. The element sticks within the nearest ancestor scroll container, not the viewport. If that ancestor is only as tall as its contents, there is no scroll and nothing happens. Measured, getComputedStyle reports position: sticky in both the working and the non-working case:

inside a scrolling container:  position = sticky
inside a non-scrolling one:    position = sticky

The computed value is identical, so the styles pane cannot tell you which case you are in. That is what makes this one expensive to debug.

3. No overflow other than visible on an ancestor between the element and the intended scroll container. This is the trap §6.14 measured: overflow-x: hidden on <body> or a wrapper makes overflow-y compute to auto, which makes that element a scroll container, which becomes the sticky element's scroll container — and since that container is not the thing scrolling, the element never sticks. Use overflow-x: clip instead, which pairs legally with visible.

A fourth, quieter one: a sticky element cannot escape its parent. If the parent is only 100px tall, the element unsticks after 100px of scrolling. That is by design — it is what makes sticky section headers work — and it is a surprise when the parent is an unexpected wrapper.

10.7 z-index and What It Needs

z-index: takes an integer and orders overlapping boxes along the z axis. It applies only to positioned elements, and to flex and grid items (which are positioned enough for this purpose even when position: static). Measured, z-index: 5 computes to 5 on a static element and has no effect; on a flex child it computes to 5 and does have an effect.

The z-index: 9999 phenomenon has one explanation and it is §10.8: z-index values are only comparable within the same stacking context. An element with z-index: 9999 inside a stacking context whose own z-index is 1 will lose to any element with z-index: 2 outside it, because the whole context is painted at level 1 and its contents are sorted only against each other.

10.8 Stacking Contexts

A stacking context is a self-contained z-ordering group. Its descendants are painted as a unit, and their z-index values mean nothing outside it.

The root element always creates one. Beyond that, a stacking context is created by:

a positioned element with a z-index other than auto
Including z-index: 0, which is not the same as auto.
position: fixed or sticky
Unconditionally, with no z-index needed.
opacity less than 1
Measured: opacity: 0.99 creates one. This is the most surprising entry on the list.
transform, rotate, scale, translate, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, clip-path, mask
Any value other than none.
mix-blend-mode other than normal, or isolation: isolate
§10.9.
will-change naming any of the above
The property does not have to have a value — declaring the intent is enough.
contain: paint or layout, content-visibility, a flex or grid item with a z-index
And elements in the top layer (§10.13).

The opacity and will-change entries are the ones that cause real confusion, because neither looks like a z-ordering declaration. A fade-in animation that sets opacity: 0.99 mid-transition creates a stacking context for the duration, and a dropdown inside that element becomes un-liftable above its siblings for exactly those frames.

Painting order within a stacking context, from back to front, is worth having:

  1. The context root's background and borders.
  2. Negative z-index descendants — behind the root's own content, which is what makes z-index: -1 on a pseudo-element work as a background layer.
  3. In-flow block-level boxes.
  4. Floats.
  5. In-flow inline content.
  6. z-index: 0 and z-index: auto positioned boxes.
  7. Positive z-index descendants, in numeric order.

Note item 5: inline content paints above floats and above in-flow blocks, which is why text overlaps a floated element's background rather than the reverse.

10.9 isolation

isolation: isolate creates a stacking context and does nothing else. It is the flow-root of z-ordering: a way to say "contain the z-index values inside me" without side effects.

.card { isolation: isolate; }

Its two uses are containing a component's internal z-index values so they cannot fight with the rest of the page, and blocking mix-blend-mode — a blended child blends with everything behind it within its stacking context, so isolation: isolate on the parent stops it reaching further back.

Use it in preference to position: relative; z-index: 0, which achieves the same thing as a side effect and is less clear about intent.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: isolation:.

10.10 Anchor Positioning: The Idea

Every tooltip, dropdown, popover and menu built before 2024 needed JavaScript, because CSS had no way to say "put this box next to that box". The element had to be measured, the anchor's position read, the result written to style.top and style.left, and the whole thing recomputed on scroll and resize.

Anchor positioning puts that in CSS. An element declares itself an anchor with a name; a positioned element refers to that name and can then use the anchor's edges and dimensions in its own offsets.

.button  { anchor-name: --menu-anchor; }
.menu    {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --menu-anchor;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
  inline-size: anchor-size(width);
}

Measured, with a 100×30 anchor at (108, 100):

anchor  108,100  100 x 30
tip     108,130  w = 100

anchor(bottom) resolved to the anchor's bottom edge at 130, anchor(left) to its left edge at 108, and anchor-size(width) to its 100px width. No script, and the browser keeps it correct through scrolling and resizing.

The pieces:

  • anchor-name: — a <dashed-ident> on the anchor element. An element may declare several names, and several elements may share one, in which case the last in DOM order wins.
  • position-anchor: — names the default anchor for a positioned element. Once set, anchor() and anchor-size() may omit their name argument.
  • anchor() — resolves to a position on the anchor: top, right, bottom, left, center, start, end, self-start, self-end, or a percentage along the axis. It takes an optional fallback: anchor(bottom, 100%).
  • anchor-size() — resolves to a dimension: width, height, inline, block, self-inline, self-block. Its main use is making a dropdown exactly as wide as the control that opened it, which is the measured example above.

An important constraint: the anchor must be an ancestor of the positioned element, or the positioned element must be in the top layer. In practice this means anchor positioning pairs naturally with popover and <dialog> (§10.13), which are in the top layer and therefore exempt.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: anchor-name: and position-anchor:.

10.11 position-area

Writing four anchor() offsets for every direction is tedious, so position-area: provides a shorthand grid. It divides the space around the anchor into a 3×3 grid and lets you name a cell or a span:

.tip {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --a;
  position-area: block-end span-inline-start;
}

Measured, with an anchor whose box runs from top=150 left=158 to bottom=180 right=258:

tip  top = 180   left = 241   right = 258

block-end put the tip below the anchor (its top is the anchor's bottom, 180), and span-inline-start made it span from the anchor's inline-end edge back towards the start — so its right edge is the anchor's right edge at 258.

The row and column keywords are block-start, center, block-end and inline-start, center, inline-end, plus span-* forms and the physical top/bottom/left/right equivalents. position-area: block-end center is a tooltip centred underneath; position-area: inline-end center is a menu to the right.

position-area also sizes the element by default: it is given the area as its containing block, so it will not exceed it unless you say so.

10.12 Fallbacks: position-try and position-visibility

A tooltip below its anchor is wrong when the anchor is at the bottom of the screen. This was the other half of the JavaScript, and it too is now declarative.

position-try-fallbacks: lists positions to try, in order, when the current one overflows:

.tip {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --a;
  position-area: block-end center;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, flip-block flip-inline;
}

The three flip-* keywords are built in and cover most cases. For anything else, @position-try defines a named alternative whose descriptors are the inset, margin, sizing and alignment properties:

@position-try --above {
  position-area: block-start center;
  margin-block-end: 0.5rem;
}
.tip { position-try-fallbacks: --above; }

position-try-order: chooses among the fallbacks by available space rather than by list order — most-block-size picks the one that gives the element the most room.

position-visibility: decides what happens when the anchor itself scrolls out of view. anchors-visible hides the positioned element when its anchor is not visible, which stops a tooltip floating detached over unrelated content; no-overflow hides it when it would overflow its containing block.

Together these four cover what a positioning library did, in about six declarations, with the browser doing the recomputation.

To have in hand before moving on: position-try-fallbacks: and position-visibility:.

10.13 The Top Layer

The top layer is a rendering layer above the entire document, outside every stacking context. An element promoted into it is painted above everything, whatever the z-index values below it, and — critically for §10.5 — it escapes any transformed ancestor.

Three things put an element there: dialog.showModal(), an element with the popover attribute being shown, and the Fullscreen API. You cannot put an element there with CSS.

This is the correct answer to the whole z-index: 9999 genre. A modal that lives in the top layer cannot be covered by anything, cannot be trapped by an ancestor's overflow: hidden, and cannot be captured by an ancestor's transform.

::backdrop styles the layer painted behind a top-layer element:

dialog::backdrop { background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5); backdrop-filter: blur(2px); }

It is a real box that covers the viewport, so this replaces the extra overlay <div> that used to be built by hand. And because a popover or dialog is in the top layer, it is an ideal anchor-positioning target — the §10.10 ancestor constraint does not apply to it.

Popover styling uses :popover-open (§2.11) for the shown state and @starting-style (§14.7) for the entry animation, since a popover goes from display: none to shown.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: popover styling.

10.14 Scroll Snap, and the Scroll Offsets

A scroll container (§6.13) can be told to settle on positions rather than anywhere.

.carousel {
  overflow-x: auto;
  display: flex;
  scroll-snap-type: x mandatory;
}
.carousel > * { flex: 0 0 100%; scroll-snap-align: start; }

snapType = x mandatory     childAlign = start
  • scroll-snap-type: goes on the container: an axis (x, y, block, inline, both) plus mandatory or proximity. mandatory always settles on a snap point, which is wrong for content of varying height because it can make some content unreachable; proximity snaps only when the scroll ends near one.
  • scroll-snap-align: goes on the children: start, center, end, or none.
  • scroll-snap-stop: always prevents a fast fling from skipping past items — essential for a carousel where every item matters.

scroll-margin: and scroll-padding: are the other half of scroll positioning and are useful far beyond snapping. scroll-padding-block-start on the scroll container, or scroll-margin-block-start on the target, offsets where the browser scrolls an element to — which is the fix for a sticky header covering the section you just jumped to with a fragment link:

:root { scroll-padding-block-start: 5rem; }   /* the height of the sticky header */

That one declaration fixes fragment links, scrollIntoView(), and the browser's own scroll-to-focused-element behaviour, all at once.

In summary, the vocabulary here is scroll-margin:, scroll-padding:, scroll-snap-type:, scroll-snap-align:, scroll-snap-stop: and view().

10.15 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • The position property has five values; static positioning ignores offsets and z-index (though they still compute), relative positioning stays in flow, and absolute positioning and fixed positioning are out-of-flow.
  • Relative positioning with no offsets is the standard way to create a containing block and to make an element z-index-able.
  • The top property, the right property, the bottom property, the left property, inset:, inset-block: and inset-inline: are the offsets; inset: 0 plus margin: auto centres an absolutely positioned box on both axes.
  • An absolutely positioned box resolves against the padding box of the nearest positioned ancestor — measured at 260×260 inside a 200px box with 30px padding.
  • A transform, filter, will-change or contain on any ancestor captures fixed descendants: measured, an identical position: fixed; inset: 0 box was 900×700 at the viewport in one case and 200×200 inside its ancestor in the other.
  • Sticky positioning needs an offset, a scrolling ancestor, and no unintended scroll container between — and getComputedStyle reports sticky in the broken case too, measured.
  • z-index: needs a positioned element (or a flex/grid item) and is only comparable within a stacking context.
  • A stacking context is created by a positioned element with a z-index, by fixed and sticky, by opacity below 1 — measured at 0.99 — by transforms, filters, clip-path, blend modes, will-change and contain.
  • Painting order inside a context runs background, negative z-index, blocks, floats, inline content, z-index: 0, then positive z-index.
  • isolation: isolate creates a stacking context and nothing else.
  • Anchor positioning uses anchor-name:, position-anchor:, anchor() and anchor-size() — measured placing a tip at the anchor's bottom-left edge with the anchor's exact width — and the anchor must be an ancestor unless the element is in the top layer.
  • position-area: names a cell of the 3×3 region around the anchor — measured with block-end span-inline-start — and position-try:, position-try-fallbacks:, position-try-order: and position-visibility: handle overflow.
  • The top layer is above every stacking context, is entered only by showModal(), popover and fullscreen, and is the real answer to z-index: 9999; ::backdrop styles the layer behind it.
  • Scroll snap uses scroll-snap-type:, scroll-snap-align: and scroll-snap-stop:; scroll-margin: and scroll-padding: offset where the browser scrolls to, which is the sticky-header fragment-link fix.

What to carry forward from this subsection: absolute positioning, fixed positioning, sticky positioning and position-try:.

Exercises

1. A modal is built with position: fixed; inset: 0; z-index: 9999. On one page it appears correctly; on another it is clipped inside a card and scrolls with the page. Diagnose it, and give both a tactical fix and the correct one.

Solution

The diagnosis: an ancestor has captured the fixed positioning.

position: fixed resolves against the viewport unless an ancestor has a transform, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, contain: paint, contain: layout, or a will-change naming any of those. Any of those makes that ancestor the containing block for fixed descendants, at which point "fixed" means fixed to the card, not to the screen — so it is sized by the card, clipped by the card's overflow, and scrolls with the page.

Measured with two identical position: fixed; inset: 0 boxes:

no transform ancestor:   900 x 700 at 0,0      <- the viewport
transform ancestor:      200 x 200 at 58,300   <- the ancestor's box

Nothing about the modal's own declarations differs between the two pages. The culprit is on the page that behaves badly, usually several levels up, and usually added for an unrelated reason — transform: translateZ(0) or will-change: transform as a "GPU acceleration" measure, a filter: drop-shadow() on a card, or contain: paint added for performance.

Finding it: walk up the ancestor chain in the elements panel and read each one's computed transform, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, contain and will-change. Exactly one of them will be non-none.

The z-index: 9999 is a second, independent symptom of the same cause: those properties also create a stacking context (§10.8), so the modal's 9999 is only compared against its siblings inside the card. Whatever the card's own stacking level is, the modal is painted at that level.

Tactical fix: remove the offending property from the ancestor, or move the modal's markup out of that subtree — typically by rendering it as the last child of <body>.

The correct fix: put the modal in the top layer.

<dialog id="confirm">…</dialog>

document.getElementById('confirm').showModal();

dialog::backdrop { background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5); backdrop-filter: blur(2px); }
dialog { border: 0; border-radius: 0.75rem; padding: 1.5rem; }

showModal() promotes the element into the top layer (§10.13), which sits above every stacking context in the document. It cannot be captured by a transformed ancestor, cannot be clipped by an ancestor's overflow, and needs no z-index at all — so the whole class of bug disappears rather than being worked around. ::backdrop replaces the hand-built overlay <div>, and the browser handles focus trapping, inert-ing the rest of the page, and Escape to close, all of which the hand-rolled modal was going to have to implement.

The same reasoning applies to tooltips and menus via the popover attribute, which also enters the top layer.

2. A table has thead th { position: sticky; top: 0 }. It works in isolation and stops working when the table is placed inside the application shell. List the candidate causes in the order you would check them, with the test for each.

Solution

Sticky has three requirements and a fourth constraint, and all of them fail silently — getComputedStyle reports position: sticky whether or not it is doing anything, which was measured. So this is a checklist, not an inspection.

1. An ancestor between the header and the real scroll container is itself a scroll container. Check this first — it is the commonest cause in a shell.

A sticky element sticks within its nearest ancestor scroll container. If a wrapper in the shell has overflow: auto, overflow: hidden, or overflow-x: hidden, that wrapper becomes the scroll container. Since the wrapper is sized to its contents and does not itself scroll, the header has no threshold to cross.

The overflow-x: hidden case deserves emphasis because it looks harmless. §6.14 measured that setting overflow-x: hidden makes overflow-y compute to auto — even when overflow-y: visible is written explicitly:

overflow-x: hidden                        ->  x=hidden  y=auto
overflow-x: hidden; overflow-y: visible   ->  x=hidden  y=auto

So a body { overflow-x: hidden } added to suppress a horizontal scrollbar breaks every sticky element on the page.

Test: in the console, walk up from the header and print each ancestor's computed overflow-x/overflow-y; the first one that is not visible is your scroll container. Fix: overflow-x: clip, which pairs legally with visible and does not create a scroll container.

2. An ancestor has overflow: hidden on the block axis for a non-scrolling reason. Same mechanism, different intent — often a card or panel clipping a decoration. Same test; the fix is clip again, or moving the clip elsewhere.

3. The sticky element's parent is too short. A sticky element cannot leave its parent's box, so it unsticks once the parent has scrolled past. For a table header the parent is <thead>, whose height is the header row — but if the shell wraps the table in a fixed-height container, the header unsticks almost immediately.

Test: give the parent a temporary outline and watch where the header stops.

4. No offset, or the wrong one. position: sticky with no top/inset-block-start never sticks. This is unlikely here since the rule declares top: 0, but check that a later rule has not reset it — and note that with writing-mode in play, top and inset-block-start are not the same thing (§15.8).

5. A transformed ancestor. Less common for sticky than for fixed, but a transform on an ancestor changes the containing block and can produce related surprises.

The related bug worth fixing at the same time: once the header sticks, fragment links and scrollIntoView() will scroll targets under it. One declaration fixes all of them:

:root { scroll-padding-block-start: 3rem; }   /* the sticky header's height */

3. Build a dropdown menu that opens under a button, is exactly as wide as the button, and flips above it when there is no room below — with no JavaScript for positioning. Then say what its limitations are.

Solution 
<button popovertarget="menu" id="trigger">Options</button>
<div id="menu" popover>
  <a href="/a">Edit</a><a href="/b">Duplicate</a><a href="/c">Delete</a>
</div>

#trigger { anchor-name: --trigger; }

#menu {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --trigger;
  position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
  inline-size: anchor-size(width);
  margin-block-start: 0.25rem;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block;
  position-visibility: anchors-visible;

  border: 1px solid; border-radius: 0.5rem; padding: 0.25rem;
  margin-inline: 0;
}

#menu:popover-open { display: grid; }

@starting-style {
  #menu:popover-open { opacity: 0; translate: 0 -0.25rem; }
}
#menu { transition: opacity 120ms, translate 120ms, overlay 120ms allow-discrete,
                    display 120ms allow-discrete; }

Each piece, and what it replaces:

anchor-name / position-anchor / position-area: block-end span-inline-end is the positioning that used to be getBoundingClientRect() plus arithmetic plus a scroll listener plus a resize observer. Measured (§10.11), position-area with a block-end row put the element's top edge exactly at the anchor's bottom edge.

inline-size: anchor-size(width) is the "as wide as the button" requirement, measured in §10.10 resolving to the anchor's exact 100px.

position-try-fallbacks: flip-block is the flip. The browser tries the declared position, detects the overflow, and re-runs the placement mirrored across the block axis — including on scroll, which is where the hand-written version always had bugs.

popover puts the menu in the top layer, which does three things at once: it escapes any transformed or overflow: hidden ancestor (§10.5), it needs no z-index, and it satisfies anchor positioning's requirement that the anchor be an ancestor or the positioned element be in the top layer — which it is. It also gives you light dismiss and Escape for free.

@starting-style plus transition ... allow-discrete animates the entry, which is otherwise impossible because a popover goes from display: none (§14.7).

The limitations, honestly:

  • This is a menu of links, not a menu widget. It has no roving tabindex, no arrow-key navigation, no role="menu"/role="menuitem", and no aria-expanded on the trigger. popover gives you dismissal and the top layer; it does not give you the ARIA keyboard interaction pattern, and a real application menu needs it. That is script, and it is the script that should have been written instead of the positioning script.
  • Anchor positioning is Baseline newly available, not widely available — every current engine has it (Chrome 125, Firefox 147, Safari 26), which means a browser two versions old does not. Until it reaches widely-available status it needs an @supports (anchor-name: --x) guard with a plain absolutely positioned fallback, or the menu appears at the top-left corner of the page.
  • position-visibility: anchors-visible hides the menu when the button scrolls away, which is right for a tooltip and arguably wrong for a menu the user has deliberately opened. Consider dropping it here.
  • The margin-inline: 0 is not decoration: a popover's user-agent styles include margin: auto, which centres it in the viewport and defeats the anchor positioning entirely. That is the kind of detail that only shows up when you build it.
SECTION 11

Colour, Backgrounds, Borders and Visual Effects

Colour in CSS changed more between 2022 and 2025 than in the twenty years before. For most of the language's life there was one colour space — sRGB — and every notation was a different way of writing an sRGB triple. Now there are a dozen, the browser computes in whichever one you name, and the choice has consequences you can see: a gradient that goes grey in the middle in one space and stays saturated in another, a palette whose lightness steps look even instead of merely being numerically even.

This section covers that, then the machinery that paints with it — backgrounds, gradients, borders, shadows, filters, blend modes and masks. Every serialisation below was read out of a real browser, and several of them are not what you would guess.

11.1 What a <color> Is

The color property sets text colour and, through currentColor, feeds most of the rest. A <color> value can be written in about a dozen notations, and the first fact to establish is that they are not all interchangeable any more.

Measured — the same declarations read back from getComputedStyle:

oklch(62% 0.19 250)          ->  oklch(0.62 0.19 250)
oklab(0.62 -0.05 -0.15)      ->  oklab(0.62 -0.05 -0.15)
lab(50% 40 -30)              ->  lab(50 40 -30)
lch(50% 50 300)              ->  lch(50 50 300)
color(display-p3 1 0 0)      ->  color(display-p3 1 0 0)
hwb(120 10% 20%)             ->  rgb(26, 204, 26)
rgb(255 0 0 / 0.5)           ->  rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)
#ff000080                    ->  rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)

The pattern is exact: a colour that fits in sRGB is serialised as rgb(); a colour in a wider space keeps its own notation. hwb() is an sRGB notation, so it collapsed to rgb(). oklch() is not, so it survived — because converting it would lose information on a display that can show it.

That is the whole reason to care about colour spaces, and §11.3 is the practical consequence.

The terms above, gathered: the color property and hwb().

11.2 The sRGB Notations

Five ways to write an sRGB colour, all equivalent:

named color
148 keywords plus transparent. Mostly historical, but rebeccapurple, tomato and gold are honest and readable in a prototype.
hex color
#rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa. Measured: #ff000080 is 50% red, so the 8-digit form is a real alpha notation and not a curiosity.
rgb()
Modern syntax is space-separated with a slash before alpha: rgb(255 0 0 / 0.5). The comma form still works. rgba() is now an alias.
hsl()
Hue, saturation, lightness. Easier to reason about than hex, and its lightness is not perceptual — see §11.3.
hwb()
Hue, whiteness, blackness. Good for "this colour, but 20% lighter" thinking. Measured collapsing to rgb().

One line each, for reference: named color and hex color.

11.3 The Perceptual Spaces: oklch(), oklab(), lab(), lch()

hsl()'s lightness is a number in a cube, not a perception. hsl(60 100% 50%) is yellow and hsl(240 100% 50%) is blue, both "50% lightness", and one of them is blinding while the other is nearly black. Any palette built on hsl() lightness steps is uneven, and every designer has compensated for that by hand.

Oklab and Oklch fix it. They are perceptually uniform: equal numeric steps look like equal steps.

  • oklch() — lightness, chroma, hue. The one to use. Lightness 0–1 (or a percentage), chroma roughly 0–0.4, hue 0–360.
  • oklab() — the same space in Cartesian coordinates. Better for interpolation, worse for authoring.
  • The lab() function and the lch() function — the older CIE Lab space. Perceptually uniform too, but with a known weakness in the blues, which is exactly what Oklab was designed to fix. Prefer the ok versions.
  • The color() function — an explicit colour space plus coordinates: color(display-p3 1 0 0), color(srgb 1 0 0), color(rec2020 ...). This is how you address a wide gamut directly.

The practical payoff is a palette that is one line of arithmetic:

:root {
  --hue: 265;
  --accent-100: oklch(96% 0.03 var(--hue));
  --accent-500: oklch(58% 0.20 var(--hue));
  --accent-900: oklch(28% 0.12 var(--hue));
}

Those three look evenly spaced, and changing --hue re-tunes the whole ramp without redoing the lightness values — which is not true of the hsl() equivalent.

Out-of-gamut values are kept, not clamped, in the computed value. Measured:

oklch(70% 0.4 145)   ->   oklch(0.7 0.4 145)

0.4 chroma at that lightness is well outside sRGB. The browser stored it verbatim and does gamut mapping at paint time, choosing the nearest displayable colour for the actual screen. So the same declaration is more saturated on a P3 display than on an sRGB one, automatically — which is the point of the wide-gamut notations, and a reason not to hand-clamp values yourself.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: the lab() function, the lch() function, the color() function and wide gamut.

11.4 color-mix() and Relative Colours

color-mix() blends two colours in a named space:

--border: color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 20%, transparent);
--hover:  color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 85%, black);

Measured, color-mix(in oklab, red 40%, blue) computed to oklab(0.522375 0.0704744 -0.13657) — the mix is resolved at computed-value time, in the space you named, and the result keeps that space's notation.

The interpolation space matters. Mixing red and blue in srgb passes through a muddy purple-grey; in oklab keeps the chroma up. As a default, in oklab for mixes and in oklch for anything where the hue should travel around the wheel.

Relative color syntax derives a colour from another one by decomposing it into channel keywords:

.button:hover { background: oklch(from var(--accent) calc(l * 0.9) c h); }
.ghost        { border-color: rgb(from var(--accent) r g b / 0.35); }

Measured: rgb(from red calc(r * 0.5) g b) computed to color(srgb 0.5 0 0) — the browser decomposed red into r, g, b, applied the arithmetic, and produced the result.

This is the feature that removes the last real reason for a preprocessor's colour functions. darken(), lighten(), transparentize() and saturate() all become one-liners that work at runtime, respond to custom properties, and can be redefined by a theme.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: relative color syntax.

11.5 currentColor, transparent and System Colours

currentColor is the element's computed color. It is the mechanism that makes a component follow its context without any plumbing. Measured:

.p { color: rebeccapurple; border: 2px solid currentColor; }

color = rgb(102, 51, 153)    border = rgb(102, 51, 153)

Two idioms worth having. An icon written as fill="currentColor" in SVG inherits the surrounding text colour, so one icon file works in every context. And border: 1px solid currentColor on a button means a single color change restyles text and border together.

The transparent keyword is rgb(0 0 0 / 0) — a fully transparent black. That matters in a gradient: linear-gradient(red, transparent) interpolates towards transparent black and goes grey on the way in sRGB. Write linear-gradient(red, rgb(255 0 0 / 0)) instead, or interpolate in oklab, where the problem does not arise.

A system color is a keyword whose value comes from the operating system's theme. The important ones are Canvas and CanvasText (the page's background and foreground), Field and FieldText (form controls), LinkText, VisitedText, ButtonFace, ButtonText, Highlight and HighlightText, AccentColor and AccentColorText, and Mark/MarkText. Measured:

CanvasText  ->  rgb(0, 0, 0)
Highlight   ->  rgba(0, 65, 198, 0.8)

They are how a page survives forced colors mode (§15.12) with its meaning intact, because they are the only colours that are re-mapped rather than overridden. Using Canvas/CanvasText as the base pair costs nothing and buys a working high-contrast mode.

accent-color: tints the browser's own rendering of checkboxes, radios, ranges and progress bars — measured applying cleanly — which replaces the whole genre of "rebuild the checkbox out of divs" component.

To have in hand before moving on: transparent keyword, accent-color:, system color and forced colors mode.

11.6 color-scheme and light-dark()

color-scheme: declares which schemes an element supports, and it does two jobs at once. It tells the browser to render form controls, scrollbars, the canvas background and the default text colour in that scheme; and it is what light-dark() (§5.10) reads.

:root { color-scheme: light dark; }

One declaration gives a page dark scrollbars, dark form controls and a dark default canvas when the user prefers dark — before you have written a single colour. It is the cheapest dark-mode work available and it is frequently missed, producing a dark page with white scrollbars.

11.7 Backgrounds

The background property is the shorthand for eight longhands, and §3.12 established that it resets every one of them. Measured on a three-layer declaration:

.a { background: linear-gradient(red, red), url(x.png) no-repeat center / cover, blue; }

image  = linear-gradient(rgb(255,0,0), rgb(255,0,0)), url("x.png"), none
size   = auto, cover, auto
repeat = repeat, no-repeat, repeat
pos    = 0% 0%, 50% 50%, 0% 0%
color  = rgb(0, 0, 255)

Three things that listing tells you:

  • Every longhand becomes a comma-separated list, one entry per layer, and the lists are matched by position.
  • Layers paint front to back: the first is on top. This is the opposite of the usual "later wins" instinct and is the commonest reason a background with multiple backgrounds shows the wrong one.
  • background-color: belongs to the last layer only, and there is one per element. That is why blue appears at the end and why the shorthand accepts a colour only in its final layer — a colour is not a layer, it is the paint behind all of them, so background-color: sits under every image the element has.

The individual longhands:

background-image: takes any <image> — a url(), any gradient, image-set(), element(), or none. background-repeat: takes repeat, no-repeat, round (scales so a whole number fit) and space (distributes without scaling). background-position: takes keywords, lengths or percentages, and its percentage is §4.6's odd one: it aligns the same percentage point of the image with that point of the box, which is why 50% centres. background-size: takes lengths, cover or contain. background-attachment: takes scroll, local (scrolls with the element's contents) and fixed.

background-origin: decides which box the image is positioned within, and background-clip: decides which box it is painted into — border, padding or content. They are separate for a reason: an image can be positioned from the padding box and clipped to the border box.

.gradient-text {
  background-image: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--accent-500), var(--accent-900));
  background-clip: text;
  color: transparent;
}

Measured: background-clip: text computes cleanly. Note that it needs a transparent color to be visible at all, and that it removes the text's contrast guarantees — check the result against §15.13's rules rather than assuming.

One measured trap, and it is §3.12 in the wild. In the same run, .b { background-clip: content-box; background: red; } came back with background-clip: border-box and .c { background-origin: content-box; background: url(x.png); } came back with background-origin: padding-box. The shorthand, written afterwards, reset both. Never write background after a background-* longhand.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: background-image:, background-repeat:, background-position:, background-attachment: and multiple backgrounds.

In summary, the vocabulary here is background-color: and background-size:.

11.8 Gradients

Four gradient functions, each with a repeating variant. All are <image> values, so they work anywhere an image does — background-image, border-image, mask-image, list-style-image.

.a { background: linear-gradient(to right, red, blue); }
.b { background: linear-gradient(in oklch, red, blue); }
.c { background: linear-gradient(in oklch longer hue, red, blue); }
.d { background: linear-gradient(90deg, red 0 40%, blue 40% 100%); }
.e { background: conic-gradient(from 45deg, red, blue); }
.f { background: radial-gradient(circle 40px at 20% 30%, red, blue); }

Read back:

d = linear-gradient(90deg, rgb(255,0,0) 0px, rgb(255,0,0) 40%, rgb(0,0,255) 40%, rgb(0,0,255) 100%)

.d is the double-position syntax: red 0 40% means "this color stop runs from 0 to 40%", which the browser expanded into two stops. Two adjacent stops at the same position make a hard edge, so this is how you draw stripes, progress bars and pie charts with no images at all.

Gradient interpolation is the modern part. in oklch (measured, preserved verbatim in the computed value) changes which colours the gradient passes through, and the difference between linear-gradient(red, blue) and linear-gradient(in oklch, red, blue) is visible: the sRGB one darkens in the middle, the Oklch one does not. For a hue-travelling gradient, longer hue, shorter hue, increasing hue and decreasing hue choose the direction round the wheel.

conic-gradient() sweeps around a centre and is what makes CSS-only pie charts, donut progress rings and colour wheels possible. Combined with an animated @property angle (§5.7), it is the standard modern loading spinner.

A repeating gradient — repeating-linear-gradient(), repeating-radial-gradient(), repeating-conic-gradient() — tiles its stop list. The classic use is a background grid or a barber-pole stripe:

.grid-bg {
  background-image:
    repeating-linear-gradient(to right, rgb(0 0 0 / 0.06) 0 1px, transparent 1px 8px),
    repeating-linear-gradient(to bottom, rgb(0 0 0 / 0.06) 0 1px, transparent 1px 8px);
}

image-set() picks an image by display density: image-set("a.png" 1x, "a@2x.png" 2x). It is the srcset of CSS, and it also accepts a type() for format negotiation.

What to carry forward from this subsection: linear-gradient(), radial-gradient(), repeating gradient, color stop and gradient interpolation.

11.9 Borders, Radii and corner-shape

border-radius: rounds corners, and it takes more than one number per corner. Measured:

.a { border-radius: 10px 20px / 30px 40px; }

border-top-left-radius = 10px 30px

The slash separates horizontal radii from vertical radii, so each corner is an ellipse quadrant. The four-value-per-side form is rare; the useful consequences are that border-radius: 50% makes an ellipse of any box, and that border-radius: 999px makes a pill whose ends are always perfect semicircles regardless of height.

corner-shape: is newer and changes the curve rather than the size. Measured working:

.c { corner-shape: bevel; border-radius: 20px; }

corner-shape = bevel

Values include round (the default), bevel, scoop, notch, square and squircle, plus a superellipse() function for anything between. It is Chromium-only at the time of writing, so it belongs behind @supports — but it degrades perfectly, because a browser that does not know it simply keeps round.

border-image: slices an image into nine pieces and stretches or repeats the edges. It is the only way to give a border a gradient, which is a common request:

.fancy {
  border: 4px solid transparent;
  border-image: linear-gradient(45deg, var(--accent-500), var(--accent-900)) 1;
}

The trailing 1 is border-image-slice, and it is mandatory. Note that border-image and border-radius do not compose — an image border ignores the radius, and the usual workaround is a padded pseudo-element with background-clip.

The terms above, gathered: ellipse().

11.10 Shadows

box-shadow: takes offset-x offset-y blur spread color, optionally inset, and any number of comma-separated layers. Measured serialisations:

0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0/.2), 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0/.15)
   ->  rgba(0,0,0,0.2) 0px 1px 2px 0px, rgba(0,0,0,0.15) 0px 4px 12px 0px

inset 0 2px 4px black   ->  rgb(0,0,0) 0px 2px 4px 0px inset
0 0 0 3px red           ->  rgb(255,0,0) 0px 0px 0px 3px

Three things follow from that listing. Layering is how good shadows are made — a tight, dark one for contact and a wide, soft one for elevation, as in the first example. A pure-spread shadow (0 0 0 3px) is a ring, which is the standard focus indicator that does not affect layout the way a border would. And an inset shadow — written with the inset keyword — is drawn inside the border box rather than outside it, which is how a pressed button or a recessed well is made; the keyword serialises last but may be written first.

text-shadow: is the same minus spread and inset. Its most valuable use is not decoration: a subtle text-shadow is how text over a photograph stays legible without a scrim.

box-shadow does not follow the element's transparency — it is drawn from the border box outward. For a shadow that follows an irregular shape (a PNG with alpha, an SVG icon), use filter: drop-shadow(), which does.

One line each, for reference: inset shadow and text-shadow:.

11.11 Filters

The filter property applies graphical effects to an element and everything inside it, in the order written. Measured:

.a { filter: blur(4px) saturate(1.5) drop-shadow(0 2px 4px black); }

blur(4px) saturate(1.5) drop-shadow(rgb(0, 0, 0) 0px 2px 4px)

The functions are blur(), brightness(), contrast(), grayscale(), hue-rotate(), invert(), opacity(), saturate(), sepia(), drop-shadow() and url() for an SVG filter. Order matters: grayscale(1) sepia(1) and sepia(1) grayscale(1) are different pictures.

backdrop-filter: applies the same functions to whatever is behind the element, which is the frosted-glass effect:

.glass { background: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.6); backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.4); }

It needs a partly transparent background to be visible at all, and it is expensive — it forces the browser to read back and re-filter the composited content behind the element every frame. Confine it to small, static regions, and respect prefers-reduced-transparency (§15.11).

Both properties create a stacking context and a containing block for fixed descendants (§10.5, §10.8). A filter: blur(0) — which does nothing visually — is a real behavioural change, and it is a frequent accidental cause of the transform trap.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: the filter property, blur(), backdrop-filter:, rotate() and scale().

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: drop-shadow().

11.12 Blend Modes

mix-blend-mode: blends an element with what is behind it in its stacking context; background-blend-mode: blends an element's own background layers with each other. Measured, both applying cleanly with the sixteen standard blend mode keywords — multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, color-dodge, color-burn, hard-light, soft-light, difference, exclusion, hue, saturation, color, luminosity, and normal.

Two idioms worth knowing. mix-blend-mode: multiply on dark text over a light photograph makes it look printed rather than pasted. And a duotone image is two lines:

.duotone {
  background: var(--accent-900);
  background-blend-mode: luminosity;
  background-image: url("photo.jpg");
}

The scoping rule from §10.9 matters here: a blended element blends with everything behind it within its stacking context, so isolation: isolate on the parent is how you stop it reaching further back than intended.

To have in hand before moving on: background-blend-mode:.

11.13 Clipping and Masking

clip-path: cuts an element to a shape. It takes a basic shape — inset(), circle(), ellipse(), polygon(), rect(), xywh(), path() or shape() — a geometry box keyword, or a URL to an SVG <clipPath>.

.avatar   { clip-path: circle(50%); }
.notch    { clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% calc(100% - 1rem), calc(100% - 1rem) 100%, 0 100%); }
.reveal   { clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0); transition: clip-path 300ms; }
.reveal:hover { clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0); }

Clipping is binary — a pixel is in or out — which makes edges hard. It is also animatable between shapes with the same number of points, which is what makes the third example work.

Masking is the soft version: mask-image: uses an image's alpha channel (or, with mask-mode: luminance, its brightness) to decide opacity per pixel. Any <image> works, including a gradient:

.fade-out { mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, black 70%, transparent); }

That one declaration is a fade-to-nothing on any content — text, an image, a whole section — which is otherwise a real nuisance. mask-size, mask-position, mask-repeat and mask-clip mirror the background properties exactly, and mask is their shorthand with the same reset behaviour.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: clip-path:, polygon(), circle(), inset(), mask-image: and path().

11.14 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • The color property takes a <color>; a colour inside sRGB serialises as rgb() and a wide gamut one keeps its own notation — measured across eight notations.
  • The sRGB notations are the named color set, hex color (including the 8-digit alpha form, measured), rgb(), hsl() and hwb().
  • oklch() and oklab() are perceptually uniform, unlike hsl()'s lightness; the lab() function, the lch() function and the color() function complete the set, and display-p3, srgb and rec2020 name spaces explicitly.
  • Out-of-gamut values are stored verbatim — measured — and mapped to the display at paint time.
  • color-mix() resolves at computed-value time in the named space (measured producing an oklab() result) and relative color syntax decomposes a colour into channels — measured turning rgb(from red calc(r * 0.5) g b) into color(srgb 0.5 0 0).
  • currentColor propagates the computed color — measured onto a border — the transparent keyword is transparent black, and a system color such as Canvas, CanvasText or Highlight survives forced-colours mode.
  • accent-color: tints native controls, and color-scheme: styles scrollbars, form controls and the canvas as well as driving light-dark().
  • The background property resets eight longhands, each of which becomes a per-layer list; multiple backgrounds paint front to back; background-color: belongs only to the last layer — all measured.
  • background-image:, background-repeat:, background-position:, background-size:, background-attachment:, background-origin: and background-clip: are the longhands; background-clip: text needs a transparent color, and a shorthand written after any of them silently resets it — measured twice.
  • linear-gradient(), radial-gradient(), conic-gradient() and the repeating gradient family are <image> values; the double-position color stop syntax makes hard edges — measured expanding to four stops — and gradient interpolation with in oklch and the hue keywords is preserved in the computed value.
  • border-radius: takes horizontal and vertical radii separated by a slash — measured as 10px 30px for one corner — corner-shape: changes the curve itself (measured as bevel), and border-image: is the only route to a gradient border.
  • box-shadow: layers, takes a spread that makes a ring, and does not follow alpha — that is filter: drop-shadow()'s job; text-shadow: keeps text legible over photographs.
  • The filter property applies functions in order and backdrop-filter: applies them to what is behind; both create a stacking context and a containing block for fixed descendants.
  • mix-blend-mode: and background-blend-mode: apply the sixteen blend mode keywords, scoped by the stacking context.
  • clip-path: cuts to a basic shape — polygon(), circle(), ellipse(), inset() — and mask-image: does the same with a per-pixel alpha, which makes a gradient fade one declaration.

Exercises

1. A design system defines a nine-step accent ramp. The first attempt uses hsl() with lightness from 95% down to 15% in even steps; the designer says the middle looks wrong and the light end is "all the same". Explain the mechanism and rewrite the ramp.

Solution

The mechanism: hsl()'s lightness is a coordinate, not a perception.

HSL is a simple geometric transformation of the RGB cube. Its L is the midpoint between the largest and smallest RGB channel, which has no relationship to how bright a colour looks. Concretely, hsl(60 100% 50%) (yellow) and hsl(240 100% 50%) (blue) have identical declared lightness and differ by roughly a factor of ten in perceived luminance.

Two consequences follow, and they are exactly the two complaints:

  • The light end compresses. Between L: 95% and L: 85% there is very little perceptual difference, because near the top of the HSL cylinder the colour is approaching white along a curve that flattens. Ten percentage points at the light end are worth far less than ten in the middle.
  • The middle is uneven across hues. If the ramp's hue shifts at all — and most do, to keep the darks from going muddy — the perceived lightness jumps, because a hue change is a lightness change in HSL.

The rewrite in Oklch, where equal numeric steps are equal perceptual steps by construction:

:root {
  --accent-h: 265;
  --accent-50:  oklch(97% 0.02 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-100: oklch(93% 0.04 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-200: oklch(86% 0.07 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-300: oklch(77% 0.11 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-400: oklch(68% 0.16 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-500: oklch(58% 0.20 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-600: oklch(50% 0.19 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-700: oklch(42% 0.16 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-800: oklch(34% 0.13 var(--accent-h));
  --accent-900: oklch(26% 0.09 var(--accent-h));
}

Three things this buys beyond evenness.

The lightness numbers are now portable across hues: swapping --accent-h to 145 gives a green ramp with the same perceived steps, which the HSL version could not do — that is the whole reason to factor the hue into a custom property.

The chroma curve is deliberate rather than accidental. It rises to a peak in the middle and falls at both ends, because maximum chroma is only achievable at mid lightness; holding chroma constant would push the light and dark ends out of gamut.

And out-of-gamut values are safe. §11.3 measured that a browser stores an out-of-gamut oklch() verbatim and does gamut mapping at paint time, so a P3 display gets a more saturated --accent-500 than an sRGB one from the same declaration. Hand-clamping to sRGB would throw that away.

Generate the ramp rather than typing it, once the pattern is clear:

@property --l { syntax: "<percentage>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 50%; }
.step { --c: oklch(var(--l) var(--chroma) var(--accent-h)); }

2. A card should have a gradient border, rounded corners, and a frosted-glass background over the page's photograph. The first attempt uses border-image and backdrop-filter and comes out with square corners and no visible frosting. Diagnose both and write a version that works.

Solution

Symptom one: border-image ignores border-radius. This is specified behaviour, not a bug. border-image slices an image into nine pieces and paints them along the border box's rectangular edges; there is no mechanism in it for following a curve. When border-image-source is anything but none, the radius is simply not applied to the border, and the corners come out square.

Symptom two: backdrop-filter needs something to show through. It filters what is behind the element and then paints the element's own background on top. With an opaque background the filtered result is completely covered, and with no background at all there is nothing to distinguish it — either way you see no frosting. It also does nothing if the element is not composited separately, which in practice means it needs a background at all.

A version that works, using a masked pseudo-element for the border:

.card {
  position: relative;
  border-radius: 1rem;
  padding: 1.5rem;
  background: color-mix(in oklab, Canvas 60%, transparent);
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.4);
  isolation: isolate;
}

.card::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  border-radius: inherit;
  padding: 2px;                       /* the border thickness */
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, var(--accent-400), var(--accent-800));
  mask: linear-gradient(black, black) content-box exclude,
        linear-gradient(black, black);
  pointer-events: none;
}

@supports not (mask: linear-gradient(black, black) content-box exclude) {
  .card { border: 2px solid var(--accent-500); }
}

How each piece earns its place.

The pseudo-element is a full-size box with border-radius: inherit, filled with the gradient. The two-layer mask then punches out its middle: the first layer is clipped to the content box and excluded, the second covers everything, so what survives is the 2px padding ring — a gradient border that follows the radius exactly. This is §11.13's masking used for geometry rather than for a fade.

The background is color-mix(in oklab, Canvas 60%, transparent) rather than a hardcoded rgb(255 255 255 / 0.6). Two reasons: it is partly transparent, which is what makes backdrop-filter visible at all; and it is built from the system Canvas colour, so it inverts correctly in dark mode and survives forced-colours mode (§15.12).

isolation: isolate (§10.9) confines any blending inside the card. backdrop-filter already creates a stacking context, so this is belt-and-braces, but it makes the intent explicit.

Two things to add before shipping. @media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) should replace the frosting with an opaque background — the effect is a genuine accessibility problem for some readers (§15.11). And backdrop-filter is expensive: it re-reads and re-filters the composited content behind the element every frame, so a page with twenty of these will drop frames on a mid-range phone. §16.12 covers measuring it.

3. Explain why each of these does not do what its author intended, with the mechanism, and give the fix.

.a { background-clip: content-box; background: rebeccapurple; }
.b { background: linear-gradient(red, transparent); }
.c { background: url("hero.jpg"), linear-gradient(black, black); }
.d { box-shadow: 0 4px 8px black; }   /* on a transparent PNG logo */
Solution

.a — the shorthand reset the longhand. §3.12's rule, measured twice in this section: a shorthand sets every longhand it covers, including the ones it does not mention. background covers background-clip, does not name it, and therefore resets it to border-box. Measured, exactly this pair produced background-clip: border-box, and the same happened to background-origin in the companion case.

.a { background: rebeccapurple; background-clip: content-box; }

The order is the whole fix. The general habit: never write background after any background-* longhand, in any rule, any file or any layer — the ordering that makes it safe is not visible from the declaration you are editing.

.b — transparent is transparent black. The keyword is defined as rgb(0 0 0 / 0), so a gradient from red to transparent interpolates both the alpha and the colour, passing through semi-transparent dark grey. The result is a red that visibly dirties as it fades, which is not what "fade out" means to anyone.

.b { background: linear-gradient(red, rgb(255 0 0 / 0)); }
/* or, better: */
.b { background: linear-gradient(in oklab, red, transparent); }

The first form fades to a transparent red, so the hue never changes. The second sidesteps it differently: interpolating in Oklab handles the premultiplied alpha sensibly and does not route through grey. Either is fine; the bug is only in the sRGB-plus-transparent combination.

.c — background layers paint front to back. Measured in §11.7: the first layer in the list is on top. So this declaration puts the photograph above the black gradient, and the gradient — presumably intended as a darkening scrim for text legibility — is entirely hidden behind it.

.c { background: linear-gradient(rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5), rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5)), url("hero.jpg"); }

Scrim first, image second. Note the scrim also needed an alpha to be a scrim rather than a solid black rectangle — the original linear-gradient(black, black) is fully opaque, so even in the right order it would have hidden the photograph completely.

.d — box-shadow is drawn from the border box, not from the content's alpha. The shadow of a transparent PNG logo is a rectangle, because box-shadow knows only about the element's box. That is correct and specified; it is simply the wrong tool.

.d { filter: drop-shadow(0 4px 8px black); }

drop-shadow() operates on the rendered image's alpha channel, so it follows the logo's actual silhouette — and it works equally on an inline SVG, a clipped element (clip-path, §11.13) and text. The trade-offs: it is a filter, so it creates a stacking context and a containing block for fixed descendants (§10.5); it takes no spread; and it is more expensive to paint. For a rectangular card, box-shadow remains the right choice.

SECTION 12

Typography, Text and Generated Content

Most of what a reader experiences on a page is type. Not the layout, not the colour system — the words, their size, their spacing, and whether the lines are comfortable to move between. CSS's typographic controls are far better than they were, and they are also the part of the language most people learn least of, because a page looks acceptable with three declarations and it takes twenty to look considered.

This section is those twenty. It also covers the two mechanisms that generate text rather than styling it — counters and the content property — because a numbered heading system, a stepped list and a quotation mark that changes with the language are all typography that CSS can produce without touching the markup.

Everything measured below was measured, and one of the measurements is the cleanest demonstration in the course of why shorthands are dangerous.

12.1 The Font Stack

font-family: takes a comma-separated list, tried left to right, with a generic family as the last resort. The five original generics are serif, sans-serif, monospace, cursive and fantasy; the useful modern additions are system-ui, ui-serif, ui-sans-serif, ui-monospace and ui-rounded, which resolve to the platform's own interface faces.

Measured, all resolving cleanly:

font-family: system-ui               ->  system-ui
font-family: ui-monospace, monospace ->  ui-monospace, monospace
font-family: ui-serif                ->  ui-serif

Two font stacks worth having as a baseline. A system stack, which costs zero bytes and matches the platform:

:root { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
code, pre { font-family: ui-monospace, "SF Mono", "Cascadia Code", Menlo, monospace; }

And a web-font stack whose fallback has similar metrics, so the swap in §12.6 does not reflow the page:

:root { font-family: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif; }

Quote a family name whenever it contains spaces or could be read as a keyword. font-family: Times New Roman happens to work because CSS joins unquoted identifiers, but font-family: "Times New Roman" is what you should write.

In summary, the vocabulary here is generic family.

12.2 Size, Weight, Style and Width

font-size: takes a length, a percentage of the parent's size, or one of the absolute keywords (small through xx-large) and relative keywords (smaller, larger). §4.3 covered the units; the rule that matters is to use rem for anything that should honour the reader's browser setting, and never a bare viewport unit.

font-weight: takes 1–1000, or normal (400), bold (700), lighter and bolder. Variable fonts (§12.7) make the whole range real rather than a set of buckets.

font-style: takes normal, italic and oblique <angle>. The difference is not cosmetic: italic selects a separate, redrawn face, and oblique slants the upright one. If the family has a true italic, ask for italic.

font-width: (formerly font-stretch) takes a percentage or the keywords from ultra-condensed to ultra-expanded.

font-synthesis: controls what the browser is allowed to fake. Measured, the default is:

font-synthesis = weight style small-caps

So a family with no bold face gets an algorithmically emboldened one, and one with no italic gets a slanted one. Both look poor next to real cut faces. font-synthesis: none turns that off, which is the right choice when you have loaded the real weights and want a missing one to be visible rather than faked.

What to carry forward from this subsection: font-width:.

12.3 The font Shorthand, Measured

font: sets font-style, font-variant, font-weight, font-width, font-size, line-height and font-family in one declaration — and, per §3.12, resets every one it does not mention. It is the most destructive shorthand in CSS, and here it is doing it:

.a { font-weight: 700; font-style: italic; font: 16px/1.4 Georgia, serif; }

weight = 400    style = normal    family = Georgia, serif

Both of the first two declarations were wiped by a shorthand that never mentions weight or style. Applied to a <strong> or an <h2>, this is how a heading silently stops being bold.

font has exactly one form worth writing, and it is the one that resets deliberately:

button, input, select, textarea { font: inherit; }

§1.7 measured why: a <button>'s font-size is 13.3333px and does not inherit from the page. font: inherit is a single declaration that fixes size, family, weight, style and line-height together, and its resetting behaviour is exactly what is wanted. Everywhere else, write the longhands.

12.4 Line Height, Measure and Spacing

Three numbers decide whether a paragraph is comfortable, and they interact.

line-height: should be unitless, for the reason §3.9 measured and this one confirms:

body { font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.5; }
h1   { font-size: 40px; }

h1 line-height = 60px

The number inherited, and the heading multiplied it by its own 40px. A 24px on body would have inherited as 24px and made the heading's lines overlap. Note also that the right number is not constant: 1.5 is comfortable for 16px body text and far too loose for a 40px heading, which wants about 1.1. Declare both.

Measure — the line length — is the number people neglect. The readable range is roughly 45–75 characters, and §4.3's ch unit expresses it directly:

.prose { max-inline-size: 65ch; }

letter-spacing: and word-spacing: take a length, and a negative one is legal. The rule of thumb that is actually true: large type needs slightly negative tracking and small or all-caps type needs positive.

h1 { font-size: 3rem; line-height: 1.05; letter-spacing: -0.02em; }
.eyebrow { font-size: 0.75rem; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.08em; }

Use em rather than px here so the tracking scales with the type.

The terms above, gathered: letter-spacing: and word-spacing:.

12.5 Alignment, Indentation and Case

text-align: takes start, end, left, right, center, justify and match-parent. Prefer start/end — they follow the writing direction, so a right-to-left page is correct with no extra rules (§15.5).

Justified text on the web is usually a mistake. Browsers have no hyphenation dictionary applied by default and only crude spacing control, so text-align: justify produces rivers of white space at narrow widths. If you want it, pair it with hyphens: auto and text-wrap: pretty, and check it at a phone width.

text-indent: indents the first line, and accepts hanging (indent every line but the first) and each-line. text-transform: takes uppercase, lowercase, capitalize, full-width and math-auto.

One caution about text-transform: uppercase: it changes appearance, not content. A screen reader announces the underlying text, which is right — but it means an acronym you uppercased visually is still announced as written, and a heading rendered in caps is still copied in its original case. That is the correct behaviour and worth knowing before you rely on it either way.

One line each, for reference: text-indent: and text-wrap: pretty.

12.6 @font-face and Loading

@font-face declares a font the browser should fetch. Its contents are at-rule descriptors (§1.2), not properties:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-var.woff2") format("woff2-variations");
  font-weight: 100 900;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
  unicode-range: U+0000-00FF, U+2000-206F;
  size-adjust: 100%;
}
src descriptor
A comma-separated list of sources, tried in order, each with an optional format() and tech() so the browser can skip one it cannot use without downloading it.
font-display:
auto, block, swap, fallback, optional. §12.6 below.
unicode-range:
Which code points this file covers. The browser downloads it only if the page uses one — which is what makes subsetting effective.
size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override, line-gap-override
Rewrite a fallback font's metrics to match the web font, so the swap causes no reflow.

font-display: is the descriptor that decides what the reader sees while the font loads, and it is worth choosing rather than defaulting:

  • block — invisible text for up to three seconds, then fallback, then swap. Never right for body text.
  • swap — fallback immediately, swap whenever the font arrives. Text is always readable; the swap can be jarring late.
  • fallback — a very short block, then fallback, and swap only if the font arrives within about three seconds. A good default for body text.
  • optional — a very short block, then fallback, and no swap at all this page load. The best choice for performance and for avoiding layout shift entirely.

Pair whichever you choose with the metric overrides. A fallback whose size-adjust and ascent-override match the web font occupies the same space, so the swap is invisible and contributes nothing to Cumulative Layout Shift.

Font loading from JavaScript — document.fonts.ready, new FontFace() — is the escape hatch for anything the descriptors cannot express; the platform APIs belong to the JavaScript course.

Formats: ship woff2 and nothing else. Every browser that matters has supported it for years, and it compresses better than anything before it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: src descriptor, unicode-range:, subsetting and font loading.

12.7 Variable Fonts

A variable font contains a continuous design space rather than a set of static cuts, with named axes. The registered axes are wght, wdth, slnt, ital and opsz; a family may define any number of custom ones.

The high-level properties map onto the axes: font-weight drives wght, font-width drives wdth, font-style: oblique <angle> drives slnt, and font-optical-sizing drives opsz. Use those wherever they suffice — they inherit properly and animate properly.

font-variation-settings: is the low-level escape hatch for custom axes. Measured:

.d { font-variation-settings: "wght" 650, "wdth" 90; }

"wdth" 90, "wght" 650

Note the serialisation sorts the axes. Two cautions: font-variation-settings does not compose with font-weight — the low-level setting wins, and mixing the two produces confusion — and because it is a single property, setting one axis in one rule and another elsewhere means the second replaces the first.

font-optical-sizing: is on by default where an opsz axis exists, and it is one of the few typographic features that genuinely improves rendering for free: the font uses a slightly heavier, more open drawing at small sizes. Measured turning off cleanly with none, which is occasionally wanted when you are animating size.

A single variable font file often replaces six or eight static files and is smaller than three of them. The break-even is around three weights.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: font-variation-settings: and font-optical-sizing:.

12.8 OpenType Features

A font carries OpenType features — alternate glyph sets the renderer can switch on. CSS exposes the common ones as high-level properties and all of them through a low-level one.

font-variant-numeric: is the one with everyday value. Measured:

.a { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums slashed-zero; }

tabular-nums slashed-zero

tabular-nums gives every digit the same advance width, so a column of numbers lines up and a live-updating counter does not jitter. Put it on every table of figures, every price, and every timer. slashed-zero disambiguates 0 from O. The rest of the family is oldstyle-nums, lining-nums, proportional-nums, diagonal-fractions, stacked-fractions and ordinal.

font-variant-ligatures: controls the ligature sets. no-common-ligatures is worth knowing for the one real case: a monospace code font whose != and => ligatures are unwanted in a beginner's course, where seeing the actual characters matters.

font-variant: is the shorthand for the whole family below and takes normal, none or any combination of their values; the longhands are what you should usually write. font-variant-caps: gives real small-caps where the font has them and synthesised ones otherwise (§12.2's font-synthesis governs that). font-kerning: takes auto, normal and none.

font-feature-settings: is the low-level route, taking four-character feature tags:

.b { font-feature-settings: "ss01" 1, "liga" 0; }

"liga" 0, "ss01"

Note that a value of 1 is dropped in serialisation, since it is the default when a tag is named. As with font-variation-settings, it does not compose with the high-level properties — prefer them and reach for this only for stylistic sets (ss01–ss20) and character variants (cv01–cv99), which have no high-level equivalent.

font-size-adjust: normalises the x-height across fallback fonts, so a fallback with a smaller x-height is scaled up to look the same size. Measured accepting both a number and from-font, which takes the value from the first font in the stack — the form to use, since it needs no hand-measured constant.

To have in hand before moving on: font-feature-settings:, font-variant:, font-variant-ligatures:, font-variant-numeric:, font-variant-caps:, font-kerning: and font-size-adjust:.

12.9 Wrapping, Breaking and Hyphenation

Six properties decide where a line may break, and they are frequently confused. Measured values first, then what each is for:

text-wrap: balance          ->  balance
text-wrap: pretty           ->  pretty
text-wrap-mode: nowrap      ->  nowrap
hyphens: auto               ->  auto
word-break: break-all       ->  break-all
overflow-wrap: anywhere     ->  anywhere
line-break: strict          ->  strict
white-space-collapse: preserve -> preserve
text-wrap:
balance evens the line lengths of a short block — use it on headings and pull quotes, where it removes the one-word last line. pretty avoids orphans and bad rag over a longer block, at a small layout cost. stable keeps earlier lines fixed while a user types.
overflow-wrap:
break-word and anywhere break a word only when it would otherwise overflow. This is the safe one, and the right answer for user-supplied content and URLs.
word-break:
break-all breaks anywhere, always, even when the word would have fitted on the next line. Almost never what you want for Latin text; correct for CJK. keep-all is the opposite and is for Korean.
hyphens:
auto uses the browser's dictionary — and requires a lang attribute, because the dictionary is per language. manual (the default) honours &shy; only.
white-space:
The old shorthand. Its longhands white-space-collapse: and text-wrap-mode: separate the two things it conflated: whether whitespace collapses, and whether lines wrap.

The overflow-wrap versus word-break distinction is the one that matters most, and the mnemonic is: overflow-wrap breaks a word as a last resort; word-break: break-all breaks it as a first resort. For a comment field that might contain a 200-character URL, overflow-wrap: anywhere is right and word-break: break-all will mangle every ordinary sentence.

hyphenate-limit-chars: constrains hyphenation — measured accepting 6 3, meaning "only words of 6+ characters, leaving at least 3 before the hyphen" — which removes hyphenation's worst results.

tab-size: sets the width of a tab character in a <pre>, in characters or a length. The browser default of 8 is almost never what a code sample wants.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: white-space:, line-break: and tab-size:.

12.10 Decoration

text-decoration: is the shorthand for four longhands, and the longhands are where the quality is. Measured:

.a { text-decoration: underline wavy red 2px; }
.b { text-decoration-line: underline; text-decoration-thickness: from-font;
     text-underline-offset: 0.2em; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; }

a:  line=underline  style=wavy  color=rgb(255,0,0)  thickness=2px  offset=auto  skip=auto
b:  line=underline  style=solid color=rgb(0,0,0)    thickness=from-font offset=3.2px skip=none

text-decoration-line: takes underline, overline, line-through, blink (ignored) and none. text-decoration-thickness: takes a length, a percentage of the font size, auto, or from-font — which uses the value the font designer specified and is the right default. text-underline-offset: moves the line away from the baseline; measured, 0.2em at 16px resolved to 3.2px. text-decoration-skip-ink: decides whether the underline breaks around descenders, and auto (the default) is right for prose while none is sometimes wanted for a deliberately heavy underline.

The practical recipe for a link underline that looks designed rather than defaulted:

a {
  text-decoration-thickness: from-font;
  text-underline-offset: 0.15em;
}
a:hover { text-decoration-thickness: 0.12em; }

Do not remove link underlines in body text. Colour alone is not a sufficient indicator (§15.13), and an underline is the only affordance a link has in a paragraph.

text-shadow: belongs here too (§11.10), as does ::first-letter and ::first-line styling (§2.13).

In summary, the vocabulary here is text-decoration-line:, text-decoration-thickness: and text-underline-offset:.

12.11 Trimming the Box: text-box-trim
