A line of text sits inside a box that is taller than the letters, by the font's ascent and descent. That extra space is why a heading with padding: 1rem never looks like it has exactly 1rem above it, and why designers' spacing values never quite match what the browser produces.

text-box-trim: removes it. Measured working:

.a { text-box-trim: trim-both; text-box-edge: cap alphabetic; }

text-box-trim = trim-both     text-box-edge = cap alphabetic

trim-both removes the space above and below; text-box-edge: cap alphabetic says to trim to the cap height at the top and the alphabetic baseline at the bottom. The result is a box whose edges are the letters, so a margin of 1rem is visually 1rem.

This is the single most useful new typography property for anyone implementing a design, because it eliminates the "the spacing is 4px off and nobody knows why" conversation. Support is not universal — treat it as an enhancement, since a browser without it simply keeps the leading.

initial-letter: does the classic drop cap properly, sinking the letter a given number of lines rather than faking it with a float and a line-height. Measured accepting 3 2 — three lines tall, sinking two.

.article > p:first-of-type::first-letter {
  initial-letter: 3 2;
  margin-inline-end: 0.1em;
  font-weight: 700;
}

Multi-line truncation is the one gap. The standard line-clamp: property is specified but was measured as not supported in the browser used throughout this course:

CSS.supports("line-clamp", "3")   ->   false

So the working recipe is still the prefixed one, and it is worth writing with the standard property alongside so that the page improves when support arrives:

.clamp {
  display: -webkit-box;
  -webkit-box-orient: vertical;
  -webkit-line-clamp: 3;
  line-clamp: 3;
  overflow: hidden;
}

What to carry forward from this subsection: text-box-trim: and initial-letter:.

12.12 Generated Content

The content property on ::before and ::after generates content that is not in the document (§2.12). Beyond a plain string it accepts:

.tag::before      { content: "#"; }
.ext::after       { content: " ↗" / ""; }          /* with alt text        */
.label::after     { content: attr(data-unit); }     /* from an attribute    */
.icon::before     { content: url("/i/check.svg"); } /* an image             */
blockquote::before{ content: open-quote; }          /* driven by `quotes`   */
.step::before     { content: "Step " counter(step) ": "; }

quotes: sets the marks open-quote and close-quote produce, and it is per language:

:lang(en) { quotes: "\201C" "\201D" "\2018" "\2019"; }
:lang(fr) { quotes: "«\00A0" "\00A0»" "\2039\00A0" "\00A0\203A"; }

Two pairs: the outer marks and the nested ones. The browser tracks nesting depth for you, which is why this is worth doing rather than typing the characters into the markup.

The / "" alternative-text syntax from §2.12 applies to all of these and should be used whenever the content is decorative.

The terms above, gathered: quotes:.

12.13 Counters

A CSS counter is a named integer maintained per element and scoped to a subtree. Three properties drive it:

ol.steps {
  counter-reset: step;      /* create it, at 0 (or a given value) */
  list-style: none;
  padding-inline-start: 0;
}
ol.steps > li { counter-increment: step; }
ol.steps > li::before { content: "Step " counter(step) ": "; }

counter-reset: creates or resets a counter on an element and its subtree; counter-increment: adds to it (a negative value subtracts); counter-set: assigns directly without creating a new nesting level.

counter() renders one counter; counters() renders the whole nesting chain with a separator, which is how you get 1.2.3 numbering with no arithmetic:

ol.outline           { counter-reset: item; list-style: none; }
ol.outline > li      { counter-increment: item; }
ol.outline > li::before { content: counters(item, ".") " "; }

Both take an optional second argument naming a counter style, so counter(step, upper-roman) gives IV.

A tooling note, because it will confuse you in developer tools: getComputedStyle(el, '::before').content returns the unevaluated value. Measured, two different list items both reported:

content = "Step " counter(step) ": "

The counters are resolved at render time, not at computed-value time, so the computed value is identical for every item and the panel cannot show you the rendered number. Read the page, not the panel.

Counters are presentational. A screen reader may or may not announce generated content, and support varies. If the numbering carries meaning, use a real <ol> — the numbers then come from the element rather than from CSS, and counter-increment is only there to restyle them.

One line each, for reference: counter-reset: and counter-increment:.

12.14 Lists, Markers and @counter-style

list-style: is the shorthand for list-style-type:, list-style-position: and list-style-image:. Measured:

list-style: disc inside url(none)   ->   type=disc   position=inside

list-style-position: inside puts the marker in the content flow so that wrapped lines align under the text rather than under the marker; outside (the default) hangs it in the margin.

::marker styles the bullet or number directly, accepting font properties, color and content. Measured:

li::marker { color: red; }

marker color = rgb(255, 0, 0)

That is a considerable improvement on the old technique of list-style: none plus a ::before, because the marker keeps its semantics.

@counter-style defines a marker system of your own, with descriptors rather than properties:

@counter-style thumbs {
  system: cyclic;
  symbols: "\1F44D";
  suffix: " ";
}
ul.approved { list-style: thumbs; }

list-style-type = thumbs

The system descriptor takes cyclic, numeric, alphabetic, symbolic, additive, fixed and extends. additive is how Roman numerals work, and extends lets you take a built-in style and change only its suffix — which is the cheapest way to get 1) instead of 1..

One accessibility rule that belongs here and is developed in §15.14: list-style: none on a <ul> can remove the list semantics in some browser and screen reader combinations, so a list styled that way should carry role="list" explicitly.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: list-style-type: and list-style-image:.

12.15 Fluid Typography and Scales

Fluid typography uses clamp() (§4.9) to interpolate a size between two viewport widths, with a floor and a ceiling:

:root {
  --step--1: clamp(0.83rem, 0.80rem + 0.16vw, 0.94rem);
  --step-0:  clamp(1.00rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.13rem);
  --step-1:  clamp(1.20rem, 1.12rem + 0.40vw, 1.41rem);
  --step-2:  clamp(1.44rem, 1.32rem + 0.60vw, 1.76rem);
  --step-3:  clamp(1.73rem, 1.55rem + 0.90vw, 2.20rem);
}
h1 { font-size: var(--step-3); line-height: 1.1; letter-spacing: -0.02em; }
p  { font-size: var(--step-0); line-height: 1.6; }

Two things make that set coherent rather than arbitrary. The sizes come from a type scale — a constant ratio between steps, here 1.2 — which §4.10's pow() can compute directly:

--ratio: 1.2;
--step-2: calc(1rem * pow(var(--ratio), 2));

And every clamp() has a rem term in its preferred value, which is what keeps it zoomable (§4.9). A scale built on bare vw values ignores the reader's font-size setting entirely.

For a component that should respond to its container rather than the viewport, swap vw for cqi (§4.5) — a card in a sidebar then sets its own type size from the sidebar's width, which is what §13.11 argues is usually the better question.

12.16 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • font-family: is a font stack ending in a generic family; system font keywords (system-ui, ui-serif, ui-monospace) cost no bytes.
  • font-size:, font-weight:, font-style: and font-width: set the four axes; font-synthesis: defaults to weight style small-caps — measured — and should be none once the real faces are loaded.
  • font: resets everything it does not mention: measured wiping a declared font-weight: 700 and font-style: italic to 400 and normal. Its one good use is font: inherit on form controls.
  • line-height: must be unitless — measured inheriting into a 40px heading as 60px — and letter-spacing: and word-spacing: should be written in em.
  • text-align: should use start/end; text-indent: and text-transform: change appearance, not content.
  • @font-face takes descriptors: the src descriptor, font-display:, unicode-range: for subsetting, and the metric overrides that make a swap shift-free; ship woff2 only.
  • A variable font exposes axes through font-weight, font-width and font-optical-sizing:, with font-variation-settings: as the low-level route — measured, and it does not compose with the high-level properties.
  • font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums stops figures jittering; font-variant-ligatures:, font-variant-caps:, font-kerning:, font-feature-settings: and font-size-adjust: complete the opentype feature controls.
  • overflow-wrap: breaks a word as a last resort and word-break: as a first; hyphens: auto needs a lang attribute; text-wrap: balance suits headings and pretty suits prose; white-space: splits into white-space-collapse: and text-wrap-mode:; line-break: and tab-size: complete the set — all measured.
  • text-decoration: splits into text-decoration-line:, text-decoration-style:, text-decoration-color:, text-decoration-thickness: (from-font) and text-underline-offset: — measured resolving 0.2em to 3.2px.
  • text-box-trim: removes the leading above and below a line so spacing matches the design — measured — and initial-letter: sinks a drop cap; line-clamp: is specified but measured unsupported, so the prefixed recipe is still required.
  • The content property takes strings, attr(), url(), open-quote and counter(); quotes: sets the marks per language.
  • counter-reset:, counter-increment:, counter() and counters() generate numbering; the computed value of content shows the unevaluated expression — measured — and counters are presentational, so meaningful numbering belongs in an <ol>.
  • list-style:, list-style-type:, list-style-position: and list-style-image: control markers; ::marker styles them directly — measured — and @counter-style defines new ones with system, symbols and suffix.
  • Fluid typography is clamp() per step of a type scale, each with a rem term so it stays zoomable, and cqi in place of vw when the container is the right reference.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: system font.

Exercises

1. A component library ships .btn { font: 500 0.875rem/1 system-ui, sans-serif; }. A consumer reports that <button class="btn"><strong>Save</strong></button> renders the word unbolded, and that setting font-style: italic on .btn--quote has no effect. Explain and fix.

Solution

Both are §12.3's shorthand reset, and the second one has an extra wrinkle.

The unbolded <strong>. font is a shorthand for seven properties, and it resets every one it does not name — measured directly in §12.3, where font-weight: 700; font-style: italic; font: 16px/1.4 Georgia, serif came back as weight = 400, style = normal. Here the declaration does name a weight (500), so .btn itself is fine.

The problem is that font-weight is an inherited property, and the <strong> inside inherits 500 from the button — and then the user-agent stylesheet's strong { font-weight: bolder } applies. bolder is relative: it moves one step up from the inherited value, and from 500 that step lands at 700… on a family that has a 700 face. With system-ui on a platform whose UI font has only 400 and 600, bolder from 500 resolves to 600, which next to 500 is nearly indistinguishable. The text is not "unbolded"; it is bolded by an amount too small to see.

The ineffective font-style: italic. If .btn--quote is written before .btn in the stylesheet, or in an earlier layer, then .btn's font shorthand wins on the cascade and resets font-style to normal. The consumer's declaration is not lost to specificity — it is lost to a shorthand that never mentions the property.

The fix — do not use font for this at all:

.btn {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  font-size: 0.875rem;
  font-weight: 500;
  line-height: 1;
}
.btn strong, .btn b { font-weight: 700; }

Longhands mean a consumer's font-style: italic survives, and a later font-weight override survives, because nothing is resetting properties it does not name.

Two refinements worth adding.

Use an absolute weight for the nested emphasis rather than relying on bolder, since bolder's result depends on the inherited value and on which faces the family actually has — two variables, neither under the library's control.

And consider whether the button should carry font: inherit instead (§12.3). That is the one legitimate use of the shorthand: form controls do not inherit page typography — §1.7 measured a <button> at 13.3333px regardless of the page — and font: inherit fixes family, size, weight, style and line-height in one declaration, with its resetting behaviour being exactly what is wanted. A button that inherits the page's type and then adjusts only font-weight is more predictable than one that declares its own stack.

2. A pricing table's figures jitter as they update, the currency column does not align, and one long product name overflows its cell. Write the typography fixes and explain each.

Solution 
.pricing td.figure {
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums slashed-zero;
  text-align: end;
  font-feature-settings: "zero" 1;   /* only if the family lacks slashed-zero support */
}

.pricing td.name {
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
  hyphens: auto;
  hyphenate-limit-chars: 8 4;
}

.pricing { table-layout: fixed; inline-size: 100%; }
.pricing td.name { inline-size: 60%; }

The jitter is proportional figures. In most proportional fonts a 1 is narrower than a 0, so a number that changes from £1,111 to £8,888 changes width, and everything after it moves. font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums switches the font to its fixed-advance figure set (§12.8, measured applying cleanly), giving every digit the same width. This is the single most valuable OpenType feature for interfaces, and it belongs on every live counter, timer, table of figures and price.

slashed-zero is a smaller win in the same declaration: it distinguishes 0 from O, which matters in an order reference or a product code more than in a price.

The alignment is text-align. Figures align on the right (or, correctly, at the end), so that the units, tens and hundreds line up in columns. text-align: end rather than right so a right-to-left locale is correct with no extra rule (§15.5). Note that tabular-nums and text-align: end are doing different halves of the job — one makes the digits equal width, the other puts the columns in the same place — and both are needed.

The overflow is a break-opportunity problem. A long product name with no spaces (or one long word) has no break opportunity, so the line cannot wrap and the cell overflows.

overflow-wrap: anywhere is the right property, not word-break: break-all. §12.9's distinction: overflow-wrap breaks a word only when it would otherwise overflow, leaving ordinary sentences alone; word-break: break-all breaks every line at the exact character where it runs out of room, so "Wireless Charging Pad" becomes "Wireless Chargin/g Pad". For a table of product names — mostly ordinary words with one pathological entry — overflow-wrap is correct.

hyphens: auto improves the result further, and it requires a lang attribute on the document or the element, because the hyphenation dictionary is per language. hyphenate-limit-chars: 8 4 (measured accepting this form) stops the browser hyphenating short words and leaving one or two characters stranded.

table-layout: fixed is the structural half. §7.13 measured it: auto sized two cells at 16/89 from their content while fixed gave 150/150 from the first row. Without it, the browser sizes columns from the widest content, so one long name widens the column even after it can wrap — the wrapping fix would appear not to work.

3. Build a numbered specification-style document: sections numbered 1, 2, subsections 1.1, 1.2, and a "Note:" prefix on any <aside>. Do it in CSS with no numbers in the markup, then state the honest limitation of that approach.

Solution 
body { counter-reset: section; }

h2 {
  counter-increment: section;
  counter-reset: subsection;      /* restart at each new section */
}
h2::before { content: counter(section) ". "; }

h3 { counter-increment: subsection; }
h3::before { content: counter(section) "." counter(subsection) " "; }

aside::before {
  content: "Note: ";
  font-weight: 700;
}

For arbitrary nesting depth, counters() replaces the hand-built chain and needs no per-level rule:

ol.outline { counter-reset: item; list-style: none; padding-inline-start: 1.5em; }
ol.outline > li { counter-increment: item; }
ol.outline > li::before { content: counters(item, ".") "  "; margin-inline-start: -1.5em; }

counters() walks the whole nesting chain of a counter and joins it with the separator, so a list four levels deep prints 1.2.3.1 from a single rule (§12.13).

The counter-reset: subsection on h2 is the load-bearing line, and it is the part people miss. Setting a counter on an element creates a new instance scoped to that element and its following siblings, so declaring it on h2 restarts subsection numbering at every section. Declaring it on body instead would number the subsections 1.1, 1.2, 2.3, 2.4 — continuing across sections, which is almost never wanted.

The honest limitation: this numbering is presentational, and it is not reliably in the accessibility tree.

Generated content's exposure to assistive technology varies by browser and by screen reader, and content on a ::before is not text in the document — it cannot be selected, it is not copied when a reader copies the heading, it does not appear in the page's text when the CSS fails to load, and it is not searchable with the browser's find-in-page in every engine. A specification whose clause numbers are how people refer to the document has just made its most important identifiers invisible to half the ways people use it.

There is also a related trap in the same family (§12.14): styling a list with list-style: none can remove the list semantics entirely in some browser and screen-reader combinations, which is why that pattern needs an explicit role="list".

So: use CSS counters for numbering that is genuinely decorative — a step indicator, a figure count, a decorative outline — and put numbering that carries meaning in the markup, where an <ol> gives you real, announced, copyable, searchable numbers. In that case CSS's job shrinks to ::marker styling (§12.14), which keeps the semantics and gives you the typography:

ol.spec > li::marker { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; font-weight: 600; }

That is the version I would ship for anything a reader might cite.

SECTION 13

Media Queries, Container Queries and Feature Queries

For fifteen years, "responsive" meant one thing: ask the viewport how wide it is and change the layout. That model has two flaws that were always there and became unavoidable once components started being reused. A component cannot know how much space it was given — only how big the window is. And a page cannot ask whether a feature exists — only whether the window is a certain size, which is a proxy for nothing.

Both are now fixed. Container queries ask about the space an element actually has, feature queries ask what the browser supports, and style queries ask what an ancestor's tokens say. Media queries are still essential, but they have shrunk to the job they are actually good at: asking about the device and the reader, which is a much more interesting question than asking about pixels.

Every query in this section was evaluated in a real browser.

13.1 What Responsive Design Is For

Responsive web design is usually described as "the layout adapts to the screen". That framing has produced twenty years of stylesheets full of arbitrary pixel numbers.

A better framing, and the one this section works from: a page should be usable under every combination of conditions the reader brings. Those conditions include the window size, and also: whether they can hover, whether they have asked for less motion, whether their system is in dark mode or forced-colours mode, whether they have zoomed to 200%, whether the component is in a sidebar or a full-width region, and whether the browser supports the feature you used.

CSS has a query for every one of those, and most of them are not about width.

To have in hand before moving on: responsive web design.

13.2 The Viewport Meta Tag

Nothing below works without this line, and it is HTML rather than CSS:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Without it a mobile browser lays the page out at an assumed desktop width — typically 980px — and then scales the result down, so every media query sees 980px and the text is unreadably small. The viewport meta tag tells the browser to use the device's real width instead.

Two things not to add. maximum-scale=1 and user-scalable=no disable pinch zoom, which is a direct WCAG 1.4.4 failure and one of the most harmful two-word additions in web development. viewport-fit=cover is legitimate and is what makes env(safe-area-inset-*) (§4.13) meaningful on a notched phone.

13.3 @media: Types and Features

@media takes a media type and any number of media feature tests.

@media screen and (min-width: 40rem) { .layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr 3fr; } }
@media print                         { nav { display: none; } }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .hero { background-attachment: scroll; } }
@media not all and (monochrome)      { .chart { --series-1: crimson; } }

The media types that survive are screen, print and all. speech exists and is essentially unimplemented; tv, handheld, projection and the rest were removed. In practice you write print when you mean print and omit the type otherwise — @media screen and (min-width: 40rem) and @media (min-width: 40rem) differ only in whether the rule also applies when printing, and usually it should.

The logical operators are and, not, only, and a comma for "or". only exists solely to hide a query from very old browsers and can be dropped. not negates the whole query, not one feature, which is why not all and (monochrome) is written the way it is.

13.4 Range Syntax

The modern media range syntax replaces the min-/max- prefixes with comparisons, and it removes a real class of bug. Measured, all three evaluating correctly at a 900px viewport:

(min-width: 100px)              matches
(width > 100px)                 matches
(400px <= width <= 2000px)      matches

The old form's problem was the boundary. (max-width: 600px) means "600px or less" and (min-width: 600px) means "600px or more", so a pair written that way both match at exactly 600px, and whichever comes later wins by source order. The usual workaround was max-width: 599.98px, which is a fractional pixel chosen to be smaller than any real device pixel — a hack that only works by accident.

The range form says what you mean:

@media (width < 40rem)  { /* narrow */ }
@media (width >= 40rem) { /* wide   */ }

No overlap, no fractional pixels, and the two-sided form (30rem <= width < 60rem) needs one query rather than two conditions.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: media range syntax.

13.5 Choosing Breakpoints

The rule is short and almost never followed: a breakpoint belongs where the design breaks, not where a device is.

Naming breakpoints after devices — $tablet: 768px — ties your stylesheet to a hardware landscape that changed the year after you wrote it, and it produces breakpoints that are wrong for every window that is not exactly a device. Instead, widen the browser slowly and add a breakpoint at each width where the layout starts to look bad.

Two practical points that follow:

  • Use rem, not px. A breakpoint in rem scales with the reader's font-size setting, so someone using a 24px default gets the narrow layout at a wider window — which is exactly right, because their text is bigger and needs more room.
  • Prefer a fluid layout to a stepped one. A fluid layout changes continuously with the space available rather than jumping at a breakpoint, and it cannot be wrong at a width you did not think of.
  • Prefer intrinsic techniques to breakpoints entirely. repeat(auto-fit, minmax(18rem, 1fr)) (§9.8), clamp() (§4.9) and flex-wrap all adapt continuously. Every breakpoint you do not write is one that cannot be wrong.

13.6 Mobile-First

Mobile-first means writing the narrow layout as the base and adding complexity in min-width queries, rather than writing the wide layout and stripping it back:

.layout { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }                  /* one column      */
@media (width >= 45rem) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr; }        /* two             */
}
@media (width >= 75rem) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr 260px; }  /* three           */
}

The argument for it is not fashion. A narrow layout is a subset of a wide one, so the base stylesheet is smaller and each query adds rather than undoes. The desktop-first version has to override the two-column rule back to one column, which means every rule exists twice and a missed override is a bug that only appears at one width.

The exception is genuinely desktop-only interface — a data table, an editor — where the narrow version is the special case and writing it as such is honest.

13.7 The Preference Features

These are the queries that matter most and are used least. Every one of them is a setting the reader has deliberately chosen, and honouring it costs a few lines. Measured, all supported by the browser:

prefers-color-scheme
light or dark. Usually better expressed with color-scheme and light-dark() (§5.10) — reach for the query when the change is structural rather than a colour.
prefers-reduced-motion
reduce or no-preference. For some readers, parallax and large transitions cause genuine nausea. §15.11.
prefers-reduced-transparency
reduce. Replace frosted glass and low-alpha overlays with opaque surfaces.
prefers-contrast
more, less, custom, no-preference. Strengthen borders and remove low-contrast decoration.
forced-colors
active when the OS is overriding colours entirely. §15.12 — the response is not to restore your colours.
inverted-colors
inverted. Mainly useful to re-invert images so photographs do not come out as negatives.
prefers-reduced-data
reduce. Skip web fonts and large decorative images.

The idiom to write, and the reason for its shape:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .card { transition: transform 200ms; }
}

Opt in to motion rather than opting out of it. Writing the transition unconditionally and then removing it under reduce means every new animation is unsafe by default until someone remembers, and a browser that does not support the query gets the motion. Writing it inside no-preference means the safe behaviour is the default and the enhancement is explicit.

13.8 Interaction Features

Four queries about the input device, and the distinction between the singular and the any- forms is the useful part. Measured on a desktop browser:

(hover: hover)          matches
(any-hover: hover)      matches
(pointer: fine)         matches
(any-pointer: coarse)   no match

hover and pointer describe the primary input; any-hover and any-pointer are true if any attached input satisfies them. A laptop with a touchscreen reports pointer: fine and any-pointer: coarse, and a tablet with a stylus reports the reverse.

The two rules that follow:

/* enlarge hit targets when the primary input is coarse */
@media (pointer: coarse) { .btn { min-block-size: 44px; } }

/* only rely on hover when *some* device can hover */
@media (any-hover: hover) { .card:hover .overlay { opacity: 1; } }

Use pointer for sizing decisions, because they should follow the input people are actually using. Use any-hover for revealing content, because hiding something behind a hover state on a device that cannot hover makes it unreachable — and the any- form is the safer test, since a hybrid device can hover even if its primary input is touch.

A hover-only affordance is a bug regardless. These queries let you enhance; they do not let you make something reachable by one input only.

13.9 Environment Features

The remaining features describe the display and the context. Measured on a 900×700 desktop window:

(orientation: landscape)          matches
(resolution: 1dppx)               matches
(update: fast)                    matches
(scripting: enabled)              matches
(display-mode: browser)           matches
(overflow-block: scroll)          matches
(horizontal-viewport-segments: 1) matches
(aspect-ratio: 16/9)              no match     (the window is 9:7)
(color-gamut: p3)                 no match
(dynamic-range: high)             no match
(device-posture: folded)          no match
orientation media feature
portrait or landscape — about the viewport, not the device, so it flips when a desktop window is resized.
resolution, color-gamut, dynamic-range
Display capability. color-gamut: p3 is how you offer a wide-gamut colour only where it can be shown, though §11.3's gamut mapping usually makes that unnecessary.
update
fast, slow, none. An e-ink screen reports slow, which is a good reason to skip animation.
scripting
enabled, initial-only, none. The CSS equivalent of <noscript>, and it works in an external stylesheet.
display-mode
browser, standalone, fullscreen, minimal-ui, picture-in-picture. How to hide a "download our app" banner in the installed app.
overflow-block, device-posture, viewport segments
Paged output, folding devices and multi-screen layout. Niche, real, and measured as recognised.

In summary, the vocabulary here is orientation media feature.

13.10 @supports

A feature query asks whether the browser understands a declaration, and it is the only honest basis for progressive enhancement. Measured, every form working:

(display: grid)                   YES
(display: gird)                   no
not (display: gird)               YES
(display:grid) and (gap:1rem)     YES
selector(:has(a))                 YES
(color: oklch(0 0 0))             YES
(anchor-name: --a)                YES
(container-type: scroll-state)    YES
font-tech(color-COLRv1)           YES
font-format(woff2)                YES

Four forms are worth knowing. (property: value) tests a declaration — and it tests the value, not just the property, which is what makes it useful for a value that is newer than its property. selector() tests a selector, which is the only way to feature-detect :has() or ::details-content. font-tech() and font-format() test font capabilities, which lets a @font-face src list skip a file the browser cannot use. And the boolean operators and, or and not compose all of them.

The correct shape of a progressive enhancement is base-first:

.gallery { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }

@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) {
  .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(18rem, 1fr)); }
  .card    { display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-row: span 3; }
}

Write the fallback unconditionally, then upgrade inside the query. The inverse — writing the modern version and a @supports not (...) fallback — fails on any browser that supports neither the feature nor @supports itself, and is harder to read.

@supports is not always needed. §1.5's error handling already gives you a fallback for free when the two declarations are for the same property:

.a { color: #5b21b6; }
.a { color: oklch(48% 0.24 295); }   /* dropped whole if unsupported */

Reach for @supports when the enhancement spans several declarations, or when the fallback and the enhancement are different properties.

13.11 Container Queries: Asking the Right Question

A media query asks about the window. A component almost never wants to know that. A card in a 300px sidebar and the same card in a 900px main column want different layouts, and the viewport is identical in both cases — so a media-query-based card is wrong in at least one of them, and the usual workaround is a modifier class that the page has to remember to apply.

@container asks about the nearest ancestor container instead:

.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; container-name: card; }

@container card (width > 300px) {
  .card { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 8rem 1fr; gap: 1rem; }
}

Measured, with a 400px container:

@container card (width > 300px)   ->  applied

The card now decides its own layout from the space it was given. Drop it in a sidebar and it goes to one column with no page-level knowledge at all. That is the difference between a component and a component-plus-a-convention.

13.12 container-type and container-name

container-type: declares what may be queried, and the choice has layout consequences. Measured:

container-type: inline-size   ->  inline-size
container-type: size          ->  size
container-type: normal        ->  normal
container-type: scroll-state  ->  scroll-state
container: card / inline-size ->  type=inline-size  name=card
inline-size
Containment on the inline axis only. The default choice, because a block's width is usually independent of its content and its height is not.
size
Both axes — which means the container's block size can no longer come from its contents. You must give it one, or it collapses.
normal
The default. Not a size container — but every element is a style container (§13.14), so style queries still work.
scroll-state
Queryable for stuck, snapped and scrollable state. §13.15.

container-name: gives a container one or more names, and container: is the shorthand — container: card / inline-size, name first. Naming is optional; an unnamed query targets the nearest size container of any name. Name them anyway: an unnamed query silently retargets the moment someone adds a container between.

The container is never the queried element itself. @container looks at ancestors, so a card cannot query its own width — which is why the pattern is always a wrapper. This is not an oversight: an element that resized itself in response to its own size would be circular.

What to carry forward from this subsection: container-name:, scroll-state query and size containment.

13.13 Size Queries and Container Units

A size query tests width, height, inline-size, block-size, aspect-ratio or orientation, with the same media range syntax as @media:

@container card (400px <= width < 700px) { .card { grid-template-columns: 8rem 1fr; } }
@container card (aspect-ratio > 1)       { .card__img { aspect-ratio: 3 / 2; } }

Pair them with the container query units from §4.5 — cqi, cqw, cqb, cqh, cqmin, cqmax — which measure the container rather than the viewport, so a component's type and spacing can scale with its own width:

.card__title { font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 1.5cqi, 1.6rem); }

Remember §4.5's measured trap: under container-type: inline-size, cqh and cqb have no container to resolve against and fall back to the small viewport. 10cqh inside a 200px-tall inline-size container measured as 70px — 10% of the 700px viewport. Use cqi/cqw unless you have deliberately created a size container.

The terms above, gathered: size query.

13.14 Style Queries

A style query tests a custom property's computed value on an ancestor. Measured applying correctly:

@container style(--variant: danger) { .title { color: red; } }

Two things make it different from a size query. It needs no container-type — every element is a style container — and it queries an inherited value rather than a measurement, which makes it a variant mechanism rather than a layout one.

The pattern it enables is a token that behaves like a switch:

.panel[data-tone="danger"] { --tone: danger; }

@container style(--tone: danger) {
  .panel__icon  { color: var(--danger-600); }
  .panel__title { color: var(--danger-800); }
  .panel__body  { border-inline-start-color: var(--danger-400); }
}

Set one custom property on a subtree and every descendant responds, with no class on each element and no JavaScript. It is the closest CSS gets to a component variant API, and it composes with §5.9's token layers: a theme sets --tone, and everything downstream follows.

Only custom properties may be queried today. A query on a standard property is specified but not shipping.

13.15 Scroll-State Queries

A scroll-state query asks about a container's scroll condition, which used to require an IntersectionObserver:

.header-wrap { container-type: scroll-state; }

@container scroll-state(stuck: top) {
  .header { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15); }
}

Measured, container-type: scroll-state is recognised. The three conditions are stuck (a sticky element has reached its threshold), snapped (a scroll-snap child is the current snap target), and scrollable (there is scrollable content in a given direction).

stuck: top is the one with an obvious use: a sticky header that gains a shadow only once it is actually stuck, which is a very common design and previously needed script. scrollable: block-end is the other: showing a "more below" affordance only when there is more below.

Availability is still limited — the @container at-rule itself is widely available, but the scroll-state container type is much newer than the size and style queries beside it. Guard it: @supports (container-type: scroll-state) measured as YES in this course's browser and is the right test.

13.16 Print Stylesheets and @page

Print is the one media type still worth writing for, and a printed page from a well-made site is worth the twenty lines it takes.

@media print {
  nav, aside, .no-print, footer .social { display: none; }

  body { color: #000; background: #fff; font-size: 11pt; }
  a[href^="http"]::after { content: " (" attr(href) ")"; font-size: 9pt; }
  abbr[title]::after     { content: " (" attr(title) ")"; }

  h2, h3 { break-after: avoid; }
  figure, table, pre { break-inside: avoid; }
  .chapter { break-before: page; }
}

Three things there are the whole art. Hide the navigation — a printed page cannot be clicked. Expand the links, because a URL that is only in an href is lost on paper; attr() (§4.13) does it in one rule. And use physical units — pt and cm — which §4.2 said had exactly one real use, and this is it.

@page styles the page box itself. Measured, all three of these parsing and applying:

@page { size: A4 portrait; margin: 2cm; }
@page :first { margin-block-start: 4cm; }
@media print { body { color: #000; } }

rules parsed: 3
@page { size: a4; margin: 2cm; }
@page :first { margin-top: 4cm; }
@media print { body { color: rgb(0, 0, 0); } }

@page's size descriptor takes a named size (A4, letter), an orientation, or explicit dimensions; margin sets the page margins. Its pseudo-classes are :first, :left, :right and :blank, which is how a title page gets different margins from the body. Note that @page also accepts ordinary page-context properties alongside its descriptors — it is the one at-rule that mixes the two namespaces.

One line each, for reference: @media print.

13.17 Fragmentation in Print

§7.15's fragmentation properties do their most valuable work here:

  • break-inside: avoid on figures, tables, cards and code blocks, so they are not split across a page boundary.
  • break-after: avoid on headings, so a heading is never the last thing on a page.
  • break-before: page for deliberate section boundaries.
  • orphans and widows set the minimum number of lines left at the bottom or top of a page; both default to 2 and are honoured for print in most engines.

The page-break-before, page-break-after and page-break-inside properties are now defined as aliases of the break-* ones. Write the modern spellings.

Two honest caveats. Engines treat avoid as a strong hint rather than a guarantee and will break anyway rather than leave a page badly underfull. And print rendering differs between browsers more than screen rendering does — if a printed output matters, test it in more than one, and consider generating a PDF server-side instead.

13.18 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • Responsive web design is about every condition a reader brings, not only width; the viewport meta tag is the prerequisite, and user-scalable=no is a WCAG failure.
  • @media takes a media type (screen, print, all) and media feature tests joined by and, not, only and commas.
  • The media range syntax — (width >= 40rem), (400px <= width <= 2000px) — replaces min-/max- and removes the both-match-at-the-boundary bug; measured working.
  • A breakpoint belongs where the design breaks, should be written in rem, and is best avoided entirely in favour of minmax(), clamp() and flex-wrap.
  • Mobile-first writes the narrow layout as the base so each query adds rather than undoes.
  • The preference features — prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-reduced-transparency, prefers-contrast, forced-colors, inverted-colors and prefers-reduced-data — were all measured supported, and motion should be opted into under no-preference.
  • hover media feature, any-hover, pointer media feature and any-pointer distinguish the primary input from any input — measured pointer: fine matching and any-pointer: coarse not.
  • The environment features — orientation media feature, resolution, color-gamut, dynamic-range, update, scripting, display-mode, overflow-block and the viewport-segment set — were each evaluated.
  • @supports is a feature query that tests values as well as properties, plus selector() feature query, font-tech() and font-format(); write the fallback first and upgrade inside it.
  • @container with container-type:, container-name: and container: asks about the nearest ancestor container; inline-size is the default choice and size requires a definite block size.
  • A size query uses the range syntax and pairs with the container query units, where cqh under inline-size falls back to the viewport — measured at 70px.
  • A style query needs no container-type and turns a custom property into a variant switch — measured applying.
  • A scroll-state query tests stuck, snapped and scrollable, replacing an IntersectionObserver for sticky-header shadows.
  • @media print plus @page — measured parsing size, margin and the :first pseudo-class — makes a printable page: hide navigation, expand links with attr(), and use pt/cm.
  • Fragmentation in paged media uses break-inside: avoid, break-after: avoid and break-before: page, with page-break-* as deprecated aliases.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: pointer media feature, selector() feature query and paged media.

Exercises

1. A card component is used in a 280px sidebar, a 620px main column and a full-width hero. It should be stacked in the sidebar, horizontal in the column, and horizontal with a large image in the hero. Write it, then explain why a media-query version would be wrong even if it produced the same result today.

Solution 
.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; container-name: card; }

.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  --img: 100%;
}
.card__img { inline-size: var(--img); aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; }

@container card (width >= 30rem) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr; align-items: start; }
  .card__img { --img: 12rem; aspect-ratio: 1; }
}

@container card (width >= 55rem) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 24rem 1fr; gap: 2rem; }
  .card__img { --img: 24rem; aspect-ratio: 3 / 2; }
  .card__title { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2cqi, 2.5rem); }
}

Why a media-query version is wrong even when it looks right.

A media query asks about the viewport, and all three placements have the same viewport. So the media-query version cannot distinguish them from CSS at all; it needs the page to tell the card which context it is in:

.sidebar .card { /* stacked */ }
.main .card    { /* horizontal */ }
.hero .card    { /* large */ }

That works, and it fails in four ways that only show up later:

  • The card is no longer self-contained. Its correctness depends on rules written elsewhere, keyed to ancestor class names. Moving the card to a new region means editing the card's stylesheet, which is the opposite of a component.
  • Each new placement is a new rule. A fourth region needs a fourth selector, and someone has to notice.
  • It is wrong at the boundaries. The sidebar is 280px at every viewport width — but a media-query rule that stacks the card below 45rem also stacks the main-column card on a tablet, where 620px is plenty of room for the horizontal layout. You end up with @media (width < 45rem) { .main .card { ... } } and .sidebar .card { ... } fighting, and a specificity ladder.
  • It cannot respond to a resizable region. A sidebar the user can drag, or a panel in a split view, changes width with no viewport change at all. The media query never fires.

The container version answers the question the card actually has — how much room do I have? — and §13.11's measurement confirms the mechanism works. Drop the card anywhere and it is correct without the page knowing anything about it.

Two details in the solution worth naming. container-type: inline-size rather than size, because the card's height comes from its content and size would collapse it (§13.12). And 2cqi in the title's clamp(), so the type scales with the container — a vw term there would make the hero's card title grow when the window widened even though the card had not.

2. Write the progressive enhancement for a gallery that uses subgrid where available, and explain why @supports is needed here when a plain fallback declaration would have been enough for oklch().

Solution 
/* base: works everywhere */
.gallery { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1.5rem; }
.gallery > * { flex: 1 1 18rem; min-inline-size: 0; }
.card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.card__footer { margin-block-start: auto; }

/* enhancement */
@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) {
  .gallery {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(18rem, 1fr));
  }
  .gallery > * { flex: none; }
  .card {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-rows: subgrid;
    grid-row: span 3;
    gap: inherit;
  }
  .card__footer { margin-block-start: 0; }
}

Why a plain fallback declaration is not enough here.

CSS's built-in fallback (§1.5) works when two declarations are for the same property and the later one is dropped as invalid:

.a { color: #5b21b6; }
.a { color: oklch(48% 0.24 295); }

A browser that does not understand oklch() discards the second declaration and keeps the first. One property, two values, no query needed — which is why oklch() needs no @supports.

The subgrid enhancement is not that shape. It is five declarations across three selectors, and they are not independent:

  • .gallery changes from flex to grid — a different value of the same property, so a browser that does not know subgrid still accepts display: grid perfectly well. The enhancement would half-apply: grid layout with no subgrid, so the cards are grid items but their internals still do not align, and the flex fallback's margin-block-start: auto has been switched off.
  • .gallery > * must lose flex: 1 1 18rem, which is meaningless once the parent is a grid.
  • .card__footer must lose the auto margin, because subgrid now positions it.

Half-applying is the failure mode @supports exists to prevent. The natural fallback mechanism operates per declaration; here the fallback is a set of declarations that must be adopted or rejected together, and only a feature query can express that.

Two details. The test is (grid-template-rows: subgrid) — the value, not the property — because grid-template-rows has existed since 2017 and testing the property alone would pass everywhere. §13.10 measured that @supports tests values, which is what makes this possible.

And the query is written base-first: the flex fallback is unconditional and the grid version is inside the query. The inverse (@supports not (...)) would leave a browser that supports neither subgrid nor @supports with no layout at all, and it reads backwards.

3. A page uses a parallax hero, an autoplaying background video, frosted-glass cards, and a sticky header that should gain a shadow when stuck. Write the query layer that makes all four respectful of the reader's settings, and say which of the four you would remove instead.

Solution 
/* 1. Motion is opted INTO, never out of. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .hero          { background-attachment: fixed; }
  .card          { transition: transform 200ms, box-shadow 200ms; }
  :root          { scroll-behavior: smooth; }
}

/* 2. Transparency has a preference of its own. */
.card {
  background: color-mix(in oklab, Canvas 60%, transparent);
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.4);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .card { background: Canvas; backdrop-filter: none; border: 1px solid CanvasText; }
}

/* 3. Contrast and forced colours. */
@media (prefers-contrast: more) {
  .card { border: 2px solid CanvasText; }
  .muted { color: CanvasText; }
}

/* 3b. Contrast, continued: nothing further needed — the system colours above
       already carry into forced-colours mode. */

And the sticky shadow, which needs no IntersectionObserver:

.header-wrap { container-type: scroll-state; }
@supports (container-type: scroll-state) {
  @container scroll-state(stuck: top) {
    .header { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15); }
  }
}

Why each is written that way.

The motion block opts in rather than out. Writing the transitions unconditionally and stripping them under reduce means every animation added later is unsafe until someone remembers to add it to the strip list, and a browser without the query gets the motion. Inside no-preference, the safe behaviour is the default. §13.7.

prefers-reduced-transparency is a separate setting from prefers-reduced-motion and is frequently forgotten. The replacement is an opaque Canvas plus a border — the border is doing the work the blur was doing, which is separating the card from what is behind it. §11.11 also notes that backdrop-filter is expensive; removing it here helps twice.

The system colours (Canvas, CanvasText) rather than hardcoded values mean the contrast block and the forced-colours case are already largely handled, because those are the colours the OS re-maps (§11.5).

The scroll-state query replaces an IntersectionObserver with a sentinel element, which is what this was before. It is guarded by @supports, which measured as YES for exactly this test in the browser used throughout this course — and the guard is not optional, because scroll-state queries are not Baseline yet and a missing shadow is a much better failure than a broken header.

Which of the four I would remove: the autoplaying background video, and it is not close.

Nothing in the query layer above fixes it. prefers-reduced-motion should suppress its playback, and CSS cannot stop a video playing — that needs script or the autoplay attribute conditioned on the preference, which is the JavaScript course's territory. Beyond motion, a background video is: a large download on a metered connection (prefers-reduced-data exists but is not widely honoured), a battery cost, a decoding cost on low-end devices, and a common cause of text-over-video contrast failures that vary frame by frame and therefore cannot be checked.

The parallax hero is the second candidate: background-attachment: fixed is a known cause of scroll jank on mobile, and the block above already disables it for readers who asked — but "correct for the people who set the flag" is a lower bar than "good for everyone".

SECTION 14

Transitions, Transforms, Animations and View Transitions

Motion in CSS has three tiers, and most stylesheets only use the first. A transition interpolates between two states the cascade already produced. An animation defines its own states and plays them on a timeline. And since scroll-driven animations and view transitions arrived, that timeline no longer has to be the clock — it can be a scroll position, or the gap between two entirely different pages.

This section covers all three, plus the transform system they mostly animate. Two things run through it: what can be interpolated at all, which is a more restrictive question than people expect, and what it costs per frame, which is the difference between motion that feels good and motion that stutters.

Everything below was measured.

14.1 Transitions

transition: watches a set of properties and, when the cascade produces a new value for one, interpolates to it over time instead of jumping.

.card {
  transition: box-shadow 200ms ease-out, translate 200ms ease-out;
}
.card:hover { box-shadow: 0 4px 16px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.2); translate: 0 -2px; }

The shorthand's four parts may be written in any order, with the first time value taken as the duration and the second as the delay. Measured:

transition: opacity 200ms
  ->  property=opacity  duration=0.2s  timing=ease  delay=0s  behavior=normal

transition: all 200ms ease-in-out 50ms
  ->  property=all      duration=0.2s  timing=ease-in-out  delay=0.05s

The longhands are transition-property:, transition-duration:, transition-timing-function:, transition-delay: and transition-behavior:, and each takes a comma-separated list matched by position against transition-property.

Do not use transition: all. It looks convenient and has three real costs: it animates properties you did not intend, including ones added later by someone else; it animates expensive properties such as width and top that you would never have chosen; and it makes the browser check every property on every change. Name what you mean.

Transitions need two states that both exist. A property transitioning from auto, or from a value the element never had because it was display: none, has nothing to interpolate from — which is §14.6's subject.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: transition-property:, transition-delay: and transition-timing-function:.

14.2 Easing

transition-timing-function: and animation-timing-function: take an easing function. Measured serialisations:

cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1)   ->  cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1)
steps(4, jump-end)            ->  steps(4)
linear(0, .25 25%, 1)         ->  linear(0 0%, 0.25 25%, 1 100%)
ease-in-out                   ->  ease-in-out

The keywords linear, ease, ease-in, ease-out and ease-in-out are all shorthands for particular cubic-bezier() curves. cubic-bezier() takes the two control points of a curve from (0,0) to (1,1); its y values may exceed 0–1, which is how you get overshoot and a spring-like settle.

steps() advances in jumps rather than continuously, and it is what makes sprite-sheet animation and a "typing" cursor work. Its second argument — jump-start, jump-end (the default, which is why it vanished in the serialisation), jump-none, jump-both, start, end — decides where the jumps fall.

linear() is the newest and the most useful of the three. It takes a list of output values with optional input positions and interpolates linearly between them, which lets you approximate any curve — including ones cubic-bezier() cannot express, such as a bounce, which needs to change direction more than once:

.bounce {
  transition-timing-function:
    linear(0, 0.55 22%, 0.9 39%, 1 52%, 0.94 62%, 1 78%, 0.99 89%, 1);
}

The practical guidance for interface motion: ease-out for things entering (they arrive quickly and settle), ease-in for things leaving (they start slowly and accelerate away), and linear only for things that genuinely have constant speed, such as a spinner or a progress bar.

To have in hand before moving on: easing function, steps() and animation-timing-function:.

14.3 What Can Be Interpolated

An interpolation exists only where the specification defines one. Value interpolation works between two numbers, two lengths, two colours, two transforms of compatible structure, and a handful of others.

Everything else is a discrete animation: the value flips from the start to the end at the halfway point. §5.7 measured this on an unregistered custom property — at exactly 50% progress it already read the end value, while a registered <number> read the midpoint.

The properties that are discretely animated by specification and that you will actually meet are display, content-visibility, overlay, visibility (partly) and any unregistered custom property. transition-behavior: allow-discrete opts them into transitioning at all, which is §14.6.

Two other rules that catch people:

  • A transform interpolates only between compatible lists. translateX(0) rotate(0) to translateX(10px) rotate(45deg) interpolates component-wise. translateX(0) to rotate(45deg) cannot, so the browser converts both to matrices and interpolates those — which produces a different, often ugly, path.
  • auto is not a value you can animate from. height: auto to height: 200px does nothing. interpolate-size: allow-keywords on an ancestor changes that, and it is the modern fix for the accordion problem that max-height hacks were invented for.
:root { interpolate-size: allow-keywords; }
.panel { block-size: 0; transition: block-size 250ms; overflow: clip; }
.panel[data-open] { block-size: auto; }

Named once more, since each is referred to later: value interpolation.

14.4 @keyframes and the Animation Properties

@keyframes defines a named sequence of states:

@keyframes pulse {
  from       { scale: 1;    opacity: 1;   }
  50%        { scale: 1.06; opacity: 0.7; }
  to         { scale: 1;    opacity: 1;   }
}

Each keyframe selector is a percentage, or from/to (which are 0% and 100%). Several may share a block: 0%, 100% { ... }. A property absent from a keyframe is interpolated from the surrounding ones; a property absent from all of them is not animated at all.

animation: is the shorthand, and its parts may come in almost any order — measured, with a name that is not even first:

animation: k 1s
  ->  name=k  duration=1s  timing=ease  delay=0s  count=1
      direction=normal  fill=none  play-state=running

animation: 2s ease-in 200ms 3 alternate both paused k
  ->  name=k  duration=2s  timing=ease-in  delay=0.2s  count=3
      direction=alternate  fill=both  play-state=paused

animation: k 1s linear infinite
  ->  count=infinite

The longhands are animation-name:, animation-duration:, animation-timing-function:, animation-delay:, animation-iteration-count:, animation-direction:, animation-fill-mode:, animation-play-state: and animation-composition:.

Two of them decide most of the confusion:

animation-fill-mode: decides what applies outside the animation's active period. The default none means the element snaps back to its cascaded values before the delay and after the end — which is why an entry animation with a delay flashes its final state first. forwards holds the last keyframe, backwards applies the first during the delay, and both does both. both is what you almost always want for an entry animation.

animation-direction: takes normal, reverse, alternate and alternate-reverse. alternate with infinite is the pulse idiom above, and it halves the keyframes you have to write.

animation-composition: — replace, add, accumulate — decides how an animation's value combines with the underlying one, which matters when two animations touch the same property.

In summary, the vocabulary here is keyframe selector, animation-name:, animation-delay:, animation-iteration-count: and animation-play-state:.

14.5 A Transition or an Animation?

The distinction is not stylistic:

Transition
A state change the cascade already causes — hover, focus, a class toggle, a media query. Two states, one interpolation, interruptible and reversible mid-flight for free.
Animation
A defined sequence that runs regardless of state — a spinner, a pulse, a multi-step entry. More than two states, or a need for looping, delay-before-first-frame, or fill behaviour.

A transition that interrupts itself does the right thing: hovering away halfway through returns from where it is, not from the end. An animation restarted mid-flight jumps back to its first keyframe, which is why hover effects should be transitions.

14.6 @starting-style and Animating to and from display: none

For years an element could not animate in, because it went from not existing to existing. The two features that fix it work together.

transition-behavior: allow-discrete lets a discretely-animated property participate in a transition — and, crucially, for display it means the element stays display: block for the whole out-transition and switches to none at the end.

@starting-style supplies the values an element should transition from the first time it is rendered:

.popover {
  opacity: 1;
  display: block;
  transition: opacity 200ms, display 200ms allow-discrete;
}

@starting-style {
  .popover { opacity: 0; }
}

Measured, the browser parses @starting-style as a rule of its own type:

CSSStyleRule        .p { opacity: 1; display: block; transition: opacity … }
CSSStartingStyleRule @starting-style { .p { opacity: 0; } }

And the transition list measured as expected:

transition: display 200ms allow-discrete, opacity 200ms
  ->  property = display, opacity   behavior = allow-discrete, normal

For a top-layer element — a popover or a modal <dialog> — one more property is needed, because the element's presence in the top layer is itself discrete:

[popover] {
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 200ms, display 200ms allow-discrete, overlay 200ms allow-discrete;
}
[popover]:popover-open { opacity: 1; }
@starting-style { [popover]:popover-open { opacity: 0; } }

overlay: is a property you never set yourself; you only ever transition it with allow-discrete, so the element stays in the top layer while it fades out instead of dropping behind the page for the duration.

What to carry forward from this subsection: overlay:.

The terms above, gathered: transition-behavior:.

14.7 Transforms, and Why Order Matters

The transform property takes a list of functions applied right to left — that is, the last one listed is applied to the element first. This is the source of a great deal of confusion, and it is directly measurable:

.a { transform: translateX(50px) rotate(45deg) scale(2); }
.c { transform: rotate(45deg) translateX(50px); }

a  ->  matrix(1.41421, 1.41421, -1.41421, 1.41421, 50, 0)
c  ->  matrix(0.707107, 0.707107, -0.707107, 0.707107, 35.3553, 35.3553)

Read the last two numbers of each matrix — they are the final translation. .a moved 50px along x and 0 along y: the rotation happened before the translate in the coordinate system, so the translate is along the page's x axis. .c moved 35.36px on both axes: the element was rotated first, so its own x axis now points at 45°, and translating along it moves diagonally.

The rule to carry: rotate then translate moves along the rotated axis; translate then rotate orbits the original position. Neither is wrong; they are different operations, and swapping two functions is not a refactor.

The functions are translate(), translateX/Y/Z(), translate3d(), rotate(), rotateX/Y/Z(), rotate3d(), scale(), scaleX/Y/Z(), scale3d(), skew(), skewX/Y(), matrix(), matrix3d() and perspective().

The individual properties are usually better. Measured, they are genuinely separate properties:

.b { translate: 50px; rotate: 45deg; scale: 2; }

transform = none   translate = 50px   rotate = 45deg   scale = 2

The translate property, the rotate property and the scale property can be set and animated independently, which is what transform cannot do — a rule that sets transform: scale(1.05) on hover destroys any translate the element already had. They are applied in the fixed order translate, rotate, scale, then whatever transform says.

One line each, for reference: the transform property, skew(), the translate property, the rotate property and the scale property.

14.8 Transform Geometry

transform-origin: is the point everything happens around — default 50% 50%, and top left or 0 0 are the two other common choices. Measured on a full-width block it resolved to 442px 0px, which is a reminder that the default is a percentage of the element's own box.

transform-box: decides which box the origin and percentages resolve against: view-box (the default for HTML), fill-box, content-box, border-box or stroke-box. Measured switching to fill-box, which is the value you need for transforms on SVG children.

perspective: on a parent gives its children a vanishing point, and perspective() inside a child's own transform gives that child one. transform-style: preserve-3d keeps a subtree in one shared 3-D space instead of flattening each child into its parent's plane — without it, nested 3-D transforms do nothing useful. backface-visibility: hidden hides an element when it is rotated past 90°, which is how a flip-card shows its other face. Measured, all four applying cleanly:

transform-box = fill-box   transform-style = preserve-3d
perspective = 800px        backface-visibility = hidden

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: transform-origin:, transform-box:, transform-style:, perspective: and backface-visibility:.

14.9 Motion Along a Path

offset-path: moves an element along a defined route, which is a genuine capability nothing else in CSS has. Measured:

.a { offset-path: path("M 0 0 L 100 100"); offset-distance: 50%; offset-rotate: auto; }
.b { offset-path: ray(45deg closest-side); }
.c { offset-path: circle(50px); }

a  path=path("M 0 0 L 100 100")  distance=50%  rotate=auto 0deg
b  path=ray(45deg)               distance=0px
c  path=circle(50px)             distance=0px

offset-distance: is the position along the path, from 0% to 100%, and it is the property you animate. offset-rotate: takes auto (turn to face along the path), reverse, or an explicit angle. ray() defines a straight path at an angle out to a named boundary, and offset-anchor chooses which point of the element follows the path.

@keyframes travel { to { offset-distance: 100%; } }
.rocket { offset-path: path("M 10 80 C 40 10, 65 10, 95 80"); animation: travel 3s linear infinite; }

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: offset-path:, ray(), offset-distance: and offset-rotate:.

14.10 Scroll-Driven Animations

A scroll-driven animation replaces the clock with a scroll position. The animation does not play; it is scrubbed. Measured, all six properties recognised:

animation-timeline: scroll(root block)  ->  scroll(root)
animation-timeline: view(block 20% 10%) ->  view(20% 10%)
scroll-timeline: --t block              ->  --t
view-timeline: --v inline               ->  --v inline
animation-range: entry 0% cover 40%     ->  entry cover 40%
timeline-scope: --t                     ->  --t

Two kinds of timeline:

scroll() is a scroll progress timeline: 0% at the top of a scroll container, 100% at the bottom. Its arguments are a scroller (nearest, root, self) and an axis. The classic use is a reading-progress bar, and it is three declarations:

@keyframes grow { from { scale: 0 1; } to { scale: 1 1; } }
.progress {
  transform-origin: left;
  animation: grow auto linear;
  animation-timeline: scroll(root block);
}

Note animation-duration: auto — a scroll-driven animation has no duration in time, and giving it one is a common mistake that makes it do nothing.

view() is a view progress timeline: it tracks one element's progress through the scrollport, which is what powers reveal-on-scroll without an IntersectionObserver:

@keyframes fade-up { from { opacity: 0; translate: 0 2rem; } to { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; } }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .reveal {
    animation: fade-up auto ease-out both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 10% cover 35%;
  }
}

animation-range: selects which part of the timeline the animation occupies, using the named ranges cover, contain, entry, exit, entry-crossing and exit-crossing plus a percentage. entry 10% cover 35% means "start when the element is 10% into entering, finish when it is 35% through covering".

scroll-timeline: and view-timeline: name a timeline on one element so another can use it, and timeline-scope: widens that name's visibility to a common ancestor, since a timeline is otherwise only visible to the element's descendants and later siblings.

The performance argument is strong: these run on the compositor and produce no JavaScript per frame. The accessibility argument is equally strong in the other direction: scroll-driven motion is exactly what prefers-reduced-motion exists for, which is why the example above is wrapped.

To have in hand before moving on: scroll().

14.11 View Transitions

A view transition animates between two states of the document, including across a navigation. The browser snapshots the old state, applies the DOM change, snapshots the new state, and cross-fades a tree of pseudo-elements between them.

For a same-document change, one JavaScript call starts it; for a cross-document navigation, one at-rule does:

@view-transition { navigation: auto; }

Measured, that parses and document.startViewTransition exists as a function.

view-transition-name: opts one element into being tracked individually, so it morphs between the two states rather than cross-fading:

.hero { view-transition-name: hero; view-transition-class: card; }

view-transition-name = hero    view-transition-class = card

A name must be unique in the document at the moment of the transition — two elements sharing one is an error that aborts the transition. view-transition-class: solves the "twenty cards, all animated the same way" problem: give each a unique name and a shared class, then style the class.

The generated pseudo-elements are what you style:

::view-transition
The root of the snapshot tree, in the top layer.
::view-transition-group()
One per named element. This is what animates position and size — style it to change the morph.
::view-transition-image-pair()
Holds the old and new snapshots together; where isolation and blending go.
::view-transition-old(), ::view-transition-new()
The two snapshots. The default animation cross-fades these.
::view-transition-group(hero) { animation-duration: 400ms; }
::view-transition-old(hero)   { animation-timing-function: ease-in; }
::view-transition-new(hero)   { animation-timing-function: ease-out; }
::view-transition-group(*)    { animation-timing-function: ease; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-group(*), ::view-transition-old(*), ::view-transition-new(*) {
    animation: none;
  }
}

That last block is not optional. A full-page morph is one of the strongest motion effects on the web, and it needs an opt-out.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: view-transition-name:, ::view-transition-group(), ::view-transition-old(), ::view-transition-new() and startviewtransition.

14.12 Performance: What a Frame Costs

§1.8 established the cost ladder — style, layout, paint, composite — and animation is where it matters most, because it runs sixty times a second.

Composite only
transform, translate, rotate, scale, opacity, and filter in most cases. The compositor can run these without the main thread.
Paint + composite
background-color, box-shadow, border-radius, color. No re-measurement, but pixels are redrawn.
Layout + paint + composite
width, height, top, left, margin, padding, font-size. The whole ladder, every frame, potentially for the whole page.

This is why "animate transform and opacity" is the standard advice, and now the reason rather than the slogan: a left animation re-runs layout for the element's whole containing block sixty times a second, while the identical-looking translate animation re-runs nothing.

will-change: tells the browser to prepare for a change, typically by promoting the element to its own compositor layer:

.drawer { will-change: transform; }

Three rules about it, in order of how often they are broken. Do not apply it to many elements — each layer costs memory, and a page with will-change on every card is slower, not faster. Do not leave it on permanently — add it when an interaction is about to start and remove it after, or use it on the handful of elements that genuinely animate constantly. And it creates a stacking context and a containing block for fixed descendants (§10.5, §10.8), so adding it for performance can silently break positioning three levels down.

If an animation still stutters after all of that, the usual causes are: an expensive paint (backdrop-filter, a large box-shadow blur, a border-radius on a big element), too many animated layers at once, or main-thread work from JavaScript blocking the frame.

14.13 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • transition: interpolates a cascade-driven state change; measured expanding all 200ms ease-in-out 50ms into its five longhands, and transition: all should not be used.
  • transition-property:, transition-duration:, transition-timing-function:, transition-delay: and transition-behavior: take position-matched lists.
  • An easing function is a keyword, cubic-bezier(), steps() (whose jump-end is the default and vanishes in serialisation) or linear() easing, which can express curves cubic-bezier() cannot.
  • Value interpolation exists only where specified; everything else is a discrete animation that flips at 50% — display, overlay, content-visibility and unregistered custom properties — and interpolate-size: allow-keywords unlocks animating to and from auto.
  • @keyframes holds keyframe selectors; animation: expands in any order — measured on three forms — into animation-name:, animation-duration:, animation-timing-function:, animation-delay:, animation-iteration-count:, animation-direction:, animation-fill-mode:, animation-play-state: and animation-composition:.
  • animation-fill-mode: both is what an entry animation almost always wants; alternate halves the keyframes of a pulse.
  • Use a transition for a two-state change (interruptible and reversible) and an animatable property sequence for anything with more states or a loop.
  • @starting-style supplies first-render values and allow-discrete lets display and overlay: transition — measured as a CSSStartingStyleRule and as a per-property behaviour list.
  • The transform property applies its functions right to left: measured, translateX(50px) rotate(45deg) ended at (50, 0) and rotate(45deg) translateX(50px) at (35.36, 35.36).
  • The translate property, the rotate property and the scale property are independent and animate independently — measured leaving transform: none.
  • transform-origin:, transform-box:, transform-style: preserve-3d, perspective: and backface-visibility: were each measured applying.
  • offset-path:, offset-distance:, offset-rotate:, ray() and path() move an element along a motion path — measured on three path forms.
  • A scroll-driven animation uses animation-timeline: with scroll() or view(), needs animation-duration: auto, and is scoped by animation-range:, scroll-timeline:, view-timeline: and timeline-scope: — all measured.
  • A view transition starts from @view-transition or startViewTransition; view-transition-name: must be unique and view-transition-class groups many; the ::view-transition, ::view-transition-group(), ::view-transition-image-pair(), ::view-transition-old() and ::view-transition-new() pseudo-elements are what you style.
  • Animate transform and opacity because they are compositor-only; will-change: should be sparing, temporary, and used knowing it creates a stacking context.

In summary, the vocabulary here is linear() easing, animatable property and motion path.

Exercises

1. A drawer slides in from the right when a button is pressed. The first version animates right from -320px to 0 and stutters on a mid-range phone. Rewrite it, and explain the frame-by-frame difference.

Solution

The original:

.drawer { position: fixed; inset-block: 0; right: -320px; inline-size: 320px;
          transition: right 250ms ease-out; }
.drawer[data-open] { right: 0; }

The rewrite:

.drawer {
  position: fixed; inset-block: 0; inset-inline-end: 0; inline-size: 320px;
  translate: 100% 0;
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .drawer { transition: translate 250ms ease-out; }
}
.drawer[data-open] { translate: 0 0; }

The frame-by-frame difference is §14.12's cost ladder.

right is an inset property, so changing it changes the element's position in layout. Every frame the browser must: recalculate style, re-run layout for the drawer and everything whose geometry depends on it, paint the newly positioned pixels, and composite. That is the whole ladder, sixty times a second, on the main thread — so any JavaScript work competing for that thread turns into a dropped frame directly.

translate is a compositor-only property. The drawer is painted once, into its own layer, and each frame the compositor simply draws that existing texture at a different offset. No style recalculation of consequence, no layout, no paint. The work happens off the main thread, so it survives a busy main thread, and on a phone that is the difference between 60fps and 20.

Four details in the rewrite that are not decoration:

translate: 100% 0 rather than translate: 320px 0 — a percentage on translate resolves against the element's own border box (§4.6), so the drawer hides itself exactly regardless of its width, and changing inline-size needs no second edit.

The individual translate property rather than transform: translateX(). §14.7 measured them as genuinely separate properties. If the drawer ever also needs a scale on some other state, transform would have the two rules destroying each other; translate and scale compose.

inset-inline-end: 0 rather than right: -320px — the element is now always at the edge and is merely displaced, which means its layout position never changes and there is nothing for layout to recompute.

The prefers-reduced-motion wrapper, with the transition opted into (§13.7). The drawer still opens and closes; it simply appears rather than sliding.

Where will-change fits: it is tempting to add will-change: transform to the drawer permanently. Do not — §14.12's rules. If the drawer is genuinely a hot path, add it on :hover/:focus-within of the trigger so the layer is prepared just before the interaction, and be aware it creates a stacking context and a containing block for fixed descendants inside the drawer.

2. A <div> popover fades and slides in correctly but disappears instantly when closed. Explain both halves, and write the version that animates in and out.

Solution

Why it fades in and not out. Almost certainly the entry is animated with an animation (which runs once when the element appears) while the exit is a change to display: none. There is nothing for the browser to animate on the way out: the element stops existing at the moment the property changes, so any transition on opacity never gets a frame.

Why a naive transition does not fix it either. Adding transition: opacity 200ms to a rule that also changes display fails in both directions. Going in, the element goes from not being rendered to being rendered, and a transition needs a "before" value that was actually in effect — there is none. Going out, display: none applies immediately at the start, and the element is gone before the first frame.

§14.3's rule is the underlying one: display is a discretely animated property. Discrete values flip at the halfway point rather than interpolating, and by default they are excluded from transitions altogether.

The version that works:

[popover] {
  opacity: 0;
  translate: 0 -0.5rem;
  transition:
