    opacity 200ms ease,
    translate 200ms ease,
    display 200ms allow-discrete,
    overlay 200ms allow-discrete;
}

[popover]:popover-open {
  opacity: 1;
  translate: 0 0;
}

@starting-style {
  [popover]:popover-open { opacity: 0; translate: 0 -0.5rem; }
}

Each piece:

display 200ms allow-discrete — transition-behavior: allow-discrete (here in its shorthand position) lets display participate. For display specifically it has a special rule: the element flips to block immediately on the way in, and stays block for the whole duration on the way out, switching to none only at the end. That is what gives the exit its frames. Measured, the behaviour list comes back per property: behavior = allow-discrete, normal.

overlay 200ms allow-discrete — overlay: is a property you never set; it tracks whether the element is in the top layer. Without transitioning it, a closing popover leaves the top layer on the first frame and spends its fade-out rendered behind the rest of the page. This is the detail that is almost always missing from examples.

@starting-style — supplies the values to transition from on the element's first render. Measured, the browser exposes it as a CSSStartingStyleRule, distinct from an ordinary style rule. Without it the entry has no "before" state and jumps.

Two things to check before shipping. The @starting-style rule must have at least the specificity of the open-state rule, or the cascade picks the wrong starting values — writing it with the same selector plus :popover-open is the reliable shape. And wrap the whole thing in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) if the movement is more than a small fade; the display/overlay lines should stay outside it so the element still behaves correctly.

3. Build a reading-progress bar and a reveal-on-scroll effect with no JavaScript. Then state two reasons a team might still choose IntersectionObserver for the second one.

Solution 
/* 1. Reading progress: a scroll progress timeline on the document. */
@keyframes grow-x { from { scale: 0 1; } to { scale: 1 1; } }

.progress {
  position: fixed; inset-block-start: 0; inset-inline: 0;
  block-size: 3px; background: var(--accent-500);
  transform-origin: left center;
  scale: 0 1;
}
@supports (animation-timeline: scroll()) {
  .progress {
    animation: grow-x auto linear;
    animation-timeline: scroll(root block);
  }
}

/* 2. Reveal on scroll: a view progress timeline per element. */
@keyframes fade-up {
  from { opacity: 0; translate: 0 2rem; }
  to   { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  @supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
    .reveal {
      animation: fade-up auto ease-out both;
      animation-timeline: view();
      animation-range: entry 10% cover 35%;
    }
  }
}

The three things that are easy to get wrong.

animation: grow-x auto linear — animation-duration: auto is required. A scroll-driven animation has no duration in time; it is scrubbed by scroll position. Giving it 1s makes it a time-based animation that ignores the timeline, which is the commonest mistake and produces an animation that plays once on load and never again.

animation-fill-mode: both (the both in the shorthand) on the reveal. Without it the element snaps back to its cascaded state outside the animation range, so it is invisible before entry 10% and also after cover 35%.

animation-range: entry 10% cover 35% — measured serialising as entry cover 40% in a similar case, which shows the browser normalising the range. entry measures the element crossing into the scrollport; cover measures its whole passage through it. Without a range the animation spans cover 0% to cover 100%, so it is only complete as the element leaves the screen.

The @supports guards are in the base-first shape from §13.10: the progress bar has scale: 0 1 unconditionally and is simply invisible without the feature, and the reveal is fully visible without it, which is the right failure for both.

Two reasons a team might still use IntersectionObserver for the reveal:

It needs to do more than animate. A reveal is often a trigger: lazy-load an image, start a video, fire an analytics event, begin fetching the next page. animation-timeline animates CSS properties and nothing else — it cannot call a function, and there is no event when an element enters its range. The moment "reveal" means "and also do X", the observer is back.

Browser support and the one-shot problem. Scroll-driven animations are not Baseline yet — Chrome and Edge since 115, Safari since 26, and not Firefox at the time of writing — so the @supports guard above means a Firefox reader sees no reveal at all. That is an acceptable degradation for decoration and not for anything load-bearing. And a view timeline is continuously scrubbed, so scrolling back up un-reveals the element — usually not what "reveal on scroll" means. Making it one-shot needs animation-fill-mode plus a range that ends before the element can leave, or it needs script. IntersectionObserver gives you a one-way entry.isIntersecting and a class you add once.

SECTION 15

Writing Modes, Logical Properties, and Styling Everyone Can Use

CSS was designed around a page that runs left to right and top to bottom, and its oldest properties still say so: margin-top, padding-left, border-right. That is fine until the same stylesheet has to serve Arabic, Hebrew, Japanese vertical text, or a reader who has zoomed to 200% and turned on their operating system's high-contrast mode.

This section is about writing CSS that survives all of those. The first half is the logical coordinate system, which replaces "top" and "left" with "block-start" and "inline-start" and costs nothing to adopt. The second half is the set of CSS decisions that decide whether a page is usable by everyone — contrast, focus indicators, motion, forced colours, and the several places where a purely visual change quietly alters what a screen reader announces.

Everything below was measured, and the measurements make the abstract parts concrete.

15.1 Two Axes, Not Four Directions

Every box has two axes, defined relative to how its text flows:

inline axis
The direction text runs within a line. Horizontal in English, vertical in Japanese vertical writing.
block axis
The direction successive lines stack. Vertical in English, horizontal in Japanese vertical writing.

Each axis has a start and an end, giving four flow-relative edges: block-start edge, block-end, inline-start edge and inline-end. In a left-to-right horizontal page they map to top, bottom, left and right — and in every other configuration they do not.

The mapping in the four common configurations, which is the whole of what has to be internalised:

configuration
block-start
block-end
inline-start
inline-end
horizontal-tb + ltr
top
bottom
left
right
horizontal-tb + rtl
top
bottom
right
left
vertical-rl
right
left
top
bottom
vertical-lr
left
right
top
bottom

Reading down the columns is the useful exercise: the block-start edge is the top in both horizontal rows and moves to a side in vertical writing, while the inline-start edge is the one that flips with direction. That is why a stylesheet written in physical properties usually breaks first on the inline axis — a right-to-left page mirrors it and leaves the block axis alone.

Every one of these four flow-relative edges has a property family named after it, and §15.4 measures the whole mapping. Which configuration you are in is decided by two properties.

What to carry forward from this subsection: block-start edge, inline-start edge and flow-relative.

15.2 writing-mode

The writing-mode property takes horizontal-tb (the default), vertical-rl, vertical-lr, and the sideways variants. It rotates the whole coordinate system, and the effect on logical properties is exact. Measured on two identical rule sets differing only in writing-mode:

.v, .h {
  inline-size: 200px; block-size: 120px;
  margin-block-start: 10px;
  padding-inline-start: 20px;
  border-inline-start: 4px solid;
}
.v { writing-mode: vertical-rl; }
.h { writing-mode: horizontal-tb; }

v:  box = 120 x 224   margin-right = 10px   padding-top = 20px   border-top = 4px
h:  box = 224 x 120   margin-top   = 10px   padding-left = 20px  border-left = 4px

Every one of the four declarations landed on a different physical edge, and the box's dimensions swapped. inline-size: 200px became the element's height in vertical writing, because the inline axis is vertical there. margin-block-start became a right margin, because in vertical-rl lines stack from right to left, so the block-start edge is the right edge.

No rule was changed to make that happen. That is the entire argument for logical properties: one stylesheet, correct in both.

Vertical writing is not exotic — it is standard for Japanese and traditional Chinese typesetting — and writing-mode also has a purely presentational use in a horizontal page, for a rotated table header or a vertical sidebar label, where it is far better than a transform: rotate() because the text still wraps and still selects normally.

text-orientation: decides how individual glyphs sit in vertical writing: mixed (the default — Latin rotates, CJK stays upright), upright (everything upright), or sideways. Measured applying cleanly.

The terms above, gathered: horizontal-tb, vertical-lr and text-orientation:.

15.3 direction and Bidirectional Text

The direction property takes ltr or rtl and sets the inline direction. Measured, with identical logical declarations under each:

.r { direction: rtl; }
.l { direction: ltr; }
.r > p, .l > p { margin-inline-start: 40px; border-inline-start: 4px solid red; }

r:  margin-right = 40px   border-right = 4px
l:  margin-left  = 40px   border-left  = 4px

The same two declarations produced mirrored results. A layout written in logical properties is right-to-left-ready with no additional stylesheet.

Set direction in HTML, not CSS. <html dir="rtl"> or <p dir="auto"> is the correct place, because direction is a property of the content, and assistive technology and the browser's own bidirectional algorithm read the attribute. The CSS property exists mainly so that direction can be inherited and queried; it should not be how you switch a site's language direction.

unicode-bidi: controls how a box participates in the bidirectional algorithm. Measured with three values:

writing-mode: vertical-rl; text-orientation: upright  ->  bidi = isolate
unicode-bidi: isolate; direction: rtl                 ->  bidi = isolate, dir = rtl
unicode-bidi: plaintext                               ->  bidi = plaintext

isolate — which HTML's <bdi> element sets for you, and which the first measurement shows a vertical writing mode implying — stops a run of text from reordering the text around it. This is the one that matters in practice: user-supplied names, filenames and search terms in a right-to-left script will scramble the punctuation of the sentence containing them unless they are isolated. plaintext additionally guesses each paragraph's direction from its first strong character, which is what dir="auto" does.

One line each, for reference: the direction property.

15.4 The Logical Property Set

Every physical property has a logical property counterpart, and the mapping is mechanical. Measured, in a default horizontal left-to-right context:

.a {
  margin-block: 1rem;  margin-inline: 2rem;
  padding-block-start: 3px;  padding-inline-end: 4px;
  border-block-end: 1px solid;
  inset-block-start: 5px;  inset-inline: 6px;
  max-inline-size: 100px;  min-block-size: 50px;
}

margin-top=16px  margin-bottom=16px  margin-left=32px  margin-right=32px
padding-top=3px  padding-right=4px   border-bottom-width=1px
top=5px  left=6px  right=6px  max-width=100px  min-height=50px
Sizing
the inline-size property, the block-size property, min-inline-size, max-inline-size:, min-block-size:, max-block-size
Spacing
margin-block:, margin-inline: and their -start/-end longhands; padding-block:, padding-inline: likewise
Borders
border-block:, border-inline:, their per-edge forms, and the corner radii border-start-start-radius through border-end-end-radius
Position
inset-block, inset-inline, inset-block-start:, and the rest
Values
A logical value too: text-align: start, float: inline-start, clear: inline-end, resize: block

Two practical rules. Adopt them wholesale, not partially — a stylesheet mixing margin-left and margin-inline-start has two coordinate systems in it and the mix is where bugs live. And note that physical and logical properties compete in the cascade by source order, since neither is more specific than the other: margin-left: 0; margin-inline-start: 2rem gives 2rem, and reversing the two gives 0.

The exceptions, where physical is still correct: box-shadow and text-shadow offsets, transform, gradient angles, and anything describing light or a physical direction rather than a text flow.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: physical property, border-block:, border-inline:, inset-block-start: and logical value.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: margin-inline:, padding-block: and padding-inline:.

15.5 Where Logical Properties Are Already the Default

Flexbox and grid were specified after the logical model and use it throughout, which is why they need no right-to-left work:

  • flex-direction: row follows the inline direction, so it reverses automatically in a right-to-left page.
  • justify-content: start and flex-start mean inline-start, not left.
  • Grid's grid-column counts from the inline-start line.
  • align-items acts on the block axis in a row and the inline axis in a column.

This is a reason to prefer flex and grid to floats and inline-block beyond the layout capability: they are internationalised by construction. It is also why justify-content: left exists and should be avoided — it is the physical escape hatch, and using it discards the property you were getting for free.

To have in hand before moving on: justify-content:.

15.6 Visually Hidden, and the Three Ways to Hide

There are three mechanisms for hiding content and they have completely different consequences. Measured, with each applied to a link that was then given focus programmatically:

.sr (the visually-hidden recipe)   focusable = true    box = 1 x 1
display: none                      focusable = false   box = 0 x 0
visibility: hidden                 focusable = false   box = 16 x 17
a normal link                      focusable = true    box = 45 x 17

Three distinct behaviours:

  • display: none removes the box and the accessibility node. Not focusable, takes no space, announced by nothing. This is the right way to hide something from everyone.
  • visibility: hidden removes the accessibility node and is not focusable — but the measurement shows it still occupies its 16×17 box. It is the right choice when you need the space reserved.
  • Visually hidden — the clip-path recipe — keeps the element in the accessibility tree and, as measured, still focusable. It is the right way to give a screen reader text that sighted users do not need.
.visually-hidden:not(:focus):not(:focus-within) {
  position: absolute;
  inline-size: 1px; block-size: 1px;
  margin: -1px; padding: 0; border: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip-path: inset(50%);
  white-space: nowrap;
}

Every declaration earns its place. clip-path: inset(50%) does the hiding without display: none's tree removal. The 1px size rather than 0 is because a zero-sized element is dropped from the accessibility tree by some engines. white-space: nowrap stops a long string wrapping into a 1px column and being announced with spurious line breaks. And the :not(:focus) guard is the important part: it lets a skip link become visible when a keyboard user reaches it, which — since the measurement confirms such an element is focusable — would otherwise be a focus that goes somewhere invisible.

The one thing this recipe must never hide is something a sighted user needs. "Visually hidden" is for supplementary text — "opens in a new window", a table caption for a purely visual table, the word "search" on a magnifying-glass button.

15.7 list-style: none and the List Role

A <ul> styled with list-style: none is one of the most common patterns in CSS — navigation menus, card grids, tag lists — and in Safari with VoiceOver it removes the list semantics: the list is no longer announced as a list, and the "list with 5 items" count that helps a screen reader user navigate disappears.

The mechanism is a deliberate heuristic, not a bug: Safari treats a list with no markers as presentational, because so many are. It does not happen in Chrome or Firefox, which makes it invisible in most testing.

The fix is one attribute:

<ul role="list">
  <li>…</li>
</ul>

ul[role="list"] { list-style: none; padding-inline-start: 0; }

Making the CSS depend on the attribute is the neat version: the role and the styling cannot drift apart, because the rule does not match without it.

Note the padding-inline-start: 0 alongside — §1.7 measured that a <ul>'s indentation comes from a 40px left padding, not a margin, which is why margin: 0 alone never removes it.

The general principle this is an instance of: a purely visual CSS change can alter what assistive technology reports. Other members of the family are display: contents on a semantic element (§7.6), order and dense packing separating visual from focus order (§8.11, §9.9), and content on a pseudo-element being announced (§2.12).

15.8 Reading Order and Focus Order

§8.11 and §9.9 established the problem: order, flex-direction: row-reverse, grid-area placement and grid-auto-flow: dense all change the visual order and leave the DOM order — which is the focus order and the screen-reader order — untouched.

A sighted keyboard user then sees focus jump backwards across the screen, which is WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) and, where the visual sequence carries meaning, 1.3.2 (Meaningful Sequence).

reading-flow: is the fix. It lets a flex or grid container declare that focus and accessibility order should follow the visual order. Measured as supported:

.toolbar { display: flex; reading-flow: flex-visual; }

reading-flow = flex-visual   reading-order = 1

Its values are normal (the default, DOM order), flex-visual, flex-flow, grid-rows, grid-columns, grid-order and source-order. reading-order: is the per-item escape hatch, taking an integer that reorders one child within the flow.

Two caveats worth stating plainly. Support is currently Chromium-only, so this is an enhancement and not a licence to reorder freely — a Firefox user still gets DOM order. And reading-flow fixes the order; it does not fix a layout whose visual sequence is genuinely confusing.

Until it is universal, the durable rules stand: order the DOM as the content should be read, use order only for genuinely equivalent items, and provide a skip link so a mismatch is survivable.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: reading-order:.

15.9 Focus Indicators

A focus indicator is the only thing telling a keyboard user where they are. Removing it is the single most damaging line in CSS:

:focus { outline: none; }

The outline property is the right tool for the indicator, and it has one property that border and box-shadow do not: it does not affect layout. An outline: is drawn outside the border box and reserves no space, so a rule that adds one on focus shifts nothing — which is why outline: and not border is what a focus ring should be made of. An outline is drawn outside the border box and takes no space, so adding one on focus moves nothing.

Measured, two useful behaviours:

.a { border-radius: 12px; outline: 3px solid red; outline-offset: 4px; }
.b { outline: 3px solid; outline-offset: -3px; }

a  outline = 3px solid rgb(255,0,0)  offset = 4px
b  outline = 3px solid rgb(0,0,0)    offset = -3px

Modern outlines follow border-radius, which is why the old "outlines are ugly rectangles" objection no longer holds. outline-color: takes any colour and defaults to currentColor in most engines, so a ring inherits the component's colour unless you say otherwise. outline-offset: pushes the ring away from the element — a few pixels of gap makes it far more visible — and a negative offset draws it inside, which is how you indicate focus on an element flush with the viewport edge.

The indicator to write:

:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--focus-ring, Highlight);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
:focus:not(:focus-visible) { outline: none; }

:focus-visible (§2.7) is the browser's own judgement about when an indicator is warranted — keyboard yes, mouse click on a button no — so this satisfies the designers who objected to rings on click, without removing anything from keyboard users. The second rule is only needed for older engines and is harmless.

The requirements, from WCAG 2.2:

  • The indicator must have at least 3:1 contrast against the adjacent colours — both the focused component's own colour and the background around it. A grey ring on a grey button fails.
  • It must be at least 2 CSS pixels thick and enclose the component (or an area of equivalent size).
  • It must not be obscured by sticky headers or footers — which is the same scroll-padding fix as §10.14.

Using the Highlight system colour as the default is a cheap win: it is the operating system's own focus colour, so it is already familiar and it survives forced-colours mode.

In summary, the vocabulary here is outline-offset: and outline-color:.

What to carry forward from this subsection: outline:.

15.10 Target Size

WCAG 2.2 added a target size requirement: an interactive target should be at least 24×24 CSS pixels, or have 24px of clear space around it. That is the AA level; AAA asks for 44×44.

CSS can satisfy it without changing the visual design, by expanding the hit area with a pseudo-element:

.icon-button { position: relative; }
.icon-button::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 50%;
  inline-size: 44px; block-size: 44px;
  translate: -50% -50%;
}

A better answer where the design allows it is simply to make the control bigger:

@media (pointer: coarse) {
  .btn, .icon-button { min-block-size: 44px; min-inline-size: 44px; }
}

§13.8 measured the pointer feature; using it here means touch devices get the larger targets and mouse users are unaffected.

15.11 Motion

prefers-reduced-motion is not a preference about taste. Vestibular disorders make large-scale motion — parallax, full-screen transitions, anything that moves a lot of the viewport — cause genuine nausea and disorientation.

The pattern from §13.7, restated because it is the one thing in this section most worth adopting:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  :root  { scroll-behavior: smooth; }
  .card  { transition: translate 200ms ease-out; }
  .hero  { background-attachment: fixed; }
}

Opt in, so that motion added later is safe by default.

What "reduce" should mean is worth being precise about, because a blanket animation: none is the wrong answer. The specification's intent is reduced, not removed: a fade is generally fine, and it is large positional movement, parallax, spinning and zooming that cause harm. A reasonable interpretation:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

That blanket rule is a safety net rather than a design. Prefer replacing motion with a cross-fade where the motion carried meaning, and keep a loading spinner — it communicates state, and a still spinner communicates nothing.

15.12 Forced Colours

Forced colors mode — the Windows High Contrast successor — replaces every colour on the page with a small user-chosen palette. @media (forced-colors: active) detects it, and the instinct it produces is almost always wrong.

The correct response is not to restore your colours. The reader has chosen that palette because they need it. What actually needs fixing is what forced colours breaks:

  • Backgrounds and shadows are removed, so anything that conveyed meaning by fill alone — a selected state shown as a coloured background, a card distinguished only by a shadow — becomes invisible. Add a border.
  • background-image is kept but background-color is not, so a gradient-only affordance disappears.
  • Icons drawn as background images vanish. SVG with fill: currentColor survives, because currentColor is re-mapped.
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .card       { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }
  .btn--selected { border: 2px solid Highlight; }
  .icon       { forced-color-adjust: auto; }
}

forced-color-adjust: none opts an element out of the re-mapping entirely. It has exactly one legitimate use: content whose colours are the information — a colour picker's swatches, a chart legend where the colour identifies the series. Using it to preserve a brand colour is the misuse the property is most often put to.

The best preparation for forced colours is not a media query at all: build on the system colours (§11.5). A page whose base pair is Canvas/CanvasText and whose accents are Highlight/LinkText is already correct, because those are the keywords that get re-mapped.

The terms above, gathered: forced-color-adjust:.

15.13 Colour Contrast

Colour contrast is measured as a ratio between the relative luminance of two colours. WCAG contrast requirements set three thresholds, and WCAG 2.2 is the edition they come from:

4.5 : 1
Body text against its background. Level AA, criterion 1.4.3.
3 : 1
Large text (18pt, or 14pt bold), and every non-text indicator — borders of form fields, focus rings, icons that carry meaning. Criteria 1.4.3 and 1.4.11.
7 : 1
Level AAA for body text.

Three things that make this practical rather than a spreadsheet exercise:

  • The 3:1 rule for non-text is the one people miss. A form field whose only boundary is a #ddd border on white is at about 1.3:1 and fails — the field is invisible to a low-vision user. So is a focus ring in a pale brand colour.
  • Placeholder text is not a label. Low-contrast placeholder text as the only label fails twice: contrast, and the fact that it disappears when typing begins.
  • contrast-color() picks a foreground with sufficient contrast against a given background, which finally makes this expressible in CSS rather than in a build step. Its availability is currently limited, so treat it as an enhancement:
.badge { background: var(--tone); color: contrast-color(var(--tone)); }

Check contrast with the browser's own tools: the colour picker in the styles pane shows the ratio and the AA/AAA marks directly, and the accessibility panel flags failures. Do that as you write, not in an audit at the end.

One line each, for reference: contrast-color() and wcag contrast.

15.14 Text Spacing and Zoom

Two WCAG criteria that are purely CSS problems, and both are usually failed by the same cause: fixed heights.

Text spacing (1.4.12) requires that the page still work when the reader applies line-height: 1.5, letter-spacing: 0.12em, word-spacing: 0.16em and margin-block: 2em on paragraphs. Content must not be clipped or overlap. A button with height: 32px fails; the same button with min-block-size: 32px and vertical padding passes.

Reflow (1.4.10) requires that at 320 CSS pixels of width — equivalent to 400% zoom on a 1280px screen — there is no two-directional scrolling. In practice that means: no fixed pixel widths on containers, no white-space: nowrap on anything long, no horizontal scroll on the body, and a layout that collapses to one column.

Both are satisfied by the same habits:

.btn   { min-block-size: 2.75rem; padding-block: 0.5rem; }   /* not height */
.card  { max-inline-size: 100%; }                            /* not width  */
.page  { padding-inline: max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-left)); }

Use min-block-size rather than block-size, max-inline-size rather than inline-size, and rem rather than px for anything that holds text. Everything else follows.

The related trap from §4.9: a font-size written purely in vw cannot be zoomed, because zooming scales the viewport too. Always include a rem term.

15.15 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • Every box has an inline axis and a block axis, with flow-relative block-start edge and inline-start edge rather than fixed physical directions.
  • The writing-mode property rotates the coordinate system: measured, one rule set produced a 224×120 box with a top margin under horizontal-tb and a 120×224 box with a right margin under vertical-rl, from the same four declarations.
  • text-orientation: governs glyph orientation in vertical writing.
  • The direction property mirrors the inline axis — measured turning margin-inline-start into a right margin — and should be set in HTML with dir, not in CSS; unicode-bidi: with isolate protects a sentence from user-supplied bidirectional text.
  • The logical property set covers sizing (the inline-size property, the block-size property, max-inline-size:, min-block-size:), spacing (margin-block:, margin-inline:, padding-block:, padding-inline:), borders (border-block:, border-inline:) and position (inset-block-start:), plus logical values such as text-align: start; the mapping was measured on twelve properties.
  • Physical and logical properties compete by source order, so adopt one system wholesale.
  • Flex and grid already use the logical model, which is why they are right-to-left-ready by construction.
  • Visually hidden content is focusable and in the accessibility tree — measured focusable at 1×1 — while display: none is neither and visibility: hidden is neither but still occupies its box, measured at 16×17.
  • list-style: none can remove the list role in Safari with VoiceOver, so pair it with role="list" and key the CSS off that attribute.
  • reading-flow: and reading-order: make focus and accessibility order follow the visual order in flex and grid — measured supported — but are Chromium-only, so DOM order remains the durable answer.
  • A focus indicator belongs on :focus-visible, uses the outline property (which does not affect layout), follows border-radius, and is tuned with outline-offset: — measured with both positive and negative offsets — needing 3:1 contrast and 2px thickness.
  • Target size is 24×24 at AA and 44×44 at AAA; a pseudo-element or a pointer: coarse query satisfies it without redesigning.
  • Motion should be opted into under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, and "reduce" means reduced rather than removed.
  • Forced colors mode should be worked with rather than undone: add borders where fills carried meaning, and forced-color-adjust: none only where colour is the information; building on system colors avoids most of the work.
  • Colour contrast thresholds are 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and every non-text indicator, and 7:1 for AAA; contrast-color() expresses it in CSS where available.
  • Text spacing and page zoom are satisfied by min-block-size over block-size, max-inline-size over inline-size, rem over px, and never a bare viewport unit on font-size.

Exercises

1. A component library's card is written with margin-left, padding-right, border-left and text-align: left. It is being adopted by a team shipping in Arabic. Convert it, and name the two things the conversion does not fix.

Solution 
/* before */
.card { margin-left: 1rem; padding-right: 1.5rem; border-left: 4px solid; text-align: left; }

/* after */
.card {
  margin-inline-start: 1rem;
  padding-inline-end: 1.5rem;
  border-inline-start: 4px solid;
  text-align: start;
}

Measured (§15.3), those declarations under direction: rtl produced margin-right: 40px and border-right: 4px from the identical rule that gave margin-left and border-left under ltr. One stylesheet, correct in both — which is the whole point, and it is why the alternative (a second right-to-left stylesheet, or a [dir="rtl"] override for every rule) is not worth writing.

Two things the conversion does not fix.

1. Content that is genuinely directional. A box-shadow: 4px 4px 8px describes light coming from the upper left, and light does not mirror with the text. Nor do transform: translateX(), gradient angles, or an icon depicting a physical direction. These are the documented exceptions (§15.4) and they must be handled case by case — a "next" chevron should mirror, because it means forward in reading order; a sun icon should not.

For the shadow specifically there is no logical equivalent; if it must mirror, that is one of the few places a [dir="rtl"] override is legitimate.

2. Bidirectional text inside the content. Logical properties fix the box, not the text. A card whose title is "Ahmed — Invoice #4021" in a right-to-left paragraph will have its punctuation and the Latin fragment reordered by the bidirectional algorithm, often producing something like 4021# Invoice — Ahmed with the dash and hash in the wrong places. No amount of margin-inline-start touches that.

The fix is at the content boundary, and it is HTML rather than CSS:

<h3 class="card__title"><bdi>{{ name }}</bdi> — Invoice #{{ number }}</h3>

<bdi> sets unicode-bidi: isolate, which §15.3 measured, and stops the user-supplied fragment from reordering the text around it. dir="auto" on the same element additionally guesses the fragment's own direction from its first strong character.

A third thing worth flagging in review, since the team is adopting rather than writing: check that the component uses flex or grid rather than floats. §15.5 — flex and grid are already logical, so flex-direction: row and justify-content: start reverse for free, while float: left does not. If the card's internals are floated, converting them to float: inline-start works but is a signal that the layout should be flex.

2. A designer asks for :focus { outline: none } because "the blue rings look bad on click". Give them what they want without breaking keyboard access, and list the three requirements the replacement must meet.

Solution 
:focus:not(:focus-visible) { outline: none; }

:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--focus-ring, Highlight);
  outline-offset: 2px;
  border-radius: inherit;
}

Why this is exactly what was asked for. The complaint is real and specific: a ring appearing when you click a button looks like a bug to a mouse user. :focus-visible (§2.7) is the browser's own judgement about when an indicator is warranted — keyboard navigation yes, mouse click on a button no, click into a text field yes, because a text field's focus is information the user needs either way. So the designer's objection is met precisely, and nothing is taken from keyboard users.

The first rule is belt-and-braces for engines that support :focus-visible in the selector but still paint a default ring on :focus; it can be dropped once support is assumed.

The three requirements the replacement must meet, from WCAG 2.2:

1. At least 3:1 contrast against both adjacent colours — the component the ring surrounds, and the background it sits on (criterion 1.4.11). This is the one most often failed, because a ring in a pale brand colour looks tasteful and is invisible. Using the Highlight system colour as the default (§11.5) sidesteps it: it is the operating system's own focus colour, so it is already contrast-checked by the platform and it survives forced-colours mode unchanged.

2. At least 2 CSS pixels thick, and it must enclose the component (criterion 2.4.13, Focus Appearance). 3px gives headroom. outline-offset: 2px is not decoration either — a ring flush against a button of similar colour is much harder to see than one with a gap, and the measurement in §15.9 confirms both positive and negative offsets apply cleanly. A negative offset is the right choice for a control flush with a viewport edge.

3. It must not be obscured (criterion 2.4.11, Focus Not Obscured). A sticky header will cover a focused element that the browser has just scrolled to. One declaration fixes it for focus, fragment links and scrollIntoView() together:

:root { scroll-padding-block-start: 5rem; }

Two details that make this shippable. outline is the right property because it does not affect layout — a border on focus would shift the page, and a box-shadow ring cannot be re-mapped in forced-colours mode. And modern outlines follow border-radius (§15.9, measured), which removes the last real aesthetic objection: the ring on a pill button is a pill, not a rectangle.

What I would not accept as a compromise: styling only :hover and :active, or replacing the ring with a colour change. Colour alone is not a sufficient indicator, and a hover state is not a focus state.

3. Audit this rule set against the accessibility material in this section. List every problem and give the corrected version.

.nav ul       { list-style: none; margin: 0; }
.nav a        { color: #8a8a8a; text-decoration: none; }
.nav a:hover  { color: #fff; }
.nav          { display: flex; flex-direction: row-reverse; }
.badge        { height: 20px; width: 20px; font-size: 2.5vw; }
.card         { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15); }
* { transition: all 300ms; }
Solution

Seven problems.

1. list-style: none without role="list". In Safari with VoiceOver the navigation stops being announced as a list, and the item count — which is how a screen reader user decides whether to explore it — is gone (§15.7).

2. margin: 0 does not remove the list indentation. §1.7 measured that a <ul>'s indent is a 40px padding-left, not a margin. The rule looks like it resets the list and does not.

3. #8a8a8a on any plausible background fails contrast. Against white it is about 3.0:1 — below the 4.5:1 body-text threshold (§15.13). It is also below 4.5:1 against most dark backgrounds. Grey-on-grey navigation is one of the commonest AA failures there is.

4. text-decoration: none plus colour-only hover. The links have no non-colour affordance, and the only state change is colour — which fails both "colour is not the only visual means" and, more concretely, gives a colour-blind user no hover feedback.

5. No focus style at all. :hover is styled and :focus-visible is not, so a keyboard user gets whatever the browser's default is — and with text-decoration: none and a colour change there is nothing to distinguish a focused link.

6. flex-direction: row-reverse desynchronises visual and focus order. §8.11 measured the effect: the DOM order is unchanged, so a keyboard user tabs right-to-left through a left-to-right layout. WCAG 2.4.3.

7. height/width plus a vw font-size on .badge, and transition: all. The fixed height clips the badge under the text-spacing criterion (§15.14); the bare vw font-size cannot be zoomed (§4.9); and * { transition: all 300ms } animates everything for everyone including readers who asked for less motion, and animates expensive properties on every element (§14.1, §14.12).

Also worth flagging: .card's shadow-only distinction disappears entirely in forced-colours mode (§15.12).

The corrected version:

<nav class="nav"><ul role="list"> … </ul></nav>

.nav ul { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding-inline-start: 0; }

.nav { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }          /* DOM order = reading order */

.nav a {
  color: var(--text);                        /* >= 4.5:1 against the surface */
  text-decoration-thickness: from-font;
  text-underline-offset: 0.15em;
}
.nav a:hover { text-decoration-thickness: 0.12em; }

.nav a:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid Highlight;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

.badge {
  min-block-size: 1.5rem; min-inline-size: 1.5rem;
  font-size: clamp(0.75rem, 0.7rem + 0.2vw, 0.875rem);
  display: grid; place-items: center;
}

.card { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15); }
@media (forced-colors: active) { .card { border: 1px solid CanvasText; } }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .nav a  { transition: text-decoration-thickness 150ms; }
  .card   { transition: box-shadow 200ms, translate 200ms; }
}

The order of the links is now the DOM order — if the reversal was a design requirement, reading-flow: flex-visual (§15.8) is the enhancement, with the DOM order still correct as the fallback since it is Chromium-only.

SECTION 16

Architecture, Scope, Performance and Debugging

Everything up to here has been about making CSS do what you want. This section is about making a stylesheet that is still workable after three years and four contributors — which is a different problem, and the one that actually consumes teams.

The two failure modes are specific and both are avoidable. A stylesheet ratchets: each change is made with a slightly more specific selector than the last, until !important is the only tool left. And a stylesheet accretes: nobody can prove a rule is unused, so nothing is ever deleted, and the file grows without bound.

CSS now has real answers to both — @layer, @scope, :where() and shadow DOM — which is a genuine change from the era when the answer was a naming convention and discipline. The second half of the section covers what makes a page fast, honestly, including which of the received wisdom about selector performance is still true.

Everything measured below was measured.

16.1 The Two Failure Modes

The specificity ratchet. A component ships with .btn { padding: 0.5rem }. Someone needs a variant and writes .sidebar .btn. Someone else needs to override that and writes .page .sidebar .btn. Six months later a change requires #main .page .sidebar .btn.btn--flush, and the only remaining move is !important. Nothing here was a mistake in isolation; each step was the smallest thing that worked.

The ratchet exists because, before layers, specificity was the only mechanism for saying "this should win". §3.2 changed that: cascade layers and scope proximity are both above specificity in the sort, and both are explicit rather than emergent.

Accretion. A rule can only be deleted if you can prove nothing uses it, and in a large application with server-rendered templates, a component library and dynamic class names, you usually cannot. So the file grows, the unused fraction rises, and eventually nobody edits anything — they only add.

Accretion is fought by scope: the smaller the region a rule can affect, the more locally you can reason about deleting it. That is what §16.6 through §16.9 are for.

16.2 BEM

BEM — Block, Element, Modifier — is a naming convention that flattens specificity by encoding structure in the class name rather than in the selector:

.card              { }
.card__title       { }
.card__title--lead { }
.card--featured    { }

Every selector is a single class, so every rule is (0,1,0) and the ratchet cannot start. The nesting that would have been in the selector is in the name instead.

Its costs are real and worth naming. The class names are long and the markup is noisy. It does not prevent a global collision — .card__title is still a global name, just an unlikely one. And it says nothing about ordering, so two rules at (0,1,0) still resolve by source order, which a bundler can change.

Native nesting does not give you BEM. §2.14 established that & is a selector rather than a string, so &__title producing .card__title — the thing Sass does — has no CSS equivalent. If you want BEM names you write them out.

BEM is still a reasonable default for a team that wants a convention and nothing else. But @layer solves the ordering problem BEM cannot, and @scope solves the collision problem, so a new codebase has better tools available.

16.3 ITCSS, Utility-First and Atomic CSS

ITCSS (Inverted Triangle CSS) orders a stylesheet from most general to most specific: settings, tools, generic, elements, objects, components, utilities. Its insight was that source order is architecture, and it is now much better expressed as layers:

@layer settings, generic, elements, objects, components, utilities;

That single line is ITCSS, made explicit and independent of file ordering.

Utility-first — the approach popularised by Tailwind — inverts the model: instead of naming a component and giving it declarations, you compose small single-purpose classes in the markup.

<div class="flex items-center gap-4 rounded-lg p-4 bg-surface">…</div>

The honest case for it: there are no names to invent, no dead CSS (a utility not used is not generated), no cascade to reason about, and the styles are visible at the point of use. The honest case against: the markup carries the design, so a change to spacing means editing every template rather than one rule; it needs a build step to be viable; and it moves work out of a language designed for it into a place with no cascade, no media queries and no :hover.

Atomic CSS is the same idea taken further — one declaration per class, generated exhaustively.

The pragmatic position most teams reach, and the one this course endorses: components for anything that repeats, utilities for one-off adjustments, and layers to keep the two from fighting:

@layer components, utilities;
@layer components { .card { padding: 1rem; } }
@layer utilities   { .p-0 { padding: 0; } }

.p-0 beats .card regardless of specificity, because utilities is the later layer (§3.6) — which is the guarantee a utility needs, without !important.

16.4 Cascade Layers as Architecture

The single highest-leverage architectural decision available is one line at the top of the stylesheet:

@layer reset, base, layout, components, utilities;

It buys four things that no naming convention can:

  • Override direction is explicit and order-independent. A utilities rule beats a components rule whatever their selectors and whatever order the bundler emits them in.
  • Third-party CSS can be subordinated: @import url("vendor.css") layer(vendor); puts an entire stylesheet you do not control below everything you write, however aggressive its selectors (§3.6).
  • Selectors can be readable again. Inside a layer you can write .card h2 without starting a ratchet, because a later layer wins regardless.
  • revert-layer gives a layer a way to step aside for one property (§3.10), which is how a components rule can defer to base without deleting itself.

Two rules of use. Declare the order once, at the top, before any layer has content — that fixes it, and layers can then be filled from any file in any sequence. And keep !important out of low layers: §3.6 measured that importance reverses the layer order, so an !important in reset is the strongest declaration in the author origin and essentially unbeatable.

16.5 What a Preprocessor Is Still For

A great deal of what Sass was for is now in CSS: variables (§5), nesting (§2.14), arithmetic (§4.8), colour manipulation (§11.4's relative colour syntax), and — where available — functions (§5.13). The honest remaining list is short:

  • Loops and conditionals at build time. Generating a 100-step utility scale, or iterating a map of breakpoints, is still a build-time job. CSS's if() is per-value, not a generator.
  • @use and @forward, which give real module scope and namespacing that @import never had.
  • String manipulation, including the &__title concatenation that native nesting cannot do (§16.2).
  • Compiling one file from many without the runtime cost of @import (§1.3).

PostCSS is the more defensible tool for most teams, because it is a transform pipeline rather than a language: autoprefixer inserts the vendor prefixes that are still needed from real support data (§1.6), a nesting plugin or a syntax-lowering plugin can compile newer CSS down for older browsers, and you keep writing standard CSS throughout. The important difference is the direction of travel: PostCSS output converges on what you wrote as browsers catch up, and preprocessor output does not.

16.6 CSS Modules and CSS-in-JS

CSS Modules solve the global-namespace problem at build time: a class written .card is emitted as .card_a3f9b and the build rewrites the reference in the component. It is genuine scope with no runtime, no new language, and no cascade surprises, and it composes with everything else in this section.

CSS-in-JS goes further, generating styles from JavaScript at runtime or build time. Its advantages are colocation and the ability to compute styles from props; its costs are a runtime, a larger bundle, and — for the runtime variants — styles that cannot be sent as CSS in the initial response, which delays first paint (§1.9).

The direction of travel is worth stating: the problems these tools were built to solve — scope, collisions, dead code, dynamic values — now have platform answers in @scope, shadow DOM, custom properties and layers. New codebases should reach for the platform first and adopt a build-time tool where it genuinely helps rather than by default.

16.7 Resets

A css reset normalises the differences between browsers' default stylesheets (§1.7). The three approaches:

  • A hard reset zeroes everything (* { margin: 0; padding: 0 }). It removes browser inconsistency and also removes sensible defaults, so you rebuild typography from nothing.
  • normalize.css preserves useful defaults and only corrects inconsistencies. It was the right answer for a long time and is now largely unnecessary — the inconsistencies it corrected have mostly been fixed.
  • A modern reset is a short list of opinions, and it is what most projects should write:
@layer reset {
  *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

  body, h1, h2, h3, h4, p, figure, blockquote, dl, dd { margin: 0; }

  html { -webkit-text-size-adjust: none; interpolate-size: allow-keywords; }
  body { min-block-size: 100svh; line-height: 1.5; text-rendering: optimizeSpeed; }

  h1, h2, h3, h4, button, input, label { line-height: 1.1; }
  h1, h2, h3, h4 { text-wrap: balance; }
  p, li { text-wrap: pretty; }

  ul[role="list"], ol[role="list"] { list-style: none; padding-inline-start: 0; }

  img, picture, svg, video, canvas { display: block; max-inline-size: 100%; }

  input, button, textarea, select { font: inherit; color: inherit; }

  :target { scroll-margin-block-start: 5rem; }

  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    *, *::before, *::after {
      animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
      animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
      transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
      scroll-behavior: auto !important;
    }
  }
}

Nearly every line there is a measurement from earlier in this course: box-sizing from §6.2, the ::before/::after selectors because pseudo-elements do not inherit it, img { display: block } from §7.5's four-pixel gap, font: inherit from §1.7's 13.3333px button, ul[role="list"] from §15.7, 100svh from §4.4, and scroll-margin from §10.14.

Putting it in a layer is the part people miss. Inside @layer reset, every unlayered rule you write afterwards beats it whatever its specificity, so the reset can never be the thing you are fighting.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: css reset.

16.8 Shadow DOM Styling

Style encapsulation is the strongest scope boundary CSS has, and it is the only one enforced by the platform rather than by a build step. Measured, with a custom element whose shadow root contains a <p>:

p { color: red; }          /* in the outer document */

shadow <p> color = rgb(0, 0, 0)      light-DOM <p> color = rgb(255, 0, 0)

The outer rule did not reach inside. That is total, and it is what makes a web component safe to drop into an unknown page.

But three things do cross the boundary, and knowing which is the whole skill. Measured on a component styled from outside with color: teal; font-family: Georgia; --pad: 12px:

host padding                = 12px          <- custom property crossed
inner <p> color             = rgb(0,128,128) <- inherited property crossed
inner <p> font-family       = Georgia        <- inherited property crossed
::part(btn) border          = 2px rgb(0,0,255)
::slotted(span) decoration  = underline
Inherited properties
color, font-*, line-height and the rest of §3.9's list inherit straight through. Measured. This is why a component looks native by default.
Custom properties
They inherit too, so --pad set outside was read by var(--pad) inside. This is a component's styling API and it is the mechanism to design around.
::part()
The component marks an element part="btn" and the outside styles it with my-w::part(btn). An explicit, opt-in hole — measured working.

From the inside, three selectors address the boundary. :host matches the custom element itself; :host(.big) matches it when it also matches a selector; :host-context() matches based on an ancestor. ::slotted() styles light-DOM content passed into a <slot> — measured underlining a slotted <span> — and it only reaches one level, so ::slotted(span a) does not work. And :host has very low precedence: a rule in the outer document targeting the element wins over :host in the shadow root, which is deliberate — it lets a consumer override the component's own defaults.

The design guidance that follows: expose a small set of registered custom properties as the component's API (§5.6's @property makes them typed and documented), mark a handful of internals as parts, and rely on inheritance for typography. Everything else stays private, and that is the point.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: style encapsulation.

16.9 @scope as an Architecture Boundary

@scope (§2.15) gives you shadow-DOM-like boundaries without web components, and — uniquely — a lower bound as well as an upper one. Measured, with a scope limited to .slot:

@scope (.widget) to (.slot) {
  p { color: red; }
}

p inside .widget, outside .slot   =  rgb(255, 0, 0)
p inside .slot                    =  rgb(0, 0, 0)
p outside .widget                 =  rgb(0, 0, 0)

The middle line is the one nothing else does. That "donut" — style everything in this region except this sub-region — is exactly the shape of: a rich-text area that must not style the widgets embedded in it, a page theme that must not reach into a third-party embed, and a design system boundary where a legacy subtree is excluded.

Three architectural properties make it good in a stylesheet rather than merely clever. It adds no specificity, so it composes with layers instead of competing. It introduces scope proximity (§3.8) — the nearer scope wins, measured in both writing orders — which makes nested themes resolve without any escalation. And an implicit scope, @scope { ... } inside a <style> element, scopes to that element's parent, which is the closest CSS gets to a component-scoped stylesheet with no build step.

16.10 Selector Performance, Honestly

The received wisdom — avoid the universal selector, avoid deep descendant chains, keep selectors short — dates from the mid-2000s and is mostly obsolete.

What is actually true today:

  • Selector matching is a small fraction of style recalculation, which is itself a small fraction of a frame. Engines match right to left (§2.1), index rules by their rightmost compound selector, and skip subtrees wholesale. * { box-sizing: border-box } is not a performance problem and never really was.
  • The cost that matters is invalidation, not matching. When something changes, the engine must decide which elements' styles are now stale. A selector whose match depends on distant relatives — a long descendant chain, :nth-child() over a large list, an unbounded :has() — widens that set, so one DOM change dirties many elements.
  • :has() is the one worth care, and the care is specific: prefer a combinator (:has(> .x)) over an unbounded descendant (:has(.x)), because the bounded form limits how far the engine has to look on every mutation. This is a real consideration on a large, frequently mutating tree and irrelevant on a static page.
  • The genuine wins are elsewhere entirely: not animating layout-triggering properties (§14.12), not creating hundreds of compositor layers, and not shipping 400 kB of CSS.

Measure before optimising a selector. The performance panel's style-recalculation timings will tell you whether it is worth anything, and it usually is not.

16.11 Containment

Containment is a promise to the browser that a subtree's effects are bounded, which lets it skip work. contain: takes four independent values plus two shorthands. Measured, all six accepted:

contain: layout   contain: paint   contain: size
contain: style    contain: strict  contain: content
layout containment
Nothing inside affects layout outside. Creates a BFC, a stacking context, and a containing block for fixed descendants.
paint containment
Nothing inside paints outside the box. Clips, and lets the engine skip painting the subtree entirely when it is off-screen.
size containment
The box's size does not depend on its contents — so you must give it a size or it collapses. This is the same constraint container-type: size carries (§13.12).
style containment
Counters and quotes do not escape the subtree.
content / strict
content is layout paint style; strict adds size.

content-visibility: is the high-level version and the one to reach for. Measured with its companion:

.section { content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 300px; }

content-visibility = auto     contain-intrinsic-size = auto 300px

content-visibility: auto tells the browser to skip rendering work entirely for a subtree that is off-screen — no layout, no paint — and to do it when the element scrolls into view. On a long page of many sections this is one of the largest single wins available.

contain-intrinsic-size: is not optional with it. A skipped element has no size, so without a placeholder the scrollbar jumps as sections render. auto 300px means "use 300px until you have measured it once, then remember the real value" — which removes the jump after the first pass.

The caveat worth stating: content inside content-visibility: auto is skipped for rendering but is still found by find-in-page and by assistive technology in current browsers, which was a genuine early concern and is now handled. Do not use it on content that must be measured by script without checking.

To have in hand before moving on: layout containment, paint containment, style containment and contain-intrinsic-size:.

16.12 Rendering Performance

Beyond §14.12's cost ladder, three things dominate:

Compositor layers. Each promoted layer costs GPU memory. will-change, transform: translateZ(0), position: fixed, backdrop-filter and content-visibility all create them. A handful is right; two hundred is slower than none, and on a memory-constrained phone it causes crashes rather than jank.

Layout thrashing. Reading a layout-dependent value from JavaScript forces the engine to flush pending layout (§3.14). Alternating a write and a read in a loop forces one layout per iteration:

for each element:  el.style.width = ...   then read el.offsetWidth   -> N layouts
read all widths first, then write all      -> 1 layout

The fix is always the same shape: batch reads, then batch writes.

Paint cost. A large box-shadow blur, a backdrop-filter, a filter and a border-radius on a very large element are all expensive to rasterise. If a scroll is janky and nothing is animating, the performance panel's paint timings are where to look.

16.13 Unused CSS and Bundle Size

The coverage tool in developer tools reports what fraction of each stylesheet was used on the current page. It is genuinely useful and genuinely misleading: it measures this page load, so anything behind an interaction, a media query or a state is reported as unused.

Treat it as a signal, not a verdict. The reliable ways to keep CSS small are structural:

  • Split by condition, not by module. §1.9's measurement: a media-qualified <link> whose query does not match is downloaded at low priority and is not render-blocking.
  • Delete on a schedule. Scope (§16.9) is what makes deletion provable; an unscoped global rule can never be proven dead.
  • Prefer one flexible rule to five specific ones. repeat(auto-fit, minmax(18rem, 1fr)) replaces three breakpoints' worth of declarations (§9.8), and clamp() replaces a size ladder (§4.9).
  • Compress. Brotli takes a 90 kB stylesheet to roughly 12 kB, which beats most hand-optimisation.

Critical css (§1.9) is the last resort, not the first: it improves first paint and costs cacheability, staleness risk and build complexity. Reach for it when a measurement says first paint is stylesheet-bound.

16.14 Browser Support and Progressive Enhancement

Progressive enhancement in CSS is unusually cheap, because §1.5's error handling gives you a fallback for free whenever two declarations target the same property:

.a { color: #5b21b6; }
.a { color: oklch(48% 0.24 295); }

Feature detection with @supports (§13.10) is for the cases that need more than one declaration to change together, and it should be written base-first — fallback unconditional, enhancement inside the query.

Baseline status is the vocabulary the industry has settled on for "can I use this": newly available means every major engine has shipped it; widely available means that has been true for thirty months. It is reported on every MDN reference page and in caniuse. Two habits worth having: check it for anything you have not used before, and re-check it for anything you learned more than a year ago — the answer changes, usually in your favour, and stylesheets are full of workarounds for problems that no longer exist.

Graceful degradation — building the modern version and patching older browsers — is the inverse and is harder to get right, because you have to enumerate what breaks. Prefer the base-first direction.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: feature detection.

16.15 Debugging

Six tools, in the order you should reach for them:

  • The styles pane (§1.10). Is the declaration struck through (lost the cascade, or invalid), present but overridden, or absent entirely (the selector never matched)? Those are three different bugs and only one of them is about specificity.
  • The computed tab. One resolved value per property, with the winning rule and what it beat, including inherited values and the ancestor they came from.
  • The layout pane. Grid and flexbox overlays draw line numbers, area names, track sizes and implicit tracks on the page (§9.16). For any grid problem this is faster than reading the CSS.
  • * { outline: 1px solid red }, temporarily. The oldest trick and still the fastest way to find what is overflowing a container. outline rather than border because it does not affect layout (§15.9).
  • The accessibility pane. The computed accessibility tree, contrast ratios, and the name each element actually exposes — which is where §15's claims are checked rather than assumed.
  • The performance panel. Style recalculation, layout, paint and composite timings per frame, which is the only honest way to answer "why is this slow".

stylelint belongs alongside them, because it catches at authoring time the whole class of thing browsers do not report: a // comment (§1.5's most destructive typo), a duplicate property, a shorthand after a longhand (§3.12), an invalid value, an unknown property. Every one of those is silent in a browser and every one is an error to a linter, which is the entire argument for having one.

In summary, the vocabulary here is contrast ratio.

What to carry forward from this subsection: stylelint.

16.16 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • CSS architecture exists to defeat two failure modes: the specificity management ratchet, and accretion — rules nobody can prove are unused.
  • BEM flattens every selector to one class; ITCSS orders by generality; utility-first and atomic css move composition into the markup; layers express all three better than convention does.
  • @layer is the highest-leverage architectural line available: explicit override direction, third-party subordination, readable selectors, and revert-layer — with !important kept out of low layers because importance reverses the order.
  • Preprocessors (sass) retain build-time loops, @use/@forward and string concatenation; postcss with autoprefixer is the more defensible pipeline because its output converges on standard CSS.
  • css modules give build-time scope with no runtime; css-in-js buys colocation at the cost of a runtime and delayed first paint.
  • A modern css reset — not a hard reset, and no longer normalize.css — belongs in a layer, and nearly every line of it is a measurement from earlier in this course.
  • Shadow dom styling is real style encapsulation: an outer p { color: red } was measured not reaching a shadow <p>, while inherited properties and custom properties were measured crossing; :host, ::slotted() and ::part() are the three boundary selectors, and registered custom properties are the component's API.
  • @scope with a limit produced a measured donut — red inside the root, default inside the limit, default outside — adds no specificity, and introduces scope proximity.
  • Selector performance is dominated by invalidation rather than matching; * is fine, unbounded :has() deserves a combinator, and the real wins are elsewhere.
  • Containment — layout containment, paint containment, size containment, style containment, content and strict — was measured on all six; content-visibility: auto skips rendering off-screen and needs contain-intrinsic-size: to avoid scrollbar jump.
  • Rendering cost is dominated by compositor layer count, layout thrashing from interleaved reads and writes, and expensive paints.
  • Unused css measurements report one page load only; the durable wins are splitting by condition, provable scope, flexible rules and compression, with critical css as a last resort.
  • Progressive enhancement rides on CSS's own error handling for single declarations and on @supports feature detection for multi-declaration changes; baseline status is the vocabulary, and old workarounds should be re-checked.
  • Debug in the order: styles pane, computed tab, layout pane, * { outline }, accessibility pane, performance panel — and run stylelint, which catches the silent failures a browser never reports.

The terms above, gathered: css architecture.

Exercises

1. A four-year-old application has a 340 kB stylesheet, 62 declarations marked !important, and selectors up to #app .page .panel .list li a.link--active. You have two weeks. Write the plan.

Solution

Week one is measurement and a boundary; week two is migration. Do not start by deleting.

Day 1 — establish what you have. Run the coverage tool over the ten highest-traffic pages and record the unused fraction, knowing it over-reports (§16.13) because it measures one page load. Count rules, count !important, and plot specificity distribution — a histogram of (A,B,C) values tells you immediately whether the problem is a few pathological selectors or a general ratchet.

Day 2 — the one line that stops the bleeding.

@layer legacy, base, components, utilities;

and wrap the entire existing stylesheet:

@import url("legacy.css") layer(legacy);

This is the highest-value change in the whole plan and it is reversible. §3.6's measurement: a (0,0,1) selector in a later layer beat (1,2,1) in an earlier one. From this moment, anything new you write outside a layer beats the entire legacy stylesheet, whatever selectors it uses. The ratchet stops that day, without touching a single existing rule.

Days 3–5 — audit the !importants, do not remove them. Sort them into three buckets: utilities where importance is the contract (.hidden { display: none !important }), overrides of third-party CSS, and escalation. Only the third needs work, and once the legacy sheet is in a layer, most of it can be replaced by a rule in a later layer with a normal declaration.

Be careful of one thing measured in §3.6: !important reverses layer order, so an important declaration in legacy is now the strongest thing in the author origin and beats your new unlayered rules. Those are the ones to remove first, and there will be fewer than 62.

Week two — migrate by traffic, not by file. Take the highest-traffic component, rewrite it in the components layer with flat selectors, and delete its legacy rules. Repeat. Each component is independently shippable and independently revertible.

Two tools make deletion provable rather than nervous. @scope (§16.9) bounds a rewritten component so its rules cannot affect anything outside it — measured producing exactly a donut. And :where() (§2.9, measured at zero specificity) lets a base layer be overridden by a single class, which stops the new code from starting its own ratchet.

Add stylelint to CI on day 2 as well, configured to fail on !important outside the utilities layer and on selectors above a specificity threshold. Without it, week three undoes week two.

What I would not do in two weeks: a full rewrite, a switch to a utility framework, or a mass deletion based on the coverage report. Each is a large risk for a benefit the layer boundary already delivers on day two.

2. A web component must let consumers set its accent colour, padding and corner radius, expose its internal button for styling, and inherit the host page's typography — while remaining immune to the host page's other CSS. Design the styling API and say what each mechanism guarantees.

Solution 
/* inside the shadow root */
@property --ac-accent { syntax: "<color>";  inherits: true; initial-value: rebeccapurple; }
@property --ac-pad    { syntax: "<length>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 1rem; }
@property --ac-radius { syntax: "<length>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 0.5rem; }

:host {
  display: block;
  padding: var(--ac-pad);
  border-radius: var(--ac-radius);
  border: 1px solid color-mix(in oklab, var(--ac-accent) 40%, transparent);
}
:host([hidden]) { display: none; }
:host(.compact) { --ac-pad: 0.5rem; }

.action {
  background: var(--ac-accent);
  color: contrast-color(var(--ac-accent));
  border-radius: calc(var(--ac-radius) / 2);
}
::slotted(p) { margin-block: 0.5em; }

<button part="action" class="action">…</button>

/* in the consuming page */
my-card { --ac-accent: oklch(58% 0.2 265); --ac-pad: 1.5rem; }
my-card::part(action) { text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.04em; }

What each mechanism guarantees, with the measurement behind it.

Immunity is total and is the default. Measured (§16.8): with p { color: red } in the outer document, a <p> inside the shadow root came back rgb(0, 0, 0) while the light-DOM <p> came back rgb(255, 0, 0). No selector in the host page can reach inside. This is enforced by the platform, not by a build step or a naming convention, which is what distinguishes it from CSS Modules and BEM.

Typography inheritance is also the default, and it is what stops the component looking pasted in. Measured: color: teal and font-family: Georgia set on the custom element from outside were both read by an element inside the shadow root. Inherited properties (§3.9) cross the boundary; nothing else does.

Custom properties are the deliberate API. Measured: --pad: 12px set on the element from outside resolved through var(--pad) inside, giving padding: 12px. Registering them with @property (§5.6) buys three things the unregistered form does not: a type, so a consumer passing --ac-accent: banana gets the initial value rather than §5.5's unset cascade failure; an initial value, so the component works with no configuration; and interpolation, so a theme change transitions smoothly rather than snapping (§5.7 measured 50 versus 100 at half progress).

::part() is the explicit hole. The component decides what is styleable by marking it part="action"; everything unmarked stays private. Measured working — an outer ::part(btn) rule applied a 2px blue border to a shadow-root button. Unlike custom properties this exposes arbitrary styling of that element, so keep the part list short and treat it as a public API with the same compatibility obligations.

::slotted() styles what the consumer passed in, and reaches exactly one level: ::slotted(p) works, ::slotted(div p) does not.

One deliberate design decision worth naming: :host has very low precedence, so a consumer's my-card { padding: 2rem } beats the component's own :host { padding: var(--ac-pad) }. That is the specified behaviour and it is correct — it means the component's defaults are genuinely defaults. Do not fight it with !important.

3. A long article page scrolls badly on a mid-range phone. Profiling shows high paint time and a large layout count. List what you would check, in order, with the specific CSS cause of each.

Solution

In order, cheapest and most likely first.

1. Off-screen sections being rendered at all. A long article lays out and paints every section on every frame that touches layout, whether or not any of it is visible.

.article > section {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 800px;
}

Measured (§16.11) as accepted together. content-visibility: auto makes the browser skip layout and paint entirely for off-screen subtrees. contain-intrinsic-size is not optional: without a placeholder size the scrollbar jumps as sections render, and auto 800px means "use 800px until measured once, then remember", which removes the jump after the first pass. On a long page this is usually the single largest win available.

2. Expensive paints. High paint time with little animation points at rasterisation cost: a backdrop-filter (§11.11, which re-reads and re-filters the composited content behind the element every frame), a large box-shadow blur radius on a big element, a filter, or a border-radius on something viewport-sized. Check each in the performance panel's paint records, and consider whether the effect can be smaller, static, or replaced.

3. Anything animating a layout-triggering property. §14.12's ladder: a top, left, width, height or margin animation re-runs layout for the containing block every frame. A scroll-linked header that animates top is the classic. Replace with translate, which is compositor-only.

4. position: fixed or sticky elements over a scrolling area. These force the fixed element to be composited and re-drawn against moving content. One is normal; four overlapping ones on a phone is not.

5. Layout thrashing from JavaScript. A large layout count — rather than a large layout duration — is the signature. Something is interleaving writes and reads: setting a style, then reading offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect(), in a loop. §3.14: reading a layout-dependent value forces a synchronous flush of pending layout. The fix is always the same shape — batch all reads, then batch all writes.

6. Compositor layer count. Check the layers panel. will-change, transform: translateZ(0), backdrop-filter and content-visibility each promote an element, and every layer costs GPU memory. §14.12: a page with will-change on every card is slower than one with none, and on a memory-constrained phone it causes crashes rather than jank. This is also why step 1 should be applied to sections, not to every paragraph.

7. Web fonts and images, which are not CSS performance but often are the real answer. A font-display: block (§12.6) blocks text for up to three seconds; images without width/height or aspect-ratio cause layout shift on arrival, which shows up as layout count.

What I would not do: shorten selectors. §16.10 — matching is a small fraction of style recalculation, engines index by the rightmost compound selector, and none of the symptoms here point at it. The one selector-shaped thing worth checking is an unbounded :has() on a large, frequently mutating tree, and an article page is neither.

SECTION 17

Capstone: Build, Audit and Harden a Real Interface

Sixteen sections of mechanism are worth nothing until they meet a page that has to work. This one is a single build, carried through from an empty stylesheet to something you would ship: a documentation site with a sticky header, a sidebar, a prose column, a card grid, a theme switch and a dark mode — then audited against everything the earlier sections measured.

Build it as you read. Every stage names the sections it draws on, so a stage that does not behave gives you a place to go back to rather than a search.

17.1 The Brief

A documentation site, with the constraints a real one has:

Layout
Sticky header, 240px sidebar, prose column capped at a readable measure, a right-hand table of contents on wide screens only. One column on a phone.
Components
A card grid whose cards align internally, a callout, a code block, a search field with real validation states.
Themes
Light and dark from the system preference, overridable by the reader, plus a high-contrast variant.
Constraints
No JavaScript for layout or positioning. Works at 400% zoom. Works in forced-colours mode. Works right-to-left. Prints usefully.

Those last four are the ones that make it a real brief rather than a screenshot.

17.2 Stage One: The Layer Order

Before a single rule, one line — the highest-leverage decision in the file (§16.4):

@layer reset, tokens, base, layout, components, utilities;

That fixes the override direction for the life of the project, independently of file order, bundler behaviour or import sequence. §3.2 measured what it buys: a (0,0,1) selector in a later layer beats (1,2,1) in an earlier one, so nothing below ever has to win on specificity.

Third-party CSS goes into its own layer at the top, so it cannot beat anything you write:

@import url("prism-theme.css") layer(vendor);

and vendor is added to the list as the first entry.

17.3 Stage Two: The Reset

§16.7's reset, in the reset layer. Every line is a measurement from earlier:

@layer reset {
  *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

  body, h1, h2, h3, h4, p, figure, blockquote, dl, dd { margin: 0; }

  html { -webkit-text-size-adjust: none; interpolate-size: allow-keywords; }
  body { min-block-size: 100svh; line-height: 1.5; }

  h1, h2, h3, h4, button, input, label { line-height: 1.1; }
  h1, h2, h3 { text-wrap: balance; }
  p, li      { text-wrap: pretty; }

  ul[role="list"], ol[role="list"] { list-style: none; padding-inline-start: 0; }

  img, picture, svg, video { display: block; max-inline-size: 100%; }
  input, button, textarea, select { font: inherit; color: inherit; }

  :target { scroll-margin-block-start: 5rem; }
}

The four to be able to justify in review: box-sizing with all three selectors (§6.2 — pseudo-elements do not inherit it and * does not match them); img { display: block } (§7.5 — the measured four-pixel descender gap); font: inherit on controls (§1.7 — a <button> measured at 13.3333px, not inheriting); and 100svh rather than 100vh (§4.4 — vh is the large viewport on mobile and is cropped by the browser chrome).

17.4 Stage Three: The Token Layer

Two levels — primitives and semantics — so that a theme is a five-line diff (§5.9):

@layer tokens {
  :root {
    color-scheme: light dark;

    --hue: 265;
    --gray-000: oklch(100% 0 0);
    --gray-050: oklch(97.5% 0.003 var(--hue));
    --gray-200: oklch(90% 0.006 var(--hue));
    --gray-600: oklch(52% 0.02 var(--hue));
    --gray-900: oklch(22% 0.02 var(--hue));
    --gray-990: oklch(13% 0.015 var(--hue));
    --accent-500: oklch(58% 0.19 var(--hue));
    --accent-700: oklch(44% 0.19 var(--hue));

    --size-1: 0.25rem; --size-2: 0.5rem; --size-3: 0.75rem;
    --size-4: 1rem;    --size-6: 1.5rem; --size-8: 2rem;

    --ratio: 1.2;
    --step-0: clamp(1rem,     0.96rem + 0.20vw, 1.125rem);
    --step-1: clamp(1.20rem,  1.13rem + 0.35vw, 1.40rem);
    --step-2: clamp(1.44rem,  1.32rem + 0.60vw, 1.76rem);
    --step-3: clamp(1.73rem,  1.53rem + 0.98vw, 2.20rem);

    --surface:      light-dark(var(--gray-000), var(--gray-990));
    --surface-sunk: light-dark(var(--gray-050), var(--gray-900));
    --text:         light-dark(var(--gray-900), var(--gray-050));
