    --text-muted:   light-dark(var(--gray-600), var(--gray-200));
    --accent:       light-dark(var(--accent-700), var(--accent-500));
    --border:       color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 18%, transparent);
    --focus-ring:   Highlight;

    --measure: 68ch;
    --header-h: 3.5rem;
  }
}

Five decisions worth defending:

  • color-scheme: light dark on :root is load-bearing twice (§11.6): it makes light-dark() resolve at all, and it makes the browser render scrollbars, form controls and the canvas in the matching scheme. Omit it and you get a dark page with white scrollbars.
  • oklch() rather than hsl() (§11.3) so the grey ramp's steps are perceptually even and the hue is one variable.
  • light-dark() rather than a media query (§5.10) so the reader's manual override in §17.9 costs one declaration rather than a duplicate of the whole block.
  • The type scale is fluid with a rem term in every clamp() (§4.9, §12.15), which is what keeps it zoomable. A bare vw would fail WCAG 1.4.4.
  • --focus-ring: Highlight — a system colour (§11.5), so the ring is the platform's own and survives forced-colours mode unchanged.

17.5 Stage Four: The Page Skeleton

Grid, with named areas so the breakpoint is a rewrite of the picture (§9.11):

@layer layout {
  .app {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 240px minmax(0, 1fr);
    grid-template-rows: var(--header-h) 1fr;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header header"
      "nav    main";
    min-block-size: 100svh;
  }

  .app > header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; inset-block-start: 0; z-index: 1; }
  .app > nav    { grid-area: nav; overflow-y: auto; }
  .app > main   { grid-area: main; }

  @media (width >= 90rem) {
    .app {
      grid-template-columns: 240px minmax(0, 1fr) 220px;
      grid-template-areas: "header header header" "nav main toc";
    }
    .app > .toc { grid-area: toc; position: sticky; inset-block-start: var(--header-h); }
  }

  @media (width < 60rem) {
    .app {
      grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);
      grid-template-areas: "header" "main" "nav";
    }
  }

  .prose { max-inline-size: var(--measure); margin-inline: auto; padding-inline: var(--size-4); }
}

minmax(0, 1fr) and not 1fr for the main column. §9.4 measured why: a bare 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr), whose automatic minimum is the track's min-content size, so one long URL or code line in the documentation widens the column and squeezes the sidebar. minmax(0, 1fr) is the spelling that means "a share, regardless of content".

:root { scroll-padding-block-start } must match the header, or every fragment link lands under it (§10.14):

:root { scroll-padding-block-start: calc(var(--header-h) + var(--size-4)); }

The sticky header has one prerequisite that is easy to break: no ancestor between it and the viewport may be a scroll container. §6.14 measured that overflow-x: hidden makes overflow-y compute to auto — even when visible is written explicitly — so if a horizontal scrollbar ever needs suppressing, it must be overflow-x: clip.

17.6 Stage Five: The Card Grid, With Aligned Internals

The requirement that separates grid from flexbox (§9.13):

@layer components {
  .cards {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(18rem, 100%), 1fr));
    gap: var(--size-6);
  }

  .card {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-rows: subgrid;
    grid-row: span 3;
    gap: inherit;
    padding: var(--size-4);
    border: 1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius: var(--size-2);
    background: var(--surface-sunk);
  }
}

@supports not (grid-template-rows: subgrid) {
  .card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
  .card > :last-child { margin-block-start: auto; }
}

Three details:

  • min(18rem, 100%) inside minmax(). Without it, a viewport narrower than 18rem makes the track wider than the container and the whole grid overflows — a real bug below about 288px.
  • gap: inherit on the subgrid. §9.13 — a subgrid does not inherit the parent's gap, and a mismatched gap is the way a subgrid looks almost right.
  • auto-fit rather than auto-fill (§9.8, measured at 295/295 versus 193/193): with two cards they stretch to fill the row rather than leaving an empty track. That is a design choice; auto-fill is correct if card width must be consistent between pages.

17.7 Stage Six: Components That Read Their Container

The callout should stack in a sidebar and go horizontal in the prose column — and the viewport is identical in both, so this is a container query (§13.11):

@layer components {
  .callout-wrap { container-type: inline-size; container-name: callout; }

  .callout {
    display: grid;
    gap: var(--size-3);
    padding: var(--size-4);
    border-inline-start: 4px solid var(--tone-accent, var(--accent));
    background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--tone-accent, var(--accent)) 8%, var(--surface));
  }

  @container callout (width >= 28rem) {
    .callout { grid-template-columns: 2rem 1fr; align-items: start; }
  }

  .callout[data-tone="danger"]  { --tone: danger; --tone-accent: oklch(52% 0.20 25); }
  .callout[data-tone="warning"] { --tone: warning; --tone-accent: oklch(70% 0.16 85); }

  @container style(--tone: danger) {
    .callout__title { font-weight: 700; }
  }
}

The @container style() block is §13.14's variant switch: one custom property set on the callout retunes every descendant, with no class on each element and no script. Note that a style query needs no container-type — every element is a style container.

17.8 Stage Seven: The Search Field

Every validation state from §2.8, with the modern pseudo-classes rather than the ones that fire on page load:

@layer components {
  .field { display: grid; gap: var(--size-1); }

  .field input {
    padding: var(--size-2) var(--size-3);
    border: 1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius: var(--size-1);
    background: Field;
    min-block-size: 2.75rem;
  }

  .field input:user-invalid { border-color: oklch(52% 0.20 25); }
  .field input:user-valid   { border-color: oklch(52% 0.14 150); }
  .field input:disabled     { opacity: 0.6; cursor: not-allowed; }
  .field input::placeholder { color: var(--text-muted); opacity: 1; }

  .field:has(:user-invalid) .field__error { display: block; }
  .field__error { display: none; color: oklch(45% 0.20 25); font-size: var(--step-0); }
}

Four things that are not decoration:

  • :user-invalid rather than :invalid (§2.8). :invalid matches from page load, so a required field paints red before anyone has typed — which makes the real errors indistinguishable from the untouched ones.
  • min-block-size rather than block-size (§15.14). A fixed height clips the field when a reader applies their own text spacing, which is WCAG 1.4.12.
  • ::placeholder { opacity: 1 } (§2.13) — Firefox applies a default opacity, and without the reset the colour you set is not the colour you get. The colour itself must clear 4.5:1; placeholder text is a frequent contrast failure.
  • :has(:user-invalid) on the wrapper (§2.10) shows the error message without a class toggled from script.

The border colour must clear 3:1, not 4.5:1 — it is a non-text indicator (§15.13) — and a #ddd border on white is about 1.3:1 and fails.

17.9 Stage Eight: Themes and the Reader's Override

Because the token layer used light-dark(), the manual override is two rules (§5.10):

@layer tokens {
  [data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
  [data-theme="dark"]  { color-scheme: dark; }

  @media (prefers-contrast: more) {
    :root { --border: var(--text); --surface-sunk: var(--surface); }
  }
  [data-contrast="more"] { --border: var(--text); --surface-sunk: var(--surface); }
}

Setting color-scheme on an element flips every light-dark() beneath it, so no token is restated. An attribute rather than a class because the two values are mutually exclusive by construction — a script writes one attribute instead of adding one class and remembering to remove another.

For the theme transition to be smooth rather than a snap, the animated tokens need registering (§5.7):

@property --surface { syntax: "<color>"; inherits: true; initial-value: white; }
@property --text    { syntax: "<color>"; inherits: true; initial-value: black; }

§5.7 measured the difference: at exactly 50% progress an unregistered custom property already read the end value, and a registered one read the midpoint.

17.10 Stage Nine: Motion, Opted Into

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  :root  { scroll-behavior: smooth; }
  .card  { transition: border-color 150ms, translate 150ms; }
  .card:hover { translate: 0 -2px; }
  [popover] {
    transition: opacity 150ms, display 150ms allow-discrete, overlay 150ms allow-discrete;
  }
  @starting-style { [popover]:popover-open { opacity: 0; } }
}

Three points from §14:

  • Opt in, not out. Motion added later is safe by default, and a browser without the query gets no motion rather than all of it.
  • translate, not top. §14.12 — compositor-only rather than the whole layout-paint-composite ladder every frame.
  • overlay ... allow-discrete alongside display (§14.6), or a closing popover leaves the top layer on its first frame and fades out behind the page.

17.11 Stage Ten: Print

@media print {
  .app { display: block; }
  header, nav, .toc, .no-print { display: none; }

  body { color: #000; background: #fff; font-size: 11pt; }
  .prose { max-inline-size: none; }

  a[href^="http"]::after { content: " (" attr(href) ")"; font-size: 9pt; }

  h2, h3 { break-after: avoid; }
  figure, pre, .card { break-inside: avoid; }
}

@page { size: A4; margin: 2cm; }
@page :first { margin-block-start: 4cm; }

The link expansion is the part people forget: a URL that exists only in an href is lost on paper, and attr() recovers it in one rule (§13.16). pt and cm are the one place §4.2 said the physical units are correct.

17.12 The Audit: Twelve Checks

Run these on the finished page. Each is a measurement from an earlier section rather than an opinion, and each has failed on a real project.

1
No struck-through declarations in the styles pane that you did not intend (§1.10). A strike with no competing rule is an invalid value, not a cascade loss.
2
Zoom to 400% and check for two-directional scrolling (§15.14). Any fixed pixel width on a container will show here.
3
Tab through the whole page with the styles pane open. Every stop must show a visible ring, and the order must match the visual order (§15.8, §15.9).
4
Check every non-text indicator against 3:1, not just text against 4.5:1 (§15.13). Field borders and focus rings are where this fails.
5
Turn on forced-colours mode. Anything distinguished only by a background or a shadow disappears (§15.12).
6
Set dir="rtl" on <html>. Every physical property left in the file shows up immediately (§15.4).
7
Enable reduced motion and confirm the page still communicates state — a still spinner communicates nothing (§15.11).
8
Narrow the sidebar and confirm the container-queried components respond, and that no cqh has silently fallen back to the viewport (§4.5).
9
Paste a 200-character unbroken string into every text-bearing component. This is the fastest test for a missing minmax(0, 1fr) or min-inline-size: 0 (§8.6, §9.4).
10
Scroll with the performance panel recording. Layout during scroll means something is animating a layout-triggering property (§14.12).
11
Print to PDF. Navigation hidden, links expanded, nothing split mid-figure (§13.16).
12
Run stylelint. It catches the whole class of thing the browser never reports: a // comment, a shorthand after a longhand, an invalid value (§16.15).

17.13 What This Section Established

Collected, in one line each:

  • The order of work is layers first, then reset, then tokens, then layout, then components — because the layer order is the only decision that gets harder to change later.
  • A css reset in a layer can never be the thing you are fighting, and every line of a good one is a measurement rather than a preference.
  • A two-level token set plus color-scheme: light dark and light-dark() makes a theme a five-line diff and a reader override two declarations.
  • A page skeleton belongs in grid-template-areas:, so a breakpoint is a rewrite of the picture and no item's placement rule changes.
  • minmax(0, 1fr) and min-inline-size: 0 are the two declarations that stop content from deciding a track's width; a 200-character string is the test.
  • subgrid is the only way to align sibling components' internals, and it needs gap: inherit.
  • A container query answers the question a component actually has, and a style query turns a token into a variant switch with no class per element.
  • Validation styling belongs on :user-invalid, not :invalid, and every non-text indicator needs 3:1 contrast.
  • Motion is opted into under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, animates translate and opacity, and transitions overlay alongside display.
  • A print stylesheet hides navigation, expands links with attr(), and is the one place the physical units belong.
  • The audit is twelve checks, each of which is a measurement from an earlier section, and each of which has failed on a real project.

Exercises

1. The sticky header stops sticking after a colleague adds overflow-x: hidden to .app to suppress a horizontal scrollbar. Explain the chain of cause, fix it, and say what the real bug was.

Solution

The chain, one link at a time.

§6.14 measured the rule that starts it: when one axis is anything other than visible, a visible on the other axis computes to auto. The measurement showed this even when overflow-y: visible was written explicitly:

overflow-x: hidden                        ->  x=hidden  y=auto
overflow-x: hidden; overflow-y: visible   ->  x=hidden  y=auto

So .app { overflow-x: hidden } silently gives .app an overflow-y of auto, which makes .app a scroll container (§6.13).

§10.6 supplies the next link: a sticky element sticks within its nearest ancestor scroll container, not within the viewport. The header's nearest scroll container is now .app rather than the document — and .app is sized to its contents and does not itself scroll, so the header has no threshold to cross and never sticks.

And the reason this is expensive to debug: getComputedStyle still reports position: sticky, measured identically in the working and broken cases. The styles pane shows nothing wrong. The declaration is present, valid, and inert.

The immediate fix:

.app { overflow-x: clip; }

clip clips without creating a scroll container — measured in §6.13, where setting scrollTop to 50 moved a hidden box and left a clip box at 0. Since clip pairs legally with visible, overflow-y stays visible and the header's scroll container is the viewport again.

But the real bug is the horizontal scrollbar. overflow-x: hidden (or clip) hides a symptom: something on the page is wider than the viewport. Hiding it means that content is now unreachable, which at 400% zoom is a WCAG 1.4.10 (Reflow) failure — the audit's check 2.

Find it instead:

* { outline: 1px solid red; }        /* temporarily — §16.15 */

The usual culprits, in order of likelihood: a 1fr track that should be minmax(0, 1fr) (§9.4 — one long code line in the documentation widens the main column); a flex item missing min-inline-size: 0 (§8.6); a width: 100vw on an element inside a padded container, since 100vw includes the scrollbar's width; or a fixed pixel width somewhere.

The capstone's skeleton already uses minmax(0, 1fr) for exactly this reason, which is why the scrollbar should not have appeared in the first place.

2. A reviewer says the card grid "looks broken with two cards" and that one card is taller than the others "for no reason". Both are real; diagnose each and give the decision you would take to the designer.

Solution

Symptom one is auto-fit versus auto-fill, and it is a design decision rather than a bug.

§9.8 measured the difference with two items in a 600px container:

auto-fill:  tracks = 193.328  193.328  193.328   items = 193 / 193
auto-fit:   tracks = 295      295      0         items = 295 / 295

auto-fill keeps the empty track, so two cards sit at their normal width with a hole at the end. auto-fit collapses the empty tracks to zero and the 1fr maximum redistributes their space, so two cards stretch to fill the row.

The capstone uses auto-fit, so the reviewer is seeing two very wide cards rather than a hole. Which is right depends on the content:

  • auto-fit when the row should always look full — a marketing page, a feature grid.
  • auto-fill when card width must be consistent between pages, so a category with two articles shows them at the same width as one with eight. For documentation, this is usually the better answer.

That is the decision to take to the designer, and it should be framed as "two wide cards, or two normal cards and a gap" — not as a bug report.

Symptom two is a real defect: the subgrid contract is broken for that card.

grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-row: span 3 requires the card to have exactly three row-generating children. A card missing its footer spans two rows' worth of content across three tracks, or — worse — has span 3 while containing four children, in which case the fourth lands in an implicit row that no other card has, and that card grows.

§9.13's measurement showed a correctly-structured subgrid landing its children on the parent's tracks exactly (127 / 127 / 127). The fix is structural rather than stylistic: give every card the same three children, using an empty element where a card has no footer.

.card > .card__footer:empty { min-block-size: 0; }

Two related things to check while you are there. gap: inherit must be present — §9.13 — or the card's internal rows use 0 and the alignment is right while the spacing is not, which is the "almost right" failure that is hardest to see. And the @supports not (grid-template-rows: subgrid) fallback must produce a coherent layout rather than a half-applied one: the flex fallback in §17.6 switches display and restores the auto margin together, which is §13.10's argument for a feature query over a bare fallback declaration.

3. Take the finished capstone through audit checks 3, 4, 5 and 6 — keyboard, contrast, forced colours, and right-to-left. For each, name one defect the stylesheet as written would plausibly still have, and fix it.

Solution

Check 3 — keyboard. The likely defect is the sticky header obscuring the focused element. Tabbing to a link low on the page makes the browser scroll it into view, and it lands under the 3.5rem header. That is WCAG 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured).

scroll-padding-block-start is declared in §17.5, so fragment links are handled — but it is set on :root, and the browser's scroll-to-focus honours it only when the scrolling element is the root. If the main column has ever become its own scroll container (see exercise 1's chain), the padding no longer applies. The durable fix is to declare it on whichever element scrolls, and to verify by tabbing rather than by reading:

:root, .app > main { scroll-padding-block-start: calc(var(--header-h) + var(--size-4)); }

A second, subtler one: .app > nav { overflow-y: auto } makes the sidebar a scroll container, so a focused link inside it scrolls the sidebar, not the page — which is correct, and means the sidebar needs its own scroll-padding if it ever gains a sticky element.

Check 4 — contrast. The likely defect is --text-muted at 4.5:1 against --surface but not against --surface-sunk. It is defined once and used on two different backgrounds — the page and the card — and the card's background is darker in light mode. oklch(52% …) on oklch(97.5% …) passes comfortably; on a card that is 8% tinted with an accent it may not.

The fix is to check it in context rather than in the abstract, and where it is borderline, to define the muted colour relative to the surface it sits on:

.card { --text-muted: color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 65%, var(--surface-sunk)); }

The second likely defect is the field border. §17.8 flags it, but --border is color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 18%, transparent) — about 18% of the text colour, which will not reach 3:1. A non-text indicator needs its own token:

:root { --border-strong: color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 55%, transparent); }
.field input { border-color: var(--border-strong); }

Check 5 — forced colours. The likely defect is the callout, which is distinguished by a tinted background and a coloured border-inline-start. In forced-colours mode backgrounds are replaced, so the tint vanishes; the border survives but is re-mapped to the same colour as everything else, so danger and warning become indistinguishable.

§15.12's rule is to work with the mode rather than undo it — restore the distinction with something structural:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .callout { border: 1px solid CanvasText; border-inline-start-width: 4px; }
  .callout::before { content: "⚠ "; }
  .card { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }
}

The .card line matters for the same reason: its --surface-sunk background is its only separation from the page, and it disappears.

Check 6 — right-to-left. The stylesheet is logical throughout, so most of it mirrors correctly. The likely defect is in grid-template-areas: grid areas do not mirror. The "nav main" row places the sidebar on the inline-start side, which is correct — grid follows the inline direction (§15.5) — so that part is fine.

What is not fine is anything physical that slipped in. Two candidates in a real build of this: a box-shadow: 2px 2px on the header, which describes light from the upper left and should stay physical (a documented exception, §15.4); and any icon with a directional meaning — a "next page" chevron must mirror, and it will not, because an SVG path is not a CSS property.

[dir="rtl"] .icon-next { scale: -1 1; }

And the one that catches everyone: user-supplied text in the search field and the table of contents. §15.3 — a Latin fragment inside a right-to-left string reorders the punctuation around it. The fix is at the content boundary and is HTML: wrap the fragment in <bdi>, or set dir="auto" on the element that holds it.

You started this course able to write CSS. You now understand what the browser does with it — which is the difference between a stylesheet that renders and one you can be trusted with.

What you can now do

  1. Diagnose a declaration that does nothing, in seconds rather than minutes. CSS error handling is specified and silent, with three blast radii: an invalid declaration costs one line, an invalid selector costs the whole rule, an invalid at-rule costs its block, and an unclosed brace costs the rest of the file. The styles pane distinguishes "lost the cascade" from "was never valid" from "never matched", and those are three different bugs.
  2. Run the cascade in your head, correctly. Six criteria in order — origin and importance, cascade layer, scope proximity, specificity, source order, inheritance — with specificity fourth rather than first. That is why a (0,0,1) selector in a later layer beats (1,2,1) in an earlier one, and why the answer to a specificity fight is usually to stop having it.
  3. Select what you mean. :has() selects an element by its contents and is not forgiving; :is() and :not() take their most specific argument's weight from what is written; :where() contributes zero, which makes it the right tool for anything a consumer must override. :nth-child(2 of .x) filters before counting.
  4. Compute in the stylesheet. clamp() replaces a ladder of breakpoints, round() enforces a grid no hand-entered number will hold, min() is a ceiling and max() is a floor, and calc() is type-checked — a length over a length is a number.
  5. Use custom properties as a real system. They inherit, so one redefinition retunes a subtree; @property gives them a type, an initial value and interpolation; and color: green; color: var(--bad) gives you black rather than green, because invalid-at-computed-value-time makes a property unset rather than falling back.
  6. Predict the box. min-width beats max-width. A percentage padding resolves against width on all four sides. Margins collapse through a parent with no padding, border or formatting context, and display: flow-root is the fix with no side effects. overflow: hidden is a scroll container and overflow: clip is not.
  7. Choose a layout mode on purpose. Flexbox when content decides the sizes along one axis; grid when the layout decides them or you need both. flex: 1 gives equal columns and flex: auto gives content-proportional ones; minmax(0, 1fr) is the grid spelling of "genuinely equal"; subgrid is the only way to align the insides of sibling components.
  8. Position without guessing. An absolutely positioned box resolves against the padding box of the nearest positioned ancestor; a transform anywhere above a fixed element captures it; z-index only compares within a stacking context, and opacity: 0.99 creates one. The answer to z-index: 9999 is the top layer.
  9. Attach a tooltip to a button in CSS. anchor-name, position-anchor, anchor(), anchor-size(), position-area and position-try-fallbacks replace a positioning library, and they keep working through scroll and resize without a single frame of JavaScript.
  10. Work in the colour space the browser computes in. oklch() gives perceptually even ramps that hsl() cannot; out-of-gamut values are stored and mapped at paint time; color-mix() and relative colour syntax remove the last reason for a preprocessor's colour functions; and Canvas/CanvasText are the pair that survives forced-colours mode.
  11. Set type deliberately. Unitless line-height inherits as a number and a length does not. font resets weight and style. tabular-nums stops figures jittering. overflow-wrap breaks a word as a last resort and word-break: break-all as a first. text-box-trim makes spacing match the design.
  12. Ask the right question about space. A media query asks about the window; a container query asks about the space the component was actually given, which is what a component wants to know. @supports tests values, not just properties, and the fallback goes first.
  13. Animate what is cheap. transform and opacity are compositor-only; left and width re-run layout sixty times a second. @starting-style and allow-discrete let an element animate in and out of display: none, and overlay keeps a closing popover in the top layer while it fades.
  14. Write CSS that works in every writing mode and for every reader. Logical properties cost nothing and survive direction: rtl and writing-mode: vertical-rl unchanged. :focus-visible gives designers what they asked for without taking anything from keyboard users. visually-hidden content is focusable and display: none content is not, and knowing which you want is most of accessibility in CSS.
  15. Keep a stylesheet workable. @layer stops the specificity ratchet with one line and subordinates third-party CSS with another. @scope bounds a component in both directions. Shadow DOM is the only encapsulation the platform enforces, and inherited properties and custom properties are the two things that deliberately cross it.

Where to go next

Nothing here is finished, and the parts that are moving are worth watching rather than learning once. @function and if() are shipping in one engine and will change what a stylesheet can express. Anchor positioning and reading-flow are close behind. Masonry is still being argued over. line-clamp and margin-trim are specified and not yet everywhere.

The habit that keeps this current is smaller than it sounds: when you reach for a workaround you learned more than a year ago, check whether it is still needed. The answer changes, usually in your favour, and most stylesheets are full of scaffolding for problems that no longer exist.

And the habit that keeps it honest: read what the browser actually did. Every number in this course was measured rather than recalled, and a surprising number of them contradicted the widely published answer. The styles pane, the computed tab, the layout overlays and the accessibility panel are all four clicks away, and they will tell you the truth about your page in less time than it takes to guess.
